CHAPTER 1 - WEST COAST WANDERING

December 30th, 1954 - January 12th, 1955

DEC 30 1954

        Had lunch with Morton, and received last minute advice from him. Mom drove me to the station, where we met Carolyn. Took the Wabash to Kansas City, where I tried to obtain space on the next train to Salt Lake City but wasn’t able to. Spent the night in Kansas City.

DEC 31

        Spent the day and night on the train. Did some reading and idle chatter with some interesting people. They removed the club car at Denver, so a very quiet New Years Eve was had by all.

JAN 01 1955

        Arrived in Salt Lake City and decided to spend the day there. Got a bath for 50¢ and began my sightseeing. Went to Temple Square, where I had an interesting tour and lecture by some Mormon layman. He explained about the fundamentals of the Mormon religion and pointed out the tabernacle, Sea Gull Monument, Temple and assembly hall.

        Walked to the Capital Building and also visited some of the earlier Mormon homes of Brigham Young. In the evening I walked out to the University of Utah campus and toured the general area. Had interesting talk with a Siam(ese?) M.D.

JAN 02 (SUNDAY - WEEK 2)

        Arrived in Las Vegas at 7:00 and obtained a room across from the railroad station. My luggage (one suitcase, one AWOL bag and some suits and an Army overcoat were quite heavy and awkward).NECESSITATED SOCA A CLOSE SBST. Roamed the streets for an hour or so, and gaped at the huge neon signs and numerous gambling halls.

        Took a tour of Boulder Dam (Hoover Dam) and it was certainly the highlight of the trip thus far. The dam is huge (700 feet) and its dimensions, intake towers, and reservoirs are gigantic. The government has a tour through the dam so I obtained a good idea of the working fundamentals, the pa__el equipment, and the cascades. The view from the top of the dam is quite impressive, since the Colorado River seems to winds its way through canyons of tremendous rock formations.

        That night - to the strip!! This little country boy had a hard time believing that such lavish places existed in this world. The hotels are truly exquisite. I had to eat at a place called D_ff_nes (bad food for the price) as the hotels were all sold out. Afterwards,  I went to the Flamingo where I stayed the evening. Played the slot machines, and by some unknown fate managed to win a dollar or so. Cashed in 20 nickels for 1 silver dollar and boldly walked to the Craps table. As luck had it, I won, plus a few more, and thus was able to wind up the evening about $10 we____. The gentleman next to me was betting $500 at a crack.)

Saw Tony Martin and a 1 ½ hour show at the cost of a 85¢ drink. (Good show) then watched the people coming and going as I waited outside for a bus or cab to get back to the hotel. The sight dazzled my eyes. Nothing but big cars, beautiful women and their sugar daddies, beautiful furs, etc. It was like a hollywood premiere, and this boy loved it. I am looking forward to visiting this place again during the summer sometime when I have make time. I am sure I would tire of the gaudiness of the place, but a week or so would be exciting.

JAN 03

        The train ride to Los Angeles was interesting, particularly the wonderful change in climate. Sat next to a very inquisitive college girl who now knows everything about me and my family. We even had a discussion on Judaism, it being started by her question of when I was going back to Jerusalem!!

        Checked in at the YMCA, and got my things in order. Went to the Station Hotel, where I bumped into Jim B_th_e, who was a former Dow Madison employee, and presently is working in the Dow L. A. sales office. Made a date for lunch with him.

        Called Ron Hou_itz (later found out he had changed his last name to Howard) and he picked me up at 10:00 that evening. Went to C__’s (Mil_ brother) and wasn't too impressed except for a girl at one of the front tables. From here we went to a Polynesian bar which was quite exotic and fascinating. (I finally was able to snatch the bill and pay it.) We ended the evening at a nice restaurant called Tail O’ the Cock which had good food.

JAN 04

        Visited with Aunt Gertie in the morning and gave her all the news of home. She has aged quite considerably since I had last seen her in 1950. Ate lunch with Jim Guthrie at the Statler Hotel, and had a pleasant conversation of old times, sales work, Los Angeles, and things in general. Jim is a very personable fellow and I had an enjoyable time. He indirectly convinced me that sales work on a salary BASIS was not very attractive, at least financially.

        Took a Grey Line tour of the city which included stops at Santa Monica beach, and Will Rogers Park; and a tour of Beverly Hills, Hollywood, Wilshire Blvd, and Los Angeles in general.

        Got in contact with Wally Batterton who had been in the Training Aide Section at Fort Leonard Wood. We had an interesting talk of Los Angeles, followed by a rehash of old times at Leonard Wood. (Wally is the person I used to drive to and from St. Louis with on the weekends.)

        Ron picked us up late in the evening and treated us back to the Coconut Grove. He even gave the head waiter $2 so that we could get a decent seat. The show was bad (Freddie Martin and his orchestra, and some Mexican entertainers), the food poor, and the prices touristly exorbitant. Nevertheless, I had been in THE Coconut Grove, for what ever that may be! Including tonight, I have not been impressed with Los Angeles’ night life.

JAN 05

        Took a bus to CBS television and hoped to take a tour of this little city. However, no tours were scheduled, and tickets had been mailed away weeks previously. Talked to an usher (implored him of the fact that I was a visiting GI and wouldn’t be able to come back) and managed to get tickets to the Art Linkletter and Bob Crosby shows.

        Both men had pleasing personalities and their respective shows were enjoyed by the GI. Farmers Market was adjacent to CBS, so I went there for lunch. Had a typical American lunch, but enjoyed the outside tables, and the crowd. The Market was something new and different for me, and was thus quite interesting.

        I decided to visit 20th Century Fox, and asked thousands of questions in order to get there. Talked to one lady who happened to be British who had been living in L.A. for some time. She said it was next to impossible to get into the studios except on tours so I decided to visit some of the places she suggested. Went to Westwood and then to U.C.L.A. Walked around the campus, and was awe-stricken by the huge and beautiful buildings. The campus was nice and the spring like weather made me homesick for school.

        In the evenings I had a date with a girl Ron suggested I call. We went to a bar and had a fair time. (Got into a philosophical argument) Horrible to think that this will be my last American date for 17 months.

JAN 06

        It rained throughout the day, consequently a USO tour of the movie studios was cancelled. Instead I decided to drive out to Exposition Park. Ron had previously loaned me use of his 1954 Buick and it sure came in handy in this spread out city of Los Angeles.

        I visited the Los Angeles County Museum and the California Museum of Science and Industry. The latter museum was quite interesting, even though one of the guards followed me around the building thinking me to be a thief because I touched one of the employee lockers in the men’s room. The Art Museum was fair, owing to the fact that my appreciation for Art seems to be quite low at the present. I feel I should visit the Art Museum, but get little out of the visit since I know so little about Art. Also, I did not seem to be able to appreciate a painting for what I may see in it.

        Later in the afternoon I drove out to Knott's Berry's Farm, which is a replica of an old Western town. They have gathered here a lot of old wagons, trains, equipment etc., and have made it into a big tourist attraction. They even have stage coaches, train rides and pony rides.

        Had dinner at the Moulin Rouge and watched the first show. The production was very elaborate, lavish and lengthy and was the best entertainment I had seen in many a moon. The show was well done, the performers were good, and the costumes beautiful. As an example of the scope of the production, they had an elephant, a giant champagne glass with a girl in it, and numerous exotic birds used in individual dancing girls hats.

        Went to the Palladium after leaving the Moulin Rouge, and was somewhat disappointed. They had Les Brown’s Band, but there were only a scattering of people on the floor and on the sidelines. Must admit that the ballroom is very beautiful.

        Went to Van de Kamp’s for a hamburger, and ate some. The roll was good, but Medart’s hamburgers are better.

JAN 07

        I had arranged to have lunch with Aunt Gertie, and consequently picked her up around 11:30. We went to Tail O’ the Cock, mainly because it was one of the few places open for lunch. The food was excellent, and the surroundings pleasant. One side of the dining room is open, and they have a flower garden and wall in its place. It is quite unusual and interesting.

        Drove around town in the afternoon, and then took Ron’s car back to the Airport where I had picked it up.

        Caught the Southern Pacific train for San Francisco, and I had at last headed for the Northwest area. The train was miserable, and I got very little sleep.

JAN 08

        Checked in at the YMCA, and took an overdue bath. The YMCA was the nicest and most ideally located of all those that I had been in previously. Checked my multitude of maps and took off in the direction of Union Square. Walked around this area, rode the trolley, walked up to Nob Hill and then through Chinatown (in an effort to get used to the Oriental flavor!)

        Walked up to Telegraph Hall and viewed the city from Coit Tower. Using the telescope I viewed the surrounding area, and was particularly interested in Alcatraz island. (Didn’t see any convicts escaping, however.) Then walked (and walked and walked) to the docks, past ships that were loading and unloading their cargo; and ended up at Fisherman's Wharf. The Wharf is interesting - especially the crabs - but very commercial. Had lunch at #9 Fisherman’s Grotto, and then bought a ticket for the tour around the bay. The day was nice, consequently the boat trip was enjoyable.

        That evening I went to the Mark Hopkins Hotel and viewed the city from its roof top bar. The view was excellent, and one could see for miles in all directions. I then proceeded to one of the top jazz spots and heard Machito and his Afro-Cuban band. The noise was overpowering and it seemed that all the Mambo they played was the same; - so I felt. Went back to the Y, and saw Donald O'Connor, Mitzi Gaynor, and George Gobel on the T.V. They were all good.

JAN 09 (SUNDAY - WEEK 3)

        Seems as if I run into rain in every city I visit. San Francisco was no exception, as it poured bucketfuls over the area. I decided to take the Grey Line tour the following day, and to go out to Golden Gate Gate Park today.

        The park used to be sand dunes and wasteland before they converted the area into a park, and is one of the few green spots in San Francisco. I visited the Museum of Science, Art Museum (same state of lethargy) and the aquarium. The latter building was the best aquarium that I have seen, and was extremely interesting. They had all types of fish and reptiles, including a lung fish (said to be a _ivile between fish and mammal), eels, octopus, rattlesnakes, and various tropical fish.

        Continued my tour, and visited strawberry hill, and the boat house. It began raining again, but I spent my time feeding popcorn to tame ducks and sea gulls. The latter birds are very interesting, especially the manner in which they maneuver, and glide with the wind. Finished my tour by looking at the deer, buffalo and other wild fowl.

        Saw the movie Romeo and Juliet, and consider it to be one of the top movies of 1954.

        Went to a bohemian night club called the Hungry I, and watched the show. The entertainers were young, but a couple of them were quite good, particularly a colored calypso singer.

        

JAN 10

        Took the all day tour of the surrounding territory, and it was worth the money. We visited Oakland, Berkeley, Richland, crossed the Bay Bridge and Golden Gate Bridge, toured the University of California campus, and stopped at Muir Woods National Park. The Univ. of Calif. Campus was as huge as UCLA, but left me somewhat cold. I imagine that for laboratory courses, this school and other huge state schools would be fine, but I think I prefer a smaller school for liberal arts, law or other discussion courses. Had lunch at the renown Claremont hotel, but frankly wasn’t impressed.

        The trip to Muir Woods was tops, and I thoroughly enjoyed my first encounter with Redwood trees. The magnificence of these giants are without words, and have no equal in nature. It looks as if Emerson’s law of Compensation was forgotten when these trees were conceived, as they seem to have perpetual life. Their only enemies are fire and man, with their asbestos bark even resisting many fires before succumbing. As Joseph Strauss wrote, “Sink down, oh traveller, on your knees, God stands before you in these trees.”

        Ate at a well known Bimbo’s 365 Club for dinner, but had a fair dinner and saw a lousy show for a high price. To top it off, the waiter didn’t even thank me for the 50¢ tip, nor did the hat check girl for a 15¢ tip. I am getting sick of this tired of this business. If it wasn’t for a drunk - Honest George - that I had talked to earlier in the evening, the first part of my evening would have been ruined. This drunk was hilarious and I had about 10 minutes of laughs. After Bimbo’s I went to a bohemian joint by the name of Purple Onion. The entertainment was good - especially a comedy team of Jane and Gordon Connell - and the people were very friendly. From there I went across the street to Opus One, and spent a couple of hours there. Had some fine conversation, and met a distant relative of the STIX family. These latter two places salvage my Bimbo’s evening.

JAN 11

        Spent the morning sleeping and packing my luggage. Took the latter to the train station, and had 4 or 5 hours to spend before my train left. Took a bus to the Cliff House, and walked around the area looking at the Seals on Seal Island, rambling through the gift shop (such junk) and walking on the beach and letting Pacific Ocean water run up to my soles. This was the first time I had been in an ocean.

        Caught the ferry for Oakland, and then hopped aboard the Southern Pacific for point North. My vacation had ended.

Route as of January 11th, 1955 – end of Chapter 1.

CHAPTER 2 - LIFE AT FORT LEWIS

January 12th, 1955 - January 31st, 1955

JAN 12

        Had a good night’s sleep on the train, owing mainly to the comfortable chair. Was sick as I took off my civilian clothes and once again became a soldier (Questionable). Nevertheless today is the big reporting day.

        Arrived at Fort Lewis around 3:00 PM and stood in line for a typical Army wait. Finally, was able to check in and they gave me 2 blankets (nothing else) for the night.

        Saw the movie “Americans”, (good adventure story - run of the mill danger + rite) and went to bed.

JAN 13

        I hadn’t had time up to now to pick up my Army duffle bag, so I wasn’t able to process during the day. Instead we sat around and waited. Had a pocketbook - Fantasy and Imagination along so I passed the time reading. Some of the stories were quite good, particularly one concerning a trip to Mars. There the explorer found chicken-wire enclosures which contained human beings. As it turned out, man wasn’t supreme on this planet, and these enclosures were food storages for huge animals who ate the humans, the latter believing this to be their natural fate. All in all, it was different and frightening.

        In the evening I obtained a pass and journeyed into Seattle to pick up my luggage. Walked around town, stopped at a bar, and then caught the Greyhound for my new home. There seems to be a large number of Servicemen in the Seattle area.

        Today was my first introduction to the Seattle rain, and I must say I do not like it. I wish somebody would turn off the faucet somewhere up above.

JAN 14         more rain.

        Today was destined to be my big day – that ominous day for assignment. While walking through the processing line one sickening, old Sgt. marked a big K on my form 20. Thus, I am earmarked for the lovely spa of Korea. Actually I all but knew I was to be assigned there, since all first 2 graders are being sent to Korea.

        We then were assigned new billets, mine being in Company B, where all Korea bound personnel are located. We heard today that probably the first boat for Korea wouldn’t leave until January 31st, so it looks like we will have quite a lengthly stay here.

        Went to the Service Club that evening, and found out that they were going to have a Dance, with the female sex coming from the Seattle USO. There were so many troopers, with only about 20-25 girls, consequently it was somewhat difficult to get to dance. I managed 2 dances and then retired gracefully to my “Korean buddies”.

JAN 15

        Didn’t do much of anything today. Straightened out my things in preparation for the weekly inspection. Visited the Main Fort for the first time, and found it to be a lot nicer than the North Fort.

        Talked to CWO Jennings (C&A Assignment) about possibilities of getting to Japan, but received little encouragement. He did satisfy my questions and attitude of trying all possible angles. I will renew my efforts over yonder.

        Began reading in earnest Dostoyevsky’s Crime and Punishment, and I believe I will like it. The Army is a good place for me to read these long novels, (560 page) since I would probably lose heart in my heretofore small reading time as a civilian.

JAN 16 (SUNDAY - WEEK 4)

        As per my request the C.Q. awakened me at 5:15, but I managed to doze off until 6:00. Hurriedly getting my things together I proceeded to wait for a bus. After nearly freezing, I hailed a cab and spent $1.50 getting to the pre-determined meeting spot. Obtained a seat on the Special Service bus, and journeyed approximately 60 miles to Mount Rainier. Rented some skis, and began my second attempt at mastering the long staves.

        Had trouble with the skis coming off but finally managed to secure them adequately. The skiing was terrific and I enjoyed immensely the 5 hours spent skiing. The snow was deep (8-10 feet) and soft and cushioned my frequent falls. The area only had rope tours which gave me trouble in the beginning, but later I managed to hold on. I still haven’t acquired the knack of turning, so I generally came “schussing” down the hill, and went into a violent snow plow in order to brake my speed. Sometimes I stopped standing up, generally it was in some snow drift on my side.

        Later on in the afternoon the snow began falling and made it difficult to see. Around 3:30 we all packed into the bus and headed for Fort Lewis. The people on the bus were quite congenial and interesting, and most of them planned to do some additional skiing the following Sunday. (Me too.)

JAN 17         more rain.

        Today was the first of two days to be spent in processing. There wasn’t much to it, consisting of a smallpox and typhoid shots, getting partial pay, checking of our records, and waiting. One thing about the Army, is that one can never predict what he will get paid. They always seem to arrive at some figure which can’t (or is difficult for my brain) be determined as to its basis. Oh well – 16 ½ more months.

        Saw Grace Kelly, Stewart Granger, & Paul Douglas in “Green Fire”. It was an enjoyable adventure movie.

JAN 18

        Spent the day completing the processing. The day consisted of attending talks and movies at Theater #5. There wasn’t too much of value in what was SAID since most of the speakers SPENT THEIR TIME making jokes of the women to be found in the Orient. Almost all of the men seem to be looking forward to such events, leaving many ties and morals at the American shoreline. (I must qualify the above statement to those going to Japan, us unfortunate being bound for Korea have different views.) Saw one U.S. propaganda film “The Hoaxers” which was well presented. It had been made by MGM and concerned Communism and what it has to offer.

        Today was the first time it had not rained since I had been in the Northwest. The sun was shining and snow capped Mount Rainier glistened in the sunshine. Such days are rare, from what I understand, but tend to make one forget the endless drizzles. There is no snow in the area and from what I am told the snow does not stick long even when it does snow. The grass is green, and the evergreen trees add color to the environment.

JAN 19

        With processing completed, nothing remains for us troopers to do at Fort Lewis while waiting for a ship, except endless details. Thus, with the first ship expected to leave no sooner than January 31st, my waking hours will be spent planning how to keep from getting involved with work. (I sure won’t know how to act when confronted with some “honest to goodness” hard work!)

        Left the post at 7:00 A.M. and went into Seattle via bus. On the way, and for a short time at the station, I completed Dostoyevsky’s Crime and Punishment, which I thoroughly enjoyed. The plot was the most interesting I have ever read.

        Completed some shopping I had to do in the morning and proceeded with my sightseeings. (I had left my camera at the Fort since I had no pass and did not want to be conspicuous.) _aged at the totem pole, and then journeyed to the top of the Smith Tower for a view of the city. It was hazy, consequently, the view was only fair.

        Took a Grey Line sightseeing tour in the afternoon, and saw many of the interesting things such as downtown, various lakes, the famous arboretum, world’s largest floating bridge, University of Washington’s campus (huge and beautiful – typical big state school), Rose gardens, etc. The trip was quite interesting.

        With the exception of the constant drizzling rain, Seattle is quite a nice town. It is nice sized – 550, 00 – and has many facilities for sportsmen such as skiing, boating, beaches and the other sports common to cities such as golf, tennis, etc.

        Saw Gina Lollobrigida in “Bread, Love and Dreams”. What a doll!

JAN 20

        Earlier in the week I had busted the buckle on my boot, and today I decided to go to the Main Fort and have it fixed. While there, I also signed up for skiing for the forthcoming Sunday trip, and spent some time at the Main Post Library. It is an adequate library, and has a music room plus most of the latest magazines.

        While leaving the PX, I had to dodge a car, and the driver turned out to be Jane Frohlichstein Dohrmann. She drove me back to the North Fort and we had a pleasant conversation concerning Army life, Fort Lewis, and happenings in St. Louis. I will try to get together with them the following week.

        Basketball and long needed exercise took up the major portion of the afternoon.

        Went to the movies in the evening and saw “Bad Day at Black Rock” starring Spencer Tracy. It was a very entertaining movie, however, the projectionist had difficulty in maintaining the proper focus. Consequently our eyes took a beating. After the show, Perry Miller and I went to the Service Club, and listened to a band concert presented by the 2nd Infantry Band. It was enjoyable, but probably could have had a better selection of numbers.

        

JAN 21

        Decided to spend the day out of the company area, so I journeyed to the Main Library. Spent the day reading magazines, listening to records, and catching up on this Daily Record.

        Had to straighten up the room for an inspection the following day, but still had time to take in the night life (Joke!) Went to the Service Club, and did some writing and watching TV. They had another USO Dance, but again it was almost impossible to dance. Managed an occasional dance or two before calling it quits and heading for 4C22 (Barracks). I would never have stuck it out for those two dances, except for the fact that I wouldn’t be doing much dancing for a long time.

JAN 22

        Visited Olympia, Washington this afternoon and night, but have to admit that there is very little to see in the Capital City. The town is small, having a population of around 15,000. Walked up to the Civic Center, which includes most of the State of Washington official buildings. The Capitol Building was open, and I walked around, looking in on the Senate and House floors, official reception room (very elegant), spire room, and men’s room. The houses weren’t in session, but there were a few members on the respective floors.

        The general atmosphere in the building was very friendly and made one feel quite welcome. There were guides to show visitors around the building and to explain the various rooms and architecture. The example shown in this building should be copied by all Government Institutions.

        Later in the afternoon I visited the Capital Museum which was typical of historical museums. They did have some fine China, loaned from the collection of a wealthy local collector.

        Completed the day with a movie, “Malta Stay” and “Down 3 Dark Streets” and a lousy meal.

JAN 23 (SUNDAY - WEEK 5)

        Today was skiing time once again, consequently, I went with the Ski Club to Rainier on the Special Service Bus. There were numerous delays getting started so we didn’t get to Paradise Inn until about noon, which only left 3 ½ hours for skiing. The weather was warm, which made the snow wet and icy – not good at all for skiing. Thus, this Alpine Scout fell quite frequently in the morning (before 1:30 PM lunch break) and the CONDITIONS made the skiing a task and chore.

        The afternoon session was different, and as 2 other fellows and myself found a small hill that wasn’t been used very much and we spent the remaining time there. The slope was fairly steep and there was a nice little bump at the beginning which made for fun and spills.

        This skiing area, being a National park, has no Chain or T-Bar lifts, only rope tows. These latter mechanisms and especially the rope became frozen and icy TODAY and made the ascent of the hills, a task in itself. Many times my hands couldn’t get a decent grip and halfway up I fell off.

        On the way back, one of the fellows (a West Point Lt.) led the bus in singing and a good time was had by all.

JAN 24

        Today was the 12th day I have been at Fort Lewis, and the 10th day it has rained. Nothing much occurred today, I spent the time packing and shipping my civilian clothes home (what a feeling!), playing basketball and taking in a movie.

        I welcome the opportunity to engage in any form of sports, as I am quite a bit out of condition. Spent a few minutes in the weight room struggling to “press” and “curl” some puny weights, but gave that up for a lost cause.

        Saw “Silver Chalice” in the evening and it was entertaining. It was one of Hollywood’s typical religious extravaganzas, with huge sets and beautiful costumes – I have seen so many of these religious movies that I won’t have to read the New Testament to find out how Christianity was born.

JAN 25

        Took a tour of the Boeing Airplane Plant located outside of Seattle. The tour originated in the cafeteria (huge – seats 1600) and progressed into the s___-assembly and final assembly sections. At the present time Boeing is manufacturing the B-52 jet bomber, which is a huge (175 Ton) 8 jet heavy bomber in the 600+ mile per hour class. The tour was interesting but other than the plane itself, I learned little of the production methods owing to a stupid guard guide.

        Earlier in the day while waiting for the bus in Tacoma, I had an opportunity to visit Point Defiance, a park in North Tacoma. They had an old fort, zoo, aquarium, etc on a well kept spot overlooking Puget Sound. The fort was closed and thus I couldn’t see the inside there, but I did go in the aquarium. They had some interesting sea life; not so much fish, as things like crabs, starfish, shrimp, and other forms of sea existence.

        Went to the Auto Show in Seattle in the afternoon and couldn’t decide which of the good looking cars I liked best. Any would do.

        Ate at the Italian Village again and, as before, I had an excellent meal.

JAN 26

        Spent the day at the Main Post Library catching up on the latest magazines, listening to records and general goofing off.

        Stuck around the barracks for a couple of hours in the evening and then went to the North Fort Library where I began my long over-due continuation of my Law Study. I hope to be more regular on this work in the future.

        My first cold since the flu shot in November burst from under cover and left me quite miserable. Got some APC pills and plan to eliminate this “friend’ as soon as possible.

JAN 27

        Another typical Fort Lewis day, with this trooper not accomplishing much. Did some reading in the morning and evening. Played basketball in the afternoon; the waiting for same precipitating an interesting altercation. Approximately 14-20 of us were waiting in line for the gym to open, when a whole bunch of fellows converged on the door at one time, having no intention of waiting in line. This didn’t seem right to me, since myself and the other boys had been waiting in line; so I dusted off the stripes on my arms, and commanded in an authoritative tone that everyone get in line. Well, almost all of them did, except for some young, punk corporal. He said he didn’t have to get in line, and also wanted to know if I was in charge. I told him no, and he proceeded to mouth off about my having no right, “that’s what’s wrong with the army, etc”. Not intending to fight or push the issue I ignored the rabble rouser and continued reading Huckleberry Finn.

        I doubt if Burt Lancaster or some other Sgt would have done it this way, but I am not their age nor did I want to lose my place in line. I figured the silent treatment works as well on ignorant folks. The conclusion was that he got in line also, but continued to make remarks. All in all, it was quite interesting.

JAN 28

        Today was a typical Army day, both in what I did and what I saw. Concerning the latter, a couple of boys in the barracks tried to “bug out” of a detail and were caught. Instead of putting them to something useful, they had to dig a hole in the ground 6’ x 6’ x 6’. When they were finished they had to fill it up and level it out as if there had never been a hole in that spot. Makes sense?

        In the afternoon they read off the names of those going on the U.S.S. Pope sailing Monday. Waited in the cold 2 ½ hours and to no avail as I wasn’t alerted. Then waited ¾ hour in the mail line. In this manner I passed the afternoon.

        Went to Services in the evening, and did not enjoy them or get anything out of them. Much of the reading and singing was in Hebrew which passed over me like a fast moving cloud. I doubt if I will attend many more Services while in the Army.

JAN 29

        Those that were not alerted yesterday, were alerted this morning. I am to have Tuesday morning aboard the U.S. General Freeman bound for Whittier, Alaska; Tokyo, Japan; and Pusan, Korea. We were told that we are to be assigned in the K Com Z (Korean Communications Zone), which is a relief from those that are to land at Inchon and be assigned to the front lines.

        Played basketball in the afternoon and worked up a good sweat.

        Went to Tacoma that evening with Bob Davidson, LeRoy Kelly and Joe Budesa. All of these fellows are above average in intelligence and have good personalities. We saw the movie “Rear Window” (which was good) and then went to an Italian restaurant for Pizza. All in all, the evening was quite enjoyable.

JAN 30 (SUNDAY - WEEK 6)

        Still had the trace of my cold, so I decided not to go skiing today. Instead I passed the time at the Main Fort Library and another movie. It sure seems as if I have seen too many movies lately, yet when I have the day off and do reading I don’t feel like doing much reading at night. Thus, I take in a movie to break the monotony for a couple hours.

        Actually the movie is usually good for the serviceman. They are cheap (.25¢), generally entertaining and keep the men from gambling, drinking and thinking of their troubles. Of course too many movies is a waste of time, there being many other things to be done under normal conditions. (I don’t consider the situation here at Fort Lewis normal!) So – my rationalizing mind leads me to my present thinking.

JAN 31

        Today was a cold and rainy day, and I felt sorry for those men that were leaving on the General Pope, and were patiently waiting out the rain for the buses to arrive.

        Very little happened today. In general I stuck around the barracks in the morning, but managed to take in a little basketball in the afternoon. This will probably be my last physical activity for a long time.

        Called home around 4:00 PM (6:00 PM St. Louis time) and it was good hearing Mom’s and Morton’s voices. Carolyn wasn’t home, consequently, I wasn’t able to speak with her. As per usual I had nothing really new to say (other than that which I had written in my last letter) but a phone call is much more personal than a letter.

Route as of January 31st, 1955 – end of Chapter 2.

CHAPTER 3 - PACIFIC TO PUSAN

February 1st, 1955 - February 21st, 1955

FEB 01

        Today is the big day! We were awakened at 4:00 AM, got breakfast, turned in our bedding and fell out on our stakes to await the buses. (Thank heavens no rain) The buses took us to Seattle where we waited a few minutes on the docks while Red Cross women gave us hot coffee and cookies. Boarded the ship – General H.B. Freeman – at 9:30 in a surprisingly efficient Army troop movement. We were immediately assigned our bunks, mine being on deck 4, compartment 2. Sorry to say that this was too close to the bow for a smooth ride. A puny Army band plus a couple spectators heralded the departure of the ship at 10;30 bound for Whittier, Alaska. We had on board about 1000 Troops, (including some Air Force personnel) and dependents for Japan who had the best quarters and facilities.

        I never realized how many people they COULD crowd in the compartments, but it sure was packed. We have about 245 men in our “hole”, stacked 4 high and mighty close together. I foolishly decided not to take any dramamine pills, and to see if my body could ward off any seasickness. I found out right fast, and was quite sick that night.

        The first night at sea was terrible, with ¾ of the men sick and heaving everywhere. Some of these with the dry heaves, made it rough on the others. The sight, noises and smell was nauseating and did little to help the situation.

FEB 02

        I took some pills in the morning, but it didn’t helped much in the morning. In the afternoon and evening I began to feel a little better, especially after forcing myself to eat.

        The sea was still “moderate” and many of the boys were still sick. In the evening I felt quite a bit better and even took in a movie. All I had done up to this time was to either sit on deck and stare or sit in the recreation room and try to doze.

        The sight at sea was interesting, especially seeing for the first time, nothing but water. The sight of the waves breaking under the impact of the waves SHIP was beautiful, particularly the aqua color in the white foam.

        I managed to get the Troop Information and Calculation job on board the ship and it should keep me out of details with only a minimum of work to do. Lets hope so!

FEB 03

        What a glorious day this day turned out to be. My sickness had left me and seemingly so, all the rest of the troopers. The atmosphere and spirit had definitely changed, with there being a lot of noise and cheerful banter. I began eating again, talking and even began reading.

        The sea was calm in the morning and afternoon, but began to roll the ship in the evening. The picture of the Navy had finally emerged, with trays sliding along the tables, and chairs slipping on the floor. I guess the ship wasn’t rolling more than 15°, but it was enough for all to hold on as they walked.

        Went up on deck in the evening and it was slightly raining, with water “sloshing” over the deck as the ship rolled from side to side. Couldn’t see much except water and blackness, but I imagine there were others out there somewhere.

        For the statistical minded, at noon today we were at -139° Longitude, 56° Latitude. We had travelled 767 miles from Seattle with 406 miles to go before we get to Whittier. Our speed was 16.24 knots

FEB 04

        Sleeping has been fair aboard this tug, with my seemingly getting enough sleep, but the noise and light in the compartment wake me into semi-consciousness two or three times a night. Generally, I get about 8 hours sleep.

        During the early part of the morning we entered the channel that leads to the Army port of Whittier. The morning was clear – but cold; and the sight was beautiful. On each side of the channel were snow-capped mountains, the sides of which ended abruptly into the green waters of the channel. I took some pictures, obtaining much needed advice from a fellow who had a light meter. I at first was going to buy a meter on board ship, but decided to put it off awhile.

        We docked around 1:00, and approximately 500 Army and Air Force personnel departed for waiting trains which came on the dock (a mammoth steel barge - like affair) to meet the ship. The air was cold, and it began snowing during the 1 hour period we were in Whittier. All the personnel were unable to leave the ship.

        The port was small, and uninteresting. The piers had burned about a year previously and the scorched remains could be seen. There were the typical Army personnel and vehicles on the dock, with a few civilian automobiles in the background. A little ways from the dock could be seen beautiful and huge buildings belonging to the Army personnel in Whittier. I understand they are relatively new, and cost about $6,000,000.

        We left around 2:00 PM, and this frozen trooper adjourned to the decks below for some warmth.

FEB 05

        We passed the Kodiak islands this morning on our route towards Yokohama. The Islands are completely covered with snow and ice, and from our ship there wasn’t any visible vegetation. The day was clear, and the water the bluest I have seen, and I hope the picture I took came out.

        The afternoon passed in a typical manner, being taken up by the same reading, talking and card playing. The sea got rough during the evening and I became quite aware that my newly acquired “sea legs” were only temporary. Thanks heavens for “dram!”

        As of noon today we had travelled 332 miles from Whittier and were at 57° Latitude and -152° Longitude.

        (I think there is only one island, with numerous peninsulas, so it should read Kodiak Island and not Islands.)

FEB 06 (SUNDAY - WEEK 7)

        I spent the morning on deck, thinking and observing the sea. We haven’t had any storms and or violent weather, as of yet, but there are large enough waves to rock or roll our little ship.

        It is interesting and thought provoking, to look out and see nothing but see and sky. We haven’t passed any other ships up to now, nor have I seen any fish or animals in the ocean.

        Someone asked me if I played bridge shortly after lunch, and I replied that I knew some of the basic fundamentals. So– I played bridge from 1:30 PM to 9:00 PM with a ½ break for supper. I enjoyed the games very much, and will attempt to get in more of such pastimes on this trip and in Korea. I think I played more bridge today than I have in the last 5 years.

FEB 07

        We had motor (engine) trouble this morning and the speed of the ship was cut from 16 to approximately 4 knots. Consequently, the ship had a tendency to ride the waves instead of cutting through them and thus we had more rocking and rolling than we have had in a couple of days.

        Today I went to the Troop Office to see what my duties as I & C NCO were to consist of. They told me I was to give a short talk on Korea and Japan. I informed them that I hadn’t been to either places, and also had some difficulty in pronouncing the names. The Lt. then decided to ask someone else to give the talk, and I was to keep attendance records. I was happy with this set up, although I wouldn’t have minded giving a current events talk.

        The Lt. told the troops that we would probably be in Yokohama Sunday or Monday which is a few days earlier than most of us had figured. He also SAID that that one couldn’t transfer from Korea to Japan for 7 months, and then only if the person would stay for at least a year. Thus it looks as if this rules me out for I only have about 1 year and 3 months to go. Nevertheless I will have plenty of time to visit and travel in Japan and perhaps other parts of the Orient.

        At noon today we were 1085 miles from Whittier, and 2312 miles from Yokohama. Longitude 172°W and Latitude 51.55° N.

FEB 08

        Man devised the Calendar and Man devised the International Date Line. Consequently, it is Man and not the Lord who decided that this day shall not exist in my lifetime. At 2:00 A.M, we crossed the International Line, making Tuesday become Wednesday, with nary a thing to write for the passing of these 24 hours. So pray tell, I will ship to the next day without nary any further adieu.

FEB 09

        Today is the day after the day that was skipped. Although that in itself was new to me, little else occurred during the day that had not taken place numerous times on this trip.

        I ate, washed, played cards, read and “shot the bull” during the course of the day. We weren’t allowed on deck (on account of the men a_ling the deck) consequently I missed the needed fresh air. The air in the recreation room and compartments gets musty and thick, and tends to make everybody sleepy and work out.

        The men generally spend their time reading and sleeping, once they have finished their details. The motion picture and pocketbook are a great boon to the Serviceman and fills much of their spare time. One thing I have not seen thus far is gambling which is something I expected to see a lot of. Perhaps there is some going on secretly, but most of the card games seem to be in fun.

        I tried my buck at Bingo in the evening but couldn’t get the needed numbers.

FEB 10

        Oh, what a day!! We ran into a violent storm and it threw around our little ship like a small twig. It began during the night and threw duffle bags and small bags all over the compartment. The rocking and rolling was tremendous, and it kept up throughout the day. We weren’t allowed on deck, but I did manage a peep through a pothole. The waves were gigantic, many times being higher than our deck. The wind caught these waves and sprayed over deck with constant showers.

        The fun really took place below, where everybody had to hold on to their mess trays with one hand and attempt to eat with the other. Every 10-15 seconds we had to balance the trays to keep the liquids from spilling. The showers were the same way, with one hand soaping up, and the other hand holding on. I think I can say that I am getting fed up with our boat ride.

        As it is, we turned South to get out of the storm and it added to our time at sea. This, plus some engine trouble earlier in the week has added a day or two on to our expected arrival time.

        I saw in the ship’s mimeographed paper that Georgi Malinkov has been replaced by Marshal Bulganin in Russia. Evidently this means the Red Army is in control of Russia, but how this will affect the Russian aims and policies, I do not know. At least we can hope for and work towards the best.

FEB 11

        For the past three or four days we have been plagued by bad weather and rough seas. These Two factors have aided immeasurably in delaying our arrival.

        Nothing much new happened today, just another day at sea. Did some reading and played cards to pass the time. Today was the first time in the past 3 days that we had been allowed on deck. Consequently, I spent about 4 hours on deck. On one occasion I saw 2 sharks about ½ mile off the starboard side. First fish I have seen all trip.

        At noon we were 1500 miles from Yokohama. Latitude 47°, Longitude 168°.

        I wish I could get some newspapers or magazines to keep up with the news. I understand that the CIO and AFL merged, but know little of the details. I am sorry to hear of this merger, as I believe competitive unions are good for the economy. Such a merger, if more than just a merger by name, will make a strong block to deal with. Time will tell, though.

        An interesting thing occurred this evening when I went on deck. I glanced at the moon and all of a sudden it seemed to jump right out of the sky. This was followed by an equally quick return to its original spot and I then realized that the movement was due to the rolling of the ship.

FEB 12

        More bad weather and more delay. Finished my big detail with the Orientations today, and also did some washing.

        Finished reading East of Eden this morning and I must say that I enjoyed the book very much. It is an excellent character study with a new and different plot. One interesting point brought out in the plot is the difference between the Old and New Testament with respect to God’s Telling Cain about Sin. In the New Testament it states that man “thou shall” rule over sin, making it a promise or command. In the old Testament it says “thou mayest”, leaving the rule of sin up to man himself. I think this is an important difference in the basic philosophies of Judaism and Christianity.

        Progress Report - 1140 miles to go to Yokohama. Latitude 45°, Longitude 160°. Sea - Very rough (snow squalls).

FEB 13 (SUNDAY - WEEK 8)

        During the late afternoon and early evening of yesterday, our ship changed course as to proceed to a helpless freighter that had developed some holes in its bow plates. The ship later wired that it was able to continue on its own, but the damage to our progress had been done. We only neted 33 miles from noon yesterday to noon today.

        The weather was still bad, and so I spent the greater portion of the day below deck. Played bridge all afternoon, and read and saw a movie in the evening. I have read all the books that I brought on board except my law Books but I have no decent place to read them so I have put them off for awhile.

        This business of being cooped up has put a definite damper on the trip. The routine becomes very monotonous and coupled with the musty air it makes for little comfort.

        Since tomorrow was supposed to be the day we hit Yokohama, we had our big meal this evening and it was quite good. We had steak, potatoes, corn on the cob, ice cream and sauce, cake, hard candy and whole wheat bread. It would be great to have such a meal every day.

FEB 14

        I think this tub is barely moving along. Today we went only 160 miles closer towards the land of the Rising Sun. This is sure a “Slow Boat to China”. They have even begun cutting rations owing to the extension of the trip.

        Spent the day playing bridge with our regular foursome. In this group, there is one good player, one fairly good player, an average or less player (me) and a learner. The games are interesting, but most of all, the time passes quite rapidly.

        Valentine’s Day – None received, one sent (many days ago). I do wish to send verbally, a Valentine of Peace and Love (?) to the Chinese Communists, for they seem to be the ones that are keeping the pot of hatred and war loaded to the brim. May it never boil over.

FEB 15

        Still crawling along owing to bad weather. Seems as if we are not destined to get to Japan, but that is mere wishful thinking.

        Played bridge, and began reading the novel, “Not As a Stranger”. It is fairly good, but mighty long – 940 pages.

        Saw the movie “Lion In the Street” and this story of Huey Long is identical to the saga of Joseph McCarthy. Both demagogues, both doing a little good, but much bad; and both, I believe, originally having good and honorable intentions, but becoming so wrapped up in themselves, that the means to the end are thrown way out of proportion. I do hope that McCarthy isn’t assassinated, and becomes a hero as Huey was.

        Progress Report - 753 miles to Yokohama. Latitude 40° Longitude 153°. Sea Rough. Wind – Westerly 15kts. Average speed 8.83 kts.

FEB 16

        We were only able to spend an hour on deck owing to bad weather and wind swept spray. Consequently I did a lot of reading, and hope to finish the book shortly as I have to turn it back to the ship library.

        Played some chess for the first time in many a moon. I remembered the basic moves, but had some difficulty in working plays. Will have to do a lot of playing and practicing in this game as well as bridge, as I think they are two games that are good to know.

        Distance to Yokohama - 386 miles. Wind - NNW 35 kts. Latitude 37° Longitude 146°40’.

FEB 17

        Sighted land for the first time since the Kodiak Islands (12 days previously) at 12:45 PM in the afternoon. From that time until we docked in Yokohama at 8 PM we assed hundreds of small junks and three or four larger ships. Each of the junks were small, built on similar lines, had 3-4 crew members, had a small sail, and were propelled by a gasoline motor.

        I wasn’t on deck at the time but understand two whales were sighted near the ship. I also was below when they moved the submarine nets to allow us passageway into the harbor. It was dark when we pulled along the dock, consequently, I couldn’t see much of the harbor. There were 4 or five skips near ours, loading or unloading.

        At the dock, awaiting the ships arrival, were approximately 100-125 husbands of the dependents that our ship carried. Many carried flowers or orchids for their (I am sure) long awaited loved ones. When they removed the rope holding them back, there was sure a mad scramble to get on board.

        They had an army band on the dock, and unlike the Seattle band, this one was quite good.

        To say the least, everybody is anxious for passes to view the “culture” in Yokohama.

FEB 18

        Early in the morning it was announced that anyone that wanted a pass could sign up for it around 10:00 AM. Consequently, I shined my shoes (first time in a long spell), took my uniform out of the duffle bag, and counted my money. (We had exchanged our dollars for MPC a couple of days previously. MPC = Military Pay Currency)

        And so I visited Yokohama, Japan – a bustling port that had more ships than I have seen in all my life. The visit was great and I enjoyed all 12 hours. We headed for 5th Street which is the main tourist street and walked for blocks looking at the people, the buildings, the cheap souvenirs, and the numerous p____ catering to the Servicemen. The street was very commercial and everybody spoke English.

        The dress of the people was mixed, with many in Western clothes and shoes, but just as many in kimonos and sandals. A lot of people had masks on their face which WAS (later explained) a Governmental decree to prevent spreading of cold germs. The mode of transportation was predominantly by foot, bicycle or motor scooter. The automobiles were mainly taxis.

        Later in the day we went down some side streets and really had an opportunity to observe the Japanese in their native environment. Here were seen the shops, food stores, speech and dress with a minimum of American customs or signs. Two of us went with a Sgt. who had been to Yokohama previously, and he explained much of the food habits, expressions and other small things I would have missed. Today, truly, was a memorable experience.

FEB 19

        About 700 men came on board ship,  destination United States via Pusan. (Sure would like trade places with any of them) Our breakfast was messed up and I missed a little of the farewell “goings on”. They had a Navy band, Japanese girls, military and civilian personnel and families of Japanese brides all performing, crying or waveing goodbye. With such an adieu, our ship put to sea about 10:00 AM. Two tugs maneuvered us out in the harbor, turned us around, and pointed our bow towards the first of the breakwater openings. There were two such breakwaters in THE HARBOR. The sea in the harbor was calm, the weather was cool and hazy, and the thoughts of those on board were varied. Those going home were happy, those headed for Pusan were wondering the assignment that awaited them. (Me in particular.)

        Later in the morning, the haze lifted and we could see hundreds of ships, many of them big cargo and passenger ships. Besides the larger ships, could be seen the tugs, harbor boats, and the ever present one cylinder junks or “sampans”.

        Around noon we slowed down, and waited while they moved the submarine nets, so that we could pass. One could see nets on each side of the ship, as far as the eye could perceive; and the opening was achieved by the moving of two barges which were connected to the nets. From this point we headed South –  destination Pusan.

FEB 20 (SUNDAY - WEEK 9)

        The good word for today, is that we dock tomorrow morning. I will truly be glad to get settled once again, even though boredom will soon enough set in. The voyage before and after Yokohama (last 4 days) has been quite pleasant, with the ship riding the waves smoothly, and the food being unusually good. I am sure the trip would have been a lot more enjoyable if these conditions were present throughout the 20 days. Nothing much happened, and I spent the day trying to keep occupied. Was an deck awhile, read and saw a movie. The cartoon with the movie was great, typical of all Tom and Jerry cartoons. I got in too late to get one of the chairs, and spent the 1 ½ hours on my fanny, and it wasn’t very comfortable. Nevertheless, good times “must” be ahead. Soooo – until the big day –

FEB 21

        Yesterday’s tomorrow has come and gone, and our “slow boat” is still miles from Pusan. We ran into some bad weather once again, particular in the Straights which separate the two Southern islands comprising the Japanese home islands. We dropped anchor and waited much of the afternoon, before a pilot came on board and guided the ship through the narrow Straight. Snow squalls added to the difficulty.

        Otherwise today was typical, and fell into the boring routine of the other 20 days. I regret running out of decent reading material a few days ago, which seemed to add hours to the days. Oh well, all I have in the Army is time, and I guess a day or two more on this ship is no worse than those to be spent in Korea.

Route as of February 21st, 1955 – end of Chapter 3.

CHAPTER 4 - Pusan If You Please

February 22nd, 1955 - April 1st, 1955

FEB 22                 Washington’s Birthday

        The spirit of Washington was with us today, as we finally docked and di_b_ched from our prison ship. Like reincarnated Columbus, we dragged (me) or carried our duffle bags to the docks and felt solid ground for a change. From here we were loaded into 10 Ton Army trucks and driven to the Replacement Depot, 10 miles away.

        The trip through Pusan was pitiful. I never saw such poverty in all my life, slums and rat holes of St. Louis included. The shacks are all wooden, and e__ide and flimsy fire traps. They are built close together with no signs of even the minimum sanitation. It is unbelievable the conditions these people live under.

        We entered the depot around 11 AM and were ushered to some huts to await reassignment. Luckily my name wasn’t included on the 8th Army shipment, although it doesn’t mean I will get a good station. We turned in our O.D’s and got O.G’s plus some other junk which fits “nicely” into my duffle bag. The food was good, and I believe I even got a stomach ache eating too much.

        Attended, or rather observed, a Washington Day party at the Service Club in the evening. Ice cream and more stomach pains later I adjourned for bed.

FEB 23

        One need only be stationed at a place where facilities are limited, to become even more appreciative of the conveniences of home. Last night we had amble blankets (4 filthy ones), but had no sheets or pillow covers. Also there was no water to clean with before going to bed, plus no toilet paper.

        Nevertheless, today was one day closer to a permanent assignment. In the morning I received my mimeographed orders, stating that I was to be assigned to Hqs 7th T Port Com C, and Pusan Military Post, APO 59, as a 1070 (Draftsman). We waited from 1:00 to 3:00, and finally got trucking to Pier #1 for our new station. At Pier #1 (where we had docked), myself and another 1070 waited for 4 hours until our transportation arrived.

        We then climbed aboard the jeep – bag and baggage– and were driven the 8 miles to 9131 AU (commonly called Hialeah Compound) which was right across the road from the replacement depot.

        Too late for dinner or a shower, we were given a place to spend the night pulse advice as to where to get some chow. They had no bunks or sheets and so yours truly slept on a mattress on the floor. Oh well!

FEB 24

        In the morning we filled out some forms and were given a brief tour of Hialeah. The compound use to be a recreation field and has fairly decent accommodations. There are about 500 enlisted men, plus some officers and some representatives of the Neutral Nations Inspection Team. The sanitation facilities are average, with American style stools, hot water in the morning and hot water in the evenings for showers. During the day there is no water at all. Water is scarce in Pusan, and only in certain places is there (1) water and (2) water fit to drink. The compound also has a nice library, PX, Service Club and Snack Bar, small gym, movie and NCO club. The latter club is quite nice with decent bands and entertainment.

        In the afternoon I was sent to Clarification and Assignment where I was informed that I would not be used as a 1070 (Draftsman) but would be the cashier at Branch 600 - the central office for the 14 PX’s in the Pusan area. I went to the office, which was located about 200 yards from Pier #1 in an old building. There are 1 officer, 15 enlisted men and about 20 Koreans working on the records of the Post Exchanges. There are also 2 civilians from the Japan Central Exchange who sort of supervise the whole operation. Other than meeting some of the personnel, I did not find out much about the job.

FEB 25

        Today was the first full day of work since December 17th, 1954 at Fort Leonard Wood. Actually, it consisted of observing Mr. Raby (one of the civilian employees of Japan Central Exchange) go about his everyday duties as temporary cashier. Besides the daily routine, there was also the monthly inventory worth to be done. This was complicated somewhat by a change in whan-dollar exchange rate at the beginning of February. More about the job at a later date.

        I ate lunch at the Harbor Lite NCO open mess where most of those living in Hialeah Compound eat when working around the Pier #1 area. I will probably eat at  the RTO mess, however, since most of the EM at Branch 600 eat there.

        Took a tour of Hialeah Compound in the evening, and also walked over to the Service Club which is just outside the gate from Hialeah. The facilities seem to be adequate and perhaps the time will move swiftly onward. Water seems to be the major inconvenience in the Pusan area.

        The weather has been quite comfortable for this time of year. While it gets cold (around 30°) at night, the sun is out during the day and the temperature rises to about 45°. There hasn’t been too much wind lately, which is a life saver, as it sure would play havoc with the dust and filth.

        All in all, my first impression of Korea (the Army facilities) is better than I had thought.

FEB 26

        Worked the major part of the day finalizing the books for the month of February. The work doesn’t seem to be very difficult, but is somewhat tedious around the end of the month. I worked with Mr. Raby throughout the day, doing some work, and observing the rest of the time.

        In the evening I met a fellow that had come over on the same ship as I, and we both went to the NCO Club. There wasn’t much going on, so we stayed a while, had a few beers and left.

        One of the unbelievable sights I have seen in Pusan, is the heavy loads balanced on the heads of the Korean women. They carry everything from pails of water to clothes, sticks, food and jars. Sometimes one will see a woman balancing some article on her head and carrying a child on her back at the same time.

        Some of the women put a piece of cloth on their head, and upon this they balance the load. Others wear nothing and balance the load on top of their hair. Old and young alike participate in this custom, and in fact one of the biggest loads I have seen was carried by a woman who must have been 60-70 years old.

FEB 27 (SUNDAY - WEEK 10)

        Such disappointment. I had planned to spend the day walking around Pusan, taking in the sight and also taking a few camera shots. But Mother Nature was not agreeable, and it rained torrents of H2O all day long. Consequently I spent the day at the Service Club writing letters.

        The Club is quite nice and has some fairly decent facilities. They have a large room, plus a writing, game, pool, music and studio rooms. They have facilities for showers, a kitchen and a snack for outside. I stayed to see a talent show, but it was only fair and I didn’t pay much attention to it. Went to the Club and had a couple 7 _eps. They had an excellent Korean band which played strictly jazz and dixieland. To say the least, the men went wild.

FEB 28

        Another full day on the February final report, but at last it appears to be completed with the exception of obtaining Whan to pay the indigenous help. Spent the evening reading – Law and a new novel I started titled Animal Farm by George Orwell.

        One of the common sights around town are men with apparatuses on their back for hauling material, livestock and almost anything imaginable. These men are actually doing work that we in the U.S would have carried in pick up trucks or on the backs of work horses.

        The apparatus is made in the shape of an A Frame, protruding from the back of which are two inclined poles that support the load. Generally the man has a hooked stick which holds it against the A frame which in turn rests on the back. The loads carried by these men are tremendous. I have seen some of these fellows carrying heavy stones, big truck tires and even a 200-300 pound hog. The frame is made of wooden poles, and bound together by rope or heavy twine. Some of the men have some padding to help soften the load on their back and against their rear end.

MAR 01

        Today was the first time I was more or less on my own. We completed the February report in the morning, and in the afternoon I laid out my balance sheet, retail and cost sheets and check form for the month of March. The only thing remaining for the month of February is to pay the indigenous help.

        Went to the movies and saw a fairly amusing show – “Tonights the Night.” The movie theater is a large quonset hut with wooden seats. It is at least better than the hole we had on the ship, although it isn’t quite as good as the Fox theater.

        The means of transportation in Pusan – and I imagine throughout most of Korea – is quite primitive by the standards we know of in the United States. For the most part it is by foot, upon earth and rock paths. The main street in Pusan is paved, but has 60 million huts in it. Some of the people have bicycles, three wheel trucks and horse drawn carts (for business). The horses are very small, about the height and size of shetland ponies. They are attached to 2 wheel carts and do much of the hauling, along with the A frame boys.

        There are some cars and trucks in Pusan, but the majority (besides the U.S. Army) belong to the ROK Army. Unlike Japan there are few taxis, and most of them are old, beat-up cars. Down the center of the main street runs a street car line, composed of cars we in St. Louis would have burned years ago. The cars manage to run, however, and have their share of customers.

MAR 02

        Had more money in my possession today than any other time in my life, although the actual worth wasn’t very great. Mr Raby and myself drew 2,200,000 whan (500 whan = $1) from the Korean Bank for payment to the indigenous help. I hated to handle the money as it was dirty and filthy and one can hardly imagine where the poverty stricken people had kept this money.

        We have caught up on all February reports so I took over the handling of the transactions for March. I don’t think I will be kept too busy at the job, and am thus looking forward to doing my letter writing and correspondence work here. One prime objective for my spare time will be to set up the work in such a fashion and with the necessary descriptions that almost anybody will be able to step in if I get sick, go on R & R or go on a leave. (Particularly the latter two!)

        The dress of the male Korean is not too different from Western garb, and there are many that wear suits and other similar clothes. The pants are more baggy (few cleaners) and many wear caps. One also sees a lot of military style clothing (black) with high collars worn by the Korean boys. The boys also wear a lot of old GI clothes, and articles made from such clothes.

        Some of the Korean farmers wear robes, particularly the older men. The garments are generally white and are accompanied by small circus type hats which indicate that they are retired. These men also have beards, many of which are quite long and make one think of the venerable Oriental thinker.

MAR 03

        Completed the issuance of the whan to the sub-branches for payment to their indigenous personnel. Caught up on the books for March, and began preparation of a setup for easy grasping of the duties of the cashier.

        Got my first haircut while in Korea, and must admit that it was a pretty fair job. Washed my hair and took a long hot shower. Decided to play Bingo at the Club, and see if I couldn’t win one of the big jackpots – $400, $300 and $200. I didn’t, but I did manage to win a concillation prize of $12.50. Really felt great.

        Korean male - The average Korean male is about 5’6” - 5’8” in height and weighs I imagine around 140 pounds. Their hair is black and in general they wear it very long. The boys complete their military style clothes with a close crew cut.

        The color of their skin is more tannish than yellow, and their eyes aren’t very slanted. The men seem to be quite strong for their __ge and can do a lot of hard work, if they so desire.

        Their obsequious attitude falls in line with what I have heard concerning the Orientals, but I think a lot of it is due to their poverty and necessity to do anything to exist. I have a hard time getting used to this type of behavior, just as I hate the tipping and waiting on others that is prevalent in America.

MAR 04

        Buses take us from Hialeah to the RTO circle near the Pier and Branch 600 in the morning at 7:300. The ride is a rough and bumpy one, as the road is very poor, even though it is the main road in Pusan. The ride generally takes approximately 20 minutes.

        The ride this morning was interrupted by a Korean parade. The parade – one band and about 400 police and 200 civilians – was for a “cleaning up the city” campaign. All the marchers carried brooms or shovels and were accompanied by one loud speaker and some signs. The brooms are interesting, in that they are made of heavy straw-like grass tied by string or rope. They are quite crude, but I imagine they are better than nothing. I would think they would wear out in a short time. Since they are a collection of straws tied crudely together, it takes 3-5 strokes more per area to do the same work as our manufactured brooms. The parade took about 5 minutes to pass where I was watching.

        On the way home in the afternoon, I was more conscious of people cleaning the streets than in the past. I saw some old women using these straw brooms to dust off the dirt and small rocks on the main road. (Actually seemed useless owing to the brisk wind and the ubiquitous dirt.) An unusually pungent odor was in the air, and it came from the sewers and other holes that were being cleaned. The odor was so bad, that one had to almost run past the immediate vicinity of the sewer or hole.

MAR 05

        Seems that the weekends are jinxed by rain. Perhaps tomorrow will be nice though, and will provide an opportunity for sightseeing and taking of pictures.

        In the afternoon I went to the bank (which was closed) and then dropped off a receipt at the Maryknoll Clinic. The Clinic is sponsored by the Catholic Church and does remarkable good to the destitute in and around the Pusan Area. The Sister I spoke to was in charge of the Social Work Section, which teaches War Widows how to sew, paint and make other souvenirs for sale in the Post Exchanges. Enough money is realized from the work of these women to support a group of about 150 women and children. (The widows do the work in their homes so they can be with their children.)

        The Sister showed me around the grounds, which is one of the nicest spots I have seen in Pusan. The land and buildings use to belong to a retired Japanese General who settled in Pusan. The ground is on a hill and overlooks part of the city, with the sea in the background. Much of the land is covered with trees and bushes, the latter which bloom in May, June and July.

        The Clinic has about 95 Sisters, Doctors and Koreans who provide free medical aid to over 2000 people a day. It is the largest free clinic in the Pusan area and probably in all Korea. The people at the Clinic work against seemingly insurmountable odds, but they nevertheless, plug away, day after day.

MAR 06 (SUNDAY - WEEK 11)

        Spent the day with R. Call and one of his Korean friends sightseeing in downtown Pusan and one of the outlying towns. The marketplace was very interesting and some what colorful. Most of the shops are small and generally specialize in one type of merchandise. There were one or two department stores in the area we visited, but they were small drug-store affairs as we know them in the U.S.

        The Koreans do not seem to have much craft ability other than some gold work and working with inlaid mother-of-pearl. Consequently, much of the goods – other than junk – were from Japan, Hong Kong and a couple other places. The Koreans are very untidy, and their shops poorly laid out.

        We visited the black market, which was displayed in open carts on some of the side streets. The displays were colorful, and one could buy nearly everything; particularly American goods and G.I. clothing. Some things were cheaper than the PX’s, others still was more expensive. Cigarettes are a premium, and sell 2-3 times what a G.I. has to pay for them. Thus, many sell their allotment (6 cartons a month) in the Black market and get whan or MPC.

        We ate lunch at an Army mess hall, but had tea at a Korean shop. It wasn’t different, perhaps a little sweeter than American brands. I had signed up for a trip to the Tong Nae temples, but since the others hadn’t, there wasn’t enough room for them. We decided to take Korean transportation to the temple and visit them by ourselves. We got on an old trolley and rode to the end of the line to a place called Tong Nae Un Chung. We walked around the town and inquired where the temples were. Although the Korean could speak good Korean, we were led astray, and took the wrong road. Consequently, we went out of our way, and almost to the top of a nearby mountain. The walk was somewhat rewarding, however, as the view was breathtaking. One could see for miles, and since it was a clear day, we could see the Seal distant rice fields on the side of mountains and other towns and villages. The mountain was steep and covered with evergreen type trees. The air was clear and it sure felt good to be in the clear, fresh country.

        We took a different trail down, and happened to come upon the KUM JHUNG temple. It was a small Buddhist Temple, beautifully located on the side of the mountain. It was old, and was styled in the familiar Oriental design – particularly the pointed roof. The beams in the ceiling were carved wood, and painted in bright colors. The inside was of wood, with mats on the floor on which the people knelt when they prayed. There was a 2’ Buddha in a glass container on a table at one side of the room.

MAR 07

        Today was the first of two Inspection days. Consequently, everything was cleaned and made “ship shape” (what a farce). Only a light colonel favored us with a visit, but nevertheless, it seemed we passed satisfactorily and can now fall back into our old habits.

MAR 08                 Purim

        I notice that today is Purim, but frankly it does not seem to phase me one way or the other. Some people say that when one “gets” in the Army (taken is perhaps a better word) that he becomes more religious. I am sure that must apply to those in battle, for those that are occupation or assisting troops become quite loose in their morals. Their one thought (as a rule) is women, and since money is the big factor, women are easy to obtain.

        Last night I went to a dance at the Service Club #6, located near Hialeah. There were perhaps 100-150 soldiers and about 100 Korean girls. The girls were all dressed in Western clothes, high heels, and lipstick. Most of them could dance the Fox Trot, and many others could jitterbug.

        Some of the fellows from the shop plus another I met at Fort Lewis decided to go so I tagged along. At first I didn’t feel like dancing, but after awhile I asked one “chick” to dance. She told me her name was Linda (laugh) and was from Seoul. Well I couldn’t speak a word of Korean, and she couldn’t make much sense in English so we had a conversationless dance. She asked me if I belonged to the Hialeah NCO club and I said Yes. She wanted me to take her, but I couldn’t see the need for spending any money for such as her. Sooo I politely said No and went on my way. I guess 80% or higher of the girls are whores and live off the GI. One interesting point is that most of the girls are from Seoul, and when the GI leaves they will then return home without people knowing what they had been. Conversely the girls up North are from the South.

MAR 09

        Very typical day in Korea. Worked at the office, ate, and studied in the evening. I have been doing a lot of studying lately – mostly law – since I am interested in getting into a routine. I generally eat, wash up and then head for the library. There it is pretty quiet, and if I put some cotton in my ears I can concentrate.

        I study from about 6:30 to 9:00 at which time they play records in the library and it interrupts my studying. I then generally read the Stars and Stripes, some magazines or even a book. Last night I read a book on “What is a Jew”. Frankly I didn’t get much out of it. They have another book on Judaism, and I will read it one night.

        During the week I had spoken to a Sgt. about working on the A-Frame paper published by the K Com Z command. It is a journalism job, but I think I could have handled it. Sooo – I went to talk to the Lt. and in turn the Colonel about the job. They said, however, that since K Com Z is phasing out shortly that in all probability so will the newspaper. I was told to call back in a week or so.

        I am looking into all angles to get out of here (even though it isn’t so bad) and try to get to Japan. After about 6 months I can put in FOR A  Intra-FECOM transfer, but I don’t think I can get it since you have to work 12 months in your new assignment. In general things are confusing with K Com Z pulling out, so I think I will sit tight and see what cooks.

MAR 10

        I saw my first real U.S.O. show today, and I must admit it wasn’t bad. Although the surroundings weren’t the typical hollow over which shells are flying and bombs bursting; still there was a genuine Army atmosphere – cheering, yelling G.I.’s. The show was held in the Service Club and perhaps 175-200 troopers were present.

        The show consisted of a 6 man colored combo (fair), a dance act (fair), two gymnasts, a man and wife comedy team and a card sleight-of-hand artist. The comedians were quite good and had some appropriate jokes and remarks about Korea. They also put on a Charleston demonstration that was the best I had ever seen.

        The sleight of hand artist was excellent and proved beyond a doubt that the hand is quicker than the eye. He pulled cards from everywhere, and accompanied his act with a pleasant and humorous conversation. The G.I’s were helping him with one act, and as they were returning to their seats he motioned for them to return. He then proceeded to return to them their wallets, watches and pens that he picked while they were on the stage.

MAR 11

        I took off part of the afternoon as it was a beautiful day. The son was out, yet it was pleasantly cool. Checked out a basketball and played with it for an ½ hour or so. Then borrowed a tennis racket and batted the ball back and forth with another fellow. It was great to get some exercise for a change.

        Korean women – It seems that many of the younger Korean women are beginning to wear Western clothes and shoes. For instance of the 6 Korean girls that work at Branch 600, 5 wear Western clothes. Almost all of the girls that go with the G.I’s or who frequent the dances dress in shirt and sweater, dress, or low cut gowns. I have seen one or two at the dance in Korean dress, but THEM seem out of place and uncomfortable.

        The Korean dress is quite ugly and uncomfortable it seems to me, although it doesn’t make much difference what I think. The dresses are quite full and hang from the shoulder in a loose manner, with generally no belt. It consists of velvet, or silk or cotton cloth wrapped around, with no buttons or ties closing the opening. (Like a nightgown only longer and fuller.) This material is generally plain, and of various colors.

        The women also wear a small jacket like coat, which comes to a position about 10” above their waist.
