Thus, it is a similar to a short jackets they wear in America, (I can’t recall the name) although the ones over here are generally of fine silk or velvet, and richly embroidered. I have seen some jackets with some beautiful needle work on them. Most of these jackets have long sleeves.

        The women generally go about bowheaded, with a few a them putting on shawls. The shoes may consist of anything, from regular shoes to sandals (not to common) to slipper like affairs with closed toe and heels. These latter shoes are the most common, and are made of cloth or rubber. Some of the shoes are painted with interesting designs.

        Very few of the women wear coats, the only visible means of protection against the cold being additional layers of under garments. They seem to keep their clothes clean even though they have such poor cleaning facilities in this country. (The children on the other hand are generally filthy.)

        The whole outfit I think is not attractive and not even practical. I don’t know if there are any customs or reasons for such dress, which could answer some of my questions. The Korean woman as viewed by the outside world is a totally clad person – from neck to ankle – and looks uncomfortable as she goes about her daily work.

MAR 12

        It was a miserable day today (with respect to the weather) and I didn’t mind working all day long. Did a little studying in the evening, and then went to the NCO club for a couple of beers, and something to eat.

        

MAR 13 (SUNDAY - WEEK 12)

        The sun was out today, but a cold breeze spoiled what would have been a beautiful day. Nevertheless, I met R. Call and his Korean friend, and we climbed aboard a trolley which carried us to Tong Nae Un Chung. We tried to get on board a Korean bus, but they were all crowded so we decided to walk to Tong Nae.

        It was a long walk – about 8 miles – but the exercise did us a lot of good. On the way the Korean fellow – Won – pointed out many sights along the roadside. He showed us the rice fields and how they were banked so that the water stayed in. He mentioned that it was a little day for the rice, but that the rains would be coming soon. Much of the land is cultivated, and the Koreans were working on Sunday as if it were any other day.

        The houses were interesting in that one could tell the wealth of the family by the construction of the house. The rich people had houses with tiled roofs and had nice looking wood work on their doors and windows. The houses were either made of dried mud, concrete blocks or wood. The poorer people had dried mud houses with thatched roofs. They looked like houses one would see in Africa.

        All the houses had outside toilets, some a little more fancy than the others. Some people had fine places that opened on one side of the house, and which tunneled under the house so as to provide heat. Now and then we would catch a smell of something cooking, but generally we caught the smell of the “Honey Pits” where human and animal feces were being fermented for fertilizer.

        One interesting point brought out by Won, was the manner of burying the dead. He showed us mounds of each on the side of the hills in which he said the person was buried. Two mounds together indicated a man and wife. Generally the mounds were unmarked and in time would look like any other part of the terrain. Some of the richer people had stone monuments, but we didn’t see too many of them on our trip. Perhaps in richer areas we would see more.

        We finally got to Tong Nae and walked around the area. There were 5- 8 buildings in which the Buddhists prayed. The buildings weren’t long, and were only about 250 years old although the original temple was said to have been built in the 600s A.D. The temples were similar to the ones we saw last Sunday; plain on the inside, mats on the floor, brightly colored wooden ceiling beams, a statue of Buddha and perhaps some others, and a table in front of Buddha on which was a gourd and stick which was beaten while they prayed. It was an interesting day.

MAR 14

        Long day at the office with not much to do. I went to the Post Office 3 times to mail some checks, but was unable to do so each time for some reason or another. Took the checks home (so as to mail first thing in the morning) before I realized I had $66,106.40 worth of checks in my possession. To say the least, I was careful.

MAR 15

        Received my income tax withholding form and then proceeded to calculate my gain or loss. As per usual I owed the government, and consequently my bankroll was set back $43 to the Federal Government and $5 to the State of Missouri.

        Today was THE day for CQ at Branch 600 so I brought all my paraphernalia to the shop. D. Call had his phonograph and records at the shop, and we listened to them during the day and in the evening. He had some classical, popular and Japanese & Korean records, which were enjoyed by yours truly. I am afraid I do not appreciate Korean or Korean music, although now and then they have a melodious song. I enjoyed the classical records very much particularly the following:

  • Finlandia by Sibelius
  • Waltz from the Sleeping Beauty by Tchaikovsky 
  • Excerpts from Les Sylphides by Chopin
  • Grand March from Aida by Verdi
  • Excerpt from 5th Symphony by Beethoven

        After the music interlude and some studying I got ready to hit the sack. All of a sudden I heard a snap, noise and a brisk movement in the ceiling near the door. I walked over and saw a long rats tail extending from a hole in the ceiling. It was moving quite rapidly but then stopped. Since my bed faced that hole I knew I would get no sleep unless I got rid of it. Sooo I got the carbine and some bullets, and I was determined to shoot it, club it, frighten it or frighten me.

        I used the butt of the weapon to hit the ceiling and as I did a rat trap fell out of the hole with the rat caught in it. I thanked my stars, grabbed the trap and got rid of both as quickly as possible. My big adventure was over but I swear I heard noises all night.

MAR 16

        Today was payday for the Korean personnel and consequently I buckled on my trusty 45, clunked into a ¾ Ton truck along with a Korean helper and rode to the Korean bank. The bank is in an old building near the center of town, and still uses the Oriental abacus, hand counting of all bills, and numerous girls performing errands and odd jobs.

        The procedure that occurs, is that when I enter I go to one gentleman who takes the check I have from JCE, and makes out some form of slip. He gives me a metal tag with a number on it and I go to the General Cashier window. There I hand him a slip telling the breakdown of the denominations (number of 1, 10 and 100 hwan notes) I need. He gives me some of the money – particularly the 1’s and any odd amounts of 10’s and 100’s – and directs me out back for the remainder.

        In the back I get the rest of the Hwan which is generally 2-5 gunny sack loads of 10 Hwan notes. My helper and I throw the sacks on the truck and then head back for Branch 600 for subsequent distribution to the Sub Branches.

MAR 17

        Back home on St. Patrick’s Day one might see a lot of bearded Engineer students celebrating their patron Saint with Engineer Days, dances, exhibits and misc. Activities. Over here the day was the same as the day before, the day before that, etc. I did have a 1 day beard but that was all.

        Tried my luck at Bingo, but didn’t even come close. Perhaps I should quit while I am ahead.

        Our branch workhouse and office is located near one of the British Compounds in Pusan. The Compound near the Pier is quite small and only has a limited number of troops – perhaps 50. The troops look basically the same as the Americans, although they seem to have an intangible “British look” about them (might just be my imagination). Their uniform is khaki, but not as new or nice as ours. They all seem to wear loosely knit sweaters which tend to give an air of distinctness and shabbiness to their uniform. Many of the troops wear the typical European beret, – even some of the officers have little black berets on their heads.

        The insignias are interesting looking, and I hope to find out what they mean before I leave Korea. These insignias and stripes remind me of the Hollywood movies concerning the British Army in India, Africa, etc.

        One interesting thing is that their guards stand post with fixed bayonets. Why, I don’t know; maybe they want to look more fierce or maybe they don’t have any scabbards.

MAR 18

        Had given some thought to taking the afternoon off but decided INSTEAD to catch up on some miscellaneous typing I had to do. In the afternoon two of the fellows asked me to come with them to a dance at Service Club #6 that was to take place in the evening. I hesitated, but agreed to go when they said they had an extra girl and that their girls wouldn’t go unless the other one went came.

        I met them at the Club around 7:30 and was introduced to the girl – Diana. (These American names give me quite a laugh.) She was about 5’4”, had a fair figure, long black hair and a very pretty face. In fact she was one of the prettiest Koreans I had seen. She spoke very good English and I learned she was from Seoul, and had arrived in Pusan at the beginning of the War. Her breath was terrible, as are many of the Korean girls, as they eat a lot of food called KIMCHEE which is a conglomeration of everything, that is purposely allowed to ferment.

        We danced awhile – she was a poor dancer  – and talked very little as I didn’t know what to talk about. I had to sit back and laugh, though, when she conversed with her friends, in a rapid gutteral type of speech. The other two fellows decided to go to the NCO Club at Hialeah so we all left early and went to the Club. They ate and drank me to the tune of about $2.25, and I was glad when 10:00 came around, and the girls had to leave. They piled in a jeep and rode downtown, I walking the 50 feet to my bed. All in all, it was quite an evening for experiences, but not too much enjoyment.

MAR 19

        I took off in the afternoon and decided to walk around downtown. Consequently, I headed South on the MSR (main road) and walked, stopped, and just gazed around at all sights; – humans and inanimate.

        In general the area was a market center and one could see all kinds of shops and merchandise being displayed. There weren’t very many shops, as we know them, but instead there were hundreds of push carts and small stands cluttering up the sidewalks and streets. The “shops or stands” generally catered to one type of merchandise, and at that the amount in stock was quite limited. Also, there would be whole streets lined with only one type of goods being displayed.

        One interesting sight is the outside, one stove restaurant. The stove may consist of a 5 gallon can which has a fire in it, and a lid; on which a pan may be heated. These restaurants had fish, cookies, potato-like food and bread. (Only one item at one place.) The person (buyer) would come up to the stand, pay the money required, and eat right out of the pan or the stove. At one stand there was a lady breastfeeding her child and tending the stand at the same time, and oblivious to the needs or desires of the baby.

        The walk was very interesting and I plan to take many of them throughout my stay in Pusan.

MAR 20 (SUNDAY - WEEK 13)

        I had signed up EARLIER IN THE WEEK for a Service Club approved tour to Kyang Ju, located about 70 miles North East of Pusan. The tour left Pusan at 7:30 AM, and via a one-car, gasoline operated railroad car, we arrived at our destination around 10:00. A truck (at least that is what it was referred to as) took us up to the Hotel Bulguksa, which is operated by the Korean National Railroad. It is a Western style hotel and is very nice. (Luxurious by Korean standards)

        Near the Hotel was the Bulguksa Temple and its adjoined Buddhist temples and buildings. The temples were similar to those I had seen on the previous two Sundays, although perhaps a little older. In one temple (temple referring to a one building about 50’ x 70’) there were two Buddhas, probably made out of wood, and covered with gold leaf. The Buddhas were about 6 feet high and had the expressionless face so typical of the Buddhas in Korea.

        I happened to be present when a Korean family came to pray, and it was interesting to observe. The family took off their shoes and went inside the building. They then kneeled on the mats, placed for such purposes, and faced the statue of Buddha. They joined their hands as in prayer, and mumbled some words, kneeling all the way to the floor as they spoke. They then rose came back to the vertical position (with their legs still resting on the mat) and mumbled some more words, and repeated their previous actions. They did this for about 3-5 minutes, and then left the temple.

        Through Call’s friend Whant, we learned that the family comes to this temple twice a year to pray. He also learned that one of the women was 70 years old, and this amazed us as you should have seen her climb on and off the truck without any help. Unbelievable.

        We ate lunch at the hotel – fair – and then began our climb to the King’s Tomb located at the top of the mountain. I had heard it was a rough climb, but rough falls flat in trying to describe the trip. The path was quite narrow and went up and around the mountain at a 50° - 60° grade in most places. It took us an hour to make the climb and I was physically worn out when I got to the top.

        At the top was a large mound of earth, approximately 100 feet in circumference, one side of which was cut in to provide space for a 15’ stone Buddha and other carved stone figures. The setting was the most impressive of the Buddha statues that I have seen. The statue was built in the 8th Century of during the Silla Dynasty. I hope my pictures come out, as they will present the figure and the setting better than I can describe it in words.

MAR 21

        Put in a full day at work today, compiling the second March Cash & Sales report, and drawing some additional hwan from the Korean Bank. Went with a couple of fellows to their barracks and took a shortcut getting there. The filth and squalor I saw were beyond description, but I will MAKE AN attempt to describe it later on.

MAR 22

        In the afternoon, Milt Raby – one of the Japan Central Exchange civilians working at Branch 600 – asked me if I would like to join their party at a Chinese restaurant in the evening. I said yes, and got some hwan needed for payment of the bill.

        We left around 4:30 and went to the CE Depot where we met the other fellow – Mr. Aloněs, Mr. Kihuchi and a Mr. Johnson. After a couple of drinks we got a ride via a CE vehicle to the restaurant which was located near the middle of town.

        Once inside they took us upstairs to our private dining room, which was quite plain in arrogance. We removed our shoes (I had boots on) and entered through the sliding door. The table was about 15-20 inches off the ground floor and had a plain tablecloth on it. There were pillows around the table to sit upon. All the men could speak Japanese and some Chinese, and after some questioning of the waiter, the dinner was ordered and a price quoted for same (5880 hwan).

        First they gave us small saucers and some sauce for the forthcoming food – soy sauce and vinegar. Next the waiter brought in hot cloths for wiping our hands. They also passed around chopsticks and much laughter was had at my expense while they attempted to teach me how to manipulate these twigs.

        The first course was a plate of hot friend shrimp. We all took from this central plate and dipped the shrimp in soy sauce which we had placed previously in our individual saucers. The shrimp was very good, and two more platters of the same were ordered. The next course was small pieces of fried chicken which I thought only fair. This was followed by sweet and sour pork which was also only fair. Soup was then brought in, included in which were pieces of bamboo shoots. The final course was fried shrimp–rice which was quite good. Fumbling and muttering to myself I manage to consume the rice using my slender twigs which slid among my butter-fingers.

        The meal was very interesting and quite tasty (in spots) and I enjoyed the opportunity of being such a “gourmet”. Milt had brought a case of beer and we made a good “dent” in the 24 can package. The evening was spiced with some interesting conversation about Japan and some kidding between Milt and Mr. Johnson concerning the catholic religion. All in all, I had a pleasant evening and experience.

MAR 23

        Today I had a good opportunity to see the inside of what may be labeled an average Korean house. It was small, with paper walls with some wood paneling around the doors and partitions. This house had no heat, no electricity, no running water, and no flushing toilets. The toilet was a hole in the floor in a small closet size room. Kerosene lamps were used for illumination. It was a typical American home of the 19th Century.

MAR 24

        On Tuesday night tentative plans were made to go on Thursday evening to a Japanese restaurant located on Sang-Do peninsula. Plans were finished during the afternoon, and we obtained the use of a JCC car to take us to this restaurant. Besides Mr. Johns, Mr. Raby and myself, a Lt. Pitts joined the party. He is a ROTC officer from Cornell and quite a pleasant person.

        The establishment was located about 100 yards from the ocean, adjacent to the nicest beach I have seen in Korea. I understand it is quite the “Coney Island” for Koreans when summer rolls around. The general appearance of the neighborhood was quite clean and there was an air of charm surrounding the homes. It was getting dark when we went, consequently, not very much of the scenery could be seen.

        The restaurant was large and was had many separate rooms for the diners. We removed our shoes at the door and walked down the hall to a room which was plain in appearance and about 10’ x 15’ in size. Over the sliding door was an Oriental painting depicting a scene of Chinese boys playing on a beach. The wall opposite the door had sliding partitions, from which the ocean could be viewed. The partitions were made of wooden designs, some of which were very beautiful.

        On the left as one came in the door, was a plain wall, which adjoined a small alcove, called TAKANOMO, and which was reserved for the guest of honor. There were scrolls on the wall (KAKEMONO) but none of the others could read Japanese well enough to understand what the characters meant.

        Mr. Johnson and Mr. Raby ordered the meal, and it was quite a feast. First they brought in the Tai-Fish which was some type of uncooked fish. I thought it was terrible. Next came fried shrimp (EBI) which when dipped in soy sauce is quite good. This was followed by the main dish which is called Sukiyaki and consists of hot beef, bamboo (TAKE) bean curd (TOFU), onions (NEGI) and CONAKO. Each of the pieces (other than the small piece of beef) are dipped in a raw egg before eating. (Of course, it is optional.) The food is hot and tends to cook the egg around it when it is dipped.

        Following the latter dish, we had rice, slice apple and DAIKON (a radish like plant) to complete the meal. I attempted to eat with chop sticks throughout the meal, but my fingers became cramped and I ended up using a spoon. I do believe I am getting a little better with the twigs, though.

        After the meal, which I enjoyed as a novelty first and satisfaction of hunger appetite second; we went back to the JCC billet and played bridge.

MAR 25

        I had set aside this evening to study, but the library was closed so I went to the Service Club and read some magazines, and watched some dancing. Typical dissipated evening.

MAR 26

        After work, I went to PX street (at least that is the name the G.I’s have given it) and checked in two sport shops for tennis rackets. I have decided to play tennis this summer, and since the Athletic & Recreation shop at Hialeah has been closed down, I must obtain a tennis racket in some way, shape or form.

        The tennis rackets shown me were not bad; one was a J.C. Higgins (7000 hwan) and another was a Wilson (7000 hwan). They also had a Dunlop which they would string for 7000. (7000 = $14). I told them the prices were too high and that a friend of mine had gotten one for 6000 hwan the previous week. The price was then lowered to 6000. I didn’t have enough money on me, so I said I would be back, next time planning to stand at 5000 hwan. (I checked later, and the J.C. Higgins they were selling for $12.00 was $10.95 + mailing charges in the Sears catalog. However, the prices over here are governed by the black market, and since 4 cartons of cigarettes – costing $4 – will bring 6500 hwan, the racket can actually be gotten for around $4)

        The fellows that I was with, then looked in some of the other shops and ___s “holes”, pricing the merchandise. Actually, they don’t have too much over here, with the exception of some inlaid pearls, gold and bronze work and some dolls.

        As it began to get dark, we headed back to the RTO (Bus depot) – passing a Korean movie which had Quo Vadis – and took in the movie “The Detective.” It was quite good.

MAR 27 (SUNDAY - WEEK 14)

        Sunday doesn’t have any particular meaning or pleasure here in Korea, with the exception that there isn’t reveille and also generally we don’t have to work. (Next Sunday I have CQ though.) I had been lagging in my studies and I spent the morning reading about Principals and Agents, and miscellaneous aspects of Agency.

        About noon I met a friend – Manse Hall – and we decided to take a walk to Yong-Do in the afternoon. Yong-Do is an island in the harbor and is connected to the mainland by a bridge. It is a good size island, and consists of hills and a small mountain.

        We took a bus to the RTO (located near Pier #1) and walked to the island. We then proceeded to begin the ascent of the mountain, talking and resting as we went. There were hundreds of shacks on the side of the mountain (South side – not as much wind) and we peeked in them as we climbed around the dirt trail.

        The houses were constructed of anything and everything. It was not unusual to see wood, cement, stone and mud for the side construction and wood, tile, metal scrap and beer can (flatten out) roofs. The stench and filth was overwhelming, and this combined with the rats we saw, really made us sick.

        The houses were typical of the slum houses in Pusan, with their dirt floors, outside privies, scant protection against the elements, sewer gutters running along side the houses, and wooden chimneys.

        After a struggle we reached the lower summit, where we could see for miles around. The day had been cold and hazy so I had left my camera behind. Manse took a few pictures, and we then proceeded down the other side as it was very cold on top the mountain.

        The other side was devoted to rice fields, occasional houses and a cemetery. One interesting thing was the bamboo irrigation pipe we saw all along the hillside. They didn’t seem very sturdy, however, we couldn’t see any leaks anywhere. I imagine the water comes from springs out of the side of the hills and the mountain.

        We barely beat the rain, and spent a few minutes in the RTO Snack Bar, resting our feet and satisfying our hunger.

MAR 28

        Inventory was taken this morning at Branch 600 and the rest of the sub-branches. Consequently, the sub-branches closed their books and brought their final Cash and Sales and checks to me for compiling into a consolidated Cash & Sales Report. Checks flooded my desk, and I had to get help to post them on a certified check list. I also began posting figures to the Balance Sheet, making up the Concessionaire and Concessionaire Insurance reports, and listing the dishonored checks for the month. It was the busiest day I have had thus far, and I am glad it doesn’t occur every week or bi-monthly.

MAR 29

        Another busy day on the “books”. This certainly is the most time consuming portion of my job. If all the sub-branches would hand in their final Cash and Sales Report plus their Concession reports ON TIME it would aid considerably in my job.

        Last night I decided to go to the little stucco house about 75 feet from my barracks door – namely the Hialeah NCO club. They had the Poppy Show scheduled, and since it was supposed to be quite good, I thought I would spend the evening bending the old elbow. The band – all Korean – was very good, and the best I had heard in Korea. The Sax and trumpet players were excellent and really gave out with good old American jazz. Besides these two players they had a bass, drums, electric guitar, piano and accordion. They played loud and sweet, and concentrated on jazz, old favorites and novel arrangements.

        They had girl singers and dancers but I wasn’t too impressed. The singers sang too high and weak and didn’t capture the American manner. The dancers – if one can call them that – wore VERY little, but I think that was to distract from their poor dancing. About all they did was wiggle a little and move their arms. However, the band more than made up for the female specie, and a good time was had.

MAR 30

        Finally caught up with my monthly finalizing and now all I have to do is wait for the 3 sub-branches that have yet to turn in their Cash and Sales Reports. Up to now I had been posting and writing up the checks on the entitled check list. Around summer time, I made my first check to see if the receipts = the checks. To my horrorI found I was $5000+ off. I figured again and I got the same answer. Decided the best thing was go and eat and then come back for another try. This I did, and although my supper was spent trying to determine where I had made my mistake or mistakes.

        I gave it another go after supper and was pleased and relieved when it came out to the correct figure. My visions of Fort Leavenworth (prison) vanished and I settled back into my life of existing. Gosh, I am sure accountants like their work, but the torture of that final push on the calculator determining whether it balances or doesn’t, must be heart fatiguing.

        I finished my annotation of the Cashier Duties and collected san_ in a pamphlet. I presented them to it the Captain who was pleased of the work. Of course, his pleasure is appreciated, but I am interested in whether it does the trick in letting me be excused for leaves and R & Rs. Every chance I get, I throw out the hint and thought of how much I want to see the Orient, particularly Japan. The big moment comes at the end of next month when I put in for a leave. Time will tell.

MAR 31

        Had C.Q. last night, and was relieved by the absence of rats AT LEAST THOSE that had chosen to keep me company the last time I had C.Q. The Captain stayed at work to write some letters, and we had a pleasant conversation after he was finished. I think he is a very capable officer, and perhaps, one of the few company grade officers I respect.

        I got back my first batch of color slides from the developer; and had a pleasant time looking at them, and re-visiting the places I have visited and the sights I have seen. I plan to use the slides as a method of describing the people and the customs, to the Werner gang back home. Once I get back the other 3 rolls I have sent I will write a description of each, and send the whole works home.

I find I am still very much of an amateur as a photographer, as my lighting and arrangement aren’t very good. The light meter seems to help somewhat, but if the pictures do not start getting better, I will start keeping track of the exposure and lens opening I allow each picture.

        Today was payday, and I was sure glad it rolled around. I was on my last couple bucks, and rationing that which I had. Got paid $250.00, which should tie me over for awhile. I sure hate that $45 income tax bite. Someday – Someday, I will get something back from the Internal Revenue boys.

APR 01

        Was C.Q. in the company during the evening; – this evidently being my CQ week, and I have CQ lined up for Sunday at the Section. Oh well, it gives me an opportunity to read, write or catch up on things in general.

        I collected the 2,500,000 hwan from the bank, and it was no problem or task. (Me and my trusty 45 frighten off all banking stick-up men) The problems arose later on when I found out that I did not requisition enough hwan for the new Post Exchanges that we have taken over. However, since the boys from Taegu weren’t due until the next day, I dished out the money I had, and settled down to the other daily cashier tasks.

We got some new men to replace those that are to leave this spa of the Orient for the hustle and bustle of the “Hew Ess A” (Don’t I wish I were that unlucky). The Captain told me that he was contemplating getting a new cashier, and use me as a working boss of the Cashier cage and merchandise control. I was interested (and pleased) with his thoughts and plans, as it would relieve me of definite duties and allow me to go on leave and R & R. (I guess when I re-read this diary it will seem as if all I think about is R & R and leave. Frankly, that is exactly what my main thoughts consist of, since I believe one can “make his own bed” in the Army.)

Route as of April 1st, 1955 – end of Chapter 4.

CHAPTER 5 - GLIDING BY

April 2nd, 1955 - May 6th, 1955

APR 02

        The Taegu boys (town about 100 miles N. of Pusan) came for their Hwan, and of course “we had a no”. I talked it over with the Captain, and it was decided to phone Seoul for a supplementary check and to send someone for the check. I wanted to go, but at first the Captain planned to send someone else as he didn’t think TDY orders could be cut for me in time. However, the clerk called A.6. and found out that I could get some orders that afternoon, so I got ready for my trip since coming to Korea.

        My orders allowed me to travel on the U.S. Army run train that ran from Pusan to Seoul. The train is a collection of old hospital cars – which serve as sleepers – and make the trip in about 11 hours (8:00 PM – 7:00 AM). Being able to speak most of the trip saves sightseeing time and also makes the trip go a lot quicker.

        After a quick shave on Sunday morning, I left the train and headed for the JCE billet where I was to meet the man with the check.

APR 03 (SUNDAY - WEEK 15)                 Seoul

        I had been told that the billets weren’t far from the RTO, so I headed in the direction of the Old Capitol and the billets.  The streets in Seoul are a lot wider and cleaner than those in Pusan, and one could see a lot more autos. The Old Capitol building (built by the Japanese) was located at the end of the main street, and is typical of the architecture one finds in many of our state capitol buildings. This building, though, was fire gutted and was not in any condition to hold legislative meetings (since the Korean War), consequently the meetings were moved to S. Rhee’s home. His house was situated too far to walk and so I decided to visit it at a later time.

        I walked to the left of the Capitol area, amid old, rotten homes, to get to a stretch of higher ground where I could overlook the city. The city of Seoul is the largest in Korea (1,500,000) and is a crowded metropolis hemmed in by huge barren mountains. The houses are built almost on top of one another, with dirt pathways or winding alleys serving as the only means to move to and fro. Actually I got lost in the maze of the alleys and spent some anxious moments winding my way in and about the homes. I wasn’t afraid of being ganged up on, but I prefer a wide street to walk upon and from which I can keep from getting close to the Korean pick pockets. I always button up my camera and light meter, and keep my wallet in a front pocket when walking about.

        After getting out of the maze, I headed for the Duk Soo Palace which was located on the main street, near the City Hall (huge white building). The buildings were originally built around 1500, and were used as mansions for princes and kings. The buildings were ruined in 1919, and rebuilt in 1938. The grounds were beautifully maintained, and it seemed that the area served as a park for the people of Seoul. Most of the buildings were designed along the typical Buddhist building – or general style of early Korean culture – which I had seen on my other trips. They also had one TWO modern buildings ONE OF which served as the National Museum of Korea.

        I then proceeded down the street past the City Hall and in the vicinity of the American Embassy. The latter building was closed, so I went across the street to the Bando Hotel – a very modern and elegant hotel. It was built to attract American greenbacks, consequently, MPC and Hwan was not permitted. I did, however, walk around the lobby, and gazed at the decorations, which consisted of both Korean and modern design. The furniture, design and lamps were mostly modern, but they had Korean pictures and paintings. It was really a lavish hotel.

        I had lunch at a Korean restaurant (850 hwan) and was indeed satisfied. The meal consisted of soup, shrimp, steak, vegetables, potatoes, rolls, ice cream and coffee. Actually it was too much, but I didn’t know what I was getting.

        After lunch I journeyed to the Thousand Steps, which was the name given to a large number of steps leading up to a Christian revival meeting. The meeting was in the Billy Graham fashion, and the charmer had about 10,000 kneeling and squatting Koreans singing and listening. It seems that the swing is toward Christianity over here, perhaps as a result of S. Rhee being a Christian. The cross on the hill consisted of two white beams, so simple that it seemed to have inherent radiance.

        I then went through the market area, to the area around the old PX. Here were many shops and fresh carts, plus one or two department stores. I ended up at the Kyong Bok palace near JCC and the old Capitol. Spent some time in the grounds, and was impressed by one huge building - KUN JUNG PALACE - which served as the throne Hall. In this area, during the reign of Sei Jong, the Korean alphabet was invented in 1443.

        It was getting late, so I ate, got a lift via JCC to the train station, and caught the 8:00 sleeper for home – Pusan if you please.

APR 04

        Today I passed the time at work catching up on the April Cash and Sales report which I had neglected while working on last months summary. It wasn’t much, so I had WAS caught up by the end of the day. At last more leisure stares me in the face.

APR 05

        A day a leisure, which I thoroughly enjoyed. I did catch up on my life work, and also spent some time looking at some pictures I got back from Kodak.

APR 06

        Heard the good news that W. Hill from the warehouse was to take my place as Cashier, thus relieving me for merchandise control work. There is already one man in merchandise control, consequently my duties will be to supervise and assist. As of now I have no definite duties, and THIS will make my position more chances for leave more likely. Of course, time and the Captain will tell!

        On the way to the RTO and to catch a bus, I saw 3 boys picking on and beating up an old man. They pushed him around, pulled his leg, and prevented him from getting to his destination. This wasn’t a new or unusual sight, as the Korean people seem to fight and push people at any provocation. Many times while walking down the street, I see little boys and girls, fighting, pushing, damaging merchandise etc. In fact once while walking on P.X. Street, I saw 2 small girls fighting with all their might, pulling hair and requiring 3 or four grown men to separate them. While one sees such fights in the U.S., the ferocity and frequency of the fights makes me feel that these people are somewhat barbaric, similar to our American Indians.

APR 07                         First Day of Passover

        Spent part of the day working with the new cashier, orientating the major phases of the Cashier job, and also checked over the daily receipts. The new Cashier is a hard headed (though likeable) chap from the poorer sections of New York City. His mouth is foul and he carries a stick on his shoulder, but oddly enough he is capable, and if he applies himself, he can do a good job.

        I left somewhat early, and played a little tennis with Manse. It was very windy and consequently most of the time was spent chasing the balls. The racket looks as if it will be all right.

        At the top of the page, I notice today is the first day of Passover. While I could go to a Sedar, somehow I have no desire to make the effort. It is funny but I am not the least bit more religious over here, perhaps if anything, any outward form of religion has seemed to HAVE left me. I still believe in mono-theism, and also feel that one should adopt a religion to ones self, and not ones self to a religion. Maybe I am still rationalizing, but I am not impressed with Judaism, nor any religion I know today. I criticize myself for making such a statement with what I know about the other religions, and yet I am not ignorant of their basic beliefs, and the knowledge of the same leaves me cold. It seems the thing for me to do is keep on learning and experimenting with religions until I become satisfied that the one I found is the nearest thing to the right religion for me.

APR 08

        Milt Raby – JCC Employee – left today to return to Japan. I was sorry to see him leave as he was a very friendly chap with a good head on his shoulders, and with a fascinating background. He gave me his address, and I will look him up in Kamakura when I get to Japan.

        It is interesting to take a night bus to the RTO, and drive through the streets of Pusan. The power situation in Pusan is bad, and most of the houses do not have electric lights. They use kerosene lamps and candles to provide the limited light they use. (Frankly I can’t see how anyone can study or read by such a light, but I guess I am spoiled)

        The bus progresses with its headlights providing the guiding light. Off hand I can’t remember seeing any street lights. Most of the push cart and other marketplace occupants continue their business by candle light. They stick one solitary candle on their cart, and sell their goods with the aid of the flickering flame. Windy nights play havoc with the trade.

        Most of the G.I installations have their own generators to provide electricity when the S. Rhee power stations become hairy

APR 09

        Worked with Hill in the Cashier’s cage, consolidating the Cash and Sales Reports and getting the Payroll sheet and reports lined up. We turned in our excess hwan to the Depot, and in general, cleaned out the safe of miscellaneous junk.

        Had an interesting discussion with a girl concerning Korea, the U.S. and her life history. Frankly, she is a whore – please do not jump to conclusions – but has a remarkable (I should say figure) grasp of the English language. Consequently, one is able to converse with her as they would with another G.I.

        She told of the early days of the Korean War, and how her family was separated. She had the opportunity to ride a truck to Pusan, and was thus able to keep ahead of the Communists. She arrived in Pusan – about 16 or 17 years of age – and managed to live off the money and few valuables she brought with her. After awhile, she ran out of money and took a job as house girl in some officers BOQ.

        One thing led to another and she soon became the mistress of the company commander. When he left she continued her trade and has been liveing with G.I’s ever since. She said that she has been proposed to 3 times, but has turned them all down. One of the 3 even went so far as to get the necessary papers needed to bring her to the states. Which of them changed their minds, I do not know, but she is still in Pusan.

        The girl said, what I had heard, that she was afraid to go back to Seoul for fear of what her family will do to her. She says that she keeps in contact with them indirectly, and is concerned about her father; her mother having passed away.

        Her knowledge about the Korean War, Truman, Eisenhower, McArthur and S. Rhee were was excellent, surpassing many G.I’s in this field. She feels that the Communists will return once the U.N troops leave, and consequently she thinks it foolish for us to pull out our troops (I wonder how much money influences her opinions!)

        It was a pleasure conversing in a normal manner with a Korean, and I enjoyed our talk very much. I was even more interested as I don’t know when such an opportunity will present itself again.

APR 10 (SUNDAY - WEEK 16)

        I was CQ at the Section today, and spent most of the day working with Call on Merchandise Control. The work consists of posting the invoice figures in the order book, and then sub-dividing the merchandise to the 13 sub-branches. The work is awful boring, but yet seems necessary. I hope to be able to give a fresh view to the set-up, but since the whole system changes next month, I am afraid innovations will be frowned on.

APR 11

        The new cashier was able to take over the cage on his own today, and I was thus able to spend more time with Merchandise Control. I am going to have a problem there as Call, an excellent worker, but sort of resents my being assigned to help him out. Actually I hope to let him do most of the work – with my assisting during the busy periods.

        Call is somewhat of an interesting human speciman. He is about 21, from Maine, of wealthy parents, slender, average looking and is Jewish. He is a hard worker, as I mentioned earlier, and has an remarkable grasp of the English language. He is sensitive, somewhat effeminate and likes to boss people, if at all possible.

        He is quite generous, and gives about 3000 hwan a week to a Korean boy by the nean name of Whang. The boy use to be his houseboy (for the barracks) and Call took a liking to him. By his giving him money, he has given the boy the opportunity to go to school, and to live a little higher than the bare minimum. I sometimes think the boy takes advantage of Call, but on the other hand he seems to be quite pleasant and honest. The relationship is interesting and I rather like to think of it being through Call’s generosity, rather than his being interested in exercising authority over some person.

APR 12

        The weather was beautiful and so I decided to take the afternoon off. (I was entitled to it since I was CQ Sunday) I called Manse Hall and we decided to play tennis at 3:00. Took care of some odd jobs at the 8131st and then adjourned to the tennis courts. Played for about 3 hours, and although I lost both sets, I thoroughly enjoyed the exercise, sunshine and company.

        The tennis courts are of concrete, and in good condition. Two of the courts have lights, which permits night tennis. The courts weren’t too crowded in the afternoon, but after supper a flood of G.I’s and officers merged on the tennis courts and the surrounding area.

        My racket seems to be O.K, my next job, though, is to get ahold of some tennis balls. The P.X. w is supposed to get some in shortly, and thus I will be able to get a hold of a can or two. Once WHEN my package comes from good old Missouri I will be set in the tennis shoes department. Once these incidentals are taken care of, my excuses will be gone, and I will have nothing to blame my poor game on except myself. Speaking of poor tennis, my backhand is atrocious. I don’t think I made a point off it all afternoon. My service was fair and my volley poor, so I can see I have my work cut of out for me.

APR 13

        Coming home from work I ran across an interesting incident. As I was walking near the RTO, I heard a voice, and turned to see what the commotion was about. I saw a Korean boy chasing a G.I., and yelling at him about some money that was due him. When the Korean got to the G.I., the G.I. began hitting him with all his might, while the boy was tugging and grabbing at the GI’s camera and clothing. The GI. (a young fellow about 20-21 years old) meanwhile broke away and walked rapidly toward the Service Club. Two other Koreans converged on the G.I., one of whom grabbed a rock and made motions that he was going to throw it.

        It was at this moment that I hurriedly decided to enter, and ran up to the fracas and separated the group. The G.I. said the boys were trying to “slicky” (steal) his camera. The Koreans said the G.I. had cheated them. They then proceeded to show me a carton of cigarettes the G.I had sold them. Inside the carefully prepared box was a bunch of old rope instead of packs of cigarettes. I then realized that the soldier had tried to cheat the Koreans, so I quickly pulled myself together and left the area. I told the G.I. to give them back their money, but he was adamant in refusing.

        It is a shame that there are GI’s who do this sort of thing, as it reflects on all Americans. Frankly, there are many occasions when I wished something similar to this on the brats, but when it happened, I guess my sadistic tendencies left me. Anyway, I boarded my bus for Hialeah and left work. RTO and another day in Korea, many miles behind.

APR 14

        It was a hectic day at work. We had scheduled the Taegu PX to draw today, and for their goods to be placed in 2 box cars and then shipped to Taegu. Everything was thrown into a dither when we didn’t get the cars until 4:00 PM. Consequently, we did little during the day as Taegu was supposed to draw and of course couldn’t. It didn’t make too much difference to me, as I have decided that I may eventually get an ulcer, but it won’t be caused by Branch 600.

        It looks as if my job will be more of a liaison butt boy between the warehouse and the front office. I think I will like the job, as it appears there will be challenging moments when things (such as the above) go haywire and last minute decisions must be made.

        I gave me request for A leave to the Captain and after a few stuttering explanation minutes on my part; plus another few minutes of silence, it he said he would O.K. it. Thus, it looks as if I will be able to take a 15 day leave in Japan starting 9 May – provided my money holds out.

        I think that one of the most nauseating sights one can see is a drunk woman. While I generally laugh at a drunk man, somehow it seems far more degrading to see a drunk woman. (double standard again?) One of the few Korean girls I know (Diana is her name) got completely pie-eyed, and it was sure a pitiful and sickening sight. I don’t think I will ever be convinced that drinking is a way to loose ones sorrow or to have a good time.

APR 15

        At work we are in the midst of a PX issue, and owing to the Taegu difficulties, plus some new men, we are running behind our schedules. Fortunately, we had an open date Monday, before we draw from Depot, and some of the postponed PX’s can be serviced at that time.

        I spent the majority of the day digging up some information concerning some dishonored checks; and assisting in a supplementary draw of souvenirs at Depot. Some of the souvenirs will be reduced in price and I will have to take a closer look at some. Most of the stuff is cheap Japanese stuff. We refused to accept any Korean dolls and trinkets as their stuff is pure junk. I even understand some of the Korean stuff isn’t allowed in the U.S for health reasons.

        In the accounting office – adjacent to the main office – there are two Koreans who can speak good English and who can teach me much about the Korean people. I hesitate to expand the relationship outside of work as the boy is a little superficial, and I am afraid I would give the girl a bad reputation. The Igno ignorant and uneducated Koreans give their own people (girls) a hard time when they are seen with a G.I. Whether it is merely a friendly relationship or that of a mistress (“maore”) they shout words of “GI whore”, slut etc. The Japanese on the other hand accept the relationship in a much more understanding light.

APR 16

        It was a quiet day of work – for a change, and I thought I would leave in the afternoon and go to training. Well, if nothing else, I would leave in the afternoon and say I went to training. This I did, and went to P.X. street to check on some stamps. The owner of the shop wasn’t in, and the boy in the shop told me to come back. I then proceeded down the street and amidst looking in the windows, I managed to buy a Time magazine for 120 Hwan and a harp (hand made) for 40 hwan.

        It began raining so I headed back to Hialeah where I turned in the 4 additional copies of my request for leave. On my way to the library I saw an officer batting a tennis ball around, so I inquired if he would like to volley awhile. He said yes, so I checked out a racket (it was drizzling and I didn’t want to get mine wet) and played for about one-half hour. It then began raining harder, so I adjourned to the library where I finished the Red and the Black by Stendhal. It was a pretty good book, but not one of the best I have ever read. I still think Crime and Punishment is the best book I have ever read.

APR 17 (SUNDAY - WEEK 17)

        It rained throughout the day, dampening any plans I had for going out in the country and taking pictures. However, since I had requisitioned a jeep, another fellow and I rode out to K-9 (to enquire about getting a flight to Japan) and to the U.N. cemetery. The cemetery is located on a hillside overlooking a valley of rice fields. The grounds are well kept, and much of the rock is whitewashed for cleanliness and looks.

        There are 21 flag poles for the 21 nations that assisted in the Korean War plus the U.N. flagpole. The graves are flat, and have at their head, a simple cross, star of David or Turkish crescent and star. These markings are white and have a nameplate and/or the dog tag of the fallen soldier. There were no U.S. soldiers buried here any more, all of the dead having been taken back to the States. There are a lot of Turkish soldiers buried here, and from what I understand, they will remain in Korea. I will return at a later date in the summer and take some photographs of the graves. An interesting note is that photos of individual graves are forbidden since some unscrupulous persons took pictures of the graves and then sold them at high price to relatives of the dead. (What people will do for a buck.)

        In the afternoon I made a stab at playing duplicate bridge. My partner and I didn’t come out so well as we ended up last, however, it was a lot of fun. One participant in the match happened to be none other than a chap by the name of Rosen who is one of the top 3 or 4 players in the U.S. At the age of 25, this wizard is already a life master and has played in many international tournaments. I was sorry that I wasn’t able to play against him as we both were South players. Maybe next time I will be fortunate or unfortunate – which ever way you look at it – to play against this meek looking soldier. Incidentally if nothing else, I have rank on this private.

        Went to see the movie Country Girl in the evening, and thoroughly enjoyed it. The main characters – gorgeous Grace Kelly, Bing Crosby and Bill Holden all did a top notch job.

APR 18

        Another typical day in Korea. Did a little work at the Section, but not much. What work I did, consisted of writing up a summary of Do’s and Don’ts on cashing checks at the sub-branches, and then talking about same to a meeting of representatives of all the sub-branches. Nothing spectacular, but a little different and perhaps a little bit of a challenge. Responsibility (other than C.S. Army crap) and challenging work has been few and far between in the Army.

APR 19

        Signed up for a class in Spoken Korean, and attended the first class at 6:30. The class consists of both officers and enlisted men, including one full bird colonel. We have a Korean instructor who pronounces the words, which are then repeated by the people in the room. The words and pronunciations sounded like Greek to me, but I imagine in time, I will catch on.

        One problem stares me in the face and that is my leave which starts in about 3 weeks. Thus it breaks in at the middle of the course, and would set me behind. Consequently, I have given thought to taking Japanese instead of Korean. First of all, it will help me in Japan, and secondly, since most Koreans speak Japanese, it will provide a crude means of communication with them. Anyway, Korean seems such a waste of time to me, as I can never imagine coming back to this land once I leave next year.

APR 20

        Got some more film back from Kodak, and I spent a couple hours looking at the slides, and writing a couple sentences about each. In this manner, I will be able to send the sides home so the folks back home can get an idea of Korea, and also I will be able to make appropriate title on these transparencies when I get home. The last bunch were the best that I have taken in Korea, and I hope it is an indication that my picture taking ability is improving.

        An interesting and amusing sight on the way to work each day is the little school boys directing traffic at the school crossings. The boys are about 10-12 years old, and they stand in the middle of the streets (with arm bands and sometimes old U.S. Army helmet liners) and motioning the traffic with dramatic arm signals. On the side of the streets, there are assistants who have colored flaps which are used to guide the driver.

        Actually I haven’t seen any of our buses stop yet, but perhaps these “cops” think they are too big to deal with. The boys remind me of our schoolboy patrol back home, with the John Brown belts, but we had nothing to compare to the color and flare of these boys. Now and then one daring kid will get a whistle and use it to assist him in his directing of the cars and buses.

APR 21

        Was supposed to get my Spring round of shots, but it was postponed for a few days. Since it was such a nice day, I called Manse and arranged for a little tennis. My game seemed a little better, but was still poor in the backhand. Manse developed a blister on his foot, and we stopped around 5:00, and adjourned to the mess hall.

        One interesting fact of Korean society is the great emphasis they place on the girl being a virgin before marriage. Mr. Kim in the other office said that if he married a girl, and found out that she was not a virgin – ”cherry girl as they call her”, that it would be legal grounds of divorce.

        The girls wear their hair in pigtails when they are still virgins, and cut it short when otherwise. It all seems to be ridiculous to me, but on the other hand, I imagine there are many American customs – such as women’s dress – that seems strange to them.

        One thing for sure, and that is that the Koreans don’t seem to believe in birth control. I think every other girl I see, has a small baby strapped to her back. They carry these babies until they are able to walk, and they seem to breast feed them up until that time also. One reason the Korean people have bow legged legs is that they are carried for such a long time on their mother’s back, and with their legs wrapped around their mother’s waists.

APR 22

        Attended my first class in Spoken Japanese, and I found it to be a little easier and more interesting than Korean. I also feel that I will get more out of the course, particularly when I am planning to go to Japan in 2 weeks (fingers crossed). The teacher is a Japanese woman who works as a DAC (Dept. of the Army Civilian) and who is competent in what she teaches; however she caters too much to the officers. An example of the latter is the fact that the officers voted, almost in mass, to cut the class from 2 ½ to 2 hours. The enlisted personnel, plus the Chaplain and one or two officers voted otherwise. The teacher, who probably is one of the officer’s mistress, went right along with the irregular action.

        My opinion of career soldiers, both EM and officers, has gone down considerably since I have been on active duty. I have met few really capable officers, most of them are average, or below, men that have found a home and security in the Army. This is especially for R.A. Sgts., who I think are almost all dumb guys that have found security and in most cases, easy, lush jobs in the Army. This might not be true for infantry men as I haven’t run across many of them, but it is sure true of specialists. I can count on one hand, the number of Sgts that I have come across in the Army whom I respect. This either means my basis for comparison is too high, or the men in the Army aren’t too good.

APR 23

        Today was more or less a typical day in Korea. Piddled around at work, doing odd jobs, reading a little and generally typing to occupy myself so that I wouldn’t get bored.

        I had planned to play tennis in the afternoon but it rained, consequently I spent the afternoon at work.

        I noticed on my way to work that the U.S. rented Korean bus that we use, had an new addition to its colorful simplicity. The driver had put up a small holder with a picture of the bus on it. Even in the states I hadn’t seen such pride in one’s equipment.

        The buses are very colorful, with many bright colors and even some fancy designs on the front. One of the buses even had curtains on the windows. The buses are built high off the ground and one has to take a high step to reach the first step. At the same instant one enters the bus, he must bend, as the doorway is not very tall high.

        The seats are placed along the side, and are very uncomfortable. They have a l__s railing along the windows which hits the rider in the middle of the back. Featherbedding is present even in Korea, for besides the driver they have 2 young Koreans opening and closing the doors. Of course, the U.S. – land of money – pays the bill gladly!

APR 24 (SUNDAY - WEEK 18)

        Today is the second Sunday after Easter and also the second Sunday after Easter that it has rained all day long.

        I spent the morning reading magazines, and looking at various books in the library. I proceeded to the Service Club in the afternoon and readied myself mentally (!) to an afternoon of duplicate bridge. I guess I didn’t do such a good job as I led my partner and I to a blazing last place. I topped this off with a pa__ of an opening 2 _id by my partner and to say the least he was perturbed.

        This fellow, William Rosen (who I found out later was the number 1 player in the U.S in 1954) was again present for the session, and I had the pleasure of playing 4 hands against him. The most I could say of the encounter was that we set them 1 trick on a 4 club bid. Otherwise he played so fast and bid (along with his partner) in such an illogical but brilliant manner, that yours truly was snowed. I enjoyed the experience, though, and hope to do it again. Perhaps next time I will watch him play all afternoon, and hope THAT I can gain something to improve my game.

APR 25

        Had some good discussions today with some of the other personnel in the office. The main jist of the talks was the status of things at Branch 600. The old timers all said things had been a lot better in the past. The newcomers defended present conditions with a cry as to the changing conditions and the phasing out program. I Didn’t say much at first, but ended up stating my philosophy on existing these two years in the Army. Basically I guess it can be summarized thusly: (1) I will do my best in my job, but do not have the initiative to extend my job (2) Nothing in the Army will worry me or get me down, particularly Army channel snafu (3) Make the most of my duty hour time and my off-duty time, and (4) Will not buck stupid officers or rulings, but instead of accepting as such, will try to avoid as much as possible.

        I truly believe I don’t worry much about the Army, and somewhat enjoy the free time to catch up on my reading and studying. I must admit that I don’t have the average soldier’s about worry about rank and money, nor the feeling of being away from my “girl”.

        I feel sorry for one of the fellows I know quite well here in Pusan. The other day he received a Dear John letter from his fiancée. It is a shame since he is a nice, upstanding guy, and she seemed to be quite understanding and faithful. Guess not!

APR 26

        Finally got my package from home – 7 weeks in route. It was good to see civilian clothes again, and I am looking forward to wearing them while on leave. Beside the clothes, I received my tennis shoes, sun glasses, American Government Book, sweat shirt and a tooth brush. It looks as if I am ready for a long stay in Frozen Chosin.

        Visited or I guess the word is attended, my second class in Japanese. They still didn’t have any books for some of the new men, and so I looked on with a Master Sgt. He knew some Japanese already, and helped ME pronounce some of the difficult words. The class is getting to be a social evening for the officers, as the class gets shorter and the breaks longer. I guess I will have to buy 2 Eagles to pin on my shoulders for attention.

        Never saw so many “mooses” (G.I. nickname for the Korean whores) at the club as I saw last night. Things must be getting a little rough for them as the troops move out. (Maybe even the price will come down). The Korean economy will receive a jolt when the American Army leaves. There are a great number of indigenous personnel working for the U.S.A, and one sees in the line in front of the labor office getting larger by the week.

APR 27

        Put in one of my busier days at the section. The auditor was here, and the Cashier needed help in reconciling the cash and refund vouchers. I also had to help in the tabulation of the inventory sheets. A system was set up for the girls to follow, but so many of the guys had “helpful” ideas of their own that it ended up in chaos. Finally at the end of the day, it looked as if we were once again getting the better of the sheets.

        I had signed up to play in a tennis tournament, and this afternoon I was scheduled to play my first match. My opponent had been telling me how good he was in college, and although his game was off, he thought he could handle me. I thought so tod too, until we began playing. His serve was easy and I was able to place the ball where I wanted. Thus it was with ease that I took the first set 6-3.

        In typical Charles Werner fashion, I thought I had it wrapped up; – that is until he beat me 6-3 in the second set. We then began the 3rd set (played more continuous tennis than ever before) and it was a see-saw affair. 2-2, 2-3, 4-3, 5-4, 5-5, 6-5, 6-6, 6-7, 7-7, 8-7 and finally 9-7. It had gotten very dark, and although we had the lights on, we had a difficult time seeing. He made a few mistakes in the last game, & so I was pushed into being the winner. My feet and hands didn’t appreciate the games, but I thoroughly enjoyed the exercise.

APR 28

        In the morning I heard that Syngman Rhee was to visit Pusan around noon to dedicate 5 fishing boats that UKNRA was giving South Korea. Took my camera and went to Port Road to await his passing. The streets were lined on both sides by school girls and boys, dressed in thin blue-type uniforms.

        Around noon we heard a whistle and from the north, coming down Port Road, was President Rhee and his party. As the automobile caravan drew near, the school kids began waving their arms and doing a half bow. S. Rhee was on the inside of a black car, and he waved and smiled to those who had come to see him. As the car passed, the people clapped approval. I took a hurried picture, but I am afraid he won’t come out.

        It was interesting, the preparations that were made for this ____ visit. Hundreds of policemen were in the crowd, all with loaded carbines and/or loaded 45 cal. For the first time I saw mounted policemen, on the biggest horses I have seen in Korea. One of the biggest farces was the throwing of water on the street to settle the dust. One would think the Lord himself was paying a visit.

APR 29

        On the way to work I saw a sight which I hope I never see repeated in an U.S. Army camp. Inside the OLD British compound (now occupied by the ROK Army) a Korean soldier – probably an officer – was beating unmercifully a Korean soldier. He was hitting the young boy with all his might in the face and head. Finally, he grabbed an end of the soldier’s carbine and began hitting him with that. The boy put up no defense, except that he was reluctant to go with the officer inside a hut when the later demanded it. The brutality of the fighting over here is without equal anywhere I have traveled.

        The rest of the day consisted of typical Friday, or for that matter, anyday events. Did a little work, played some tennis, and attended my Japanese class.

        I went to the NCO club around 9:15 and found out to my sorrow that it was free night. By the time I had arrived all the drinks, except cognac (bad stuff) was gone, including the food. It was quite apparent that it was free night, as there were a lot of high spirits and drunk soldiers. I guess I had better inquire about such nights at the ends of the subsequent months.

APR 30

        Most of the enlisted men at Branch 600 were reassigned from 7th TPC to KComZ; at least until KComZ phases out. As of the present I haven’t been advised to move my billet, and frankly I hope I do not have to. Constant changing is one of the worst parts of the Army. However, until the situation over here becomes settled, it looks like moving will be a common occurrence.

        Took off part of the afternoon and visited a stamp shop located on PX street. I was unable to bargain him down, so I had to settle for his prices. Bought 4000 hwan worth of Korean, Japanese, and Chinese stamps. Had 6 identical packages made of the Japanese stamps for myself, Morton, Alan B, Peter B, Carol B, and Trip S.  I will try and get them some more colorful stamps when I hit Japan. His “pretty” stamps were too high.

        Speaking of my leave, I was disappointed that they left Hong Kong off my leave papers; and unless I can get them changed, I guess I will spend the 2 weeks in Japan. Really doesn’t matter, although I had decided to try and go to Hong Kong. Getting free hops is the major problem, and since one can’t pre plan free trips to Hong Kong, I thought I would try and go there each leave and R & R I took to Japan.

MAY 01 (SUNDAY - WEEK 19)

        The sun was beaming during the morning and part of the afternoon and sports activity at Hialeah was at a seasonal high. I played about 3 hours of tennis in the morning, included in which was my second tournament match. The match was somewhat even at least in the final 2 sets, as we split 6-2, 2-6 before he rallied and went on to take the 3rd set 6-2. He was a better all around player than I, and played towards my weak backhand. I surely have to try and do something about my backhand as I find myself running over to hit the backhand shot with my forehand.

        Went to the duplicate bridge late in the afternoon and watched Rosen and his partner play. I don’t think I learned anything as Rosen seemed to play by card sense as against any strict system. For instance he bid 1 NT, one hand with only 13 b___r points, and made the contract. His partner was very good, also, and together they make a formidable pair. I had to laugh once when his partner accidentally threw away a contract. I thought Rosen was going to bite his head off. To say the least, his partner felt a little bit bad about it.

MAY 02

        Checked with the Airport concerning flights to Japan, and found out that there are fewer this month than in April. Checked at the Orderly Room and Personnel, and arranged to have Hong Kong added to my orders.

        I then went to see Mr. Cain, CWO in Personnel. The irony of the situation is that he was the CWO at Fort Leonard Wood who put me on the levy. About 2 weeks ago I saw him and he asked me what I was doing. When I told him that I worked for the Post Exchange, he advised me to stop by and see him concerning requesting assignment in my MOS. Consequently, I talked with him in the afternoon and he composed a letter for me to send through channels.

        At the present I am a little reluctant to do it as I might be getting myself into a more chicken s_ _ _ outfit. However, the more I think about it, the more I feel that the chance is worth a gamble. The best I could get would be Japan. The worst would be the front lines, however a compromise is more likely. Anyway, I shall give it a lot more thought before I act.

MAY 03

        We got some new men at the section, and it now seems that we have too many for the amount of business that we do. Oh well. I guess I will continue to glide by as before. In one way, my initiative is being stymied, but if I can use the time for constructive purposes, it won’t be a total loss. However, since I have left the solitude of the cage, it is getting more and more difficult to read and concentrate.

        I got a letter from Je__ Lumsden, and it was quite informative about the goings on at Dow. I reconciled it with the one from Rheinecker and together they gave me a look from 2 sides. Production is up, but they still are low in initial efficiency in the Mill. Since the major part of the program is in the mill, they will have to improve in order to begin to realize a profit.

        It is interesting to observe the change in personnel at the plant. Of the three men who originated the program – Haney, Watters and McNulty; Haney is now gone and both Watters and McNulty have been demoted. All of them were good technical men, but their personality had something lacking. I guess I was sorriest to see old Haney go. He had some dynamic ideas and I believed I learned something from him. From all of them I learned that personality and getting along with people are an important facet of any job and task.

MAY 04

        Got a ride out to K-9, the airport near Pusan, and talked with a marine corporal about getting a ride to Japan on Saturday, plus a hop on Sunday to Hong Kong. I then went to Hialeah where I handed in my request for assignment in my MOS. I sure hope my gamble works out, but frankly I have NOT raised my hopes. Perhaps when I come back from my leave I will have received an answer.

        Some Korean troops took over the British compound adjacent to Branch 600, and they provide an interesting subject for observation. I notice where the men sleep on the floor, although there are some that have cots. They have a few women in the Korean Army, and this compound has about 10-15. They sleep in a little hut separate from the men, and don’t seem to mind the uncomfort of Army life. Frankly, my opinion of what they do in the Army is not the highest, yet I do not know for sure.

        The worst part of the set-up is the smell that floats over the barbed wire into our section. Sometimes the smell is like garbage, and perhaps that would be an adequate name for the food. Rice is their main food, but they tend to make some real concoctions with greens, onions and fish. I am afraid it would take me some time to get use to the Oriental diet.

MAY 05

        Checked with the Captain and he said he would let me off duty on Saturday so that I could catch the morning plane. Soooo if things don’t foul up, I will leave Saturday. My orders say “o/a May 9th” which means on or about May 9th, so I assume I can legally leave a little early.

        Went out to Finance to get a partial pay, and was told I needed a slip from the personnel section, and besides I couldn’t get it until after the 7th of the month. I thanked the trooper and turned to leave. A friend of mind noticed me leaving, and came up to me and asked if there was anything I wanted. I told him the story and he said wait a moment. In about 3 minutes I had my $50, and with a minimum of questions asked. It is the same old story, “Its not what you know but who you know.”

MAY 06

        The last day of work before I go on my leave. Worked with Hill and the Cashier’s duties to get most things wound up before I depart. He had lost 2 Bank deposit slips, so we had to send in the final cash and sales not knowing whether we were $5 over or $10,000 short. Oh well, time will tell.

        Just my luck to get a case of the GI Shits. Nothing particularly wrong, just the runs which would prove a nuisance on the trip. Went to the dispensary and got some white, bad tasting medicine which seemed to do the trick.

        Our unit was stood retreat, however since I work for a section which actually belongs to K Com Z, no one called the section to get me and of course I didn’t come forward. I saw a part of the marching and felt sorry for the boys in their O-G’s with the hot sun up ahead. From what I heard later, the parade was very bad, and it has the all earmarks of a lot of future practicing. But as for me – I shant be there.

        Did some last minute shopping, and turned in early.

Route as of May 6th, 1955 – end of Chapter 5.

CHAPTER 6 - LONG-AWAITED LEAVE

May 7th, 1955 - June 4th, 1955

MAY 07

        Stood reveille, signed out (as of 9 May), collected my gear together, put my bedding in my duffle bag and headed for the motor pool. Arranged a jeep ride out to K-9 airfield, and checked in at the Marine Liaison office around 8:30. The Marines were the ones WITH whom I had arranged my flight, as they have a bi-weekly flight from IWAKUNI, Japan to Hong Kong. As luck would have it, I was bumped from the plane as more marines turned up than there were seats scheduled. So I went to the Air Force and found out that they had 2 flights available. I couldn’t make the flight to Tokyo, so I arranged to go to Ashiya, located on the Southern island of Kyushu and not too far from Iwakuni.

        I spent the day at the library, and part of the evening too, since the flight was 4 hours late. (This killed my chances of getting to Iwakuni on time) While I was passing the time I happened to pick up Frank Bettger’s book, “How to Multiply your Happiness and Income in Selling.” I wasn’t able to finish it but the amount I read, I enjoyed very much. He sure has some dynamic thoughts on selling and the “science” that goes with it.

        I caught the flight out of K-9 at 11 PM, via a C-119 and landed in Ashiya around midnight. Found out that there was a flight to Okinawa on Mon. morning, so I signed up for it and went to my bunk for some long needed sleep.

MAY 08 (SUNDAY - WEEK 20)

        First Mothers Day I haven’t been home, but circumstances “tend” to prevent me from wishing Mom all the joy and happiness in the world. Distance can never silence that which emanates from the heart.

        Checked around for things to see near Ashiya and was told that Fukuoka (sometimes called Hakata – pop. 300,000) was located about 1 hour away by train. Caught the train, and arrived in Fukuoka around 11:00. Began to walk here and there, and also wandering through the large and small stores. The town is quite nice, with seemingly good streets and transportation, and with quite a few new, large modern buildings. The people seemed friendly, happy and a large percentage were dressed in Western style clothes. The department stores were modern, and had an innovation of children’s amusements on the roof. The day was dreary and rainy and I only took one or two pictures.

        I happened to come across a Japanese movie house which had a Japanese picture. I decided to invest 150¥ and went inside. The place was jammed tight, and still the usherettes forced in more people. I stood in the back and tried to follow the story and also see if I couldn’t make out a word or two that I had learned in my class. Sorry to say I had a rough time with both, but I did enjoy the afternoon.

        Ate at the Fukuoka Imperial hotel for dinner and had a fair meal. The most surprising thing happened when I asked the waiter in Japanese where the toilet was and she understood. Bengyo wa, doko ni arimasu ka?

MAY 09

        Up bright and early, and thence to the terminal. Boarded another C-119 for Kadena, and again labored as I had done the previous night, with my parachute and May West. They sure load one down with equipment, but since it is for my own benefit, I really couldn’t complain too much. They give everybody a 10-15 talk on how to operate the stuff, and I was ready and able (?) to jump.

        3 ½ hours later and without being able to prove or disprove my boast, the plane landed in warm Okinawa. Since I wouldn’t be allowed to leave the Airfield in Formosa, I decided not to go there, instead I would go to Clark where Field (P.I.) where I could catch my ride to Hong Kong.

        While waiting around the terminal for the flight to leave, I sat outside, writing this and observing the scenery. One thing I did observe was the multitude of jet planes coming and going – I bet 20-30 jets passed me as I waited. Looks like we are prepared for anything. At least I hope so.

        We flew from Kadena to Clark via a 4 engine C-54, and it was a good ride. Checked in around 5:30 PM and then I got my first blow. I was told that there were not any more flights to Hong Kong and that I would have to go by commercial airline. This was a jab at the old pocketbook to say the least.

        Stayed at the base that night, but did take a 3 hour jaunt to Angeles a small parasite town near Clark Field. Rode in a horse pulled hackney to one of the hundreds of night clubs where I had a few beers.

MAY 10

        Got up early, checked with the R.A.F., but still no luck in getting a hop. I missed the Air Force bus so I went to Manila via a Filipino bus. It was quite an experience, riding through the small towns and back routes on the way to Manila. At every stop boys and girls would climb on the bus and try to peddle their wares.

        The countryside looked dry, but I think the rains are coming slowly. Saw water buffalo in the field for the first time. Also saw a couple wallowing in a mud hole. Decided to make the Port of Manila Military Base my billet as I anticipate a shortage of money.

        After lunch I went (via jeep-taxi affair (5¢)] to the old walled city, in which, still standing, was is the St. Augustine church, oldest in the Philippines and built in 1599. From here I went to Taft Avenue, on which was WERE the Capitol Bldg., City Hall, Dept. of Finance and Agriculture, and one or two other government buildings. Attended briefly one of the sessions in the Senate chamber, but couldn’t understand their broken English.

        Caught a taxi down to the center of Manila where there are a lot of shops, movies, colleges and book stores. Manila seems to have quite a few places of higher learning. After taking in a movie to cool off, I went to Dewey Bldg whereupon I waited until the sun set over the bay.
