        Had a few drinks with a couple of Americans who lived in Manila, and I must say I wasn’t impressed. Had dinner at the ritz Hotel Manila. In an adjoining room the vice pres. was given a dinner for a rep. from Egypt.

MAY 11

        Today was a mixed up mess. Last night I had decided to go to Hong Kong and save the much needed $30 which I could get on a Cathay flight. I tried to call them when I got up, but no one answered. Since the plane didn’t leave till 12:30, I thought I had time to go out to Santo Thomas Univ. founded in 1611, and used as the allied civilian concentration camp by the Japanese during World War II.

        I hopped on one of the thousands of jeep-taxis and made it across town in pretty good time. I put in another call to Cathay, and then the fun started. I had to get 3 additional copies of my orders, get pesos and an authorization from the Finance Officer, – and all by 10:00. I dashed across the street, took 1 quick picture and caught another jeep-taxi. Back at Manila Military Port, I talked and waited, and answered questions, and thought the Filipenos would never finish the work; but finally I got the necessary stuff.

        Got the ticket, some greenbacks, talked a cabbie into taking me to the airport for only 63 pesos, and I was on my way. Filled out the papers, and boarded the plane at 1:30 PM. It took us about 3 ½ hours to get to Hong Kong, and I must admit I was glad to land. We hit some rough weather and some of the “others” gave up their recently acquired lunch. Frankly, I wasn’t feeling so good myself.

        Checked in at the International Hotel, and got my things unpacked. Had a Chinese dinner, and walked the streets, window shopping before turning in.

MAY 12

        I had hoped that the day would turn out nice, but was cloudy and misty all day. I caught the ferry for Hong Kong Island and went to Fenwick Pier to change some money and get some information. The exchange rate in Hong Kong fluctuates, today it was $5.85 HK = $1. From here I walked and rode to the Victoria Peak Tram which was an electric car going up to the top of Victoria mountain or hill.

        While waiting for the car I began talking to an English Soldier by the name of Ronald Dent of the Dorset Bn. We rode up the steep ride together, walked to the utmost peak, and as it turned out I spent the day and evening with him, that is until he left at 10:30 to eat go back to his ship in the harbor. I enjoyed his company very much and we discussed everything from politics to the Army to Chinese women with their skin tight dresses and slits up both sides. I really enjoyed being with him as I learned a lot about the English soldier and their thoughts.

        From Victoria Height (where there are huge apartment projects for English servicemen) we viewed the island and the peninsula town of Kowloon. We then rode back down, and walked through the streets observing the way the Chinese lived, worked and loafed. Saw one factory of about 8 machines and 10 women in a space 10’ x 10’. I am afraid our labor unions would object slightly. Visited the fabulous Tiger Balm Garden (which I shall describe later), the Cheero Club (British) and did much more walking. Revisited Victoria Heights at night, and even though there were some clouds obstructing the view, we could see the thousands of bright lights shining below.

MAY 13

        It was a beautiful day and so I decided to spend the day touring Hong Kong Island and taking pictures. I went first to Tiger Balm Garden, which appeared more fascinating than the previous day owing to the brilliant sunshine. The Garden, built by  millionaire philanthropist AW BOON HAW, is made up of hundreds of statues, carvings and colorful paintings. Most of the work explains some phase of Oriental history or legend. The Garden is for the Chinese inhabitants of Hong Kong as all the titles are in Chinese. Topping the whole area is a 156 ft. Pagoda, which I am sorry to say, was closed today.

        I next went by bus to Aberdeen, a large fishing village on the SW side of the island. Here were thousands of junks and sampans, with fishing being the main occupation. One interesting sight consisted of 3 school children walking to the waters edge and waiting for their mother to come get them via a row boat. Some of these people are born, live and die on these small boats, and I sure have to thank my stars that I am as fortunate as I am. One girl pleaded with me for about 10 minutes to take a sampan ride out to one of the famous floating restaurants. I kept on saying no, and adding that all I wanted was a girl. After I went out to the boat – via the sampan – and returned, she slapped herself on the hip, winked an eye and said “How much?” I laughed and she walked away.

        I next went by bus to Repulse Bay, where I had a great lunch for $8.50 HK (about $1.50 U.S). The beach looked good and I will have to returned later with my bathing suit. Before I returned back I also visited the small village of Stanley, and its Chinese inhabitants

MAY 14

        The Goddess of Weather seems to be on my side, for today turned out to be another glorious day. Consequently, I gathered my swimming gear together and headed for Repulse Bay. Repulse Bay is located on the other side of Hong Kong from Victoria, and is separated by a row of mountains. The view one obtains going over the mountains is breathtaking, and I only wish the bus didn’t jiggle as to make it impossible to take pictures.

        Besides the ritz hotel where I ate yesterday, there are also a smaller hotel on the beach and about 60 or 70 tents where one can change his clothes. My bathing suit was sort of short, but it was all I had, so it had to do. Swimming in salt water was a first time for me, and I really can’t say I enjoyed it any more or as much as fresh water. There were too many times when I opened my mouth when I definitely should have kept it closed. Most of the swimming consisted of going to and from floats set out in the bay and which were not too close to shore. Like a goof I used no suntan oil and I reddened fast. I had intended to leave earlier, but I met my airline stewardess and her boy friend and I talked with them until I got burnt. Some people will never learn

        Went to the local Chinese Opera (movie) at night, and I understood it as much as I do the title, – . All I can say is that it was a novelty. Met a Chinese girl by the name of Ching Ching Wa, and had a nice time talking to her. She told me – in broken English – how and why she left China, about Chinese customs, etc.

MAY 15 (SUNDAY - WEEK 21)

        The sunshine began to show its effects on me, and I wasn’t feeling very good all day. I sure hope it taught me a lesson about going out in the sun, and using of suntan oils.

        I got up late, and had a small breakfast. The food in Hong Kong has been good and reasonable. I rarely spend over $1 or $1.50 U.S money for any meal. Walked down to the ferry, and spent the 10¢ (H.K.) it costs servicemen to go across. For 1st class fare it is 20¢ (H.K.) or about 3¢ U.S. Ratio is about 6 to 1. The ferries are modern, numerous, and efficient and it doesn’t take long to go from the mainland peninsula of Kowloon to the island of Hong Kong. I stopped by the cricket field and was told that cricket is a winter sport.

        Having nothing particular to do, I just walked around, taking pictures, watching the people go by, and observing that Sunday doesn’t seem to be any different than any other day to the Chinese. The Chinese dress is interesting, in that the majority of the men and relatively few women wear Western style clothes. The women wear two types of clothing; – a pajama like affair, which is Cantonese, and more of a working or everyday outfit, and a slick, body tight, no belt dress with two long slits up the sides. This later dress is overwhelming and WHEN a Westerner first sees it, as ones his imagination goes wild wild. When the girls sit down, the slits extend way up their lap, and this old boy, as others do, looked out of the side of ones his eyes and drooled. Definitely the best of the Oriental dress.

        Took a bus to Shek O beach in the afternoon, and just watched, – no swimming this day. The beach seemed a little better, but the atmosphere not as nice as at Repulse Bay.

MAY 16

        Had somewhat of an interesting and exciting morning. I purposely got up early and caught the 8:45 AM train to Sheung Shui, which was the closest railroad station that I was allowed to go, the other one Lowu being right at the British-Communist border on the Sham Chun River. The ride through the New Territories was enjoyable, even though it consisted of mainly farms and small villages.

        I got off the train at Sheung Shui and walked along the highway until I came to a road block. Here I was told I could go no further. (It was manned by Pakistani troops, the reason being I AM TOLD IS that the Chinese are very class conscious, and look down on anyone blacker than they. Thus, these men could do an efficient job if trouble arose, whereas the Hong Kong Police – Chinese – might tend to go over to the Reds) I turned around and headed for the train station.

        Since I had an hour to kill, and as there were no guards or signs telling me otherwise, I decided to walk along the tracks, and perhaps climb a hill and look into the Bamboo curtain. Well, I walked and walked and finally came upon the station of Lowu. To my surprise the bridge over the river was just ahead, and about 30 yards in front of me was a Chinese flag. I took 2 shots of the flags, and was about to take some more when a voice yelled at me. I turned and found a quite excited British Hong Police Inspector, who told me to come inside.

        I went inside, and soon was peppered with questions as to how I got here, who I was, didn’t I know it was an offense to be here, etc. I told them the truth and I think they believed me. Anyway, another officer offered to take me in his motorcycle sidecar back to Sheung Shui where I could catch a bus back to Kowloon. I thanked him, and rode back to the town where I proceeded on to Kowloon. He was quite decent and said there would be no sweat, even though I did take somewhat of a risk. Frankly for the first time in my life I was actually innocent of what I did.

        When shopping in the afternoon, but bought nothing – Prices didn’t seem to be much cheaper relatively except in clothes and I have little use for good clothes in Korea.

MAY 17

        Had a great time last night but since I had neglected to check with the Air Force about the flight Wed, I decided to try and catch the Marine flight. Went out to the Airport around 7 AM, and found out that they had room (In a sense I was somewhat disappointed!) The plane took off around 8, landed for lunch and refueling at Naha, Okinawa and then proceeded on to Iwakuni, Japan.

        The next flight to Tokyo wasn’t until 1 PM the next day, and so I spent the night at Iwakuni. I must say it was a lousy nite as they gave us 2 blankets, 1 sheet and that was all. I managed to get ahold of another blanket, but still had a lousy nite.

MAY 18

        Got up later than I wanted, but my alarm (in my head) let me down for about the first time in many a moon. Debated about going to Hiroshima for a half hour or so, but decided against it as I didn’t want to take the chance of getting stuck in Hiroshima and thus missing my plane.

        Consequently I just goofed around the base, – got a haircut, went to the library, had lunch and then meandered out to the airport. We flew up to Haneda (Tokyo International Airport) in my old companion the C119. Once again luck held up and we made it safe and sound.

        From the International Airport we (O__ Sa_by) and I went by subway to the Gajoen Kanko Hotel. It is a Special Service Hotel located on the outskirts of Tokyo. For $3 a nite it isn’t bad, however, it is a little out of the way

        In the evening we caught one of the subways and went to Yurakucho station near 2 Ave and the famous Ginza Area. We walked around, looking in the windows, observing the Japanese people in comparison with the Chinese, and in general got a little taste of Tokyo nite life. We didn’t stay long as it was late and we were tired so we headed back to our hotel.

The hotel has many services and features such as PX, nite club, grill, bar, movie etc. Thus one could spend most of his time (and money) here and not venture much into Tokyo. There are even plenty of “local” girls nearby to satisfy that whim.

MAY 19

It was a beautiful day today, but instead of sightseeing, I thought I would get some of my tasks done. Consequently, I headed for Yokohama, with the intention of obtaining some type OF letter saying that a vacancy I could get a drafting job here if I can be released in Pusan. It was a long shot but I thought I would gamble a day.

        I got off the train at Yokohama and then the fun started. I found out that the Yokohama Engineering Depot was divided into sections and the people I asked did not know where the C & A section was. I got in a cab and went to the nearest YED detachment, where I was told that the place I wanted was about 25 miles away. I was told to wait for a sedan which went there every hour, and so I stuck around until such time. While driving out to this place, a couple of GI’s in the car said my best bet would be AFFK headquarters at Camp Zama, so I got off + out and hitchhiked the 4 or 5 miles to Zama.

        At Camp Zama I asked a million questions, and finally found the right section. I talked to a Captain who informed me that 1070’s were surplus here, but that they needed some S&P 1391’s on Okinawa. Sooo he said he would check on my qualifications, and perhaps transfer me to Okinawa. Anyway, time will tell, and if nothing else, I will probably be taken out of the PX and put in some form of drafting work.

        Went to Sushiros for dinner and had some of their famous Sushiyaki. A girl cooked in right at my table (bench?) and sat and talked to me throughout my stay. Sort of beisha type, I guess.

MAY 20

        As you would guess, it rained all day, just because I was set to do some sightseeing. Anyway I headed for Veno Park in the morning and stopped briefly at the National Museum, the Art Gallery and the Science Building. Almost all the titles were just in Japanese so it made it a little difficult to appreciate.

        Caught a taxi and went to the Sumo Wrestling stadium. The wrestling goes on during the day and consists of a match between 2 bronze, generally big and muscular (or fat) men who try to either push the other out of the ring or throw him on the ground. Some of the matches are over in 15 seconds, others take up to 2 or 3 minutes. The pairs of wrestlers come in a steady stream and I guess the undefeated one at the end of the 15 day session is champ. People watch from small boxes surrounding the ring; in the boxes there being mats to sit or kneel upon. I enjoyed the show, especially the loin cloth affair they wore, and some of the size of the boys.

        Shopped for presents in the afternoon and I can’t say I enjoy the job. Had trouble getting Mom a necklace of black pearls, as the nice ones cost around $100-$200. The cheaper ones are too irregular. Saw one nice pair and probably will buy it tomorrow.

        Went to a Japanese stage show in the evening, – called Kabuchi. It consisted of various plots and acts, and I had to marvel and at the scenery and staging. The actors all wore Japanese kimonos, and the women were generally portrayed with that typical white make up.

MAY 21

        In the morning I finally got my American Dollars converted into MPC and yen. I could kick myself a thousand times for not buying my yen in Hong Kong. In H.K. the rate is 450 to $1 whereas in Japan it is 360 to $1.

        Walked to the Imperial Palace, and took pictures of the bridge, houses and foliage. Only those in scheduled groups are allowed on the inside, so I had to be satisfied to be on the outside looking in. Saw a couple of gents in brightly colored kimonos and took pictures of same. From the Imperial Palace I went to the Diet Building, a beautiful Capitol building built in 1936 to house the House of Counsillors and Representatives. Neither house was in session so I had to settle for a guided tour and explanation of the major rooms. The guide pointed out the room the Emperor stays in when he opens the new session. It was a richly decorated room with silk walls, solid gold fastenings, inlaid pearl panels etc.

        Decided it best that I do my shopping, so I headed for Ginza street.  I went to the place where I had seen the strand of black pearls for Mom and I bought it, reminding the lady that I will have to check the quality with a friend. Next I went to Mikimoto and purchased the necklace for Carolyn. As I was leaving I asked if they would appraise a necklace for me, and they said they would. They checked the black necklace, and told me that it was a desirable buy. Feeling relieved I thanked them, and went out to buy the binoculars for Morton.

        Went to Takarazuka Revue in the evening. It was an elaborate extravaganza with an all girl cast.

MAY 22 (SUNDAY - WEEK 22)

        Caught the early train for Kamakura, which was about 1 hour away from Tokyo. I had a little trouble in getting about, as I didn’t see any Westerners, and there were very few English signs. Found one boy who could speak English and he pointed out the correct bus to take to see the Great Buddha, a tremendous bronze figure of Amila. The Buddha was truly awe inspiring and fell in the class of such statues as the Lincoln Monument, Statue of Liberty, and Thomas Jefferson. The figure is seated, with legs crossed and hands touching. The head stares down at the visitor before it. I was very much impressed with this Buddha, which I think is the 2nd largest in Japan

        After lunch I visited the Haciman Shrine, and also took in the museums located in the immediate vicinity. One of the museums had many old figures and statues of the Kamakura period (around 1000 - 1200 AD) The other museum was a new building and housed a Museum of Modern Art. I walked through it quite rapidly.

MAY 23

        Well my leave ended today, and so I met the airport bus at 5 AM, and rode out to Tachikawa Air Field. Boarded the plane at 8 AM and soon was wingeing towards Korea. We stopped for about ½ hour at Nicho, Japan, but soon were back in the air headed for home – Pusan. The trip was a little rough, and I was thankful when we landed.

        Hitched a ride back to Hialeah, dropped my junk at my bunk, and gave one long sigh. I think the sigh was a result of my having to return to Pusan, and being somewhat relieved of the constant traveling which was does get fatiguing.

        I sauntered over to the orderly room, and while singing in I received some news, – my visit to Camp Zama had paid off and I was soon to leave for Okinawa. I looked up Mr. Cain and he told me the full scoop: I was to be reclassified S&P Type A – Mechanical Engineer Ass’t, and my new address would be Okinawa Engr. District, 8103 AU, APO 331. He also informed me I was to leave around June 5th.

        I can’t say I was overjoyed with the news, although I am glad to again be designated S&P. I think it is a good MOS, and since only the Adjutant General can ess with you, it is not likely I will get screwed by these lower commands. They say Okinawa isn’t bad, at least it is better than Pusan. Anyway it will be something new for a couple of months.

MAY 24

        Back to work, although it was more a matter of speech than actual work. Spent the morning and most of the afternoon talking to the fellows (and Korean girls) and reading my mail. Had somewhat of a backlog of mail, and it will take me centuries to catch up.

        Things have been jumbled up at Branch 600 since I left, (not because of my not being there) mainly as a result of the P.X’s phasing out in the Pusan area. I think about 6-10 P.X’s are closing out, and consequently, they are bringing their stock down to us. The stuff is in b__ lots and is going to be a headache when we inventory and move.

        Getting back to Korea, and comparing this country with what I have seen in the Orient, doesn’t speak favorably for Korea. I think the people are dirtier, less energetic, and have a tendency towards complacency. Other countries have been conquered and defeated but the Koreas of them all, seem to just move aside and either let the world pass, or someone else do the work. The Japs and Chinese were much different, with the Filipinos between the two groups.

        I still marvel at Tokyo, for it is as New York as our large city itself. Just exchange the populace and one would have difficulty in knowing which was which. (N.Y. does have taller buildings – Tokyo and Japan being somewhat prone to earthquakes.)

MAY 25

        Another full day at work, but I am afraid my new job prevents me from devoting my full attention to Branch 600. The Lt. asked me to work on some consumer reports for the 1500-2500 people that will continue to be serviced by Branch 600 after July 1st. He said to take my time, so instead of disobeying an order I worked on the above, while also shooting the breeze with the “gang”.

        Things are beginning to change quite rapidly in the Pusan area. The troops that are to stay are being billeted in the 8069th, 32nd QU and Hialeah areas. The other troops are either be being shipped up north or to Japan and a few to Okinawa. All the P.X’s in the area will close except the one at the 8069 Replacement Depot, thus leaving Branch 600 with about 6 or 7 scattered PX’s. Most of the Snack Bars are also being closed,  except the one in the 8069 Compound. The RTO area along with Pier #1 will be turned over to the Koreans and some civilian outfits such as KCAC. Transportation is becoming more difficult each day as they cut the bus schedule by ½ and also have turned in or shipped up north many of the Army vehicles.

        In general this Pusan Area Command is undergoing some vast changes in personnel, physical layout and scope of operations. Actually, with things consolidated so, I would think the living conditions will continue on a fairly decent level. They won’t be as good as before – say at Hialeah – as one will have to go farther to get to the PX’s, snack bars etc.

MAY 26

        One of the men in the Orderly Room called me up and informed me that my new orders had been cut for Okinawa, and also orders changing my MOS from 1070 to Type A, S & P (1391). I had arranged with Manse Hall to play tennis, so I got off work early and picked up some copies of the above orders on the way to the tennis court. (incidentally I got walloped in great fashion today, 6-1, 6-1, 3-2. Whew was I bad)

        I had to laugh when I looked at my orders as they had a couple of mistakes (I hope) in the LTS and other dates. First, they had me down for a 3 year enlistment. Next my EDDFEC was Feb 56 (more likely Apr 56) and finally they had me for an ETS of April 57. Man, – me with only a year left from next monday, and they try to stick me for another 11 months. Never hoppen GI! I checked with personnel and they said no sweat, that I shouldn’t worry.

        It is entertaining to look back in hindsight and see if I goofed about getting to Japan. Earlier this month they had asked those desiring to go to Japan or Okinawa and with a year to go, should sign up. I debated and then decided against it for the following reasons: (1) they might not have told me before June or July, and I would then have had to extent a month or so, (2) they wouldn’t say where you would go or what you would do and, (3), I am still kicking around the idea of putting in for an early release for school. So, all in all I gambled with the odds and facts, and hope the Okinawa deal justifies my selection.

MAY 27

        Johnny Grant, Debbie Reynolds and a levy of 4 girls plus 3 other men came to Pusan to give the boys a show and a look at stateside women. I didn’t go to the previous evening show; instead I decided to go to the 14th Port and catch the 9AM show. 2 other fellows and myself left Branch 600 around 8:30 and walked at a killing pace up the MSR and the “mountain” that led to the 14th Port. We got there a little late, but managed to find a spot to stand for the 1 - 1 ½ hour show.

        Johnny Grant has been overseas 6 or 7 times and is an excellent Master of Ceremonies. He cracked jokes about the Army, Basic Training, Officers and things back home, and had yours truly and the thousand or two other soldiers laughing in the aisles. I believe he is a disc jockey back in Los Angeles. Three girls came out at different intervals and either sang or danced, but mainly presented huge (real or padded) breasts that had the man stamping their feet or hitting their heads. They were poor performers but provided the men with a thrill.

        Then there was Debbie the sweetheart of America? She sang, danced and joked around and showed herself to be a 1st Class Trooper. She was very cute, but much smaller and thinner than I had pictured her to be. I had to laugh at the general comment as we left, “I thought Debbie was cute, but for me, give me the one in greeen!!”

MAY 28

        Rained all day, and thus knocked out a tennis match I had arranged. Somewhat disappointed, since I had hoped to get in some practice so as to make amends for my pitiful showing of two days ago. Soo, I stuck it out all day at Branch 600, not doing much of anything.

        One thing quite interesting occured down at the old section today. It seems that with the cut in troops and PX’s to be serviced by Branch 600, special service has decided to cut the number of men (EM) that would be kept by Branch 600. They decided on 5, but said the Lieutenant should select 7 and 2 would be pruned. I was interested in whom he would select, and tried to figure which of the 15 odd men at 600 I would keep if I were in his shoes.

        Well, the list was given to the clerk for typing in the afternoon and with such a ____, it became common knowledge. I was somewhat shocked at the list and disappointed in the Lt’s selection and Jerry Turnquiests taint approval. Only one of the men working at 600 when I came was to be kept, the rest being those men that came from 601(3) and 647(3). I told Jerry that I thought they had made a poor selection but he said it was mostly the Lt’s work. Basically it confirms some of my fast or low thoughts of the Army and how it operates. If nothing else, the timing of this list was extremely poor, as 600 is to move shortly and the men that are leaving have developed the, “I don’t give a damn anymore.” attitude

MAY 29 (SUNDAY - WEEK 23)

        Where did the day go? Slept late and missed breakfast. Took a shower, ate lunch and went to the library. While reading I fell asleep twice, so I decided to go back to my bunk and make myself a little more comfortable. Hit the sack at 1:30 and slept off and on (fighting flies and music that poured out of the NCO club) for about 3 hours. Couldn’t fight it anymore, so I adjourned to the club and had a drink while listening to a half drunk friend tell me his women problems and watching the floor show. They had a great saxophone player who was quite a performer. He played on his back, on one leg and in all kinds of positions. Probably the best I have seen in Korea. (ONLY 1 MORE WEEK!)

        It looked like rain, but the clouds never opened up to pour forth their water. Instead it was a nice sunny day. It rained all day Saturday, and turned the sidewalks and roads into seas of mud. The mud went over ones soles as he walked, and just oozed everywhere. My thoughts drifted to the war and the fighting at that time on the hills and in the mud. I guess I don’t know how lucky I am.

        The flies and mosquitos are starting to come, and the DDT and malaria pills are being taken from the storages for use. With my first couple of bites I have to think back to Manila for I was really eaten alive in that town Tow n. I think I was one big bite when I left. Didn’t have many mosquitos in Hong Kong or Japan.

MAY 30         1 MORE YEAR

        Notice please everybody under the sun, the statement at the top left corner of the page. Yours truly, the United States’ gift to the Army, has only 1 more year in the Army, – about 10 months in Okinawa, the remainder in Japan. (Communists willing)

        The day was a holiday for most of the troops, and the weather even cooperated with some beautiful sunshine. Played about two hours of tennis in the morning, took a brief nap, and played about an hour and ½ more of tennis in the afternoon. I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and although my game is still quite low, my serve did pick up a little.

        Did a little work on the General Insurance Correspondence course from Aetna. It is a pretty good course and I think I am learning some basic facts concerning general Insurance. My law has been neglected, however, and I will have to get on the ball. This great weather has sure made my “summer” sick if there is such a term.

        Saw the old Italian movie, Shoe Shine, in the evening and while it was entertaining I don’t think I thought it to be as good as the critics have acclaimed it to be. The ending was sudden and far fetched and left me quite cold. Perhaps that was the intent, in that case they did a creditable job.

MAY 31

        Well, I began my last week in Pusan and at Branch 600. Continued to do odds and ends, plus mucho goofing off. Bought a bracelet from Siam on sale, and I hope I enjoy giving it to somebody. I don’t know, seems as if either I am tight with my money, am a cautious buyer or don’t know much about jewelry and silverware. Anyway, any buy is a problem and a challenge to me, and I am always hesitant and perhaps afraid that I made a poor buy. Will have to do some self analysis on this problem.

        One thing that interests me, is what could be done to some of our major scientific problems if we applied money and talent to them as we did the atomic bomb. Of course the major problems would be disease and health, but also there would be such things as food and water shortages. The latter problem has become more important to my thinking the farther I travel from St. Louis, where we have almost unlimited supplies.

        First I hit Los Angeles and Boulder Dam, and the crying need for water in the Southwest. Then there was Korea, where water is turned on only certain hours of the day, and men sell water out of wagons in the street. I hit Hong Kong at the tail end of a 4 day rain deluge, which filled the reservoirs and made it possible to have water 9 hours a day instead of the previous 3. The answer to all the above is obtaining cheap water from salt water. Seems that someone would have solved it by now, but no such luck. Oh I am sure it is possible, but the problem is cost. Anyway, I don’t think we will have to wait too long before it is done.

JUN 01

        Not much doing at work. Piddled around in the morning, and listened to records in the afternoon. At first I thought I would buy some of the records that were on sale – great bargains – but I chickened out and didn’t buy a one. They had a good set PAIR of binoculars on sale, but I had just finished buying one for Morton, so I didn’t even buy it. Consequently, in the 3 ½ months I worked at the PX I didn’t acquire one single bargain or advantage. Not that I couldn’t, but I guess I am too tight with my money.

        Drove down Port Road, one of the two main roads in Pusan. Besides being a smoother road, it is also more intriguing than the MSR. One portion of the road is devoted to outside markets, and one can buy any type of food or clothing at the outside stalls. The women or men have little straw mats on which they pile their goods and from which they sell. Generally, they sit next to each other, and form an almost continuous line of peasant women and men. They spend the whole day in this fashion, selling their meager goods and conversing to the persons on either side.

        Another section of the road runs next to the water, and as one drives by he can see the large and small fishing boats and cargo junks unloading or loading at crude piers. None of the big ships are docked in this particular section, but as one continues towards Pier #1, the Army influence takes is evident. First there are the storage yards for the Army, next the LST docks and finally the 2 large piers for ocean going vessels. At this time the docks are loaded with equipment, since the Army is shipping out a lot of its heavy vehicles and equipment. Sufficient equipment is being left here, however, for the Koreans to use and acquire knowledge of. One use to see troop transports atAT Pier 1, but they are now being diverted up to Inchon. LSTs are about the largest U.S Gov’t vessels that now come to Pusan.

        One thing that warrants mentioning are the thousands are OF crude, flimsy, filthy huts and shacks that line Port Road. These are the slums of Pusan, and I am sure will stand up against slums anywhere in the world.

JUN 02

        Went to the Orderly Room in the morning, and received the necessary paperwork and instructions for cleaning the post. First I went to the Library, then A&R, then the Post Office and finally Branch 600. At Branch 600, Lt. Cramer gave me my efficiency rating – Superior (what a farce) even though he barely knows me. From here I got a physical check (on paper) and then clearance from the Orderly Room itself.

        The next place was Personnel, and so I gathered all my paraphernalia together and headed for the busy section on the 2nd floor of the old Hqs 8131st Bldg. My records were checked to see if they were in order, and then I signed a slip assuming responsibility for my 201 file as I was to hand carry it to Okinawa. While checking my 201 file, I noticed that they neglected to mark down my last 15 day leave, so maybe I will get an extra 15 day leave. Most likely, though, they will check at Okinawa and catch it there. (Hope not!!)

JUN 03

        Next to last day in good old Pusan, the flower (hinchi perhaps) of Korea. I had acquired a foot locker to ship some of my goods and personal items to Okinawa, so I went to the Motor Pool to get a jeep. Waited a few minutes and finally obtained the use of a jeep to take myself and the foot locker to the Post Office. Weighed the box at the P.O. and found out it weighed exactly 70 pounds, the limit one is allowed. Went to branch 600, and banded the box to insure safe shipment. Took the box back to the Post Office where the man told me that it waited 70# 1 oz. After sweating a few minutes he accepted it and relieved me of the Herculanean (sp?) task of toting it up to Inchon. The cost was only $1.19 plus .39 for insurance, which was cheap enough to ship the box to Okinawa.

        Spent part of the afternoon walking around in the downtown area, taking pictures and observing the people and Pusan for the last time. Witnessed a parade of school children – tens of thousands of school boys and girls – called by the National Government to protest Japan’s proposed trade with North Korea. Some of the signs were very anti-Japan and reflected the bitterness the Koreans have for their masters of old who are now trying to walk a middle line. Can’t say that I think the Japanese are wrong, but on the other hand I believe I understand how the Koreans feel. Sort of feel that a spontaneous parade, even if it were a lot smaller, would have been more effective than a government sponsored parade. (Also, I think they could use a little music to excite the people).

JUN 04

        The Big Day! Called the RTO (Train Station) in the morning and got a birth on the evening train for Seoul. Didn’t do much of anything in the morning; – read a little, completed one of the insurance courses and ambled around the compound. In the afternoon I visited the NNIT Compound and said goodbye to Manse Hall. Of the men in Korea that I met I believed I enjoyed his company the most, and will correspond with him so that perhaps we can arrange a leave to Japan at the same time.

        Saw Call at the Snack Bar and so I stopped by Branch 600 in their new quarters at 8069th. The office is in an old mess hall, but the excellent location outshines any cramped office or warehouse storage. Reiterated my good bye of the day before, and went back to Hialeah for the final events. Ate, washed, had a beer with Jerry Turnquiest (JCE) and rode to the RTO. Waited a short time and then boarded the train for the North. I had a halfway decent birth so I slept most of the way, making the trip pass quite rapidly.

        Funny what one notices on the last trip from Hialeah to the RTO. First the ubiquitous rubber shoes; the goods carried on the heads; the flowing, ugly Korean national dress, and last but not least, the poor, bumpy roads. Glad to be leaving Korea and Pusan, too; however I must admit my stay wasn’t bad at all. The job was easy and the compound quite decent.

Route as of June 4th, 1955 – end of Chapter 6.

CHAPTER 7 - ENGINEER ESTIMATIONS

June 5th, 1955 - September 3rd, 1955

JUN 05 (SUNDAY - WEEK 24)

        We arrived in Yong Dong Po around 8:30 A.M. and waited for a bus to take us to the Inchon Replacement Depot. A lot of troops had left the Depot in the morning to board the General Sultan (States bound) and so the compound was relatively empty. We found out that we wouldn’t process until the following day. Consequently after lunch we had our time for ourselves.

        Walked up to the PX, looked around – seems that since I worked in a PX, that I have to inspect every one I come upon – and then had a strawberry sundae at the Snack Bar. Meandered over to the Service Club and looked into the magazine pile. Here as in most Doctors’ Offices, the magazines were yellow (?) with age.

        Saw a fellow I came over on the General Freeman with, and talked with him a few minutes. He has a soft job in the Service Club alongside of American women! Also ran into a stupid master sergeant I had known at the 6-3 Training Aids back at Leonard Wood. He bleated out a few incoherent words and that was the extent of our brotherly greeting.

        Outside of one or two fellows back in Leonard Wood, I haven’t met anybody I knew before I came into the Army. Maybe once I get to Okinawa I will run across some good old fashioned Missourians from University City.

        

JUN 06                                 GOODBYE KOREA!

        Mark this day and mark it well for this is the day this trooper blew goodbye kisses to Korea and headed for civilization. I hope that my 3 ½ month visit was the first and last time I see or visit Korea. I guess I sound bitter, but actually I am not. My stay in Korea was just long enough to get to learn about the people, their habits, customs and even a little of their basis for thinking and doing. My living quarters at Hialeah were perhaps the best and in Korea consequently I really didn’t suffer much or any for that matter.

        My job was easy, and I had ample time to read, take pictures and just do nothing if I wanted to do that. I didn’t come across any of the real scum of the Army (the Infantry) but I did meet a lot of unusual and interesting people. They came from all over the U.S, and freshened my understanding of the American people.

        On the other side of the ledger, the water problem and sanitation in general was WERE prevalent and my stomach never did seem to function properly. I learned little from my job and outside of a month or so as cashier, I contributed little to branch 600.

        All in all it was an experience, a 3 ½ month experience that I feel has broadened my understanding of the human race. I hope my next assignment will continue to educate my up to now narrow contact with all kinds and types of people.

JUN 07

        One whole day doing very little except some reading. They have tagged me as being on Air Alert for Okinawa and consequently not eligible for pass or even to leave the area. Sooo I found an empty room in the barracks, hauled over a mattress and alternated reading and dozing. However, the frequent voice over the “bitch box” and the “fallout at the speakers stand” provided too many diversions and interruptions to get much done. I went to the troop movement office and found out that almost all air shipments to Okinawa are at night consequently my plans for Wednesday will be made accordingly.

        Bumped into a fellow by the name of _______ who had been at Hialeah and was now assigned to Camp Drake. We talked of old times and the great deal he has at the present. Camp Drake is situated about 1 ½ hours drive from Tokyo and has many fine extra curricular things to do. Their PX is the best I have seen, and the Snack Bar opens early and closes rather late. The theater is huge and the Service Club holds 1400. The library is well stocked and they have a gym, raft shop, swimming pool and American women. What more can a man ask. 

        For the first time in a couple of months, I began thinking of what I will do when I get out of the service. I think I have narrowed it down to Law or Sales Work, with a minor interest in Government work. I believe I have discounted Industrial Engineering almost completely. Nevertheless, I have a lot more thinking to do on the subject.

JUN 08

        No one awakened me in the wee hours of the night and so I realized when I got up in the morning that I was in for another boring day of waiting. Fell out for the 6:00 formation and after that I ignored all formations and calls during the day. In the morning I did A little of reading, writing of letters and off and on dozing. In the afternoon I went to the gym and played basketball for about an hour and one-half; – the first exercise I have had in some time.

        Around dinner time I once again checked to see if they had heard anything about an air shipment but the wise guy said he didn’t know anymore than I, and was equally as wise when he refused to write down my bed number, I said _ _ _ _ it, and took off. Went to the North Camp and saw a lousy movie. Then strolled over to the NCO club which was unpretentious on the outside but very elaborate and beautiful on the inside. I happened to hit the dance night, and ate a fine combination salad to the music of a top notch Japanese band and voluptuous, half naked girls. The food was cheap, the room huge, they had smartly dressed boy waiters, table cloths and candles on the table; and I still preferred the rough, intimate club we had at Hialeah. Granted such a club wouldn’t do for American dependents, but one could sure release his inhibitions in such a place.

        For a floor show they had Larry Adler and I really enjoyed his harmonica playing and idle chatter. Whew, what he can do with that little old harmonica!

        

JUN 09                                OKINAWA

        I am writing this page while sitting in my own room, sweating my water from the last week and listening to whining jets coming and going from Kadena Air Base. Yes sir I am in Okinawa for at the most 11 months and 21 days but perhaps a little less.

        Going back to the morning, I awakened to the sound of somebody yelling over the intercommunications system – ”Sgt Werner, Cpl Neglie, you have 5 minutes to catch your flight to Okinawa.” Actually I didn’t understand a thing until I heard OKINAWA. Jumped out of bed – (4:10 A.M.) – and checked in at the skipper room. Washed and shaved and then was driven to Haneda Air Field where we waited 2 ½ hours until our flight left. (Hurry up and wait) Stupid Army. If the guy had only taken my room & bed number he wouldn’t of had to wake up everybody, but oh no, he couldn’t or wouldn’t do such a thing.

        Well, I left Tokyo with a slight bad taste in my mouth from Camp Drake, but a longing in my bones for Tokyo and Japan. Since I have 50 leave days left I shall be back.

        We flew non-stop in a C-54 to Kadena, and had a pleasant trip. I slept 2 ½ hours and thus the time passed quite rapidly. Arrived about 1:30 PM and was driven to the Okinawa Engineering District. Had expected concrete billets, but found samo samo quonset huts. However, everyone had a private room, so things shouldn’t be so bad. Walked around a little, but will have to wait before giving forth any impressions.

JUN 10

        Whew is it hot. I don’t believe I have sweated as much in many a moon. Took two showers today and changed clothes twice although the latter is a luxury which I am afraid I will have to eliminate. In the morning I went to the Quartermaster and got a lot of clothes, worn out pieces of which I had turned in up at Inchon. I then moved again, this time to the hut on my right, closer to the latrine (30 feet) and in which some of the other S & P’s live. As before I have a room by myself, and once I get settled I will have to obtain by hook or crook, a table and a fan. The room is large (8’ x 12’) and I believe I couldn’t ask for better living conditions.

        In the afternoon I reported to Personnel, but outside of 2 interviews, I didn’t get any inkling as to what I will be doing. Perhaps I will be in the field as an inspector, or on a board (hope not) Doesn’t make much difference either way.

        Played volleyball in the evening and besides welcoming the exercise, I met quite a few of the other S&Ps. Most of them are between 23-27, and have worked a couple of years after school. They, like me, were draft dodgers who were finally caught. Latter on in the evening I met SFC Upson, an (National Guard) Civil Engineer who came in about the same time as I and who was is working as an S&P. We went to the Crystal Terrace, a very fancy civilian night club, and had an enjoyable conversation over a few drinks. Returned to Hut 725, washed, and crawled under underneath the mosquito netting for the night.

JUN 11

        Had about 8 hours sleep, but it was so sultry that it seemed as if I had gotten hardly any sleep at all. Didn’t do much in the morning except read and put away some of the clothes I had gotten the previous day. In the afternoon I went to Rycom Plaza and bought a pair of pants and a sport shirt. Would of bought another pair of pants but they didn’t have my size.

        I stopped at Sukeran in the afternoon and looked up Lyle Nelson, Carol Chervitz’s fiancée. He has been here 7 months and I found him to be somewhat bitter (to say the least) about Army life and living on Okinawa. I haven’t talked to anyone in sometime who wanted to get home as much as he did, and consequently it seemed as if he made it that much harder on himself. He did does his job and probably did does it well – but other than eating, sleeping, SEEING A movie and occasional cards, he did little to pass the time or break up the daily routine. Perhaps I will feel the same as he after 7 months, but I think he could make it a little easier on himself. Once I get settled, I will give him a phone call and we can get together. Oh yes! - he did say that Norty was going to get engaged next month. To think that Norty has finally and actually fallen stunned me, but wonders are a part of everyday life. It was good to hear the news as I have met the girl and she is very nice and will make a fine wife.

JUN 12 (SUNDAY - WEEK 25)

        Went into Naha, the capital city of Okinawa, this morning with three other fellows. We took an Okinawan bus, which happened to be the first bus in a long time, as American troops are not allowed to travel in Korean buses. True to form it rained off and on all day long, and since our G.I raincoats are too heavy, I thought I would do without and suffer in the rain.

        Naha was completely leveled during the war, and consequently has many relatively new buildings. The buildings in town are of wood or concrete and provide a refreshing change from the dingy stores on the MSR and Port Road back in Pusan. The main streets are paved, and some of them even had sidewalks; however there were many that were dirt and rock.

        We stopped at a ceramic store and pr___ed some of the bowls, tables, trays etc that were made out of wood and baked lacquer. They had some nice napkin rings and wine glasses and I think I will get some in the near future. I didn’t buy anything but a couple small odds and ends but the other fellows bought abacuses, robe, fans, besides looking in almost every store we passed. Basically the market was the same as in Pusan, with the open shops, crowded but colorful displays, and whole families operating one store. One would see everybody from the baby girl and boy to the old grandmother, with her wrinkled fore and sometimes tattooed knuckles. The market is always fascinating and I can spend many enjoyable hours just walking around.

JUN 13

        I thought I would not have to go on the range today, however, I was rudely awakened at 4:30 AM and informed that I “too” had been selected. Sooo, I put on my fatigues and new boots, ate, and checked out a carbine. The range was quite a distance from Camp Kue so we were driven out in the backbone of the Army – the 2 ½ ton truck.

        I was in the 2nd Order, and when it came my time to shoot, I found that I enjoyed it and appreciated the opportunity to improve my aim. Don’t get me wrong, – the early hours and deep mud distracted plenty from any little enjoyment I received. Everyone fired 40 rounds, part of which was in slow fire, the rest in sustained or rapid fire. If the man in the pit was accurate (and didn’t go out of his way to help me) I shot 181 out of 200 which is fair. Must admit though that I used the sandbag at every opportunity. My most difficult position was standing, and my arm wavered as if I had been on a weekend binge. All I could do was start at one side of the target and move across the bulls eye, squeezing the trigger when I passed over the bulls eye. Best I could do was a 4, 3, 3, and 5.

        No one called me in for interview, so I had the rest of the day off. Slept and read in the afternoon, and I played volleyball and read (plus a lot of hot air) in the evening. Doesn’t seem to be much more to do than in Pusan, although the private room is great. Will have to begin looking for some tennis partners.

JUN 14

        When I was at Personnel last Friday, the Sgt said he would contact me when he wanted me to continue the interviewing. Consequently, I have done little of anything, sort of waiting until he decides to process me further. It is not that I am interested in doing work, but I am curious as to the type of work I will be performing while on Okinawa. I think I would rather do field inspection instead of drawing board work.

        Had a pretty good discussion in the evening with a couple of the boys concerning the economic status of our country in relation to the common man, TVA and religion. It was a pretty good discussion with intelligent reasoning on both sides. I am for the common man or denominator having a higher and higher standard of living if together with this material increase, society allows and pushes forward those that are more talented and creative. Everyone, poor or rich, should have the opportunity to make the most of his ability, whether it be in science, art, literature, music etc. Only in this way will we be able to reap the benefits of our talented people so as to raise our standard of liveing.

        One fascinating interesting thing concerning Okinawa is the tremendous (permanent type) building the U.S. Gov’t is performing. Everywhere one goes he sees new barracks, installations, homes and recreation facilities. The program will be finished in a year or so and will make Okinawa our main bastion in the Pacific.

JUN 15

        Even though this is the rainy season I actually don’t mind the rain too much, for it cools off the weather. I have been comparing the temperature in Okinawa with that in Pusan, and find that they are very similar. The main difference is the humidity and “whew” it sure makes a difference. The humidity in Okinawa must be 105%, for I don’t believe I have sweated this much, without doing much physical exercise, in many a li even in sultry St. Louis.

        I received 4 boxes of my slides back, and eagerly opened them to see how they came out. Surprisingly so, the majority are much better than I expected, and consequently makes me quite happy. I still should receive more boxes of photos I took in Hong Kong; both rolls being damaged somewhat, perhaps the reason for the delay. My pictures of the Tiger Balm Garden in Hong Kong are very colorful and do justice to one of the most interesting spots in the Orient. (Actually the sun was brilliant that day, which made it easy to take pictures)

        Other favorite shots are: the bridge at Lowa, separating Communist China and Hong Kong; the sunset in Manila Bay; a shot of the old Walled city in Manila; a anti-Japanese parade in Pusan, and a couple shots of the great Buddha in Kamakura. The fellow in the next room, Al Chapman, said they have a projector at Sukeran, so I will have to take my slides there to look at as the small hand viewer I had borrowed is quite unsatisfactory.

JUN 16

        180 years ago today the Corps of Engineers was established, and which along with the Quartermaster, Finance and Adjutant General. Not that I really am interested, however, the District Engineers were interested and decided to have a huge birthday party at the Crystal Terrace Club. All persons having anything to do with the Okinawa Engineering District were invited to partake in the free eats and drinks.

        The club – built by the Gov’t for the civilian employees – is located about ¾ of a mile from Camp Kue (where I am billeted) and is quite a lush establishment. They have a number of rooms, one box being air conditioned, and a huge ballroom with very lovely decorations. Nightly they have a Filipino band and singer, and one is able to get 30¢ drinks and reasonable food. They also have 2 nice tennis courts, which I hope to make use of once the rains leave.

        I went up with 3 other fellows and we had an enjoyable evening, eating, drinking and making a lot of noise. Some Filipinos put on some costumes and performed some of their nature dances, which although interesting weren’t very exciting. They did have one number called the Bamboo dance that was unusual and somewhat fascinating. It consisted of 2 persons kneeling on the floor, about 10 feet apart, holding on to 2 bamboo poles. They moved the poles together, apart and to the floor to a rhythmic temp, while another couple danced in and around the poles. The performers didn’t make any mistakes and even moved with graceful dexterity as the tempo increased. All in all, the evening turned out to be a fine success.

JUN 17

        It was the morning after the party and many of the fellows had a hard time falling out for duty. With the whiskey taste still in their mouth, each drink of water was like another drink, making their stomachs groan that much more. I had about3 scotch and water plus two sodas, and didn’t have much of a hangover if any.

        I am not sure what keeps me from getting drunk for last night was a great opportunity, with the unlimited free drinks and food. Basically, I just feel it is because I don’t like whiskey, consequently I generally have to push myself to drink 2 or three drinks. Possibly, my dislike is an outward manifestation of my sub-conscious which refuses to allow me to let myself go completely. Always there seems to be some restraining effort to any tendency towards lowering myself in the eyes of others. Whether this is good or not is a question that puzzles me, for there are times when I feel that the letting off of steam and pressure is good for the human body. I generally counteract the above, with the philosophy that a gradual release is better than periodic total releases, and for an over indulgence in anything usually produces more harm than good. Perhaps the best policy at the present is the latter policy and so I will follow it, modifying it as I grow older and as I emerge into new and different environments.

JUN 18

        We had a brief inspection in the morning and the captain informed me that my carbine was still dirty. Nevertheless, I returned it to the gun room, hoping that I will not have to mess with it any more while at Camp Kue. One thing that interested me at the inspection was the absence of most of the other SFC’s and M/Sgts and I will have to check into this for the future.

        Played volleyball for about two hours, and got a little sun burnt from the blazing sun. Began laughing at my poor playing and the other fellows on our team, and soon found that I barely had enough energy to hit the ball over the net. After losing 4 games we found finally quit, and retired to the showers.

        Watched a ball game at Camp Kue in the evening for about 1 ½ hours, before my seat became sore and I called it quits for the evening. They have a pretty nice ballpark (lights inc.) but the brand of ball is only fair. There is a league on the island and the 6 teams play against each other. I guess I shouldn’t be very critical of the ball playing here, for the St. Louis Cardinals are sure doing lousy. Hard to believe that they are in 7th place, 19 games out of first place.

        Got my last two boxes of slides back from Kodak, and I enjoyed reliving my leave in Hong Kong. Some of the shots turned out very well, and I am quite pleased with the shots I took on my leave.

JUN 19 (SUNDAY - WEEK 26)

        Went with Al Chapman to Kadena, where we joined a Service Club sponsored camera tour of the northern part of Okinawa. The group left around 9 AM via 2 ½ ton truck, and I was soon wishing they had gotten buses instead. The seats were hard, particularly on the gravel roads, and the dust completely covered the back of the truck and the inhabitants thereof.

        The trip turned out to be a long, truck ride, with little opportunity to take pictures as we drove. There were three breaks, one at lunch, and one each in the afternoon and morning for drinks. Al and I had gotten box lunches from the mess hall which filled our stomachs, and, sigh, that was all. Drinks were provided by the Service Club.

        Can’t say that the trip was all bad, for I did enjoy the opportunity to see more of Okinawa, and visit Motobu Peninsula which is somewhat off the beaten path. We also went to Nago, the second largest city on Okinawa, and spent some time there. One thing that impressed me (other than the fact that the villages and people are similar to those in Korea) was the were the beautiful children that we saw. I don’t think I have ever seen so many cute and pretty little boys and girls, and that includes all the kids that I have seen in the Orient. They leave the white babies far behind.

JUN 20

        Read all morning, and joked around with the maids at various interludes. I think they higher brass have decided what to do with Charlie Terry (the other NEW boy) and myself, but they haven’t gotten around to telling us yet.

        In the afternoon we went to the golf driving tee, but found out, to our dismay, that it was closed on Monday. Then hopped an Okinawan bus and got off at Sukeran where we visited the snack bar, library and post office – in that order. The library of Sukeran is pretty good, and they have one or two books that I haven’t read as yet. Happened to glance at a list of 100 top novels, and I was ashamed to find out that I had only read about 10. Only goes to show what a poor literary background I have had.

        Earlier in the week, I had talked to a lady at TI&E concerning teaching of USAFI courses. She said to call back on Monday, and when I did she said that I was to teach the Foremanship and Supervision Class. She showed me the two textbooks, and gave me some general information about the set-up. The job should be interesting and challenging, besides somewhat remunerative. However, the books are old, 1938 & 1941, they have no teachers guide and there is little reference material. The one catch is that they have to have 6 people in the class at all times are or they disband the class. Sooo it looks as if I will have something to keep me busy on Tuesday and Thursday nights.

JUN 21

        Rumor has it that I am to go to Operations and work as a Contract Assistant. However, since the silly Army has to cut orders in order to assign someone, nothing was yet official. Don’t know much about the job except that it will be a desk job.

        Nothing else to do, so I read all morning. Caught up on my magazine reading, and also dived into a book on the Far East by Mrs. Roosevelt. Of the part I have read, the book is very interesting, however, I have the fel feeling that she is sugar coating a lot of the things she writes about. This is, of course, only a guess or presumption on my part, but things just seem too rosy with respect to other material I have read on the Far East.

        In the afternoon, Charlie Terry and I decided to take a hike to the Plaza, which is located on a cliff about 3-4 miles from Camp Kue. to go by bus it takes 1.2 hour, so we thought we would walk (and climb) the distance and see if we couldn’t get there in faster time. We first passed through Jagaru, the Okinawan village next to Kue, then cut across some fields, and finally arrived at the base of the cliff. The cliff was steep and covered with tall grass and big bushes, and we thought we had come up against a dead wall. However, we found a winding path and followed it up the cliff. When we got to the top we found that we had forgotten to check our watches, and besides we were too pooped to care. Needless to say, we took a bus home.

JUN 22

        Put in my first day of work in a long time, and as fate would plan it I dozed off once or twice. Woke up twice last night, for no particular reason than the mosquitos and their cohosts. I think my legs are nothing but big red welts and bumps. Guess it only goes to prove how sweet I am!

        As I had heard via the grapevine, I was assigned to the Construction Branch of the Operations Division. My job it appears will consist of doing contract modifications and some estimating. Had a little fling of the latter during the day as another man and I rode to the Naha Housing Area to check a rain gulley that was eroding and causing damage – A contractor went with us, pointed out what he planned to do, and from this the other fellow wrote up an estimate. I threw in a word or two, but mostly listened as much of this is new to me.

        The job will prove interesting for awhile owing to its newness, but I am hoping that there are enough different modifications to keep my interest for about 10 months. All the men I will work with are civilians, with their being a mixture of Americans, Filipinos, and Japanese. It will take me years to get to remember the names of the latter two groups, as they aren’t like the Chinese with their one syllable. Very few Okinawans work in the office, although some of the women are Okinawans.

JUN 23

        My first full day of work, and also two week anniversary of my arrival on Okinawa. Purchased a fan ($11) and now I need only a table and a comfortable chair to make life easy.

        At work, I was assigned to go out on another estimate, this one being in the Naha Port Area. It concerned a section of land which was too low, consequently all the water was draining to this spot. The problem was to figure out the cost necessary to remove some of the old base material, replace it with about 3” of new material, and then place asphalt over the base. All of this was new to me and I was quite interested in the problems involved. The Filipino chap that I was with seemed quite competent, and did not let the contractor put anything over on him.

        Went back to the office in the evening and began writing some long overdue letters. I am mighty far behind and no one will write anymore unless I get hip.

        Saw Robinson Caruso Crusoe in the evening and wondered what I would have done if I were placed in the same circumstances. I doubt if I could have existed for the 28 years that he was supposed to have lived on the island and I also believe that I would have made more attempts of building a boat to escape in. Perhaps not, – maybe the solitude would have been a pleasant escape from this upturned world.

JUN 24

        Another week gone, and almost another month. Time is passing quite rapidly, and I think it will continue to do so provided I don’t get the urge to make a big calendar and mark off the days.

        Worked the whole day in the office on a contract modification, which appears to be my main job. Right now I am laboring over a modification to supplement a contract which originally called for spread columns, and now piles were to be driven for the foundation. My boss – Joe Alfonsi – seems to be quite decent, and willing to explain much that I do not know about construction. A good example was the difference between spread columns and pile foundations, which I was in total ignorance of.

        The modification work consists of first preparing a finding of fact and then writing out the changes or supplementary work in contract form. There are standard paragraphs and forms to use, and so I have to decide which are the correct phrases to use to explain the work. The work isn’t hard, but at present is a little confusing.

        I sat in on a negotiation conference between the Engineer District and some Japanese contractors concerning a modification in a different contract. Am afraid the Engineers and estimaters were a little confused and the contractors got more than they should have, – at least my boss thinks so. Reminded me of the Job Evaluation meetings I use to sit in on. Hope I will have more opportunity to do this type of work.

JUN 25        

Every Saturday we have t__ming which consists of various different ways of passing the time, – such as TI&E talks, Chaplain lectures, care and cleaning of the weapons, inspection and drill. Today we had the first three items listed above, and all of them together produced one large care of anoyance annoyance. The Chaplain was bad, and kept on referring to the American way of life as being the only way of life. I missed the TI&E lecture, and did a sloppy job with my Carbine. They gave me a new one to clean after I had spent about 2 hours cleaning the one I fired on the range, so I cleaned the bore, wiped her down good and left it at that.

Played volleyball in the afternoon then spent an hour or so using the ball as a basketball and hitting the ball into the air with one of the maids – Iniko. Funny, but it seems that all of the girls have their names ending in “iko.” e.g., Yoshiko, Hediko, Yoiko, Iniko, Kumiko, etc. Asked one of the girls why it was like that, but she couldn’t give me a decent answer.

The maids make about $20 a month which is fairly good for them, as none of them are married and consequently they live at home. Most of them are young, hard working girls who seemingly are much friendlier and meeker than the Korean women. On the whole, I think the Okinawans are quite a friendly people who respect and perhaps enjoy the Americans in one sense, but wish we were gone and they were more independent on the other hand. One big argument presently going on concerns the $22 per acre per month we pay for land rental. The Okinawans believe that is for too small a price, especially since they claim we have taken the best rice paddy and farm land. From what I have read, the U.S. is presently renting 40,000 acres and plans to rent 12,000 more.

One big bane of contention to the Okinawans concerns the fact that there doesn’t seem to be anywhere they can complain if they feel the $22 is too low. In other words, they say, it is $22 or nothing for the Americans are going to take the land in the long run. A Congressional group is coming to investigate the Okinawan problem in the fall, so perhaps we might get a couple of political arguments going.

JUN 26 (SUNDAY - WEEK 27)

        Had a company picnic today, and the weatherman cooperated with a nice sunny day. I missed the bus going, and consequently had to hop an Okinawan bus to get to the picnic area. There was a lot to eat – chicken, hot dogs, potato salad, potato chips, beans – plus beer and soft drinks. I guess there were about 70 men, wives and children present.

        Four of us decided to wade and swim to a little island off shore. It turned out to be much further away than it appeared plus the fact that it was very shallow and rocky. Many stumbles and bumps later we “crawled” ashore and started to investigate. The coral rock got the best of my feet and I took a breather, while 2 of the group walked around the island. Rested a moment and then headed back. One thing for sure, most everybody was sunburnt.

JUN 27

        Told my maid – oh hum – not to put so much starch in my shirts, but I still had one or two starched ones to wear. Needless to say, I suffered, as the stiff shirt didn’t feel to good on my raw skin. (When will I learn to invest in my suntan oil?)

        Seems as if I am beginning to get on to the modification work, and it looks easier and more of a routine job as I become more familiar. Finished my first modification today, and started on the second. This one was a little different from the first as it was a change order (to the contract) whereas the first was supplementary work. My boss – Joe Alfonsi – seems to be a nice fellow, and is willing to help me with the job and particularly in understanding construction terms. I am really a novice at the latter.

        Stayed at the office after dinner and wrote 6 letters and a postcard. Finally, my correspondence pile is beginning to dwindle a little. From here I went to the library where I read the Stars and Stripes and thence to the ballgame being played at the Camp Kue field. There is a 6 man team league in this area, and there are is usually one game a night. The game this evening was surprising good and free of errors, that is until the last of the ninth when the Mauraders scored twice (both not earned) to win 2-1. Got a hamburger and a lemonade and went to bed.

JUN 28

        Surprising how few times I find myself leaving the Camp Kue Area. There are pretty many things to do here, perhaps as much but maybe not as good as say Sukiran or Kalena. The movie is hot, but shows the same movies perhaps 2 weeks later than Suhiran. The PX is fair; library fair; restaurant pretty good; ball diamond good; Castle Terrace Club, good; volleyball, horseshoes, tennis and other sports; barber shop; and a few miscellaneous other activities.

        Tonight I drove some golf balls, and surprisingly enough I did better than I thought I would. Hit the balls solidly, and about 150 yards, although some were too high and others faded to the right. Guess I will try my shill on a course, but I anticipate the worst.

        From 9:00 PM to 9:30 PM the Island underwent a blackout and mock air raid. All lights were turned off when the sirens squealed at 9, and shortly thereafter jets took off from Kadena and Naha Air Bases. Around 9:15 AA guns began firing and one could hear and see the shells bursting in the air. Read in the newspaper that the drill was a success, so I guess we are somewhat prepared.

JUN 29

        I had taken a driver’s test on Tuesday and today I picked up my pass. Now all I need is a car! Samo-samo at work. My boss had the afternoon off, so since I couldn’t get some answers from him, I did some personal typing, which consisted of compiling some phrases, statements and articles of things I felt to be outstanding and worth keeping. Seems so often one runs across a good statement or wording of an old idea, and two days later can’t remember where he saw it or what some of the words were. Perhaps I can capture the brilliant remarks of my more illustrious human beings, even if I can’t contribute anything

        Finally got around to doing a little studying. About time to say the least. Received my chapters on Agency in preparation to taking the final. Actually I can’t decide if I made a mistake with this Law Course. I don’t think it is very good, but of course I haven’t done much studying. If I didn’t have it, I would do more reading of good novels, – or would I. Presently reading Franklin’s Autobiography which I find to be very good.

        Found the battle of the mosquitos in my room this evening. Must of killed 15 and I don’t think I dented the environment. One thing good is this DDT spray bombs we have. It attacks their nervous system and I get sadistic enjoyment in seeing them run, then flop over, hack and die. Guess it is how a human being would react to nerve gas.

        

JUN 30

        Pay day today. If I remember correctly that stood for – – • –, the letter Y in morse code. Of course I could be way off, for that was way back in the Air National Guard. Anyway, it was Payday and I got my $147. Was also reminded that I would be a Specialist 1st Class as of tomorrow, – no longer would be a NCO. Doesn’t matter for me, for as long as I receive the pay of a SFC, I don’t care what they call me. Matters to my maid though, as she has to change all my emblems and stripes. The new emblem is an eagle with spread wings, and 2 gold stripes. It is much smaller and less attractive than the other stripes.

        Took off early and played some tennis. Didn’t have anybody to play with so I just batted the ball against the boards. It was really hot and after 45 minutes I threw in the rag.

        Went back to the office and reviewed my Agency a little more before taking the test. The test consisted of 20 questions, most of which were quite easy. It is good though to do a little thinking and use some of the material that I am studying. If nothing else, it will perhaps be easier in the future if I ever need to study it any further.

JUL 01

        The beginning of another month, which means that much less time in the Army. Surprisingly as it may be, I really don’t hate the Army, however I must quickly state that I have no intention of staying in. I have never had so much free time, – time to read, play ball, and do as I desire, – outside of my summers when I was going to school. This free time is somewhat of a challenge, as it dares the person to make the most of it. I am sorry that I haven’t made better use of my free time in the past 13 months, and I hope to do better in the months to come.

        The travel bug has really bitten deep. I am looking forward to the time when I get out, as I plan to do some traveling when I get separated. Besides for these plans, which seem far away, I hope to take some leave time in Japan and possibly Southeast asia. I had given some thought to taking the latter trip in September, but after looking at some weather averages for temperature and amount of rainfall, I think I will have to postpone it until November or December. Perhaps I can visit Japan in September.

        I don’t think I should have much trouble getting released from my section and is one of the reasons I don’t mind working where I am. Yesterday I didn’t have any trouble in taking an hour off in the afternoon, and today I went on a tour of the northern part of the Island. Sooo things look pretty good.

JUL 02

        Had our typical Saturday morning “training” which is nothing more than a farce. Nevertheless it wasn’t difficult or very irritating so it passed quite rapidly. I had planned to play tennis in the afternoon but torrential rains – the first in some time – put an end to that.

        Arnold Pernado and Charlie Terry decided to do some shopping and looking so I said that I would join them in their tour of Central Okinawa. We went by bus and got off at a town near the Plaza House. We headed for the Plaza House, which is a souvenir haven, having many nice expensive and attractive gifts from Okinawa, Hong Kong, Japan, Siam etc. I look at some Hong Kong work and also some black pearl earrings for Mom, but couldn’t decide on anything to buy. (I will have to spend more time here)

        We then headed for New Koza and Koza and wandered in and out of the hundreds of little shops that lined the streets. Most of them had similar goods to offer, such as china, lacquer ware, bronze and brass objects, nick nacks etc. It was interesting to visit the quaint shops, watch the salespeople and the prospective customers and especially notice the well behaved children sitting to one side getting amusement from some simple toy.

        Koza, or Old Koza as it is called, is strictly commercial, and caters to the GI. This includes women, and I must admit I never saw so many whores on the street trying to peddle their wares at 4:00 PM in the afternoon. The outfits these gals had on were really humorous and I had a great time watching them and the boys they tried to coax in.

JUL 03 (SUNDAY - WEEK 28)

        Strolled up to the tennis court in the morning, hoping to find an opponent, and luck was with me as there was another man looking for some “easy meet”. I sure filled his bill, for after taking the first game from him, he proceded to blast me off the court and the set ended 6-1. I then banged the ball against the backboards awhile and departed for my hut, much redder than when I had left. My nose and forehead are as red as a beet, and they both feel like broiled lobt lobster.

        Al Chapman and I decided to go out to White Beach in the afternoon and take some pictures of some of the Navy ships in dock and at anchor in the so called harbor. We rode out in buses, and took in the scenery on the way. The day was wonderful and everything looked green after the recent rain. This was also rice harvesting season and everywhere one looked he could see rice drying in the sun.

        When we arrived at White Beach we found out we could ride out in one of the launches to the carrier Hornet anchored a couple of miles out. I was somewhat excited as I had never seen a huge ship like this before. The sight of the ship as we drew near was overwhelming and from what I found out later, it is about 14 stories high.

        We climbed aboard, and spent some time wandering around the flight deck and the hanger deck underneath. They even had an escalator between these two decks, so that it saved a lot of wear and tear on the pilots. (Seems reasonable)

The planes were bunched up quite close on the deck, and their wings were folded for closer storing. We were told there were 80 planes, including fighters (jet) night fighters (late models of the McDonnell Banshee), reciprocating engine planes and one helicopter. Couple fellows also pointed out the wires used to stop the planes and the Norwell and Davis barriers when the planes missed the wires.

        One fellow, then showed us around – including supper – and pointed out the catapult machines, quarter (troopship memories!), 3 blue bomb casings supposedly for A-Bombs, and other highlights. All in all, the visit was thoroughly enjoyed.

JUL 04

        Twas a lazy day for me, outside of some tennis in the morning and evening. The latter game was one of my best and I attribute it to the fact that the sun was behind some clouds and consequently didn’t get into ones eyes when he served or make it overly hot.
