        Wrote letters in the afternoon and for the first time tried to explain somewhat what I have been thinking up to now concerning my proposed traveling after I get out of service, and also the type of work I will do. Will be interested to hear the family’s comments.

JUL 05

        Finding out how hard it is to get back to work after a 3day dayoff, I wonder what it will be like after 2 years? Today was a very typical day, and I am afraid that I didn’t accomplish very much. Continued to work on Modification at work, and am getting to know the job a little better as the days pass by.

        Wrote a preliminary draft of a letter I plan to send to the legal departments of some of our larger companies hoping to acquire some more information about law and its relation to industry. I am afraid the letter is too long, but perhaps the people will answer one or two questions providing me with a little bit more data. Law and sales seem to be my main job prospects when I get out, although law will mean further studying. Seems as if I have put Industrial Engineering and Government work out of the running, at least for the present.

        Finished reading Ben Franklin’s Autobiography and Assorted Short Tales tonight and enjoyed the book very much. He was quite a remarkable man, perhaps the first outstanding man in America. He reminds me much like Winston Churchill, especially with all his talents. His story, “Way of Wealth” is chuck full of great sayings and if one followed them to the letter he couldn’t help but be a great man.

JUL 06

        Stopped by the Education Center to get some more information about the Foremanship and Supervision course that I am to give. The lady informed me that about 10 had enrolled so it looks as if the class will meet a couple of weeks at least. I don’t know though, – with my poor teaching they might all quit at the end of the first week and leave me without a job.

        Actually the job isn’t bad, and I will appreciate both the experience and the money. The 2 booklets that accompany the course are quite poor and I imagine I will have to supplement them with a lot of outside information. However, since the test will be over the material in the book, I will have to give a few minutes discussion to the main ideas. At the present my plan is to spend the first 30-45 minutes on the book. Then have a 30 min or so discussion on human relation problems that face the forman. I then plan to wind up the class with some discussion and facts of basic Industrial Engineering courses.

        Went on my first estimate today and it was a fairly easy one to start out on. It concerned relocating 8 switch boxes from the inside to the outside of the PX Warehouse building. The work had already been done by the time our department was told to give an estimate, so my job consisted of looking at the work, determing or find out how much it cost to chip the concrete in order to place the switch boxes, and what was needed to cover up the holes on the inside. I found the Inspector (a Filipino) who took me to one of the Japanese foreman and we three went to the jobsite.  My job was made easier by the fact that the foreman said it had cost 50¢ to chip the concrete, and that there were no holes to fill out (this was obtained thru much language difficulty – Japanese English to Filipino English to me!)

        Back at the office I made up a brief report of my findings and thus completed my first estimate (?)

JUL 07

        I am afraid that I am getting tired already with doing Modification Revisions and the accompanying Finding of Facts. I guess, though, that if he (MY BOSS) doesn’t mind my occasional “personal work” I will be able to survive. (There are worst jobs in the Army!)

        Typical night, – read and then went to Camp Kue Restaurant (fondly known as the Chinamens) for a sandwich and lemonade. Seems as if I get something to eat and/or drink every night. Actually, most of my money is spent in this manner.

        For the first time, in I would say 2 months, I really did some studying. Read Torts for about 2 ½ hours and refreshed my memory about same. Actually once I finally sit down and study, I find that I enjoy studying law, but I must admit, I am lazy.

JUL 08

        Guess I have the tennis bug. Got off work a little early and went to the tennis courts located adjacent to the Castle Terrace Club, about ½ mile - ¾ mile from my hut. The courts are cement but are in good shape, and besides they lend people rackets, balls and even give free lessons if desired. Well today, my 3 ½ carton Korean racket gave out and a couple of the “unbreakable” strings came loose. I left the racket to be fixed as it is one of the few things I bought in Korea.

        The game wasn’t bad, although my partner and I lost 3 sets to two out other fellows from Kue. The sun was behind some clouds most of the afternoon and provided our noses with some welcome relief from Old Man Sun. Tennis affords some good exercise, and also there isn’t the squabbling that has developed in volleyball. Looks as if my my main exercise while on Okinawa will center around tennis.

        Today marks my 1st month in Okinawa, and I must admit it passed quite rapidly. I hope the remaining 10 ½ months pass as quickly. I think I will like it here better than Korea, and I am glad I made the change. I am waiting to hear from a couple of people back in Pusan to get the latest poop, as to what is happening at Branch 600 and also Hialeah Compound. Sounds familiar, ni!

JUL 09

        Don’t know if my horrible handwriting will show an improvement, but if it should as a result of my getting a table from supply. I was just about to buy one when I decided to ask for the last time, – and low and behold they decided to issue them instead of keeping them locked up in a room.

        Went into Naha in the afternoon to do some sightseeing and to look for a comfortable chair. My poor back is taking a beating, sitting on a card table folding chair, balancing the chair on two legs as I while I lean against the wall. Probably will end up buying a wicker chair I had seen when I was in Naha a couple of weeks ago, but I wasn’t able to find the place this afternoon. Did buy a desk lamp for 130¥ (120 yen = 1 dollar)

        Walked around Naha, taking picture, watching the people go about their shopping, and in general tried to absorb some of the nature atmosphere. As usual, the beautiful Okinawan children fascinated me and I was constantly watching them and their antics. Their older sisters paraded around with colorful umbrellas to protect themselves from the hot son. The rest of the family seemed to be busy buying or selling or watching camera loaded American personnel walk by.

        Went to Koza in the evening and enjoyed teasing the many whores out selling their trade. The three other fellas I was with were convinced that I wanted to buy some of this 200 yen stuff but I had too good of time kidding the girls and making comments to them as we strolled by.

JUL 10 (SUNDAY - WEEK 29)

        Played a little tennis in the morning, and spent the rest of the morning reading or shooting the breeze. Took a shower around noon, ate, and caught the bus for the Plaza. Three other fellows (Chapman Terry & Fox) joined me in an afternoon trip to the Plaza (Post Exchange – best on the Island), Plaza House – civilian souvenir store and thence to Shuri via Naha.

        Shuri is where the University of Pryuhyu is located and is the first stop on a list of things to see while in Okinawa. Might as well, for besides presenting a clearer picture of the people and their environment, it also keeps one out of trouble.

        Took a bus (6 yen) from Naha to Shuri and got off at the end of the line. We then climbed a small hill where we found 2 dormitories for out of town (or island) students. The buildings were new and represented some of the huge construction programs in Southern Okinawa. Naha, the Capital, has an especially heavy construction program going on. Up a road and on the top of a hill is located the University, with 2 modern permanent buildings, 2 more under construction, and a number of wooden classrooms.

        The students seemed young, but I am a terrible judge of Oriental age. They all seem young, and then they seem to bypass middle age to get to the old age class. Then to make it a little more confusing, the Orientals count their age a little different than we. There weren’t very many students around although there were a few studying, some playing musical instruments and others in the dormitories. The view from the campus is tremendous. One can see for miles, particularly to the Southwest, where the whole city of Naha is unfolded to the eyes. In the far distance one can also see other islands comprising the Ryukyus Islands.

        The ca University is located on the site of the old Shuri Castle, the house of King Shotaikyu. The castle was destroyed during World War II as well was much of the housing and historic treasure on the Southern part of Okinawa. The present Administration Building is built on the former Throne Room of Shuri Castle.

JUL 11

        Typhoon Clara was the topic of discussion throughout the day. According to the weather station a 135 mile per hour wind was moving towards Okinawa and was supposed to hit early Tuesday morning. Consequently, during the evening all the windows were covered, loose objects stored inside, and conditions were readied for the fury of the winds.

        It was interesting to observe the people – some were pressing the panic button and were moving as if their heads were severed from their bodies. Others took the show calmly, prepared for the typhoon and then sat back and waited. Not knowing what to expect, I bought two candles, some ritz crackers and settled down for the evening.

JUL 12

        Unless the typhoon doubles back, it looks as if we will not witness our first typhoon of the year. Some heavy rain and wind awakened me around 4 AM, but outside of some showers in the morning things quiet throughout the day. Condition One (there being 3 Conditions, for designating the stages of the typhoon and its proximity) was announced for the day so we didn’t go to work – just goofed and idled the time in and near the barracks.

        The morning consisted of reading, sleeping and teasing the maids. The afternoon consisted of reading, bridge (bad playing all around) and teasing the maids. The evening was passed with a couple games of volleyball, writing and reading. Not a very eventful day at all.

        The typhoon canceled the class, and so I guess I will have to wait till Thursday before I begin to start in the teaching profession.

JUL 13

        The typhoon is supposed to be about 200 miles from Okinawa, not moving in any particular direction. Consequently, work went on as usual today, and I encountered a nice juicy estimating job. The job consisted of estimating the labor needed for setting up antenna poles and guy wires on some of the outlying Ryukyus Islands.

        My first problem consisted of interpreting the blueprints in order to obtain an idea of the job. Took me some time to get orientated, mainly as a result of lack of practice. I then had to attempt to set up my same form of system or method for doing the job, so that I could determine the labor needed. At this point I talked it over with my boss and asked him to have one of the other estimators assist in figuring out the labor. Mr. Delmendo started to work with me, and we accomplished some good by the end of the day. Perhaps, tomorrow will even be more profitable.

        Nothing much new happened, except we had some strong winds all day, perhaps an aftermath of the typhoon. Actually the coolness of the air the past few days has been a relief to the heat we have been having on Okinawa. Noticed in the paper that St. Louis has had 90°-97° temperatures for the past few days. Still nothing like the 115° temperature we had last year during basic at Leonard Wood (God, am I getting to talk about “when I was in the Army, things were much worse!”

JUL 14

        Well my first night of teaching was somewhat of a dud. Only one man showed up (of 12 that had registered for the course) and consequently all I did was shoot the bull with the fellow. He was an SFC RA SGT, who had thought the course was more about Supervision than foremanship. Have my doubts whether he will come to class next Tuesday. The lady in charge said that most of the 75 RCT were out on the range and that was the reason for the low attendance. I hope so, or it looks as if I will be a classless teacher.

        While waiting for “the hoped for” pupils to come, I heard through the windows the familiar shout or song of delayed cadence – one – two – three – four, one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four. It sort of cleared my brain of any dislikes of Camp Kue, and for me to realize how lucky I have been in the Army.

        Actually I have no gripes coming. Am getting a chance to see the Orient, to “step back” and see where I want to go, and to spend 1 ½ years in the Army in relatively good jobs. I just finished reading a story in Look Magazine about some POW during the Korean War and what he went through. I just thank my lucky stars that I wasn’t in it, nor had to endure what the POWs went through. I wonder if I could or would have stood it all, or whether I would have cracked. The POW problem is touchy and needs a complete going over. One can not expect a human being to adhere to the completely idealistic practice of giving to the enemy only the name, rank, serial number and date of birth. I am sure that those that stuck by that standard in Korea are now dead, (perhaps we haven’t given them their due homage) are or in such poor medical condition that they are a living dead. Now I am not saying collaboration, nor anything near that; – but there seems to be (or has to be) some middle ground where a man can give a little more than the idealistic minimum (T____ who is to define what is to be given and what not?)
        In other words for a man to sign a slip of paper advocating peace, doesn’t seem to me to be so bad. Nor should a tortured confession end in a 10 year or 20 year sentance at hard labor. Just seems to me that the Army hasn’t given enough attention and advice to the troops about being captured by the barbaric countries of the world, and one should act.

JUL 15

        Went to Services in the evening, the first that I had gone to since Fort Lewis. Here as it was there, the Service was principally in Hebrew and left me quite cold. Frankly, I doubt if I go back other than for the high holidays in September, and maybe not even for them. Met a few people, one or two I had seen at Kue, but the spark I need to participate and give of my self in order to receive or get something from the religion, is lacking. Maybe eventually, – maybe never – I will obtain the form of religion that is closest to my own views on religion. (And this is the way it has to be, not my view conforming to a religion.)

JUL 16

        Got up early, ate breakfast and then went with an estimator in our office by the name of Delmendo, to Machinato. There, by pre-arrangement, we boarded the S.S. Hua Lien, a Chinese vessel from Formosa which carries Cement Aggregate from Motobu to Machinato. We had been given a list of damages done to the vessel, of which estimates were to be made so that negotiations could be agreed upon and the contract completed.

        For nine months the quarry in Motobu had been producing the rock, crushing it and then transporting it aboard ship by modes of a conveyor set-up built on the pier. The ship then carried the rock to Machinato where cranes removed the aggregate and stored it for use in concrete. The cranes had caused the aforementioned damage, and the U.S Government had to mend the damages as part of the agreement.

        The ship was of a medium freighter class, 1 stacker, and had two holds - 14’ x 28’ and 14’ x 52’ (20’ deep). The crew were Chinese, flew the National China flag, and I presume, profess to be violent anti-communists. The first mate was very friendly, but spoke a mumble jumble form of English and it had both Delmendo and myself cocking our ears to understand. Actually, Delmendo got a little seasick at the beginning of the trip and I had to do most of the checking of the damage.

        The damage consisted of a few bent beams, hatch coamings, ventilators, awning stanchions and fender fittings. A couple wooden awning beams have to be replaced plus a wooden fender and sounding pipe cover. We plan to work up the estimate on Monday, so we took it easy the rest of the trip. The trip was uneventful, and only lasted about 2 ¾ hours.

        At Motobu we watched then load for awhile – fascinating and tremendously efficient conveyor – and then caught the bus for Kue. The bus ride took about 2 hours and was made uncomfortable by heavy rains necessitating the closing of the windows. Before we could get any sleep, the bus was at Kue, and we hopped off to get some chow. Thus ended my sea career for another couple of months.

JUL 17 (SUNDAY - WEEK 30)

        Visited the Futenma Shrine, which is a Shinto shrine built about 1450. It consisted of a couple Tor_s, and a cave where the praying and offering were done. The shrine is dedicated to Futenma Gaugin, the Virgin of Futenma and Guardian Spirit of Voyagers. Legend says that if a person makes a prayer and offering for a person going on a trip, that the voyager will receive good luck and health while on his travels.

        Walked around the village and noticed the ring worm or sores prevalent on the heads of many children. I guess it is a result of filth and lack of sanitation, but can’t seem to remember it in Korea. Such a shame as the kids are so cute, well behaved and friendly and it hurts to see these afflictions.

JUL 18

        Rush job all day concerning the estimate for the repair job to the ship. Delmendo and I figured, then refigured and finally came up with an estimate of around $500, versus the $1400 estimate the Works Division had prepared. We probably are low, yet they are probably high, so somewhere in the middle the negotiated settlement lies.

        Thought I would walk through one of the villages in the evening, so I took a bus to Fatina located near Sukiran. The town is small, and caters a lot to the G.I, having beer or tea establishments, miscellaneous carts, whore houses, furniture stores (all hand made and quite cheap), and the movies. The streets were unpaved, being composed of dirt and rock and of course, rubbish. Most of the houses were one floor affairs, occasionally there would be a two story house.

        On the houses one could see inside, I noticed the typical Oriental floor matting, low table, no chairs, minimum number of cabinets, generally one electric light and people of all ages squatting, sitting and lying about. The electric light was different, as very few of the houses in Korea had electricity, – mostly kerosene lamps.

        No one seemed worried about what they had on or what they were doing. It is not unusual to see a man taking a leak alongside the road, and little children going even farther. People generally stopped and stared at me as I passed, but then casually resumed what they had been doing.

        One interesting thing are is the woman barber seen frequently in the barber shops. In fact the first haircut I got in Okinawa was given by a woman or lady barber. At the end of the job, the barber – man or women – always massages the neck and back muscles and actually does a “relieving” job. I will have to go to a hot bath up in Japan.

        Of course similar sights were present on my walk as on previous walks here and in Korea. There was were the simple houses, the ever-present and numerous children, the general inactivity of many of the grown ups and the filth and lack of sanitation. The walks are quite an eye opener and one sees a lot he wouldn’t get if he stuck mainly to the Army compounds.

JUL 19

        Taught my first class tonight, and I guess it went along all right. The lecture part seemed to snow them, but they participated activly actively in the discussion phase of the class. There were 3 fellows present (all RA Sgts) and unless I can get 6 by Thursday, the class will be discontinued. I hope not as I think I will enjoy the teaching experience if the class lasts the 10 weeks.

        Heard that the Army authorities were having a little trouble with some of the Okinawan farmers. Seems that the farmers don’t want to sell their land, and are resisting. Will wait till I hear more before I put further anything down in the book.

JUL 20

        Since I had worked last Saturday, I figured that I should have a morning off, since “it just isn’t right to put in more time than one has to.” I told Joe (my boss – Joe Alfonsi) that I wouldn’t be in all day Wednesday, as I also had training to make up in the afternoon. Also arranged with Sgt Hunt to overlook me at 7:15 formation.

        Hopped an early bus and went to Awase Meadows Golf Course, where I rented some clubs, bought 2 old balls, bought some tees and got a caddie. “Loaded for bear” I tackled the course and to say the least, it threw me. Ended up the first night with a 53 and was just about ready to quit. Decided to play a little more, and I was happy I did, for a blazed in with a 40. Must admit I was unusually lucky, particularly with my short irons. The greens (actually sand greens) which had been my Waterloo the first nine, were up my alley the second nine, and I putted many of them. All in all, I enjoyed it, and will have to return.

        Attended training in the afternoon, which consisted of 4 hours of movies. Two of the movies were in color and concerned God at the Atom, and God and the Universe. Outside of some inane words about Jesus Christ, the movies were enlightening. Also enjoyed one movie about Escaping. Actually I think I learned a little from the movie, but I hope I never have to put it in practice.

JUL 21

        Spent most of the day working on an estimate for Antenna Farms for 4 outlying islands. Seems to be a little ridiculous not to visit the islands in person, but they are a little out of the way.

        Attended class again tonight and had only one pupil show up. INstead of discontinuing the class this evening, they decided to give it one more chance, meanwhile they were going to contact the TI&E NCO’s and see if more interest could be aroused for the USAFI classes. Since I didn’t give the class, I am prepared for Tuesday, and for whatever happens. Plan to hit my Law Books pretty hard if the course officially folds, – now that I got my new chair. Oh yes, I must make mention of my wicker, wrought iron shell type chair I got at the Plaza House. Got it half priced, – ($3.60) – as it is damaged in the front, but I can fix that fairly easy. Need a couple 2x4 boards under the front lip and it should make for comfortable reading. As it is now, the back is a little too straight.

        Went over to the Sukiran Library after class, and read a little about Hinduism. The religion is a mystery to me, and I would like to find out a little more about it before I visit the country. (Wishful plans!) From what I can figure out, endless reincarnation is the bane of Indian life and every good Hindu wants to rid himself of it, and thus reach salvation. Various sects preach different ways to this salvation, – knowledge, devotion or sacrifice. Perfection of these will mean MOKSHA (salvation)

        

JUL 22

        Typical day in Okinawa – work, eat, kill time and sleep. The kill time sometimes varies, thus providing the incentive to keep going. Already I have begun planning for my next leave, and if things work out I will take it the first couple of weeks in September. My present plans are to spend two weeks in the Kyoto, Osaka and Nara area. Kyoto is a former capital of Japan and has many priceless places and objects of historical interest that one “has” to see when he visits Japan. Osaka is also supposed to be a great city to visit, – it being the 2nd largest town in Japan.

        Went up to the Castle Terrace with a couple of the boys. Had a couple of beers, and a cheeseburger to round out an evening of boisterous fun. The fellows I went with, plus two others from Kue that we met, became quite tanked up, and the conversation got humorous and loud. Stayed the latest I have been at the club – 12:30 AM – before flopping in a taxi with the boys and heading for 725, Camp Kue.

        The Club is nice, and provides good food and drink at reasonable prices. The Filipino band and singer do an adequate job on the American songs, but I wish now and then they would since a few Japanese songs. Actually if they substituted American waitresses for the Okinawan girls, it would be impossible to tell the difference between this and a nice American night club.

JUL 23

        Rain, rain and more rain. It rained constantly throughout the day and night and came down so heavily at Suppertime that a couple other fellows and myself were caught in the mess hall for about one half hour. Morning training consisted of movies, and owing to the fact that I had gotten only 5 hours sleep the night before, I half slept and was half miserable. If nothing else, movies are better than inspections and lectures.

        Stayed in the hut all afternoon, – reading and talking to my maid Suziko. For awhile 2 other fellows were in my room with me, and the 3 of us were teasing and kidding with the josan about herself, Americans, Okinawa, Jagaru (where she lives) etc. She is a smart cookie and threw back a relentless tirade of nonsense to us, perhaps getting the best of all 3 of us G.I’s.

        The other 2 fellows left after an hour and I spent about an hour talking to Suziko about her “boyfriends”, and when was she going to catch a honey. (G.I slang for steady; – samo samo as Moose in Korea) She said she didn’t have a honey, and started kidding me about how much I would give to “catch” her as my honey. I said I didn’t know, and wanted her to set a price. Well, this went back and forth for awhile before one of the fellows called me to play volleyball, and so I told her we would continue the conversation later. Can’t say that I am not at all interested, for I would be a lier if I did; yet I hope my better judgment keeps me away and leaves it in the teasing stage.

        

JUL 24 (SUNDAY - WEEK 31)

        Still more rain. I don’t think I have seen so much rain in many a day. I am anxious to see in the morning paper how much rain has fallen in the last few days, – there must have been at least 5-7 inches. Reminds me of the monsoons that one reads about, but seldom witnesses in the USA.

        The climate on Okinawa is very similar to the summers in St. Louis. The days are hot and sultra, with humidity getting up to 90% or higher (it seems). The nights are pretty cool, and makes for fair sleeping; however, it gets hot about the time to awake in the morning, thus sweating up the bed and making it seem as if the peron had only gotten a couple hours of sleep.

        There are a lot of mosquitos and flies in our huts, but we are issued spray bombs to kill them off. The DDT is effective and I do not get many bites any more, however I still sleep under the netting. The DDT is fascinating (sadistically speaking) and I like to watch it take effect on the winged pests. They shake off the spray for a few seconds, then fly or walk wobbly and finally fall to the floor, turn on their backs and give a few final kicks of their legs. All in all, the whole procedure is quite cruel, but “it is either them or us”. (I can imagine how how the nerve gas works on us humans!)

JUL 25

        Need I mention it – yep, more rain. Rained throughout the day, coming down in force in the afternoon. According to the paper, we had 10 inches of rain from Friday night to Sunday night. St. Louis barely manages to get 30 inches of rain all year round.

        Received a batch of slides back from Hawaii and enjoyed viewing them in my small viewer. On the roll of film were about 10 shots of Pusan, which came out quite good. They included scenes taken on the MSR, PX street and the street leading to Hialeah compound; of the main Pusan movie house; and a shot of Hialeah Compound looking down from the baseball field toward the Library! Couple of shots I took of Korea and Okinawa from the airplane weren’t too good, mainly because I didn’t have a haze filter. The rest of the shots are of Camp Kue, and general scenes of Okinawa including our Sunday visit to the carrier Hornet. The scenes of Kue should give the folks back home a little better picture of life on “the Keystone of the Pacific”.

        Went to the Castle Terrace Club for a couple of beers and a way to pass the evening. Worked out in a small room they have at Kue, in which they have weights, prior to going to the Club. Had to laugh at my self, for I did more exercise on my own than I ever would do in a me__ of PT classes. Typical I guess!

JUL 26

        More rain. Probably more rain in one period of time than I have ever experienced. Finished a Contract Modification that I was working on at work plus receiving the estimate of the Antenna Fields. The Contractor estimates were from $800 to $7000 higher than ours, and I will be interested to see how the negotiations turn out. I am sure the Contractors pad their estimates the way the Union Representatives at Dow use to pad their point evaluations. (They would be fools not to, for negotiations many times result in “dividing the difference.”)

        Well it looks as if my brief career as a teacher has come to the end of the line. Only 1 fellow showed up at class this evening thus precluding a discontinuance of the course. Oh well, made a little money besides having the experience of teaching one class.

        The new Reserve Bill has most of the fellows discussing and arguing the relative merits. The House and Senate were supposed to be voting on the revised bill and soon we should hear as to our fate once our 2 year hitch is complete. I hope I don’t have any more reserve obligation.

        Still thinking about what to do when I get out, – whether to serve 24 months and go into sales; serve 24 months, travel, and then go to law school; or serve 21 months and go to law school. Still have plenty of time left, but it is getting closer to the big day. I hope the letters I have written to these firms regarding employment of lawyers with technical backgrounds, will help me come to a decision.

        

JUL 27

        Guess what – yep more rain. Lets see, it has now rained 6 days straight and I imagine about 15 inches have fallen. Actually it hasn’t been too much of a bother, although it has eliminated the possibility of playing any tennis or golf. The ground is becoming quite soaked and indirectly has forced me to buy another pair of low quarter shoes, since my other ones are constantly getting water logged.

        Didn’t do much at work today, mostly worked on my own personal work plus some preparation for negotiation on the Antenna fields. The negotiation is at eight tomorrow and I am interested in seeing what develops. I feel perhaps that our estimate is a little low owing to the fact that the terrain is tougher and more hilly than we anticipated.

        The people on Okinawa are quite friendly, perhaps as friendly a group of people as I have ever met. They are always smiling and seem to laugh and giggle a lot. Physically they aren’t too attractive, although there are some that have cute looking faces. Most of the girls are squat and have small breasts. The men are not so squat looking, but are slight built. They have long black hair and are very obsequitous.

        Most of the grown-ups have bad complexions which add to their gold teeth. It seems that everyone has at least one gold tooth, and always in the front of the mouth. I like the Okinawans as they show me a lot more than the Koreans, under very similar circumstances.

JUL 28

        Most admit that the weather man held back somewhat today as we only had a slight drizzle of rain. The lack of rain, however, was sure evident as the atmosphere and humidity was almost 100% water. It drizzled around supper time to cool things off a bit.

        I sat in on a negotiation today which was somewhat interesting and also boring. The estimates for the Antenna Farms didn’t come up until after lunch, so I sat and listened (and kept hitting myself to stay awake) throughout the morning. The afternoon session was somewhat jumbled as the Government wanted the Contractor to do certain things – and be paid for some – and the Contractor just as soon have the Government do the work. One of the issues concerned transporting the poles (25’-85’) to the island of Okino and installing them at the transmitter and receiver sites. The Contractor said that it would be quite difficult getting the poles from the dock to the sites owing to the narrow roads. The meeting adjourned until Friday at which time the Gov’t will present the views of the Contracting Officer – Col. Miller.

        Five men sat in on the Contractors side and three for the Government. Of the five, – two were project engineers, one was a Hawaiian liaison man, another was an interpreter, and the fifth gentleman was Kokuba (No. 3), one of the 5 Kokuba brothers who has built up a lucrative construction company on Okinawa. The men were cool and collected, seemed to know what they were talking about and in general gave me a favorable impression of their actions.

JUL 29

        Turned out to be a nice day on Okinawa, and I attempted to make the most of it by playing some tennis. Took off work around 3:30 and walked the ¾ mile to the courts. The sun was blazing and the sweat poured out while I batted the ball against the backboard. I sure tired easily, and after about an hour, collected my junk – sun glasses, sunburn cream, racket, balls – and headed for Hut 725.

        The supper meal was pretty good as our are most of the meals at the mess hall. (relatively speaking). The mess hall is a large wooden building, divided into 3 eating sections – G.I’s, Japanese and Okinawans – each separate and distinct from the other. The food is served cafeteria style, and we use trays and plates. The tables seat four, and the chairs are comfortable padded ones. There are about 5 Okinawan girls to bring water, set the tables, get bread, etc., and as they are for the most part friendly girls, they provide a pleasant atmosphere to our meals.

        Some of the girls are nice looking (as Okinawans go) and laugh and kid around with the fellows. A few of the fellows date the girls, but it consists of nothing more than taking them to the Camp Kue movie. The girls are generally afraid to be seen in public with G.I’s as they feel they would be labeled “honeys” or as we call them – mistresses. From one or two fellows who have been here some time, I have been told that one or two of the girls have gone with G.I’s at Kue, probably more for friendship and accompany that money.

        The girls live in a woman’s compound located at the North end of Kue. They work 24 hours and have 24 hours off, plus 1 day off a week. They sleep in a dormitory type hut ,and eat the same food as we do. My curiosity is aroused concerning whether these girls, now that they are accustomed to a higher standard of living, whether they would be satisfied with marrying an Okinawan and living in the villages. Seems hard to believe they would, yet I guess love triumphs over most obstacles.

        One unusual thing, is that the Okinawan girls don’t believe in getting married until they are 22-25 years of age. Haven’t been able to find the reason for this as of yet.

JUL 30

        Pay day today, and I welcomed the $146 dollars that was coming to me. Quickly paid out $10 to my maid, $2 to the girls in the mess hall and $.60 for the man who cleans the latrine. Didn’t mind it though, as I enjoy the luxury.

        Worked this morning, which consisted of sitting in on the negotiation of the antenna fields. The contractor proposed $12,000 versus the company’s estimate of $7500. The meeting stalled on the question of transportation to Okino, one of the offshore islands, and neither side would give in. Mr Carlton of the Government team, checked with the Colonel, and proposed a split of the difference – $10,000. Agreement was soon reached. (Why need have the estimate!!)

JUL 31 (SUNDAY - WEEK 32)

        10 more months and all is behind. Won’t be too long I guess, at least if it passes as rapidly as the first 14 months. I got up early in the morning and met a fellow by the name of Parriott at the tennis courts. We played two sets, before he went to church, and he won both of them 6-4, 6-2. He was quite good, and beat me handily even though his game was somewhat off. He was the No. 3 man on the tennis squad that played in the AFFE tennis tournament.

        I waited around a little before going back to the hut, resting a few moments, and then headed for the mess hall. For the first time since I had been at Kue, we had something besides fried chicken, – and it turned out to be lousy boiled ham. Ate what I could and then adjourned back to the courts. Volleyed a few minutes with a Mister Peterson who was quite good, and who introduced me to a Col. Newcomer when he had to leave. Volleyed a bit with the “Old Man” (39 and a full bird!) and then had the audacity to suggest a set. Split the first 2 games before he blasted me off the court 6-1. I believe he was one of the best tennis players I have ever played. The Colonel and I then stood Perriott and Alfred in a game of doubles, which we proved victorious 6-4. It was an excellent game, including or in spite of my many errors.

        Thus I had a very enjoyable day of tennis together with a tender case of too much sun.

AUG 01

        At the end of last week, Mr. Kent, head of the Construction section of the Operations Division of OKED (of which I am a minor worker) said that he would like me to visit the 5 “J” Sites on Okinawa and the off shore islands so that one member of the section would be familiar with the work going on and particularly the terrain. As a further result of the conference, I contacted Capt. Griffin of the Air Force Division, who was the project officer of these projects. He told me that Phase III of the program was to start soon, and that an organized tour of the sites was to be taken starting August 1st, so that the contractors could see what was to be done and where it was to be built. He invited me along on the tour, and thus lined up an interesting week of visiting new places.

        The first place on the agenda was Miyako, located about 160 miles south of Okinawa. Flying was the logical method of getting there, so we met at Naha Air Base where we were flown in C-47’s down to Miyako. The flight lasted approximately 1 ¼ hours each way and was relatively smooth flying. Will have to admit that the dependable old C-47 is one of the best airplanes there is.

        Landed around 1:30 PM, and were was taken to the port where we were shown by Capt. Griffin and a civilian side kick, the approximate located of the 2 tanks to be constructed, the necessary piping and harbor facilities and the proposed improvement of the roads to the tanks. One tank is a 6000 gallon gas container and the other is a 1000 barrel Diesel Oil Tank. We then drove to the camp site and the miscellaneous roads and other improvements were pointed out on the way.

        Miyako is a fairly large island and I am told has about 100,000 native population. The land seems quite arable and the people typical of the small town Oriental. About 100-125 U.S. Servicemen are stationed here, and lead what I would imagine to be a quiet and dull existence. New barracks, recreational facilities, and other buildings are being built for this radar site, but very little has been completed up to now. When the 3 phases are completed living conditions will be 1000% better and should make life a little more endurable down here.

        Arrived back at Kue at 6:10, too late for Army chow, so I decided to eat at the Castle Terrace. The food was great, but I must admit my bank roll can’t take too much of such a luxury.

AUG 02

        Nothing was scheduled for today, so I worked in the office on an estimate and also did a little work on Contract Modification.

        Asked to have the afternoon off, and being that it was granted, I went to the Plaza PX and bought a hat (for tennis), alarm clock, Selsum shampoo (at a nearby pharmacy), gum, magazine & toothpaste. Looked at some ivory figures, meandered about the store and then caught the bus to Sukiran. Returned an overdue book, met a fellow I had bumped into on my Hong Kong trip, and found out I was too late to pick up my shoes. Back to Kue and supper, writing letters and bedtime.

AUG 03

        Today we drove up to Motobu Peninsula to a camp site called Yaetake. There the Captain pointed out to the Contractors the work to be done in the forthcoming Phase III – same as Miyako – and answered all questions concerning same.

        The Contractors then left and the Army personnel ate lunch at the camp – located at the top of a mountain – before looking over the work that was being done in Phase II. As at Miyako the army and air force personnel lived in temporary quonsets and tents, waiting the completion of the new buildings. These men operated the radar “ball” on a 24 hour basis and also did other jobs to make the camp self sufficient. The radar was is located on what use to be the tallest peak on Okinawa (before they cut it donw) and provides early warning of approaching aircraft.

        From the peak where the radar was located, one could get a tremendous view of the surrounding countryside and particularly of Ie Shima an off shore island in the Ryukyus Island Chain. It was on this island that savage fighting took place during World War II, and is probably best known for the fact that Ernie Pyle was killed here.

        I was informed that security regulations wouldn’t allow any picture taking, even if I took them only of the surrounding scenery. (Stupid non-enforced regulation, but I happened to be among some RA officers) The visit lasted all afternoon and was very enlightening.

AUG 04

        Today we visited the “J” site at Yozadake which is located on the Southern tip of the island. To get there we drove through Naha and Itoman, the later town being new to me. The roads were bad and we bumped along, talking about things in general. The Colonel who was along, began kidding the driver (a 60-65 year old civilian employee) about his “roving” eye, and out of the blue the old man divulges his love life. Frankly I was amazed at what he said for I always assumed old men to be nothing but onlookers. Well, – live and learn!

        There were no soldiers or Air Force personnel at Yozadake, as the radar equipment has not been installed. However, the new 160 man barracks is about 90% completed and I imagine troops will be sent down in a month or so. This particular contract is being done by Kokuba Sumi, an Okinawan Construction firm. The people in the firm are very friendly, and eager to do a good job. They have a lot to learn, but they realize it and welcome construction comments. Besides the Army work, the company is also doing a lot of building in and around Naha. For instance, one of their latest projects is a modern, air conditioned theater soon to be opened to the public.

        While walking around the area, one of the men pointed to a ridge, beyond which he said, was Suicide Cliff where many top ranking Japanese committed _au-_au at the end of the Okinawan campaign. I will have to visit the cliff in the near future.

AUG 05

        Got up early and together with another GI Engineer, Bill Cornell, were taken to Naha Port via Army transportation. There we boarded the LSM A63 at 6 AM along with 4 other Army personnel, 2 civilian OKED employees and about 30 Japanese and Okinawan contractors.

        The ship sailed promptly at 6:05 and we headed south for the Ryukyun Island of Kume. The trip took about 5 hours, and was relatively smooth – the first leg of our voyage. I had only gotten about 5 hours sleep the previous night, so I headed for the sack shortly after breakfast. We were quartered (Bill and I) in the officers section but ate on the enlisted side. The bunks were better than those we had on the troop ship, but they still were 3 high and jammed tightly in a small room. On the trip to Kume I alternated sleeping and sweating for the two hours I lay in laid in the bunk. Around 11 AM I was told that we had arrived at Kume, and I hurried to the deck in time to see them lower the front landing ramp – typical of these ships – and enter the small dock area at Kume.

        At Kume we were shown where the two storage tanks and pipelines were to be installed and then were driven to the compound on the top of the highest hill. The road leading from the pier to the compound is to be improved and was thus pointed out to the contractors. It was about 1:30 when we arrived at the “peak” and since we had about 5 hours till the boat was to leave, Bill and I walked around the compound, sticking our noses everywhere.

        We visited the radar sites, which is the purpose of these “J” sites, and were able to get a Lt. to explain the workings of the system. Basically, at the present, they have 2 main radar equipment; – one that judges height of objects in the surrounding area, and the other that determines within a 500 mile radius the location of ships and planes. He said that they knew whenever Chinese planes flew in this area, what ships were passing, etc. Within 3 minutes word can be radioed to Naha, and within 10 minutes jet fighters will be in the air.

        Visited some of the construction presently going on, and “shot the bull” with some of the boys at the PX. We ate chow at their mess hall, and around 5 PM headed for the ship. At 6, we departed for Okino and it proved to be a rough trip.

AUG 06

        I hit the sack early and was awakened around 2 AM Saturday morning to the pounding and vibration of the ship on the waves. (I think that is correct, as this was a flat bottom ship) From 2 AM to around 5 AM, I didn’t sleep very soundly, owing to the rough weather.

        At Okino we anchored off shore and boarded a small LCM for transportation to the island. The dock facilities were poor, and even the small craft was only able to enter and leave the so called harbor when the tide was in. Since the tide was to go out at 11 AM, we were told to hurry up on our tour in order to be able to leave the island without having to wait till nighttime.

        The tour first visited the water supply which consisted of an underground spring which fed into a reservoir located in a cave. The water was then pumped 60 feet to the first station, and then to the campsite located as the others were, on the highest point of the island. The cave was interesting and while on my way to its entrance I saw bamboo growing for the first time. The stalks or stems or very straight and from what I gather, grow quite fast

        We then visited – via a tremendously rough road – the proposed airstrip, roads that were to be improved, and the new docking facilities. We passed through one of the most primitive villages that I have ever seen, and which seemed shut off from the rest of the island and world. From all indications the village had been there a long time, but still existed on what they grew and made. Also had an occasion to visit a small tea plantation, and saw how tea grew and how it was dried and cured. We then hurried back to the boat, whereupon we set sail around 11:30 AM and got back at Naha at 7 PM.

AUG 07 (SUNDAY - WEEK 33)

        Called Lyle Nelson, Carol Ann Chevitz’s fiancee – shortly after breakfast and found out that the dinner at the Seaman’s Club that we had planned together had to be moved up to lunch on account of he had to go to work in the evening. Consequently, he, I and 3 of his friends conveyed on the Seaman’s Club in Naha shortly after 1 PM and there devoured 1’ thick, well-done steaks. The price was high, but the food was worth it. As a rule a thick steak doesn’t send me into ecstasy, but this steak hit the spot.

        Caught the bus back to Kue, and upon returning, engaged in a little tennis.

AUG 08

        Back to work for a change. After a week of doing nothing but walking, riding and travelling by ship and plane to the J sites, it was somewhat difficult to sit in one chair for the whole day. I still had an estimate to work up for Miyako, consequently it occupied most of my time. This was really my first estimate by myself but I only had to estimate the labor, – the Government furnishing the materials. After witnessing the negotiations on the Antenna Field, I am anxious to see what happens to this estimate.

        In the evening I caught a local bus and for 13 yen I road to Naha. The city is really being built up, and I believe I am more conscious of the construction that is going on, every time I visit Naha. This was the first time I had been in Naha in the night time, and I stood outside the movie theater for about a half hour before going in. The streets were crowded as many people were coming home from work. It was interesting to see the people pass, the expressions on their face, and the type of dress they had on. Now and then a couple of young men passed or went in the show, clothed in a robe with a sask sack and wooden sandals. The women for the most part had Western type clothing on, although occasionally some old women passed dressed in these robes. I have to chuckle at these women, for they wear nothing under the robe, and when they go to get their belongings they have placed under the robe, they expose their wrinkled bodies to the public.

        The movie consisted of a double feature – a French film and a Japanese film. The French picture was in color and even though it I couldn’t understand the words, the acting and story didn’t impress me. The Japanese picture took place in Rio de Janero, and had all the ear marks of being halfway decent. However, the film must have broken earlier in the day and when they went to splice it, the spliced it all wrong. Some scenes were out of place, others were repeated twice and thus confusion, added to my lack of understanding of the language prompted me to walk out.

        Downstairs from the movie house was a night club, and I dropped in for a “quick one”. Decided on a plain 7 up which I sipped while I watched the other people. A “B girl” was sent to sit with me (and dance also if I wanted) but other than saying she could sit down I ignored her completely. After my drink I caught the bus for Kue. I will have to come back, but next time with a bunch of boys to kick it up!

AUG 09

        Finished my estimate on the Miyako overhead power line, and instead of requesting another job, I took it easy in the afternoon. I spent the time reading from a book on basic mechanical and chemical properties of materials, plus typing an occasional letter to a Patent Attorney in St. Louis. I am writing to 10 such lawyers, in conjunction with the 33 letters I wrote to large corporations requesting general information of their Legal Departments. Incidentally I have received 8 answers, most of which are from 2-3 pages in length. The replies are interesting and I believe I am going to get some valuable information.

AUG 10

        Since I missed training on Saturday, I had to make it up this afternoon, however training today consisted only of watching movies at the Camp Kue theater. The first one was on Map Reading, and since I have seen it ten thousand times before, it lulled me to sleep. The next movie was a captured German movie and showed the Germans capturing a bridge in the Netherlands. It was quite interesting and showed the German soldier in good light. (Actually any winning team looks good)

        The next movie concerned the assault on a small island in the Pacific by the Marines. To say the least it was a bloody picture and really illustrated the horrors of war, and in particular, was fought by having to take hundreds of well fortified small islands. The last picture was on supply economy (and the $15,000 pencil!) and as the first, it was somewhat boring.

        Ate chow – played volleyball – worked out a little with some weights, and then headed for the Castle Terrace. On Wednesday and Saturdays they have amateur night and unlike the two previous shows, the talent tonight was great. First came a Japanese dance followed by a member of the 8105 singing “The Jones Boys”. The show was then “stolen” by a 11 year old violinist who was terrific. She played Ava Marie for a 2nd number and proved she was not just a rote musician. A G.I. comedian was on next and put on some good acts. The last number was a Filipino singer who was only fair but didn’t distract from the show. Even the food – egg salad sandwich – was good tonight.

AUG 11

        Found out today that I probably goofed with respect to the color shots I took on our trip the past week. Can’t say where I got the idea, but I was of the opinion that it was possible and desirable to use filters with color film so as to bring out certain colors, etc. Consequently, I wrote home to Morton to send me his, and received them about 2 weeks ago in a package. On Okino in particular I used the light yellow and light green filters, and am interested to see the mess I created by using the filters. I am sorry of what has happened – glad that I found out in time, however – for it is not likely that I will visit Okino again.

        In the evening, Bob E_cson and I went to play tennis, but found that the courts were taken when we got there. We were able to get up a doubles game, and took a beating from 2 Filipinos. Not that they were good, it was through our really poor playing, however, I guess in the long run they could beat us more than we could beat them.

        The Filipinos are as a rule, quite friendly and do pretty good work. They have the same privileges as the Americans, although they do not get the same money for equivalent 65 ratings. Many – perhaps 90% – are here without their families, and they treat the Okinawan women the same as the G.I’s. Generally, they have their own groups, and stick in them for the most part. Many of them live at Camp Kue, and have the same living quarters as the G.I’s. They speak Spanish among themselves, but are all able to speak English and some Japanese.

AUG 12

        In the afternoon I had a field trip to make and drove (actually was driven in a sedan) down to the Machinato Service Area. There I checked the location of the new boiler house, and the piping that was necessary and which I was to bid on make an estimate on.        Back at OKED I checked the Engineering drawings and found out that the pipe should have been there before, and by its omission, would require tearing up of pavement to put it in. Checked further into the new work required, and found that some of it had been completed by the Past Engineers. Well, after getting nowhere, I went to see Army Construction, but the particular men interested were not in, so I will check with them on Monday.

        In the evening I had my first date with Okinawan girls, and it turned out that I had to take 2 girls, as this was the Okinawan custom (of some) when the girls are afraid what others might think if they were seen paired with a GI. Well, to make a long story short, Larson, who prodded the whole deal with me at the Castle Terrace Club on Wednesday, “chickened out” and “old watash” (I) had to take the girls to the local cinema.

        The girls waited till the other people had gone in, and then joined me at the front door. I sat down first – in the middle of 3 seats – but they decided to both sit together on my right. The conversation was mainly between themselves, with my getting in one or two words. After the show was out, we went to the ball field and watched for a few innings before I took them home. Some date!

AUG 13

        Samo-samo training. Five boring films that put me to sleep but fast. The trouble is that theater seats aren’t the greatest for sleeping, and the back of my neck suffers so that the rest of my body can have some peace.

        In the afternoon some of the fellows decided to rent a boat and go out to some nearby reefs and do a little skin diving and fishing. I said I was interested and so the 7 of us piled into 2 cabs and went to the small town on the sea shore where one can rent a boat. We haggled a little with the papasan, and finally rented one of the sanpans for the afternoon for 600 yen. The boat was one of these gasoline put-put jobs and we plowed along at high speed until we came to the area where there were coral reefs.

        It began raining when we arrived at the reefs, and along with the indecision among the boys as to where was the best spot to drop anchor, we drifted aimlessly for about a half hour. The rain then subsided and we all jumped in to either skin dive or keep from getting sea sick as the waves were really rocking our little boat.

        I didn’t have any equipment, so for the first portion of our stay, I swam and treaded water as it was too deep to stand in the water. After awhile one of the fellows got tired and I borrowed his face mask, fins and snorkel arrangement. I had difficulty with the snorkel as I was constantly getting water in my mouth and my mask also clouded up to give me trouble.

        I finally borrowed one of the fellows mask which had a built in snorkel. It was very easy to use, and I had a great time floating along, face down, peering at the new world below. We had dropped anchor on a coral reef and the bottom was quite irregular in that it had its valleys and hills made up of the porous, sharp pointed coral rock.

        Brilliant colored fish swam by and it seemed as if artists had dabbed each of them with the brightest colors on their eisel. Some of the fish were black with light blue stripes, some were yellow and black, others were almost colorless. Also on the reefs were the small sea urchins, the sea horses, plant life and everything imaginable. After awhile, we decided to head for shore, but not before I had vowed to myself to get a mask and continue my newly found interest.

AUG 14 (SUNDAY - WEEK 34)

        Seemed to be a typical goof off day, as I did very little all day. Read, talked, slept and wrote in this diary. Had planned to play some tennis, however I went to our 10’ x 15’ gym and worked out instead. Did some exercises and then grunted and groaned and swet sweated in attempting to press some weights. Right at the present I am laboring with 50lbs, although it seems like 150. Some of the fellows suggested a couple of sitting up and back exercises which I did, but not with any ease. Hard to realize how out of shape and weak I am, and but  maybe I will get enough ambition to do something about it.

AUG 15

        Finally decided to put in for a leave from 6 Sept. to about the 17th . Stopped in the Orderly Room on the way to work, and had the Clerk type out the form. Then I hand carried it to my section where Mr. Kent signed his name to the slip, thus making my release from the section official. This leaves signatures by the 1st Sgt. and Company Commander and I will be all set.

        Some boat mail came in today, and I received my weekly Post Dispatch. This time I got 2 issues, and I spent the evening reading back papers, plus the Time magazine that I get through the mail on Mondays. It is really good to get the home town papers, as it brings one up to date on what is happening with the folks back in old St. Louie. In this way I will be somewhat cushioned for the shock of being away for over a year and a half, and having to get accustomed to all the new construction and projects.

        I was really pleased to read in the paper a little while ago, of the passage of a $110 million bond issue which will be used to improved “dying” St. Louis. Much is needed to keep St. Louis from falling by the wayside, and although it took a couple submittals to the populace before it finally was passed, it is better late than not at all. I understand that the Plaza project is on its way, and soon there will be a decent section of town from 12th street to Kiel Auditorium. Then of course there are the improvements with the highways, streets and other long range projects.

AUG 16

        Hate to admit it but it seems as if I am beginning to get in a rut. If it was a constructive rut, I guess I wouldn’t mind, but I am afraid it is too much dissipation. My day generally consists of awakening at 6:15, doing some pushups and bending exercises, glancing at Dickie’s newspaper and then going to wash and shave. I then return to the hut, get dressed and head for the mess hall. Breakfast consists of cold toast, milk and 2 eggs, and usually lasts approximately 25 minutes. Back to the company area, brush my teeth, stand reveille, shoot the breeze for 10 minutes, and then walk the ¾ - 1 mile to work.

        For awhile I began the morning by typing a letter or two to the corporations that I have been writing too, but now I goof around, and finally start work about 8. My work consists of estimating or contract modification, primarily the former, and of which I am a total novice. Lunch is about 12 to 12:25 and the other 35 minutes is spent washing my face, teasing the maids and reading. Back to work at 1 and usually it is spent like the mornings. At 4:30 I generally pull out my typewriter and bang off a letter or two before chow. Chow takes about 30 minutes – depending on who I sit with or how much time I talk to the waitresses. Volleyball follows the supper meal and after a couple games I generally, or as of late, go to the gym for a little work out. Then its a shower and either dress for reading or going out. Going out mainly means the Castle Terrace although occasionally I go to Naha or the show. So now I am tired, and it is bedtime around 11:15 or 11:30.

AUG 17

        Was assigned a real lulu of a job in the office today, – that of estimating a cost per acre for topsoiling, spot sodding and sprigging. I didn’t even know what the last term meant and had to look it up in the erosion section of the contract. Actually it is nothing more than planting individual grass sprouts in the ground, somewhat similar to planting of rice.

        My boss and I decided to visit Chinen, where the work on the above was to be done, so as to obtain an idea of the terrain. Chinen is located on the Pacific Ocean side of Okinawa, about 10 miles to the Southeast of Kue. It is a secluded camp; very hush hush in nature. I am told that very few people know what goes on there, and that there are certain areas and warehouses where only screened personnel can enter. The camp is self sufficient, and has all the conveniences within the area. The military personnel do not wear their uniforms and mix in with the civilian Government employees. (Perhaps I should have asked one of the Okinawan maids what went on down there, as they always seem to know everything)

        Speaking of maids, I think mine just got a “honey”, a marine jarhead to top it all. Oh well, I HAD my chance and flubbed it I guess, but maybe I could switch maids?

AUG 18

        Spent the day at work trying to come up with some reasonable estimate for the topsoiling, sprigging and strip sodding that is to be done at Chinen. I checked with the estimating section of Engineering plus some of the men in our department, and I was at least a couple thousands dollars per acre apart. Finally said to heck with it and developed my own price which came out to be $947 / acre. The contractor’s proposal was $700 / acre and so it seems as if I allowed too many labour, trucks or something. Frankly, the Contractor’s price is very reasonable and I am wondering exactly what he intends to do. Oh well, that is the problem of the Project Engineer.

        Had some good volleyball games in the evening, in which I began laughing so hard I barely had enough strength to hit the ball over the net. One of the fellows is a great spiker and the game generally revolves around whether he is in fou__, which means bullet like blasts coming from his side of the net. My main problem is eating early enough so that I can digest my food before I play.

        I had good intentions to study this evening, but a couple of the boys stayed to shoot the bull. This was followed by an invitation to the Castle Terrace and there went my evening. For the first time our favorite waitress waited on us (Chizuko) but she was pissed off at me for kidding her too much the evening before. Thus the love of my life (on the Rock) had snuffed out my flaming heart! (Whew – )

AUG 19

        I guess I must be getting into a rut, for things are becoming so regular that I have little to write about except a few trifles concerning my daily work. Today I started on a new estimate concerning connecting a 36” concrete drain pipe to an inlet, and to better acquaint myself with the job I took a field trip to the site. The drain pipe had already been laid and the connection made, so I wasn’t able to learn much. Will continue on it on Monday.

        One good discussion subject among some of the boys, is the “right” or “rights” we have here on Okinawa. Some say we are taking too much good (and much needed) ground for projects, and which were rice fields handed down from generation to generation. They go on to say that the $22 / acre we pay isn’t enough to support the families even though it may be the actual worth of the land. A few people go even farther and believe that we should pay the Okinawans what they ask for the land, and those that do not want to sell, should not be forced to sell.

        On the other hand, the people argue that Okinawa has been decided by our military planners to be the U.S. bastion in the Far East. Consequently, a semipermanent type of installation is to be built which requires a lot of Okinawan labor and land. The wages to the labor help make up for some of the deposed land owners, and the skills they are learning, will in time raise their standard of living, and change their economy from strictly an agricultural economy to a mixture of agriculture and small industries. To say that we should pay what the Okinawans demand, or to turn back if they refuse to sell, seemingly cannot be tolerated. Surely an equitable price should be paid and to that end a fair and non-partial appeal board has to be set up. Actually it is no different than eminent domain back in the states.

        I guess I lean towards the later view, particularly if a fair and equitable board is set up. I believe that an island like Okinawa, with a limited population of say 800,000, is easier to disrupt and then provide for than a country such as Japan. It is inevitable that the standard of living will rise here, and that even though the Ryukyans don’t admit it, they are in a way appreciative of the opportunity to further themselves. Still, I believe they prefer going back to Japan as against home rule, and herein lies a problem for the U.S.

AUG 20

        Training today consisted of a Character Guidance lecture from the new Reform Jewish Rabbi, which was fair, and a mine laying technique lecture. The latter was given in Futima (near by) and took about 1 ½ hours to present a 20 minute talk. During the practice portion of the program, some of the 8105 boys, including myself, laughed at some of our “morning-after” boys, and I think we have heard just the beginning. A Lieutenant and Major from Rycom got quite provoked and voiced their disapproval to our 1st Sergeant. A 1st 3 Grades meeting has been called for Monday!!

AUG 21 (SUNDAY - WEEK 35)

        Well it finally happened; – after putting my watch in my pocket, on the latrine shelf, and every other conceivable place, I finally put it some place where I can’t remember where it is. Thus it looks as if I have lost my watch, and I am very sorry that it happened. I guess I will buy one of these small pocket watches to tide me over until right before I leave when I will buy a very good wrist watch.

        Played tennis in the morning after a long respite from the game. Didn’t play too good though, in fact I stunk. In the afternoon I went to the PX to buy some odd items that I need, and finished my shopping by buying 2 stamp envelopes filled with Japanese stamps. My chagrin came to a head very fast when I found that the stamps were mostly duplicates and to top that, they were still on the envelopes. Well, after a few minutes of muttering I finally steamed them off, and will send them to Alan and Peter.

        In the evening Dicker (MOT) and I went to a social gathering of the Okinawan Jewish clan. It was held at a Kadena mess hall, and consisted of bingo, bridge, cake and ice tea. It wasn’t too bad, although I didn’t win any prizes. At the end we took 3 cakes back to Kue and the so starved personnel therein.

        I met the new Rabbi and at first opinion,  am not too impressed. He probably just came from school and seems quite immature to fill the shoes of somewhat to pick up the spark of Judaism on “the Rock.”

AUG 22

        My faith in my fellow man was renewed this morning when I went into the Orderly Room to see if I could post a notice about my misplaced wrist watch. The First Sergeant said,  “Is this it?” and opened his desk drawer. Sure enough, there big as a cow, was my watch, smelly band and all. He said that one of the G.I’s in the unit had found it in the latrine and had turned it in Saturday morning. Whew was I glad and so was my pocketbook. Now perhaps I will be a little more careful with the few valuable possessions that I have.

        I stayed late at work this evening, and wrote four overdue letters. With the exception of 5 letters that I have recently received, I am now caught up on my correspondence. I will answer the above mentioned letters when I return from my leave.

        On the way back to the barracks around 7:30, I met Bill Numacher who is in our unit and who is scout master of one of the troops on the “Rock.” He invited me to sit in on a Board of Review for one of his scounds scouts who was attempting to pass 2nd class. I decided to do so, and for the next 45 minutes to 1 hour, I relived a portion of my life that took place 13 years ago. The boy was a good looking chap, who was quite nervous and not too well prepared. Still he did a fair job in answering the questions, and Mr. Kent passed him. Sure seems a long time ago that I was a scout, but I can recall the fun and knowledge that I got from it.

AUG 23

        Things really popped today at work. I had 3 rush jobs to do, each of them being vague in scope and detail. Checked with a project officer and then with some Okinawans in regard to supplying dirt and rock for some fills in the Futenma Housing Area. It was sure hard to get across to the Okinawans what we wanted, and I really don't think they ever did understand. Still I got some general information which I can use.

        In the afternoon, a Major from Air Force construction came in and wanted a rush-rush job concerning an estimate for an insecticide they were thinking of using. The trade name of the liquid was Chlordane, but we had not much else to go on. Check with materials section, purchasing, post engineers, engineering and quartermaster, and managed to scrape together some rough facts as to price, % concentrate etc.

The evening's entertainment consisted of volleyball, weight lifting, and Bingo. Yep, I broke down and decided to invest $1 in a card. Naturally I didn't win, and to be frank, I didn't even come close enough to say “ Oh Shit” the G.I term for Bingo. The crowd was huge and I would estimate about 600 people played. They bought $1,200 worth of cards plus drinks and eats, and consequently did quite well for the Castle Terrace. They gave out $890 in prizes plus 10-20 bottles of whiskey. Many Filipinos played each week, but they didn't seem to be any more luckier or "more clever" than the others disclaiming some rumors that I have heard. Bingo has sure good over Big in the U.S. world of entertainment.

AUG 24

        Funny how some days a lot of mail will come in and other days there will be hardly enough to take more than 1 or 2 minutes to read. Monday I received 9 particles of mail, including a Time magazine which I get every Monday. Today I received only 1 letter, and it wasn’t very interesting at that. Well, who knows, perhaps Friday I will get a lot. Airmail only comes in 3 times a week, and boat mail about once a week. This differs from Korea where mail came in daily.

        So far I have keep up a fairly good correspondence, although I do notice that as time goes on my letters and those of the other writers are spaced further and further apart. For awhile I tried to answer no more than 1 month after I received a letter. At the present, it is 2-3 months and might become longer after my forthcoming leave. Lets see, I have 5 replies to answer, and most of them are about 1 - ½ months old. As I mentioned earlier I will probably answer them after I return from leave when I have more to write about.

        Went to see “Glass Slipper” at the theater in the evening, and thought it was somewhat entertaining. Thence to the Chinaman’s for something to eat, and back to hut 725. Started to read my Torts when Charlie Terry came in and we had an interesting conversation about the Army, Okinawa, life in general and other “discussable thoughts.” Nothing earthshaking, but it was interesting to hear what the other man has to say about problems that affect the both of us.

AUG 25

        Work, I find, is becoming more interesting as the weeks go on. Seems like all the estimates are different and for the most part, new to me. Consequently, I generally have to labor OVER the date or blueprint for some time before coming up with a reasonable amount. Today I spent my time checking some figures proposed by a Contractor for some additional work he was to do. Since I am quite a beginner with plumbing, I solicited the help of Fujiwara, a Japanese engineer who works in our section.

        Subsequent to my earlier efforts at “picking off” the additional work, Fijiwara methodically showed me how what (and why) was needed and how much it cost. After gathering all the information I retired to my typewriter to bang out an estimate.

        Had some plans for the evening but nothing very exciting happened. Tossed a football around for an hour or so, and then shot the breeze for a few minutes more. Took a shower and then proceded to the day room for a chess game. Waited about 45 minutes for the game in process to end, and then I played. The game lasted over an hour and a half, and to say the least, I got quite tired. Finally in a flair of action we ended the game and I went back, sleepily, to the hut. Chess is all right and even a lot of fun, but it isn’t much enjoyment if the other player is so slow. I think some of the skill lies in summing up the situation in a hurry – or a small period of time – and executing the plays in that manner. When I play slow, my thoughts drift, and I lose the continuity. (Some call it rationalisation!)

AUG 26

        For awhile I thought we had endured the rainy weather for 1955, but I must say that any hopeful signs were erroneous. For the past 5 or 6 days it has rained every day, and almost 12 of every 24 hours in those days. The ground is saturated and in many places there is from ½” to 1” of water lying about. I finally switched to my boots yesterday, as my other shoes were getting soaked, likewise my socks. I really don’t mind the rain during the week, but I don’t care much for rain on the weekends.

        I can’t complain about the weather, though, since I have been noticing in the Stars & Stripes that St. Louis continues to experience 90° weather. I imagine that these high temperatures coupled with the usual high humidity has made St. Louis a haven for air conditioning salesmen. On the other hand, things have been pretty good here on “the Rock.” Sure it has been hot and sticky, but still I can’t complain, as there haven’t been any typhoons (knock on wood) or any extremely hot weather. The temperature generally varies between 75 and 89° and the relative humidity from low to the saturation point. It is when it (humidity) gets high, that I wish I were located in Hokkaido, Japan.

        Took my slides to work today, hoping to ride write or type a couple sentences about each one. However, I spent so much most of the time – between 4:30 - 5:45 - showing the slides to various individuals that I never got very far. Will have to finish it Monday.

AUG 27

        Tokusan rain! It has been raining off and on all week, and there seems to be no let up in sight. Today was typical training day, and we saw about 5 movies, one of them a general movie about power; two of them concerned atomic energy; and the last two were about the infantryman. Actually, I thought the first movie about power was the worst even though it was made by the Norfolk and Western Railroad. All through the movie there were references to this “great country of ours”, “how wonderful everything is”, “how much better we are” etc. I am a firm admirer of what has been done in the past, and also what has to be worked on in the future – but trite sayings such as the above get me quite sick to the stomach. Definitely not the type of movie to be shown overseas, or even to the American public for it tends to make people complacent and to rest on their laurels.

        Owing to the rain I stayed in all afternoon and did some reading. I bought a small pocketbook on about places of interest, etc on this here Rock. one of the festivales – Obon – takes place the latter part of the week, and I was interested in acquiring a little background about it. I asked one of the waitresses in the mess hall about the festival but for some reason or another she didn’t know anything about it. Finally I changed my pronunciation slightly and she said, “Oh, Obon!” She laughed so hard at my mispronunciation that I wasn’t able to learn anything from her. Incidentally, this particular waitress was born in Peru, and can speak English, Spanish and Japanese.

AUG 28 (SUNDAY - WEEK 36)

        More rain, plus some pretty stiff winds. Consequently my day was spent inside, with reading, writing and talking occupying my time.

        Last night some of the boys in the unit, plus a few others, had a party at Dave Rinker’s house – supply sergeant. The party lasted quite late – 4 AM to be exact – and when they arrived back at Kue they made a little noise. Actually, they made enough noise, plus waking up people, that a lot of the troops were cogniza cognizant of what time they came in. Today most of the fellows were either talking about the good time they had or the ungodly time in the morning that they were awakened.

        In our hut, two of the fellows participated, two were quite pissed off, two were somewhat neutral and I didn’t hear them. At lunch time I sat with one of the fellows that was somewhat perturbed, and he voiced his comments concerning the fellows and their weekly and bi-weekly d__nks. At supper time, I sat with the two that were quite loaded, and they laughed throughout the mail about the good time they had falling all over themselves.
