        I guess I don’t care what they do, as they don't seem inclined to come in my room at night to wake me up. Oh, if I hear them, I might get momentarily provoked, but I generally fall asleep soon and forget about it. Can’t see much sense in complaining, for it doesn’t happen too often, and I know that if I were living in a barracks, the occurrences would be more frequent.

AUG 29

        I will be glad when I get to Japan and have something interesting to write about. Unlike Korea, there are stretches of 4 and 5 days when I don’t leave Kue and thus am not in contact with the native Okinawans. Work continues to move along okay, and life in general isn’t bad. Still the rain, but by now it doesn’t phase me.

        I generally spend part of my Monday evenings reading the Time magazine that I receive in the mail. It keeps me up to date on the news and miscellaneous events that occur in other activities. Right now things look like good in Europe, fair in Asia, and bad in North Africa and the Middle East. It just seems that the French do not have a decent Colonial policy and in most of their remaining possessions, the Nationalist movements have erupted into bloody fighting.

        The United States is always put on the spot in those international problems, for it was only 180 years ago that the 13 Colonies fought the British for their independence. Today the movement is strong everywhere and can be seen in French North Africa, Cyprus, Crete, Sudan, and French Indo China. Africa is about the only major area where colonies are still remaining, and I don’t imagine we will have much peace and tranquility there for many years to come.

        The Israel-Egypt mess is just that – a mess. Both sides are stubborn and refuse to give in a little to arrive at a compromise. It is such a farce when one stops to think of the benefits that could be derived from the money now going into the war machine.

AUG 30

        9 more months and I’ll be out, – honey, honey! Won’t be long? With every ship that leaves Okinawa, a few of the boys in camp Kue leave for the “Hew Ess A.” The longer that I am here, the better I get to know most of the fellows, and the sorrier I am to say good bye. Oh, I guess I can’t really say that I am sorry, for I am happy for them that they are leaving for the states; and also, there aren’t any of them that I spend most of my time with.

        On the boat leaving Friday, Charlie Whitmire and Leonard Poole are the ones that I know best who are leaving. Charlie was the TI&E clerk and is from salem, Missouri – near the Current River. He went to Missouri University and will probably go to work for his dad at the 1st National Bank in Salem. Len worked in Finance and is from Belleville, illinois. He is a school teacher, and will probably follow that profession unless he goes to work for his father in the building weatherizing business. Both of the fellows are real nice guys, with good senses of humor and whom I wouldn’t mind seeing back home.

        Len is a very shy fellow with women and treats them all as if they were perfect angels. Lately he has been dating Yoshiko, one of the waitresses in the mess, and although he knows she use to sleep with one of the boys in the outfit (since got home) he talks to her and respects her like any “nice girl” back home. In fact my curiosity is aroused as to whether he has ever kissed her! Still I respect him for his attitude and wish more American G.I’s had it.

AUG 31

        Got paid first thing in the morning, and then signed up for sick call, thinking that Pay Day would be a good day to go to the dispensary. Had them look in my ears for wax, and when I was told that there was quite a bit in the ear, I told them to go ahead and take it out. Actually I am a little leary about letting the G.I’s in the dispensaries mess with my ears, but there is not much else that I can do since a lot of wax cakes around my ear drum. If they use too much pressure I generally tell them, so that they don’t blow a hole in my head. The fellow who did it today was pretty good, and it didn’t take long.

        On the preceding page I wrote about Poole and Whitmire, but I didn’t mention one of the outstanding things that they did. They and Campbell, found out that Junko, Campbell’s maid, was a high school graduate and was different – or better – than the average lot of maids. They decided to send her to the University of the Ryukyus, and made the preliminary arrangements. She wasn’t able to start this fall, so instead they are sending her to a 8 week night school in which she can improve her English and prepare for the entrance exams. Then if she passes the tests, they will pay the $150.00 needed to send her to school. If she doesn’t pass, they will then pay for another Okinawan to go to college. Sounds great to me and I am really pulling for this girl.

SEP 01

        Another day at work, and one less to do before I go on my leave this coming Sunday. Borrowed another AWOL bag and it looks as if I am all set. Even got my money lined up that is, I bought 2 $100 MPOs and plan to take the remainder in MPC.

        Today, as were the two preceding days is a big holiday for the Okinawan people, and most Buddhist people throughout the world. Here on Okinawa, it is called Obon, and it commemorates those who have passed on to the next world. The people pray, leave food and drink at the tombs and then on the 3rd day, dance and sing.

        Chapman and I decided to go to Nago to see the dancing and singing, and so around 6:00 we headed for the above city which is the 2nd largest on Okinawa. It is about 40-50 miles north of Kue, and has very few American troops in the surrounding area. We had our transportation problems, and after standing, cramped sitting, riding the wrong bus, hitch hiking and then taking another bus, we finally arrived around 8:00. We walked around the town, asking where the dancing was, but nobody seemed to know. We did find out that the last buses left around 9 PM, but we didn’t believe the people; at least we didn’t think they understood us.

        In the distance we heard some noise and decided to go investigate the source. It turned out to be a group of male dancers, dancing and singing to the tunes from 3 samisens (3 string guitar) and a couple of drums. The group – about 25 – danced in a circle, with a couple movements in towards the center. They were dressed in white, had a white band on their head, and carried little white fans with a red spot in the center. Groups of children and adults gathered and listened to the young men. Three lanterns were carried which had decorated sides and 4 or 5 lighted candles on the inside. After staying in one spot for awhile, they would then move on to a different area.

        Around 9 PM we met a waitress that works in the mess hall, and we asked her when the last bus went goes to Naka. Sure enough, the last bus had left or was about to leave in a few minutes. We hurried to the bus station and boarded the bus. Before this, a little boy (8 years old) had followed us as we walked around. He was quite friendly and full of pep and energy, so we decided to buy him a soda and some gum. He really was a sight, dressed in a little kimono and drinking a Pepsi-cola. After talking to him awhile, he said Sayonara and went home.

SEP 02

        I finished my last estimate early in the morning, and spent the rest of the day doing nothing. My boss – Joe Alfonsi – told me that he was going to be sent to Formosa in about a week, and that I probably wouldn’t see him for a while. I am sorry to see him go, for he was a good guy along with being a fair and understanding man. He is relatively young – 31, and I am somewhat surprised at his attitude of staying in the Orient and “why” attitude towards getting married and settling down. Still, he likes what he is doing, so I guess that answers my questions.

SEP 03

        Training was mandatory and consisted of some 4 hours of messing with mines, and pertinent information relating to the laying of a mine flied. I was only one half awake all morning, so I guess I must of missed the interesting part, for the portion that I heard was sure boring.

        Saw “Slick” E_mlick at lunch and he jabbered something about tennis, and so after chow I put on my tennis duds and headed for the courts. We volleyed for awhile, and when he left, I played some with a navy boy who was at the courts. My lack of exercise soon became apparent and after a couple hours, I retired to my hut for an easier life. Showered, and then packed my two AWOL bags and readed myself for the “hoped for” midnight plane ride.

        Instead of waiting for the call, I joined a bunch of the boys at the Castle Terrace for something to eat and drink. They had their usual huge Saturday night crowd and we were stuck way in the back. However, our own noise and entertainment made up for what we couldn’t hear, and the party was in full force. Around 10:30, the “Jarhead” Drum and Bugle Corps arrived and played a few numbers for the customers. The band was quite good and of course had the sickening Jarhead precision. I thought it time to check the airport, and adjourned to the lobby to call Operations at Kadena Air Base.

        Operations informed me that I was on the manifest, and so I returned to 725, put on my uniform, gathered my bags and miscellaneous junk, and caught a taxi for Kadena. The plane left at 1:30 A.M. and arrived at Nagoya  at 5:30 A.M. It was a smooth and pleasant ride.

Route as of September 3rd, 1955 – end of Chapter 7.

CHAPTER 8 - JAPANESE VACATION

September 4th, 1955 - September 17th, 2021

SEP 04 (SUNDAY - WEEK 37)

        Three fellows that were on the same plane, called the motor pool, and we got transportation to the RTO in Nagoya. I asked a taxi where I could get some M.P.C. cashed into yen, and he said the hospital, so I went to the U.S. Hospital in Nagoya. Across the street were some transient billets, and after having only 3-4 hours sleep, I checked in (free) and slept a couple hours.

        Around 10:30 I walked to the PX, ruins of Nagoya Castle (not very interesting) and to Noritake China factory (closed). My sightseeing luck hadn’t been good up to now, and I thought I would give it one more chance and visit the Atsuta Jingu Shrine (2nd largest in Japan). I took a trolly car as it was a lot cheaper than the tours, and luckily got off at the right stop. The shrine was quite interesting and was a Shinto Shrine unlike the many Buddhist temples I will later see. I watched the people bow, clap their hands, and deposit a few coins in the ever present coin boxes. I later visited a department store which was as busy as a dept. Store back home on Christmas Eve. The store was very modern and even had escalators.

Since I had about seen all there was to see in Nagoya, I decided to visit Gifu, and its famed Cormorant Fishing. The train ride was about 1 hour long, and at the Gifu Station – after much misunderstanding – I took a taxi to the river. There were many boats on the river, and in most of them, gay, noisy parties were going on. (Mainly Japanese). At 8:30 the fishing boats came by and the boats on shore went out to meet them, and then drifted with them downstream. The fishing boats had a basket of fire in front of the boat, and 5-10 Cormorants on rope along side. After the Cormorants had 4 or 5 fish in their mouth, the fisherman would squeeze it out of their neck and mouth. Their necks were tied so that the birds couldn’t swallow any fish. My flash was all messed up, and I don’t think I got any decent shots.

SEP 05                 LABOR DAY

        I got up relatively early and caught a cinder belching steam engine for Toba in Ise Shima National Park. At Toba I disembarked and strolled down the street to Mikimoto's Pearl Island. Actually, not much of the pearl industry is on this island (although located in the nearby vicinity) and I think it is here to commemorate Mikimoto’s first success with cultured plants. The island was quite commercial, but was interesting as it had the dining girls in their white outfits, a small museum, a mock factory with explanation of the process, and other related spots.

        I then tried to obtain directions to the Grand Shine at Ise, but wasn’t having much luck. I spotted an American and her Japanese friend and asked them. They said it was were they were going and that I should come with them (to Nakiri). While on the electric train they suddenly realized exactly where I wanted to go and said it was in the other direction but I decided to stay with them and visit Nakiri. After a long train ride, followed by a bus ride we arrived in Nakiri and the girl proceeded to show us the sights.

        We visited the lighthouse, fishing dock, and park. Along the way we discussed things in general that I wasn’t too clear on, and also various customs we saw along the way. I took their picture and the girl (about 18 years) asked for a copy, so I guess I am somewhat indebted to follow thru. All in all I had a very pleasant afternoon.

        Using their “new” directions I went to Ugiyamada where I visited the Grand Shrine at Naiku. It was about 6 PM, consequently I couldn’t take any pictures, but it truly is one of the beauty spots of Japan. The grounds were immaculate and the huge, straight trees reminded me of the Muir Woods in San Fran. Caught the night train and arrived in Nara at 10 PM.

SEP 06

        Stayed at the Nara Hotel, a huge establishment run by the Japan National Railroad. There were very few people at the hotel, I guess it must be an off season.

        I started out about 9:30 AM and walked all day, covering much ground, and seeing almost every important temple and shrine within walking distance. Basically everything I saw is in or around Nara Park, a huge (1250 acres) park in which tame deer roam about and eat from your hand. In fact they are so friendly that if you have food in your hand and don’t feed them, they butt you or lick your hand. Near the hotel is Kofukuji Temple and from its top floor I viewed the city and the sights I was later to visit. These sights included the Nara National Museum (contains some very old Buddha and other statues); Nanendo Temple (where I watched the Buddhist ritual of prayer ring gong, clap hands twice, bow, say prayer, place burning incense in front, give money); and the Todaiji Temple (biggest wooden building in the world, and headquarters for Buddhism in Japan. Also contains the Daibutsu or Great Buddha 53’ high)

        While visiting the Nigatsudo Temple I spoke a few words to a Japanese young man, and it blossomed into an afternoon acquaintance. His name was Dr. Shigeo Gondó and he was visiting Nara in between medical conventions. Actually he is a resident at the Univ. of Kyushu Medical School Hospital. We then visited Sangatsudo Temple (combination of Nara Period and Kamakura Period work); Tamukeyama Shrine,  Kasuga Shrine (many lanterns and vermillion colored walls), Shinyakushiji Shrine, Sagiike Pond,  Ichi-no-Tani, etc. He explained many of the objects and made my afternoon 100% improved. I think we both enjoyed each others company.

SEP 07

        Checked out of the hotel and signed up for a sightseeing trip to Hōryū-ji Temple, which has the oldest wooden buildings in Japan and most likely the world. The temples were well preserved and contained many old and valued Buddhas and other Buddhist statues. I sure have seen a lot of Buddha temples, both in Korea and Japan, and I guess I should be an authority on the religion. (but I am not)

        Our bus had a load of people visiting Nara, probably for the first time. They were for the most part, from the same village (Dente sp?) and wore little blue ribbons with the village name on it. Mot of them were old women and they wore drab looking kimonos or old women’s dresses. The guide was a cute young girl who did a fine job, at least it seemed that way, for she spoke entirely in Japanese and I didn’t follow one word. Nevertheless, once we got to the temple I went on my own, thanks to a leaflet in English.

        Caught the 12:48 train for Osaka, and arrived about an hour later. Checked my bags at the station and took a trolly to Osaka Castle, a huge castle overlooking the city. The walls are tremendous, and some of the stones therein are the largest I have ever seen. The castle has been reconstructed, but still retains some of the historical flavor.

        Ate dinner late, because I decided to sleep in a Japanese hotel, and surprising as it may seem the cab driver didn’t know exactly where to go. I guess some Japanese hotels don’t want Americans. Finally got situated in the Ang___ Hotel, and after a hot bath, I went to the Metro Club. This club is the most elegant that I have ever been in, and has hundreds of girls to dance with. I am ashamed to say that I watched the show and the people and did no dancing.

SEP 08

        Had an interesting day today, which erased the bad impression I was having ACQUIRING for Osaka. I changed hotels – from Japanese to American – and found that the facilities more than made up for the extra charge. I went to Tennoji Park in the morning and early afternoon and visited the Botanical Gardens (fair), Art Museum (Fair) and zoo (Very Good). I then visited Shitenmo-ji Temple which is similar to other Buddhist temples except instead of preserving the Buddha as he was, they have given him a new gold paint covering, and it is quite attractive.

        My first enjoyable series of experiences today, took place when on 3 separate occasions, young Japanese college students approached me and offered their services to show me where I was attempting to go by myself. I had a soda with one of them – economics student at Kyoto University – and we talked for about 15-20 minutes. He asked me if I mamboed, and I said that the movies tend to exaggerate things in America. I had to laugh when he said that he thought all Americans were interested in “carnal.”

        Later in the afternoon I visited Shinsaibashi Street which is one of the top places to see in Japan. It extends for a couple miles and is loaded with many shops and outdoor selling booths plus colored lights. It is narrow, and no automobiles are allowed on it which adds to the street. I walked up and down, and likewise in the evening, and saw many a good looking Japanese girls. In the evening I also played “Rocket Ball” the successor to Pachinko, the new Japanese craze. Broke even and was quite satisfied. Also saw 3 innings of the pro baseball game which was exciting. With 2 outs and none on and losing 2-1 (9th), an Osaka player hit a foul homer before bouncing out.

SEP 09

        I got up somewhat early, and took the trolly to the station. Here I took an express to Kobe, and got off at the Sannomiya Station. I had decided to visit some industrial plant, consequently I went to Kobe Steel Works, which was suggested to me by my hotel clerk. As I walked in the gate I noticed a group of men sitting around and all of them had on red arm bands. I soon found out that the plant was on strike. I turned around and began walking towards the piers. I noticed a large factory on my right, and thinking nothing could be lost, I decided to see what they made and if I could tour the plant.

        It turned out to be a British run plant – Dunlop Rubber Company – and they referred me all the way to the president. He was quite nice, and asmed a Mr. English (Production Manager) to show me about. He talked to me for about 45 minutes, including a spot of tea, and then we toured the plant for approximately 2 hours. He was extremely nice, showed me the complete process, and answered all my questions. He told me about the particular problems they had when Japan gave them back their factory in 1949, their sterling–dollar–yen difficulty, labor relations, etc. I thoroughly enjoyed the visit from beginning to end.

        Next on the agenda was to visit some shipping firms and to get some information about future travels. Took a short walk to the dock, and then along the waterfront before going back to Sannomiya Station via Motomachi Street (similar to Osaka’s Shinsaibashi, although not as good). Stayed at the movie theater and saw new “Blackboard Jungle” which was excellent. Caught the express back to Osaka and went to the Daik_zi Theater where I saw and heard Japanese Singers (More of a novelty than pure enjoyment.)

        Later on in the evening I visited the other entertainment section of Osaka, and had coffee at the Moko Coffee Shop.

SEP 10

        Took the morning train to Kyoto and checked in at the Hotel Matsubara, a Japanese style hotel, although my room had a bed in it. Perhaps before I leave I will be brave enough to sleep on the floor – Japanese style. I had to cash an M.P.O., so I went to Camp Otsu located near Kyoto. It use to be a large Army Camp, but most of the men have been transferred away. Got my money, and had my shoes fixed and bought a couple items at the PX. Also compared camera prices (JCE vs RCE) and looked at a Patina III C. I am undecided about buying it although it has some good features.

        Back in Kyoto I got a map with English words and began my sightseeing. Before dinner I visited the Higashi Honganji Temple – which is a huge wooden temple. It is the center of the Shin Sect of Buddhism, the most influential of all Buddhist Sects. One of the most interesting temples that I have seen is the Sanyu Sanjinko Temple which is 396 feet long and has 1001 Korean statues lined up in rows. Although much of the gold foil has worn off it is quite a sight.

        In the evening I walked my fool head (I should say feet but my head led the way) off, and for 3 hours I trodded around Kyoto looking in shops, watching people, having a beer in a small booth lite bar (with 2 waitresses or B-girls who sat with me & poured my drink) and even__ samples some rice. In one section – Shimabara District – I saw row upon row of whore houses with the mamasan sitting at the door and the girls next to her. I passed by around 7:30 and being that it was early and not many men had come, I had a lot of offers. Prudence won out although I would be interested in seeing how fast they can get in and out of a kimono.

        On the way home I went through the Gion District where apprentice Geisha entertain. These are real Geisha & not whores – I saw three of the girls and they had beautiful kimonos with a long sash.

SEP 11 (SUNDAY - WEEK 38)

        The sun shone brilliantly all day, but I absentmindedly forgot an extra roll of film, consequently, I only took about 12 pictures. Started off with breakfast at the Kyoto Hotel, and from there I went to a lacquer factory near Okazaki Park. Here they explained the complete process and one was also able to see a few of the workmen going about their craft.I never realized so many steps went into one finished product.

        Heian Shrine wasn’t far away and so I sauntered over in that direction. I spent about 2 ½ hours in the general vicinity of the shrine, mainly to watch the Japanese people. First there were the thousands of students who were at the shrine, painting and colored what their eyes dictated. Then there were the visitors and sailors (Japanese) who came to see the beautiful shrine and its outstanding garden. In front of the shrine were athletic fields, and I watched some girls and boys teams playing a game similar to volleyball. The girls particularly amazed me as they were graceful and quite good.

        Near the shrine was a hall which I first thought to be the Art Museum but it wasn’t. While walking through the hall a Japanese boy said hello, and I stopped to talk. It so happened that a recital was to take place and he invited me into a nearby room. In the room mothers and various men were helping their daughters with kimonos, ___s, white powder etc. I felt a little funny but was very interested in the prim_ing an the dance that followed. I ran out of film – drat it – but got a few shots. One girl, a friend of a dancer was extremely pretty and I had a hard time keeping my eyes off her.

        After the recital, the fellow and his friend went with me to visit other temples and shrines and thence to Daimaru Department Store. I sampled Soka (macaroni) but can’t say I enjoyed it.You should have seen the Japanese laugh at the crude way I used the chopsticks.

SEP 12

        How the time does fly. One week from today and I should be back at work. That is, if I get a flight home. Had a big breakfast and walked to the Imperial Palace. However, since the tours started on the hour I decided to visit Kyoto University first. A lady in public relations showed me the campus and pointed out the main buildings. She said that this was a National School (8000 students) and charged 6000¥ a year. Private schools charge from 15,000-30,000. I then took the trolly to the Palace and joined in the foreign tour. The place grounds were quite beautiful, particularly the garden. From what I understand all Emperors have their coronation here. Five American women (on a round the world cruise) were on the tour with me, and lived up to the picture I had imagined for stupid American tourists. I hope I never show my ignorance and “real reason for touring” (to impress people back home) as these women showed. Oh yes, I had an occasion to use the Japanese bengō (floor level_ and must confess I wasn’t very adept at it all.

        Next I toured Nyo Castle which was quite interesting. It is 350 years old, and well preserved. Besides, they had English signs and booklets plus guards to help one understand. Walked to Seyō Station and took the electric train to Takarazuka a nearby resort. It is fam famous for its revuse revue, which is an all girl musical, quite elaborate in costume and scenery. I missed about ½ but really had about the right amount as amyn Foreign spoken production gets tiring if too long.

        Sampled Tempura (fried shrimp, fish & other food) and thought it to be fair. Can’t really say I like Japanese food. Seems to be too fishy and full of carbohydrates. Visited a coffee shop after dinner and listened to a Japanese jazz band.

SEP 13

        One of the most favorable impressions that I will take back with me to J Okinawa and the U.S. is the friendliness of the Japanese people,  – particularly the University students. Since as a rule they can speak and understand the most English, I have made it a point to ask any questions to these fellows. Many times they take me to the shrine or temple in question and an enjoyable hour or two are spent in talking about various things that we see on the way or have questions in our mind.

        Today I visited Ryusan-Ji Temple which is noted for its simple but interesting rock garden. There are 15 rocks spread out in 7 groups, in an area of about 20’ x 40’. There is no grass, although some of the rocks have moss around their base. The ground is covered with white rocks which is raked to make a neat pattern.

        I tried to visit a textile factory but the best I could do was to see a couple weaving machines in action. One was supposed to be the oldest in Japan, and another was one of the latest designs. With this latter machine and cheap Japanese labor I can understand why the textile companies in America and Great Britain are crying for protective tariffs.

        Went to the Kabuchi theater in the afternoon and even evening (4:30-9:30) and I did my best to stay awake. I guess I didn’t understand more than 10 words in the 5 hours. The program consisted of 3 plays, with the middle play capturing my attention throughout. The plays are very colorful, and the costuming is old Japanese; all the parts (Geishas too) are performed by men. They had one scene where one of the men cut off another’s arm, and the props they used really made it realistic and gory.

SEP 14

        When I was at the PX at Camp Otsu on Saturday, I noticed that it would be closed on Thursday. Consequently, I decided to go to the PX today and also make some telephone inquiries regarding planes going to Okinawa. I bought a wood carving for my collection and also bought a set a wood block prints. I checked with Base Operations at Iwakuni Air Base and they said there would probabably-ably be flights on Saturday and Sunday so I decided to head for Hiroshima and thence to Iwakuni.

        Checked out of the hotel and took the afternoon train to Osaka. Spent the remainder of the afternoon buying some Japanese stamps and looking for gifts that I could send home. Either I am awful stopid or have no imagination, but I will be darn if I could find anything to buy. Pottery, lacquerware, textiles etc. don’t seem worthwhile to me, so I decided not to send home stuff just to be sending it home.

        The main reason for stopping in Osaka (besides shopping) was to attend a concert at the Sankei Kaikan Concert Hall!! It was an all Tchaikovsky program and included the Symphony No. 6, “Piano Concerto No. 1” and “Overture to Romeo and Juliet.” The interesting thing was the contrast in the audience tonight with the audience of the Kabuki. At the latter most of the people were middle age or older, and many of the women had on kimonos. At the concert, 95% of the audience were young people with very few kimonos to be seen. I think Japan has become quite Westernized in the past 10 years and if given a chance, the younger generation should be a guiding light in Asia. One bad point is the difficulty of college graduates getting decent jobs. Sometimes such groups of people can become restless and easily stirred up.

SEP 15

        After a miserable all night ride to Hiroshima I finally arrived at 6 AM. I was covered with black soot from the lousy steam engine and dead on my feet as I don’t think I slept a total of 2 hours. I had decided to stay at a Western hotel and told the taxi to take me to the New Hiroshima Hotel. It is a brand new hotel, and was built close to the apex of the Atom Bomb burst, back in August, 1945. I checked in, took a shower and hit the sack for 3 hours. Decided that I could sleep back on Okinawa, so I got up, dressed and went to the train station. Had a lousy lunch (I am not crazy about Japanese food) and took the train to Miyajima.

        As you would guess, I didn’t get off the right stop, so I had to take a bus part of the way and walk the rest to the Miyajimaguchi. There I boarded the ferry and went to the famous shrine built so that when the tide comes in, the shrine and its equally famous, huge red Torii appear to come from (or float on) the water. The tide was out, so I wasn’t able to view the above, but was able to go out to the Torii and examine it at close hand. Also, I enjoyed watching many women and men digging for clams in the sand. They used pieces of metal which they scraped away the sand, about 203 inches deep, and sifted for the small clams. Some of them had quite a pile collected.

        Didn’t know exactly what to do in the evening so I went to a Japanese show. (fair) I had seen an adventurement of “Soldier of Fortune” but couldn’t read where it was. Wouldn’t you sh know that when I left the show and turned the corner, there big as life was the theater that had Soldier of Fortune. Ah me, such is life!

SEP 16

        It was a nice day for walking, and that is what I did – all day. Walked all around Hiroshima, visiting every tourist attraction listed in my brochure. I started by visiting the A. Bomb Memorial Museum which is a very modern building built on columns and in which are many photographs, maps, charts, pieces of clothing, tile, stone and even in one instance, pieces of flesh. It is a very gruesome exhibit, but does illustrate the tremendous destructive force of the atom bomb, and it gives suggestions as to how much more powerful and destructive would be the Hydrogen bomb – supposedly 1000 times as powerful.

        I then walked around the new Peach Park, and took pictures of the Memorial Cenotaph which was erected in memory of the fallen thousands (approximately 200,000 killed), the not yet completed Peace Memorial Hall, and the new City Auditorium – Hotel Building. Not too far from this area is the Industrial Exhibition Gallery, or at least the ruins of the building. On August 6 1945, at 8:15 A.M. a bomb exploded 500 meters above this building, and caused the destruction of the city. This building is the only remaining ruins of the A. Bomb attack, and its scary dome is a grim reminder. The rest of the city has been rebuilt, including a new Peace Blvd. down the center of the town.

        At one end of the Peace Blvd, located on a hill, are the buildings of the Atom Bomb Casualty Commission. This jointly US-Japan financed commission examines about 44 people a day (annual visits) and collects and segregates data concerning the effects of the bomb on the people and their future generations. There are about 700 Japanese technicians and 55 foreign nationals working at the Commission.

SEP 17 - ROSH HASHONAH

        I reported in at Iwakuni yesterday evening and got a bunk, a blanket, sheet and mattress cover for comfort (?). Got a good nights sleep and had breakfast at the mess hall. (Once again dressed as a little toy soldier) Around 7 PM I arrived at the Operations Building and inquired about flights to Okinawa. The fellow at the desk said that a plane was to leave in about an hour and that I would be able to get a ride. Things worked out great and by 8 AM we were in the air headed South. The flight was not very interesting – there were only two passengers – and I tried to sleep as much as I could. Coming in for the landing, the pilot nosed down too sharply and the plane suddenly veered for the ground. Luckily a Major was at the other controls and he took over and brought the plane, and I, in safely.

        Didn’t do much in the afternoon, except do a little reading, get a overdue haircut, and do a lot of talking. Many of the fellows are planning trips to Japan in October, and they asked a hundred questions. Oh yes, I decided to change maids and told my old maid that I wanted to switch. She was so nice about it, that I felt a little bad, but I had already made up my mind.

        Back in the swing of things – but fast. Joined the boys at Castle Terrace and had a few brews plus making a lot of noise. Had more beer tonight than on my whole trip. They had a huge crowd at the Terrace and also some guest entertainment to provide a good floor show. The comedian was good once he warmed up, and soon had everybody laughing.

SEP 18 (SUNDAY - WEEK 39)

        I didn’t go to services this weekend, however, I plan to go to Yom Kippur services next week. I guess I am drifting further and further away from Judaism, but I don’t feel too bad about it. If it were a drifting away from a belief in One God, then it would be time to pull up reins and examine things, but being a part of a religion in name only means absolutely nothing.

        Today was a day that was important to the day that it was the day before I reported back to work, but other than that, it was a typical Sunday. I played tennis in the morning and wrote letters in the afternoon. Actually it was a single letter to the folks back home, but it consisted of 5 type-written pages (both sides) and took me 2 ½ hours to finish. Took in a movie in the evening and that was Sunday, September 18th, 1955.

        While up in Japan I tried to compare the Okinawans and Japanese people, but my only conclusion is that they are similar in most respects. I think the Japanese are more industrious and perhaps harder pressed to earn a bare living. The northern people are more educated and having 100 times the population, have more good looking women, perhaps even percentage-wise. (Especially the cities). I guess in boiling it down, the country people in Japan are similar, whereas the city folk are more advanced and have adopted more of the customs and habits of the Western world.

        The Japanese make better use of the land, and I guess are about the best farmers in the Orient. Every flat or semi-flat PIECE OF land is a rice field with the exception of city parks and city and country school yards.

Route as of September 18th, 1955 – end of Chapter 8.

CHAPTER 9 - BACK TO THE ROCK

September 19th, 1955 - December 31st, 1955

SEP 19

        Started off the day bucking heads with the personnel clerk, a stupid RA SFC with whom it is almost impossible to talk to. He showed me where the two days that I left prior to 4 September are to be counted on my leave, consequently since I had asked for 11 days, I was actually 2 days AWOL. The Company Commander decided to extend my leave for the 2 days (13 days instead of 11) and thus make it officially legitimate. I now thus have 37 days of leave remaining and I have already begun planning for my next leave, probably in December or January.

        Back to work and it was rough trying to get back into the grind again. My old boss – Joe Alfonsi – had been transferred to Formosa, and a fellow by the name of George Sauer has taken his place. Seems to be a pretty decent fellow and I hope he doesn’t bother me. Frankly I am up to my dick in correspondence, and I would hate to have a slave driver for a boss, for it makes it a lot easier if I just do what I want and not have to be bother by too many “Big Brothers.”

        Pachinko and Rocket Ball are the latest rages in Japan and to some extent Okinawa. Both of the games involve hitting small balls, and watching them bounce off little p___ or pieces of metal and hope they fall into prize winning slots. Most of the players have their own special method of playing – some spin the shooter, hit it easy, hit it hard, combination, etc. Some establishments let you cash in the balls for money, others for prizes. In the big towns the parlors are everywhere, each having bright lights and loud, hypnotizing music. I believe Pachinko has been banned in Tokyo although I don’t know why.

SEP 20

        While on my vacation, I decided to change maids, and consequently shortly after I arrived back at Camp Kue I told my former maid that I was terminating her services. She took it quite well, and I was sure relieved for I felt a little ashamed about firing a pregnant woman. Yep, she was about 5-6 months gone (I have only been on Okinawa 3 months, and besides she was too horrible to yo touch) and was beginning to swell quite a bit. Nevertheless, I wasn’t completely satisfied, so I switched to Junko, who was Campbell’s old maid, and the girl whom Campbell, Poole and Whitemire are sending to school.

        The girl finished high school (Miyako) and came to Okinawa to get a job. Being a maid isn’t the greatest of jobs, but they are able to make 2400 yen a month, which isn’t too bad. I believe she said she pays 400 yen for board, and I am sure rice costs next to nothing. Her biggest expense is transportation to and from school which is located in Naha. She goes to night school 4 nights a week, and she is learning English, both reading and speaking.

        She read a little for me out of Time magazine and did a pretty good job, although she didn’t understand what she read. It was about Robert E. Lee and I had a rough time trying to explain about General Lee, the Civil War and the North and South. Still she seemed interested, so I got a map, a Japanese-English dictionary, and did my best. I told her to bring her lessons to Kue and at lunch time I would see if I could help her. Will have to wait and see if she does.

SEP 21

        I thought that once I returned from my leave, that the days would pass quite rapidly, at least for awhile. So far this week the days have been moving as slow as a 7 year itch, but perhaps the reverse of my thought would come about, and after a slow start, the days would roll on.

        Only worked a half day today as I had to attend training in the afternoon. As usual, the afternoon consisted of movies, and we saw about 5 movies, 4 of which were about the Atomic Bomb. I never saw so many atomic explosions in all my “merrie days”. A couple shots of Hiroshima were interesting because I had just been there, but the rest were quite boring.

        During my absence, and for the first 3 days of this week, I received enough mail to last me 10 years. It seems that all the literature, papers, magazines and letters that I was expecting, arrived at the same time. So far I have read 4 St. Louis Post Dispatches, 3 Time magazines, a ANCL paper, a AIIE journal, and about 10 letters. Received some more law school catalogs, reprints from Life’s Religious series, letters from lawyers, and the remaining books from LaSalle University. (Mistake)

        Outside of the 1 letter home, I haven’t done any writing, but have set Friday evening aside as a beginning. Funny how one looks forward to letters, and when they arrive one at a time, how eagerly they are read. When everything comes in at once, they are lucky to be scanned much less read throughout. Generally I stick the letters in a box and reread later in the future and in this way enjoy what the others have written.

        

SEP 22

        I received some of my slides back from Hawaii and I enjoyed viewing them in my slide viewer and recalling the places where I have been and things that I have seen. The first batch of pictures were taken when I was on a trip to Kume and Okino. A few slides turned out all right, but I ruined about 8 by using a green filter which I thought to be the thing to use. Also took some pictures of the “Oban” (Okinawan dancing) in Nago, but had considerable trouble with my flash and thus had a couple black slides.

        This flash trouble followed me to Gifu and I lost about 5 slides trying to take pictures of the cormorant fishing, but each time the flash failed to go off. Managed to get one picture of some Japanese people in a boat eating supper, prior to the fishing, but that was all I got. The other slides concerned Nagoya, Toba and Naha I hope the other slides are better as I am not too satisfied with the results.

Work continues to move along, although not fast enough for me. Oh well, 100 more days this year, 150 next year and that, I hope, will stamp be finis to me military career..

SEP 23

        See this was a long week. But it is almost over and this means one less within the U.S Army. I am still working on the Maintenance Hangar estimate, and have just got started ,for it is a big job. Had to chuckle to myself today when my boss told me that I was doing a good job and he liked my latest reports (of course was appreciated) but sort of stunned me, for if anything I expected a bailing out owing to my doing of other things while at work, plus being absent for periods during the day. Funny world!

        One interesting in Japan is to walk down the main streets at night time, particularly in the small times. In Naha I spent one evening doing this, and had a fascinating time watching the men and women, their dress, things they were doing and objects they were buying. This particular night in Naha, there were hundreds of school children who had come to visit Naha, their ancient capital. There were hundreds of black and white uniforms, and groups of the children were roaming up and down the street, looking in stores, and buying souvenirs to bring back to their home towns.

        There were many men dressed in robes on the street, and they looked quite at ease in these loose fitting garments and the wide sash. Many of the women also had robes on and a couple were in kimonos. The shops stayed open to about 10:30 PM, and one could buy almost anything they desired. Especially numerous were small eating and drinking shops, souvenir stores and art and book shops, plus of course, a lot of small hotels.

SEP 24

        Again training. Seems as if all I have been doing lately is going to training. Read a pamphlet throughout one of the talks, and the M/Sgt came up to me afterwards and told me to never read in his class again or he would lower the boom. Such is life and the composition of RA’s, but no sweat, it won’t be long before this joker is out.

        Did a little shopping in th afternoon and bought some sympathy and wedding cards. Also pu__ced a skylight filter and some ivory earrings. Looked at some cameras, although I am not particularly in the market for one. Still trying to make up mind whether to buy a good camera, or use the old betsy I have at present. I guess it really hinges on whether I go into photography for an earnest hobby or whether I am just interested in pictures of my travels.

        While in Naha one evening, I spent part of the time watching people on the street, and ended the evening by going to see “Violent Saturday.” It is a good movie and captured my attention throughout the picture. In fact until the lights went on I had forgotten where I was, and didn’t give much thought to being in a foreign country. However, when the lights came on, I recognized the universal school uniforms of the predominantly male audience. One could hear nothing but wooden shoes as the people left the theater, with many of them heading for a special parking lot in the patio where there were about 45 bicycles and motorcycles parked. In fact a traffic snarl developed as they all tried to leave at the same time.

        I stopped for a lemonade at a restaurant in the theater building, and sipped a refreshing drink. Many theater buildings in Japan and Okinawa have restaurants or cabo_ts in them.

SEP 25 (SUNDAY - WEEK 40)

        Tried to play tennis in the morning but the courts were crowded. Went back to the China Sea Racquet (Racket) Club in the afternoon and managed to sweat out 3 sets. It was really hot, but a nice cool breeze took away the high humidity. Called baseline shots for a tennis tournament they were having at the courts, but decided to quite after the first set as I had been in the sun 4 hours and was starting to broil.

        One of the fellows in the tournament finals is an Air Force light colonel, and one of the poorest sports that I have seen in a long time. He constantly bitches, mainly about his own play, but also about his partner’s play and the “lucky” shots of the opponents. I began to laugh at his childish remarks but was told to be quiet by one of the other officials. This plus my sun burn prompted me to head for Hut 725.

        Went to Yom Kippur services in the evening and was a part of a fairly large Jewish turnout. Even recognized a fellow St. Louisian, and will try to get an opportunity to talk to him tomorrow. The services were short and uninteresting, and a great deal of the speaking was in Hebrew. The Rabbi is a very young man, and I am not too impressed by his actions nor his mind. His sermon was general and dull, although perhaps I do him the injustice of comparing him to the speaking ability of the late Julius Gordon. Concerning Shaare Emeth, I am interested in how the new Rabbi is getting along and whether he will be able to fill Gordon’s shoes as an orator. There will be no problem for the spiritual shoes.

SEP 26

Being a good Jew I took the day off, and stuck around the area until 3 PM. Then boarded a bus for Kadena and attended concluding Yom Kippur services. The services were primarily in Hebrew and lasted 2 long, tiring hours. No sermon was given and the main chanting and reading was performed by a former Cantor student who subsequently to his tour of duty, married an Okinawan and settled down to living on the “Rock.” He wasn’t bad, but the service in general was boring, repeated several times and lost what little interest I might have brought to the chapel. Am convinced that the Orthodox religion is not for me, whether it be in Judaism, Catholicism or Protestantism.

The services were followed by a meal, in which we had dumplings, gafilta fish (sp?) and chicken. Wasn’t bad but wasn’t very good either, so I satisfied my hunger with a cheeseburger.

        I spent most of the day reading, but naturally had time to converse with my maid. She is about the smartest of all the maids, having finished high school, but being new to Kue, does not speak very good English. I feel that my talking to her and explaining things, helps to improve her English which she will need if she goes to school. I asked her what religion she believed in, but she said “none” at the present. She remarked that she would probably become a Christian in the near future.

        With request to marriage, she said that she probably wouldn’t get married until she was about 23 (she is 19 at the present) and that she would pick her husband. It seems that the procedure of the past whereby mommasan picks the boy is gradually being ignored.

SEP 27

        A typhoon was in the near vicinity, consequently Condition Two was proclaimed for our unit, and the other units on the island. This meant that we had to stay within our compound at night, in case the typhoon would venture near enough to the island to cause any damage, or necesitate human labor to get things straightened out. Other than the brisk winds, the troublesome typhoon didn’t affect the daily rut one bit, and life and work continued as usual.

        Continued to work on the Maintenance Hangar estimate, and found myself batting my brains out trying to get prices that were not available, or interpreting difficult drawings. My general background helped some, but not near that which a background of civil engineering would have done.

        I imagine that the typhoon has hit the Okinawan whores right smack in the pocketbook, for restrictions make it difficult for the trooper to frequent a cat house. Okinawa is loaded with them, and I guess the price is as cheap as there is in the world – 200 ¥ or about $1.65. The girls are generally located outside the Army gates, or in localized spots for which there is a well earned publicity – New Koza, Shimabuku, etc.

        Red light districts are common in Japan, and it is interesting to hear the hotel owners speak of the fact that the girls “have moved on to better locations.” One interesting spot was Shimaba___ with its numerous cathouses and money hungry mommasans peeking out the doors.

        Business has been a little tight on Okinawa since two Okinawan kids were raped by Americans. The press played it up and the 11 PM curfew was clamped on a little tighter.

SEP 28

        There seems to be a new policy at work, that is; if at all possible, each request for an estimate should be personally checked by one of the Construction Branch estimates. Consequently, a job came in for which one of the Japanese engineers was assigned; and since he couldn’t speak very good english I was sent along, somewhat as a liaison man. Well, the job was somewhat complicated and the brief research that I did before I left the office didn’t help very much. Consequently, I was snowed whenever they asked me questions or referred things to me. Can’t deny but that it was interesting, although I will have to develop a “know it” attitude to cover up my brief indoctrination.

        Went to the Castle Terrace Club in the evening and enjoyed the final talent show of a series they have had on Wednesday and Saturday nights. The worst part about it was the judging, which was left to old man Cowan’s hearing of the volume of clapping for each contestant. Since he is partial to Okinawans, they generally won, particularly if they were young and cute. This evening a 7 year old Okinawan tap dancer fit the picture, and won the $50 prize money. While she was cute, she certainly wasn’t the best as far as talent goes, although I guess Cowan nor the audience cared very much. One of the contestants gave a monologue that was excellent and showed that he had professional inclinations. Still, he got very little applause and was thus snowed by the 7 year old.

        The other contestants were also good; and included 2 dancers, a singer, a comedian and a duet composed of 2 fellows from our unit. These latter boys were better than I expected and put on a nice act.

SEP 29

        Played some volleyball after work, and had some pretty humorous games as the wind played havoc with the ball and whenever a server hit the ball too high, it was sure to float outside. I think my team lost all but the first game, but I am sure we made more noise.

        I went to the office after the games, and started to catch up on my correspondence. Two of the letters I hated to write as they were sympathy letters to the Barron and Les Sherman families, since Mrs. Barron and Mrs. Sherman had passed away in August. Both of the women were fine women and mothers and I feel bad about their deaths.

        The Okinawans and Japanese treat their dead a little different than the Western world, but the main difference is what happens to the dead and not so much the burial ceremonies. The Japanese cremate most of their dead, although I did see some small crowded cemeteries. The Okinawans bury their dead in tombs, some of which are shaped in the form of turtles, and others in square cave-like tombs on the sides of hills. (Also location of turtle tombs)

        The Okinawans leave food and drink once a year for the deceased so that they won’t be hungry, and also, on occasions, communicate with the spirits of the dead. They pray often to the deceased, and part of Buddhism and Shintoism religions are based upon homage to the dead or so called ancestor worship. Taoism, incorporated in the above 2 religions believes that after seven generations, ancestors become divine, consequently the emphasis on humoring and honoring the dead.

SEP 30

        Spent the whole day typing, although I did take the necessary “breaks” to relieve the monotony. Mr. Fugewa and I had worked together on the mechanical phase of the estimate and I decided to type it up in the final form. Today was also payday and I was glad to receive the monthly MPC plus the 3 months clothing allowance they owed me. Socked a great part of it away in the bank for future traveling purposes.

        Decided to stay in the hut in the evening and start to weed out a lot of junky reading material and other stuff I had laying around the place. Reread a batch of Work Simplification booklets I had had Morton send me when I started to teach the Supervision course back in July and August. Some of the booklets were well written and proved good reading, one in particular, was from the Maytag Company of Newton, Iowa. Their booklet was spearheaded by numerous clever cartoons and pithy remarks and I felt that such a booklet aids considerably in putting over any Work Simplification program.

        Reread all the letters that I have received in answer to my questions that I had sent to 33 corporations and 10 patent attorneys in St. Louis. Some of the replies were 4-5 typewritten pages in length, and represented a lot of thought and time on the part of the correspondent. I believe I learned a great deal from the information, and have pretty well came to the conclusion that I am not too inclined toward Patent Law or perhaps general law, both in private practice or corporation law. I am interested in labor law, and therein would be my specialty if I undertook the profession of law.

OCT 01

Today was my first big inspection since I have been on Okinawa, and Colonel Joyce, with his parachute pin blazing on his left shirt pocket, inspected the 35-40 men of the 8105 AU detachment assembled before him. We had drawn carbines prior to the inspection, so with the little babies slung over our shoulder we awaited the personnel inspection of the bird colonel.

I happened to be the first man in the first rank and consequently he inspected me after the platoon sergeant. He asked me my name – ”SP1 Charles A. Werner, SIR”, how much longer I have to do in the Army, “8 months, sir”; what I would do then, “work, sir”; where “back home, sir;” when I polished my boots last, “this morning, sir, we have just finished drilling, sir;” and to tighten my pistol belt “yes, sir.” He also commented that I needed a haircut, and two hours later I had my pass pulled for the weekend on account of “shaggy looking hair on the nape of the neck.” So goes the Army, and bird colonels who have nothing better to do. Oh well, as long as my maid – what would I do without her – shines my shoes and brass, and the arms room men clean the carbines, I had just as soon stand inspection every day of the week, for we were released at 10 AM.

Invited Lyle Nelson to the camp in the evening, and after chow in the mess hall, we saw “Stalag 17” plus the remainder of the evening at the Castle Terrace. Tonight was the final night of the Talent Contest and a colored army sergeant (singer) and a combo tied for the $175 first place money. An air force choral group came in 2nd.

OCT 02 (SUNDAY - WEEK 41)

        Somewhat of a boring day, but there was nothing I could do about it. I had decided to take some ektachrome slides, however, the pass pulling had a lot to say about it. My arm was giving me a little trouble, so I decided not to engage in any sports, which consequently eliminated many things that I could do. Sooo, I took it easy.

        Slept a little longer than usual, read and shot the breeze with the boys. Later in the afternoon I went to the Castle Terrace and got my much publicized ha__ient. Then I meandered down to the tennis courts, where I proceed to get sick to the stomach listening to the poor sportsmanship talk of my Air Force Colonel “friend.” He really nauseates me and I sure hated to see him win the doubles championship of the island.

I guess the thing that I disliked most in Japan were the taxi drivers. They have adopted the worst habits of New York cabbies, and have put all other cab drivers over the world to shame. They weave in and out of traffic and many times my heart was in my mouth because I didn’t think we had a ghost of a chance of coming out alive. The fares range from 60 ¥ to 100 ¥ to begin with, mainly depending upon the size of the cab. American cars (taxis) charge 100 ¥ whereas the small European and Japanese makes scale down to the 60 ¥.

Twice I caught cab drivers trying to cheat me, and each time I refused to pay what was on the meter. One driver was glad to see me go, whereas I had to argue with the other one. What makes it so bad is that 40-50% of the cars on the road are taxi cabs.

OCT 03

I had finished typing the mechanical part of the estimate for the Maintenance Hangar, and I now waited for the electrical part so that I could complete this huge project. The estimated amount via Engineering was $58,000.00. I will be anxious to find out the Contractors bid for the proposed work.

One of the fellows, Bill Cornell, just came back from Hong Kong Hollywood, and I was really interested in what he did and how he enjoyed himself in this Oriental town. As usually occurs, the slit shirted babes captivated him, and he spent 90% of his time in the company of some English speaking Chinese whore, I mean girl. His concluding remarks, “I’ve got to go back!

While visiting Osaka I spent part of one morning in the New Osaka Hotel’s lobby. While munching on a sandwich, and taking it easy, I watched some business meetings between some Japanese men, and women. The women undoubtedly were wives, but they sat in on the meetings, smiling and nodding their heads, and looking pretty in their brightly colored kimonos.

One man interested me, as he was quite huge, and sat on a small sofa. His belly protruded and he sat erect looking like an old time Japanese war lord with his wife at his side. The only difference was the western dress he had on, as did all the businessmen.

The men bowed 2-3 times when they greeted each other and seemed to make the meeting as casual as possible. There was one old man present, and everybody looked his way and gave him the most attention.

OCT 04

This evening was one of the most enjoyable that I have had in the Orient, and I am looking forward to other such evenings. It began a couple days ago when I decided to go to the new Japanese OKINAWAN theater that had just opened in Naha. I asked my maid Junko about it, and when she said she had never been there, I asked her if she would like to go. Actually, I feel funny when I take her out, not because of comments about me, but what others think of her. I am sure they all conclude that she is some G.I’s slut. Actually the relationship is strictly platonic, for my interest is in the movie, and in showing her things that she has never seen.

Well, I met her at the show at 7 PM, but we couldn’t get in until the next show at 8:30. I asked her if she would like a drink (soda) and she said “Yes,” so we went to the Taiko Club, where many G.I’s go. She was really bashful about going in, and I guess felt funny the whole time we were there. She had a sandwich and a drink, and I had a drink, and we sat watching the dancing. I asked her to dance a show number, but she said she didn’t know how and was scared to get on the floor. After awhile, I showed her – with my fingers – the basic box step, and she went out on the floor with me. Her eyes were glued to my feet, but by the time we had danced 2 numbers she was doing quite well, and looking over my shoulder and not at her feet. She has a lot of rhythm and in no time could be a fine dancer.

We then went to the show and saw a fair American picture. The climax to the evening came on the bus, when with bubbling enthusiasm she said how much fun she had and what a wonderful evening it had been. I was really pleased.

OCT 05

        After waiting a week or so for my shoulder to get better, I finally decided to go to the dispensary and see what the doctor had to say. Af I waited for over 2 hours and finally was called in to see the doc. I told him about the shoulder, and after he examined it, he said that I probably had a minor case of bursitis. He suggested heat treatments and massages for 5 days, after which, if he it doesn’t get any better, that it might be a good idea to have an x-ray taken. The arm doesn’t hurt when I do everyday activities, although when I raise it over my head it bothers me a little. The main soreness comes when I engage in tennis or other active sports, and I am anxious for it to clear up as soon as possible for I am getting mighty lazy.

        I asked the doctor what was a good cure for dandrift, and he suggested an egg shampoo. Soooo— I finagled 2 eggs from the mess hall, and when the shower room was empty, gave myself an egg shampoo. It was really messy and unless I notice an immediate end to dandrift, I doubt if I shall try it again.

        Read awhile in the evening, and then journeyed up to the Castle Terrace with Al Chapman and Charlie Terry; perhaps they are the type I enjoy myself the most with. They are smart, plus having a fairly decent personality. It is interesting how the 2N Engineers have split into definitive groups, with only occasional intermingling for chow and after duty hour events. Up to now I have been inclined to go out with everyone, but lately I have found myself favoring one particular group. Don’t really think that is the best, however there are some I just had soon say “hi” to and leave it at that. I am interested in the basic between the fellows, and sort of plan to delve down into the roots of the situation if at all possible. There are some that drink to an excess and think it is the thing to do. There are others that don’t spend their money at all, and are called stingy. Some are married and still like the ladies, although for the most part the married men don’t mess with the Josans.

        None of the Engineers are dumb, for they all have at least one college degree. However, some are typical Engineers in that they have received a narrow type of education, and are not interested in other subjects outside of say sports or women. The thought that keeps on coming back to me, is whether this is a typical cross section of our educated youth. In some ways I guess it is, but on the other hand I wish it weren’t, for I am not too overly impressed. True the fellows are nice fellows, and easy to get along with, but I think that they are shallow in my respects. I will be interested in a latter observation and study of the group.

OCT 06

        Got my second heat treatment, but I can’t say that I have noticed any improvement yet. The fellow giving the massages was new, and I think he did more harm than good, for he gave my arm a big jerk and said, “there, did that hurt?” Went back to work after dinner and completed writing up a sentence or two of each slide. I find that I continue to enjoy my slides, and I am anxious to see some of the early ones that I took 7 and 8 months ago.

        Am a little puzzled as to the outcome, but my maid asked me if I wanted to take her to see the football game tomorrow night. She is a good athlete and is interested in seeing what would be her first football game. I said “yes” and quickly got another fellow to go with us.

OCT 07

        Last night I received the somewhat discomforting fact that I had to give a lecture on Carbine marksmanship at training on Saturday morning. Knowing so much about the subject, I headed straight for the library to check out a 7M series pamphlet on the topic. I decided to take the morning off so that I could read up on the interesting subject of marksmanship and subsequently jot down some notes so that I don’t make a bungling idiot of myself in the morning. Spent the remaining two hours at the dispensary where I got my third heat treatment. The fellow seemed to know what he was doing and I think my arm is getting better.

        Went to the movie in the evening and saw “Roman Holiday”. I had seen it a couple of years ago, but enjoyed it just as much. That Hepburn babe is really a doll. It rained during the movie, and consequently I was glad that I had decided to go there instead of the football game. However, after the show was over, we journeyed past the Camp Kue Baseball-Football field and decided to stay awhile.

        The half time ceremonies consisted of a band (Army) plus some Okinawan students performing on the bars and giving exhibitions of karate, the deadly hand-to-hand-fighting developed by the Okinawans in the 19th Century when the Japanese forbade them to have armor. The fighting is done by deadly kick, and blows to strategic parts of the body, and is aimed at a quick, one blow death. The exhibitions were of course just “going through the motions”.

        The second half began, but was interrupted by rain and being soaked I headed for the hut. I believe the Marines were leading 21-7 when I left.

OCT 08

        I gave my talk on Marksmanship and I am glad to say that it went off easy. The talk lasted 20 minutes and we sat around and shot the breeze for the rest of the 50 hour minute period. After the class I headed for the dispensary and got my 4th breakdown heat treatment on my shoulder; all the time “bugging out” of an inspection and P.T. Got back just in time to hear the Sergeant say, “Thats all for today.”

        Decided to test the shoulder and play some basketball in the afternoon. Played one game, plus about 1 ½ hours of shooting and retrieving the ball. Had all kinds of people playing with me, – maids, Okinawan guards, & G.I’s. The playing didn’t bother the arm very much although on one or two occasions I noticed a slight soreness when I attempted to make a hook shot. However, things seem to be O.K., and I will begin to play in the daily volleyball games.

        The weather has turned quite chilly, and for the first time I dragged my blanket out and used it to good advantage last night. I guess, no longer will I be able to lie around in my underwear shorts, or go to the shower with hardly anything on at all. I have given some thought to have my blue jacket with the yellow lining, sent to “the Rock.” Otherwise, I guess I have sufficient clothing for the winter, as it doesn’t get too cold here, although the high humidity makes it somewhat uncomfortable.

OCT 09 (SUNDAY - WEEK 42)

        Typhoon Nora was burning in the South Seas, and as a result we had advance winds on Okinawa which got up to about 40 mph. The winds also brought along rain and thus today was one of the most dismal, cool days that I have yet encountered on The Rock.

        I stayed in the hut in the morning and read from my Gulliver’s Travels Book, which I have found to be quite a humorous and interesting book. Decided to trust my skill at shopping, for the last and perhaps final time – but I when I arrived back in the company area at 5:30 I had only bought 2 Japanese dolls for Carol and Jane, plus a scarf for Mom. The Plaza House had some goods and objects from countries all over the world, but I couldn’t help but feel that most of it is just junk.

        Arnold and I walked up to Koza and Shimaboku around 2:30 and did a little store visiting on the way. None of the stores offered much, but I did price some row silk which Mom has indicated she might like to have. The material sells from 75¢ to $1.50 per yard, and some of it would make nice drapery material. Will send the price quotations home and await further word.

        Koza is geared to the G.I. pocketbook, and one finds many souvenir shops, beer halls, and whore houses. It has been at least 3 months since I last walked through the general area, and it seemed as if there weren’t quite as many girls standing about. However, I saw many more dance halls and cabarets and I imagine that is where the girls are. Still of the opinion that Okinawa has more whores proportionately than any place that I have visited.

OCT 10

        Back to work, but I didn’t do much work in the morning as I went to Sukiran to see a welding exhibition. There wasn’t much to the exhibition, but it brought back some memories of the welding I did when I worked at the St. Louis Car Co. At that time I use to spend my Saturday mornings practicing the welding technique under the tutorship of Norm Brauss the Welding Engineer. I think I usually spent a good portion of the time taking off my shoes in an effort to get rid of the molten metal that had fallen into my socks and shoes.

        Near the site where they were holding the exhibition, I noticed that the contractor had gathered in one pile, many old and rusty pipes, valves, etc. Consequently, I walked over, and with the help of one of the Japanese engineers, identified many parts that I have been making estimates on. Also, not very far away, work was progressing quite well on the new training building, and so I decided to roam about watching the Okinawan laborers.

        On one occasion I watch 2 men remove a scaffold, and in the process one of the men fell in a hole and scraped his back. He had a small pick in his pocket and I at first thought he had fallen on it, but when I saw the wound there was no sharp puncture to indicate such an injury. A nurse came to the scene and administered first aid, and I then decided to move on. Oh yes, a major came up to the scene of the accident, and after inquiring how the man got hurt, asked me why I was here and what I was doing. My answers seemed to satisfy his curiosity and so he walked on, I guess somewhat frustrated as he had no legitimate excuse to bawl me out.

OCT 11

        The weather is now much cooler than it has been, both during both the day and at night time. I would never had thought 2 months ago that I would be sleeping under a blanket, and once in awhile, 2 blankets. One good feature of the colder weather is the fact that mosquitos do not seem to thrive in cold weather, and consequently I have even been brave enough lately to ignore my netting.

        One of the highlights of my trip to Japan was the side trip to Kobe and a subsequent visit to the Dunlop Rubber Company. The plant is quite old, and during the war when the Japanese took over, they ran the machines to their maximum with only a minimum maintenance and replacement. After the war a caretaker Japanese group ran the company for 3 years until they returned it to the British firm that owned it. They also did not rebuild but continued to take without putting back anything.

        The company was the largest rubber company in Japan before the war, but as a result of the war they relinquished their lead and in fact dropped to bottom among the big 6 companies. Since 1948 the company has progressed, rebuilt and through shrewd business policies have advanced to 3rd place.

        Mr. English, the Production Manager, invited me into his office for a spot of tea before taking me on a tour of the plant. He spoke of some of the difficulties encountered by foremen working in Japan. First of all currency problems is utmost, for the Japanese government will only let them send out a certain percentage of their profits. When buying equipment and replacement machinery, in order to send money to the States or to England, they must first get approved from the Japanese Government. Then if a comparable price is made in Japan, the Government generally turns them down and advises them to buy the Japanese product, even if it is not exactly the same.

        While touring the plant I inquired about the Union, if any, – “Yes, a company union;” and the type of incentives they had. He said that there were not any price rates, although there was a day rate with incentives. The men and women worked hard (lunch: 115-125) and seemed to do quite a proficient job when working with their hands. Mr. English said that on machinery, the Japanese were not quite as good as Westerners.

        The plant produced all types of rubber products, which included automobile and truck tires, scooter tires, bicycle tires, football bladders, hot water bottles, etc. I truly enjoyed the trip and hope to visit other plants when I return to Japan.

OCT 12

        Carolyn’s birthday, whew, hard to believe that she is 23. Likewise it is hard to believe that I will soon be 26. Man I am getting old. Work continues to progress all right, and of course on days like today when I had the afternoon off, I enjoy everything that much better. Spent the entire afternoon talking to my maid Junko, and it was really interesting to hear her comments and views. She is getting much better with her English which makes it easier to converse.

OCT 13

        Am presently working on a big estimate for some air force dependent housing, and it is a labor. The contract is a huge one – $8,000,000 – and it is as confused as it is huge. The prints are poor, and I find myself thumbing back and forth trying to determine the elevation, sections, etc. To make it more complicated, there are 4 kinds of houses and thus 4 sets of blueprints. Nevertheless, it is interesting and I am learning a lot of basic facs about construction, particularly housing construction.

        While in Japan, and specifically Kyoto, I spent 5 days in a Japanese style hotel. They did have some rooms with beds in them, and I partaked of this form of luxury. The rest of the hotel was Japanese, in that the dresser was small and had a minute, slender looking glass; Japanese bath and Japanese toilets. The bath consisted of a tub of hot water, wherein one was to sit to feel relaxed and relieved. Before the bath one was supposed to wash himself with either a wash rag and pan or in a shower.

        The toilet was the typical hole in the floor, and I am glad to say that I did not have to partake, as I made it a point to take my morning constitution at a Western type hotel. This hotel did have toilet paper, although many places do not furnish toilet paper for ones use.

        One bad feature was that there were no screens in the curtains, thus letting in a lot of mosquitos. The thin walls on the other hand did not bother me.

        At this hotel were 2 servicemen from Korea, and they paid the manager $65 for a weeks room and board plus a girl.

OCT 14

        Lately I have had a tendency to “goldbrick” and today was a typical example. I needed some general information about housing and checked out a sedan to go to the Sukiran housing area. There I wandered in and out of some of the houses under construction, and observed the men at work. I was primarily interested in seeing some furring and metal lathing, but only saw a little bit on some of the wall corners.

        The houses are uniform, that is, in each type, all houses are the same. There are two, three and four bedroom houses and two bedroom duplexes. Also, there are several 2, 3 and 4 houses built adjacent to one another. The houses are of concrete block construction, concrete beams, pre cast concrete roofs, and “shotcrete” walls. Depending upon the number of bedrooms, the houses cost the government from about $7000 to $10,000 and I imagine they would cost more in the states, since labor is so cheap here. A laborer gets $1.00/day, plumber, $3.50/day; electrician, $3.30/day and so on. Actually these are the labor costs the Government pays the contractors, but I am sure that the contractor pays the Okinawans less than the above.

        Upon arriving back at Kue, I went to my hut and joked with the maids for a few minutes after going to the supply room. I then went back to work for the rest of the morning. In the afternoon I went to the dispensary, and didn’t get back to work until 4 PM. Put in an hour of work and before I looked up it was chow time.

        In the evening Chapman and I went to the Naha Air Base to hear a music concert which was enjoyable. I especially liked a colored singer who sang “Danny Boy”, “Lord’s Prayer”, & “I’ll Never walk Alone.” We roamed around Naha for about an hour before heading for Kue.

OCT 15

        Ever since the RA, no good, Colonel inspected the ranks, our Saturday morning training schedule has been tailored to his views. Consequently, today we had an hour of character guidance, an hour of dismounted drill and an hour of PI. The morning was concluded with a few volleyball games.

        The character guidance class was a farce as it usually is. The Chaplain is a white haired old stoggy who preaches and lectures as if it were a Sunday School class of 10 year olds. The main points were reiterated: women, drink and the other sins that the G.I. gets mixed up with . The example he used today, was, that it would be much better to take the 10,29,39 or even the 40 dollars a person might spend for liquor in a month and light a match to it, instead of bringing it into ones body. Frankly, I think the best thing would be to get some of the old alcoholic and V.D movies and scare the boys. Sure the educators say that it is much better to talk and reason than to scare and punish, but I have heard a lot of former soldiers say that the only thing that kept them from running around with wild women was the V.D. film and its realistic portrayal of men and women who have advanced cases of syphilis.

        Back in the company area, we marched to the sorrowful bleating of 2 RA sergeants. For once I really disliked the stupid right and left flanks, to the van and columns left and right. I even got a pain in my side and was quite happy when we had our break.

        Then came the physical training, and owing to my arm I was in poor shape which really showed up fast. I am sure I will feel it tomorrow.

OCT 16 (SUNDAY - WEEK 43)

        The day was halfway decent and after listening a few minutes to the Navy – Penn State football game, I journeyed to the tennis courts for my first tennis since 3 weeks ago. I favored my arm awhile, but soon found that there was no pain and I attempted to blast across a serve that was “not there.” Had a good match with Chapman, and then he and I teamed up against a father and son team, and ended up getting beat 6-4.
