The two hours of exercise were a lot of fun and really needed.

        Went to the Plaza PX in the afternoon to do a little shopping. Couldn’t find a thing (sounds stupid to admit) but actually there wasn’t anything I thing thought to be practical and reasonable. Did end up buying some Christmas cards, but other than that, I came back to Kue, my shopping being a total loss. I will go to Naha next week and see if I can’t get something, and have decided this to be my last shopping spree for a long, long time.

        While walking through Naha the other night I passed a place in which I noticed some men preparing Soba, a Japanese dish of cold noodles. This and the other Japanese food I tasted up in Japan left me with a so-so attitude, – I guess curiosity would be the right word. Tempura isn’t bad, but it is too rich and fishy to make it a steady diet. The tea I thought to be terrible, and rice is the same throughout the world. The JApanese meals lacked green vegetables and I found myself eating at Western style restaurants to balance my diet.

OCT 17

        Feeling mighty stiff and sore from the tennis games, I managed to make my way to work and therein continued my slow progress on the Air Force housing estimate. The blueprints continue to cause me trouble and at times I think I am hardly moving along.

        I had planned to see the movie “Marty” in the evening, however, as luck would have it, the movie schedule was changed and I will have to plan to see the movie at either Sukiran or one of the other theaters on the island. The movies progress in order down an established schedule, and consequently, if I miss it at Kue, which is about #8 on the list, I will still be able to see it at a movie further down the list.

        My weekly Post Dispatch arrived, and after reading it and the Stars and Stripes, I was talked into going to the Castle Terrace. Since Chapman and Terry leave tomorrow on a 30 day leave, I decided to join their little party, even though I had decided “to stay home tonight.”

        I believe I mentioned a little about the recital I saw in Kyoto, however, there is perhaps a trifle bit more to say. The Japanese, while are definitely swerving away from the kimono and Geisha girl atmosphere of the past, still relish it a great deal, and generally dress up in kimonos for weddings, when having portraits taken and other notable occasions. (Two of the maids in our hut recently had a picture taken, and they wore kimonos, probably for the first time)

        The girl in the recital was young – perhaps 18-20 years old – and wasn’t very pretty, although she had the serene, calm look generally associated with Geisha girls. She had a beautiful kimono on, which was very bright and colorful. They put white powder on her face, accentuated her eyes, and tied her hair together so that the wig would go on. The wig or hairdo of a Geisha is very important, and is one of the trademarks of a Geisha and her apprentice the Gi_n.

        The hair is, of course, black and voluminous, with various combs neatly placed. The girl had on the gita and the white boot sock that goes with it. All in all she looked quite picturesque.

        She danced to the tune of a sam___n, and performed a tea ceremony and other dainty acts. In one portion of the recital, a small girl came on stage and performed like a miniature Geisha. She was even dressed in a kimono and wig and drew applause from the audience when she came on stage. I am sure sorry that I ran out of film and thus wasn’t able to take more than 2 pictures.

OCT 18

        Rained today, and made the atmosphere quite humid and sticky. Seems to rain at meal times, and today was no exception. However, luck was with us as we managed to beat the rain to the mess hall, although it paused while we ate and even throughout the rest of the lunch hour. I am afraid we are in for a damp winter, which will be quite disagreeable, although I can’t say that it is too different than St. Louis weather, for without a doubt St. Louis weather is one of the most humid in the U.S., both in winter and summer. Oh well, once I am back in St. Louis, I am sure I will cripe about the “lousy” weather.

OCT 19

        Late yesterday afternoon we received word that Typhoon Opal was was near by and that the island was now in Condition II. The typhoon moved closer to the island and on the 7 AM news we heard that it was only 50 miles away and we were officially in Condition I. Rain poured all morning amid winds and gusts ranging from 25-40mph. Electricity remained on, consequently there was no inconvenience and since we did not have to work, I got in some reading. I completed Gulliver’s Travels which is a mighty fine book, and one that takes a college student (age group) to get all of the meat of the book that Swift put in it. His witticism on social conditions and society in general, are great and somewhat applicable to the present.

        The all clear signal sounded was given at 1 PM and everybody was supposed to go to work. However since no one came around to “pass the word” the fellows in our hut stayed in the hut and either read or played bridge. The rain stopped and it was an ideal day to read and take it easy. I had planned to take off one afternoon this week so didn’t feel too bad about “goldbricking” during the P.M.

        The typhoon never came any closer than 30 miles to the island, and actually didn’t affect the weather too much. We had rain and moderate winds during the morning and previous night, but both rain and winds left in the afternoon, even though the typhoon was almost due East of us. It was headed NE and consequently shouldn’t hit Japan and spoil the leaves of a lot of fellows from the Rock presently in Japan.

​​OCT 20

        The day off in the middle of the week is a great idea and I am hoping for 32 hour weeks in the Army. Today seemed like Monday and with Friday being only a day away, this will indeed be a short week.

        Joe Alfonsi, my former boss, came back for a week (he is presently the honcho down in Formosa) in order to clear up his personal matters and to arrange to take his car back with him. He rain into some difficulty though with his car, and consequently will have to wait a couple of days before he can get passage on a boat for the automobile. He asked me if I would mind taking care of it for the few days after he leaves and before the boat sails, and I said all right. Sooo— it looks as if I will have some “wheels” for a couple of days. Don’t know where I want to go, but that is besides the point, – I guess!

        The weather is sure getting cool during the night, and I even sleep with 2 blankets and one window closed. I hope it doesn’t get much colder – say 50° or so – for I guess I would freeze, chicken that I am. I wonder what would have happened to me if I had remained in Korea, and during the phase out, they shipped me to the front lines. “Our father, who art in heaven…”

OCT 21

        Last Friday when at the dispensary I made an appointment to see the dermatologist at the hospital, and consequently I left work in the morning and got a lift to Mercy Hospital. Although my appointment was supposed to be for 9:30, I had to wait an hour before I was admitted. The waiting room was filled with pregnant women and small children, and was unusual in the respect that it had up to date magazines. I was finally ushered in to the Doc, and I peppered him with questions about Acne, Dandrift and my Arm. He seemed to know what he was talking about, and gave me some junk to cure the dandrift. Actually I am not bothered much with dandri acne, but I thought I would have him check my prescription to see if I should continue to use it. Concerning my arm, he said not to worry, but that it was probably old age creeping up on me, but if it got worse, I should come back.

        My maid was dying to see a football game, and she finally talked me in to taking her to the Naha Eagles – Marauder game which was to be played at the Kue Football field. The Eagles are bad, although the Marauders aren’t good either, but the latter team managed to come up with a 13-0 win. The game was boring and beset with poor officiating. Tried to explain the game to Junko, but I sure had a rough time. Of course I had to start from scratch, and to make it more difficult, our basic terms are quite different than their translation in Japanese. Still I think she picked up the basic fundamentals and had a good time. I froze sitting through the game for I haven’t received my coat as yet.

OCT 22

        Last night before I went to bed I asked the company clerk what was on the schedule for training for today. He informed me that I was to give a 2 hour talk in Carbine Marksmanship. Sooo–today I got the fellows in the day room and for 2 hours we read newspapers and magazines. Probably I will hear about it later, but they could at least inform me a “little sooner!”

        Joe Alfonsi left today and turned his car over to me. I am to take it to the ship next Friday where it will be shipped to him on Formosa. Meanwhile I have it for my use, and it was great driving around in a car once again. Actually I am a little clumsy with the controls, but it wont’ take me long to get back in the swing again.

        In the afternoon I took a Service Club Sightseeing trip to the Southern part of the island. We went to Naha and then via mighty poor roads to Homan, the largest fishing village on the island. We past passed through, passing somewhat slowly to get pictures and a chance to watch the people at work. The women in the village are supposed to be quite the saleswomen and also enjoy equal rights with the men which isn’t too common in the Orient.

        From here we drove to the Virgin’s Cave, where 122 young Okinawan students of the First Girls High School were either killed or committed suicide during the wiping up phase of the Okinawan campaign. No one were really knows what happened; – some think that they were killed by Americans when they refused to answer when challenged. A Japanese movie version of the story shows armed Japanese soldiers preventing surrender. The cave is actually a huge hole in the ground, with some caves leading off from the hole. There are two monuments commemorating the spot.

        From here we went to Suicide Cliff, which marks the spot where Generals Ushijima and Chō committed hari-kari at 4:10 AM on June 23, 1945, the last day of organized Japanese resistance. Near by are also some bones, skulls and other reminders of those Japanese soldiers who were killed or who committed suicide to prevent being captured. So many souvenir hunting people have taken some of the bones, that they are not now encased behind a stone wall.

        At the base of the cliff can be found the tomb of students from the Okinawa Teachers Training School who died helping the Japanese Army by running messages, patroling, etc. Their tomb is known by the name of Kenji-no-to.

        It began to get late, and so we climbed into the trucks and headed back to Sukiran and thence to Kue.

​​OCT 23 (SUNDAY - WEEK 44)

        Played some tennis in the morning, but it wasn’t too enjoyable as another fellow and I played with a young man and woman who weren’t too good. Nevertheless it was an opportunity to get some exercise

        I used Alfonsi’s car and went to the Plaza PX and the Plaza House and again attempted to buy something for home. About all I accomplished was to obtain some raw silk samples to send home for Mom’s concurrence. From here I went to Naha where I left the car for some repairs that had to be done. Spent the next 2 hours walking around Naha, looking at the goods on sale.

OCT 24

        The 1st Sgt. called me in this afternoon and said that he wanted to see me in the Orderly Room. Five minutes later I received the ‘good” news that as a result of the noise that I and 3 other fellows made coming back from the Castle Terrace on Saturday night, that we had to clean the Orderly Room. Since two of the fellows were to bowl tonight, it was decided that Tuesday night would be the big night.

        In the evening I decided to go to the Kadena NCO club and see what it was like. It is not that I am really interested in the Club, or in other NCO clubs, but since I have the car, I thought it would be a good opportunity to drive the 7 or so miles to the club. The building was nothing pretentious, and actually was somewhat shabby. It cost $1.00 to join for a month, and being a member of one NCO club, it is then possible to visit other NCO clubs around the island.

        The band was composed of Filipinos and there was a female singer that did a good vocal job. Actually I think the band is just as good as the band signed at the Castle Terrace Club. One good feature, at least for the fellows who like to dance but who do not have “honeys” or wives, are the dancing girls available for the boys to dance with. Most of them can dance fairly well, and can speak a little English, at least enough to carry on a limited conversation. The girls do not go to the individual tables, but sit instead near the dance floor, thus saving the Airmen from buying unnecessary drinks.

OCT 25

        I thought that EM were the biggest goof offs in the Army, but it appears that one of the Majors in Army Construction takes the cake. He asked me about one of the estimates that I had made, and before I could explain much of anything, he said, “Let’s take a field trip to the sight.” Sooo we got a sedan and proceded to Naha where we viewed the land that was to be paved. From here we went to the Port and thence to the Depot and Post Office and managed to kill 2 ½ hours in total.

        Concerning the estimate, I think he, like many of the others, has the wrong attitude. He takes the Construction Branches estimate and compares it with the Contractor’s bid. If there is a difference he assumes that the Contractor is right, and looks to see where the Construction made a mistake. Besides being the easiest to do – relation wise – it is generally easy to analyze the Construction Branch’s estimate since it is generally broken down into components whereas many times the Contractor comes in with lump sum quotes. At times it is quite frustrating.

        In the evening I took Joe’s car and went for a ride up the Eastern side of the island. The evening was cool, but made for good riding. Coming back I followed Route #13 hoping that it would hit $5, but I overshot the mark and landed in Yonabaru way south of Kue. Cut over to Naha and thence back to Kue for a 70 mile automobile ride. It was great to be behind the wheel again, but I must admit my legs got a little tired.

OCT 26

        Today was really a day of do nothing, – in the morning I went with Major Ejan to view a job that we were working on. From here he visited Naha Port, MSA and finally we went back to Kue. Got back at 11:30, and cooled it until lunch time. In the afternoon I was supposed to teach a 2 hour class in marksmanship, but we managed to compact everything in about 20 minutes, and since this was the only training scheduled we were off for the rest of the afternoon.

        Played some tennis in the afternoon, but the lay off of the past few days took its toll, for I was really stiff. After leading 4-2 I managed to lose the next 4 games and came out on the short end 4-6.

        Didn’t feel like reading all evening and decided to see the Camp Kue movie, “A Bullet for Joey.” Although E.G. Robinson and G. Raft were in the picture, it was one of the worst that I have seen in a long time. I believe I fell asleep 4 times and still do not know how the final scene came about. I struggled with myself t concerning whether to get up and get out leave, but finally I decided to stay in hope that it would get better, – but it never did.

        Mailed some packages home – one to the Barkers, and one to 520 – and was overwhelmed at the 2.60 postage cost. Whew, I imagine that if I would total up all the stamps and postage fees since I have been overseas, it would be tremendous. Oh well, guess one has to mail something to receive news from home.

OCT 27

        The one day respite that I had in the middle of last week was sure missed this ye week. Consequently, when today dawned bright and early, I was already looking for tomorrow and then the weekend. Estimating was becoming more interesting as I begin to learn about the various equipment, rental and usage information and construction practices. Today I talked to the Project Officer in charge of roads, etc, and he gave me the scoop concerning asphaltic concrete and the preparation that is necessary.

        Upon acquiring this basic information, I checked some of the contractors proposals and it disturbed me to see the huge profit that they have included in their bids. I talked to the Major and told him they were getting away with murder, and that the $2200 bid of the Contractor was too high, perhaps $800 higher than the Government Estimate. He said, “well he thought he could get the Contractor down to say $1800, and with the 15% allowance in the Government Estimate, that there would be only $200 difference.” I said that $1400 should be the limit, but he didn’t pay any attention. Don’t know exactly how to handle him, as he is RA, even though quite pleasant at times. Perhaps I should say that he’s literally giving the Contractor an extra $200. On the other hand, maybe I should say nothing further, as it really isn’t my problem once I make the estimate. I think I will wait until Monday, as the negotiation is to be held at that time and the Major said that I would be invited.

        While frustrating and disturbing at times, still it is interesting, and a beneficial experience. This year although not connected with Industry, still, the engineering experience will be so valuable as if I had been working for Dow, St. Louis Car Company or some other firm.

OCT 28

        The day passed quite rapidly, and before I knew it I was heading back to Kue and the final meal of the day. The meal wasn’t too good, so I had to get a couple of sandwiches later on in the evening.

        Received two St. Louis Post Dispatches today and was swamped trying to catch up with the news back home. The more I read, the more I feel that St. Louis has finally begun to get out of its shell, and with the $100,000,000.00 Bond Issue under its belt, things are picking up. In all phases – highways, culture, social, etc – improvements are blueprinted and it won’t be long before St. Louisians will have some additional interesting sights and events to publicize.

        While writing this, I have been listening to the radio, and recently a few minutes ago they mentioned that 400 Okinawan families were to depart soon for re-settlement in Bolivia. It seems that since there isn’t enough land for everybody, that some of the people have migrated to other countries; – Bolivia being the major country. One of the waitresses in our mess hall has spent much of her life in Bolivia, and she says that the family is beginning to giving a lot of thought to going back. Perhaps when the grandfather dies, they will move back, but he would like to die in Okinawa.

        The U.S. indirectly sponsors the movement, and furnishes many for medical supplies and agricultural equipment. Especially with the recent acquisition of much land in Okinawa for military purposes, the U.S. is interested in resettling as many families that can as possible. However, the Oriental tie to the ancestral land is very strong and there haven’t been too many that have immigrated.

OCT 29

        We were awakened at the horrible hour of 5:45 AM and reminded that today we were to go to the 1000 inch range for practice firing with the Carbine. The buses came at 7 and we headed for Early Range, about an hour and a half ride from Kue. The buses were about the best type of transportation provided as the 2 ½ ton truck and jeep being quite rough.

        THe group divided, with the Carbine men being coached by Lt. Dero_nes and the pistol group by Capt. Schl_y. The Lt. is a good man and directed the proceedings with a “I don’t give a damn and lets get this over with” attitude. He could joke, made fun of some of the stupid Army strictness and made the morning pass quite rapidly and with everybody getting their turn and at the same time, observing all the safety rules.

        The sun came out, then went in, rain came and then it left and in general the weather was all mixed up. I stayed in part of the afternoon, played cards, and finally got up enough energy to play some basketball. The fellow who I was playing with decided to go to our “big” gym (15’ x 25’) and I said that I would join him. He showed me how to hit the punching bag, but I could never get it going for any time duration. Once I stood too close to the bag, and on the rebound it hit me in the face. Didn’t knock me down, but did sting quite a bit.

        The evening was a typical Saturday night, and I spent the evening at the Castle Terrace. It was Halloween, and the Club was packed, however, we sat with a couple of the boys in the bar. Weren’t many costumes, although I had to chuckle at one 45 year old woman who came wrapped in a Turkish towel. She was quite a sight!

OCT 30 (SUNDAY - WEEK 45)

        It was a typical Sunday morning, although I did not play any tennis. Awakened about 7 AM, and listened to the Navy-Notre Dame football game prior to eating breakfast. After breakfast I returned to the hut and listened to the remainder of the game. Notre Dame outplayed Navy and walked off with a 21-7 victory, much to my sorrow.

        At 10:00 I listened to the football scores, as did the rest of the fellows in the hut, and received the sad news that once again I had lost in our weekly football pool. As a football prognosticator, I stink; however a couple of the victories that I was hoping for did come in. Missouri upset Colorado for their first victory this year, and Washington University beat Washington and Lee, 27-0. Also heard that the Baltimore Colt pro football team won again and are in 1st or 2nd place, I can’t remember. “Weeb” Ewbank, the Washington U. coach of 1947-49 is the coach of the Colts, and it seems that he is doing quite a creditable job.

        Took Alfonsi’s car to a Car Wash shop in the afternoon and got a wash and wax job for 150¥ (about $1.15). Four men worked on the car and they completed it in about 1 hour. They did a pretty good job although they didn’t put much wax on the car. Joe’s car has sure come in handy over the week or so that I have had it, but I must admit that it is more of a luxury than a necessity. I have taken a couple of rides in the evening, and have used the wagon to get to a couple of places in Sukiran and Auo__ that I wanted to go to. I am supposed to call tomorrow to see if the ship has arrived and when they want me to bring the car down to the dock. Anyway, it was great while it lasted.

OCT 31

        Another month – 7 more to go. Actually could be 4 more to go if I decided to try and get an early discharge. Will write to the draft board in the morning concerning a statement that I read in the World News & World Report, “that any person serving a minimum of 6 months cannot be drafted.” I sure hope that is true, for then the draft board can not hold anything over my head if I got out early.

        One of the problems that I face concerning getting an early discharge to go to school, is the fact that my 21 month tour will not end until 29 February 1956. Consequently, I am unable to go to semester schools, the only hope being the few quarter schools throughout the country. Of course there is always the possibility of going to school in Australia, where the seasons are the reverse of those in the United States, – thus the fall semester begins in March. I already have some information with respect to the Universities of Melbourne and Sydney, but will write further to obtain the latest catalogs. I have also written to the Missouri to find out if the 1 year at an Australian law school would be acceptable to the Board of Bar Examiners.

        A couple good features of going to school in Australia are: (1) getting out of the Army 3 months early, (2) getting to see Australia and per haps New Zealand and (3) being able to tour Southeast Asia from October to January, which are perhaps the best months to visit these hot countries. On the other side of the ledger are the points that (1) I wouldn’t get home until January 1957 and  (2) cost of school and the trip. If nothing else, I could go in the March-May term, and (1) see if I really want to continue in law, (2) get out of the army early, and (3) still be in Asia and thus able to do the touring that I am looking forward to.

        I guess I would really be a stranger to the family if I decided to go to school in Australia, for it would be over 2 years that I would be away from St. Louis. Actually that isn’t too long, as there were many soldiers away from their families for 3-4 and even 5 years during World War II.

        In the evening I went to the Top three club, the local Army NCO club. My membership card from the Air Force NCO club entitled me to go to the club and I decided to take advantage of the fact. Being payday night the club was crowded but we found a table near the door. The band was good and the singer was also good. Food and drink was cheap and all in all I had a reasonable and enjoyable evening. THe bad feature is the distance from Kue which is a little far by bus or cab.

NOV 01

        Called the Port about Joe’s car and finally got the word that the ship is to be in Naha at 6 tomorrow and that I should bring the car down to the dock around 8:30. And so ends what will probably be my first and last use of a car on Okinawa.

        Was informed that we were to receive shots today and I am glad that we weren’t given any advance notice. I meekly walked through the shot line and proceded to get 4 shots including a Small Pox scratch. My arms didn’t bother me for awhile but before I went to bed my left arm began hurting and gave bad signs for the following day.

NOV 02

        My arms were a little better today although I acquired a slight headache. Most of the fellows in the unit had the same trouble, and it was humorous to hear everybody ask each other, “How is your arm feeling?”

        Did very little actual work today, for in the morning I took Joe’s car down to the dock and turned it over to the proper personnel. They said that I had to wait until they checked the car for scratches, etc. Consequently, I waited around for 1 ½ hours until somebody made a quick survey for scratches, dents, broken lights and other items that the shipping company doesn’t want to get stuck for.

        In the afternoon a I went on a brief field trip to Machinato to check on the progress of a small drain. The only work the contractor had done was deliver some concrete pipe so my task was quite easy. I goofed in one way though for I assumed that the pipe was 30” diameter pipe, but I later found out that 24” pipe was being used on the same job and my assumption could have been wrong. It turned out that it was 30” stuff, but shows that one has to do a better job if he intends to get ahead. Perhaps it is necessary to get all the information asked for, plus trying to visualize some of the problems that could come up. I am always reminded of the man who had 3 sons working for a large company, one of whom was a $800/month man, the next was a $400 man and the third was $250/month. The father went to the General Manager and asked why there was such a difference in the salaries of his sons when he thought they were about equal in talent. The General Manager said, “I’ll show you,” and he called the sons in individually and asked each to obtain some information about a shipment of goods that was due in. The $250 son checked and came back and said that it hadn’t come in as yet. The $400 son said that it hadn’t come in, but that he had checked and that the goods had left 3 days ago and should be in tomorrow. The $800 man said the same as the $400 man, but he also checked for when the material was to go into production and since it was due on the midnight shift he telephoned the foreman and had other arrangements made. The General Manager then remarked to the father and said that he thought the answers explained the difference in salaries.

        Went to the American Consul and got some more information about getting a passport. Made an appointment for 10 November. Also wrote letters to the military attaches of each of the countries I hope to visit asking for a letter stating that I have their permission to enter. Phew – what Army hogwash!

NOV 03

        Finished reading the book, “The Age of Conformity” by Alan Valentine. While there was quite a bit that I did not agree with, still some of the basic premises are worth thinking about. The U.S. is without a doubt the greatest materialistic nation in the history of the world, and the production prowess is also tops. However, the social and cultural progress has not progressed at the same rate and consequently there is much to be desired along these avenues. Too many Americans are sold on the “average” or “common man” denominator for the U.S. Consequently they dislike high and low brows and strive fervently to be good middlebrows. (Later, on this same subject)

NOV 04

        Went on a field trip in the afternoon and witnessed how a contractor can get himself into trouble if he does do not give some thought to the estimate. Kokuba Gumi, the largest Okinawan contractor bid $.60/cy for 267,000 cy of excavation, and $.80/cy for Bo_row. The area was composed of small hills and former rice paddies, the latter having no drainage. Consequently, in order to obtain the necessary compaction, the contractor had to remove a lot of muck, some of it 6-10 feet deep; fill in 2-3 feet of sand and then add b_rrow and compact as usual. Bulldozers weren’t able to remove the muck, and thus crane-shovels and Pans had to be used. The muck then had to be disposed of in the ocean. The sand is being obtained from the ocean and 2 pans, 1 shovel and some men are working during low tides to get the sand. All of these factors cost a lot and should remove any profit the contractor had figured on.

        In the evening we had the second practice Air Raid Drill since I have been on the “rock”. At Approximately 7:00 PM, the siren sounded and most of the lights went out. A couple of minutes later a siren sounded too soon and most of the lights went on in the Sukiran, Kue, and Kadena Areas. A plane flying overhead was brox broadcasting during the blackout and it was humorous to hear him complain of “all the lights still on in the Kue – Sukiran area, even the football stadium lights.” About the football game – it was pretty good, and served to provide something different in the way of entertainment.

NOV 05

        Saturday morning training again. The training open up with an inspection in ranks by the 1st Sgt. While he was inspecting the troops the air raid siren sounded and everybody scattered to the dispersal areas. Our area is #6 and is located in the hills in back of the camp. We double timed up the hill and found spots on the side of a hill to sit and await the all-clear signal. The practice this morning was the second half of the 2 day training and it is designed to get the troops orientated in case of a real air raid, and also remind the indigenous people that Okinawa is a prime target for enemy airplanes if there is a 3rd World War or even a small war such as Korea.

        Speaking of Korea, I read an article in Saturday Evening Post about Korea and it was one of the most accurate articles that I have ever read concerning S. Ree’s country. It discussed the poverty and disease, the difficulties encountered by Army relief agencies, S. Ree and his proud nationalistic attitude the new, “huge”, Korean Army and life in general. Since much of the description was about Pusan, it was that much more familiar to me. Korea is unlike any country that I have visited in the Orient and perhaps has problems unique among the other Asiatic people. They have been under denomination by a foreign power for such a long time (1910-1945), and of course the Korean War, that they have not yet developed a recovery plan that is workable. Perhaps things will work out, but the Koreans will have to help themselves more (countrywise not individual wise) and also be more appreciative of the help other countries want to give them.

NOV 06 (SUNDAY - WEEK 46)

        Bill Cornell and I went to Kadena Village in the morning to take some pictures of a track meet that was to be held. However we found out that it was a cross country race and no one knew when it was to start. We decided to stick around a few minutes, and also look the area over. On the top of a nearby knoll we found half (or more) of the village excavating behind the shrine, and removing the dirt in bags or on pieces of cloth. It was 100% hard labor, performed by 90-120 persons, and doing the work of one small bulldozer. Perhaps, though, it will be “everybody’s” church and in this manner will mean much more to them.

        In the evening I went to Sukiran and saw the 2nd All Army Show, titled “Rolling Along.” The numbers are all winners of sectional talent contests and each were tops in their fields. The show was great and moved along fast throughout 1 hour and a half, and without the services of any master of ceremonies. ONe skit was a tamboueline SPT number in which 2 fellows did almost unbelievable stunts and somersaults. The band members were individual artists in their own right, and each gave special numbers besides performing well as a group. The two comedians were New Yorkers from the Bronx and they had some excellent jokes and animations. Other numbers were: harpist, colonel vocalist and quartet, top notch hillbilly singer and a concert pianist. I guess I can say that this was the best show I have seen in the Army.

        

NOV 07

        This normally would be birthday week, but for the year 1955 it is going to have to be a long distance or via Airmail birthday week. Hard to believe that I will be 26 in a day or so, but that is the age I will have attained on 9 November 55. Oh well, no sweat, time marches on; for in order for me to be getting closer to ETS day, I also am getting closer to doomsday. (Joyful thought!)

        Can’t complain in any way. Have my health, good family relations and a desire to learn as much as I can. My life thus far has been easy, with few periods of extremely hard work. As a matter of fact, most of my life thus far has been in school and with society providing the meat and water. Actually society is too broad and also not entirely correct, for Mom has been the driving force behind our family, depriving herself so that the 3 kids can finish college and have a good basis for setting out in the cruel or demanding world.

        Thus far I have no obligations other than to make sure Mom is comfortable and provided for. Not being married I have no obligation in that respect and should thus be able to do whatever I want without having to keep someone in mind when deciding. My materialistic outlook of my high school and college days is vanishing and I find myself searching for a vocation where I can not only serve my family but society as well. And while attempting to accomplish this end I must be satisfied with my work, for doing something distasteful would lead to a neurotic state of mind.

NOV 08

        Have been working on two estimates in the Naha Air Base and made a 3rd field trip to the air base. Obtained some information concerning excavation of the Air Police building, and compared it with the proposal of the Contractor. The Contractor’s bid is high, and its his rental notes were from 3-5 times as h that of the Government. Using his quantities for equipment and labor, the Government estimate was about 20% of the Contractor. I suggested to let our estimates go through like this and show the inane proposal on the part of the Contractor, but my boss decided to modify our proposal and include items necessary to meet Government specifications which are omitted in the first estimate.

        Major Eagan called me and questioned a $.98/cy price for B_rrow versus the Contractor $1.25. He said that the contract price for Excavation, unda_fied was $1.00 and that the Contractor wasn’t going to accept a price $.02 less when he had to get the b_rrow from outside the area. I said that the $.98 was a good price and that since Contractors are accepted on a lump sum basis, and thus individual items could be wrong, at which the $1.00 figure is a good example. I told him that I wasn’t going to change my price and he said I was off base and would have to go over me. And with that I left, as any additional discussion would be futile.

        Went to the Terrace in the evening, which was the first time in about 10 days. Had a couple of beers, a sandwich, garlic bread, french fried onion rings and came home.

NOV 09                        CHARLES’ 26TH BIRTHDAY

        Happy Birthday. God it is awful to be 26. Oh well, I guess I had better start acquiring some age to go with the grey hair I am growing on the top of my skull. Jake Fox shook my arm in the morning around 6:30 AM and yelled a husky “Happy Birthday,” – and thus did the anniversary of my birth start. Received a Happy Birthday from the waitresses in the mess and a couple of people at work. All in all it was a fine birthday, and with its passing, should mean the last birthday that I have to spend in the Army.

        Work was the same as usual and consisted of working on some estimates. In the evening I took one of the fellows CQ for him while he went to the show, and spent the time writing letters and reading the October 9th section of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch.

        Read in the local paper where the Marine that raped a 7 year old Okinawan girl about a month ago, got sentenced to life imprisonment. This case and another rape case stirred up a lot of trouble and some acrimonious blasts in the Okinawan papers. For awhile there was some tails of putting the village off limits, but there wasn’t much to the rumor and I am sure that the Okinawan businessmen wouldn’t put up with it. The 2nd case comes to trial at the end of the month and should be a sensational trial since in this case the little girl died as a result of the rape. If the life sentence from the other trial is any basis, this shoulder could get death. I am sure that the Okinawan papers, some Communist agitators and other civilians would then be satisfied. The fact that both rapes came within 1 week of each other is the reason for the tremendous adverse public opinion.

NOV 10

        Typical goof off day. Worked awhile in the morning and then went to the American Consul, where I filled out the necessary papers for my passport. Also, got to talking with the fellow preparing the necessary forms and data and found out that he is a Foreign Service Official who joined in 1942, but who did not have to take the test. He has been around the world serving in various posts. Actually talking to him sort of brought out some of the routine and somewhat boring duties of some of the Foreign Service. Actually, few jobs are the policy jobs we read about, with the majority of the work consisting of the handling of registration and passport duties for American citizens abroad.

        From the Consul’s office I learned that I would need visas and that some of them took a couple of days to get. They also told me that some of the airlines would get the visas for a fee. I thus journeyed to PAA and the lady said that they would mail my passport to Tokyo to obtain the visas, and it shouldn’t take too long. I got the necessary applications, and also had the reproduction lab at OKEO make me 20 additional photos of my passport picture.

        There is sure a lot to do in order to travel, particularly when one is in the Army. If I wasn’t in the Army I wouldn’t have had to write to the Military Attaches nor get a visa to the Philippines. Oh well, the monetary savings by catching military planes is worth the extra work.

        Saw a half of the Marine football game at Kue Field and it was an exciting scoreless tie.

NOV 11

        It was great to have a day off and I enjoyed every minute of it. It either rained or threatened to rain all day long, consequently I spent the day indoors. In the morning I completed filling out the applications for visas to India, Indonesia and the Philippines, and will take them to PAA on Saturday morning. Read the newspaper in the afternoon and began writing and completing my Christmas Cards. Am using the Cards to catch up on some of my correspondence – Cheating, I know – and I think I am only 3 letters behind all of which I have just recently received.

        Sat through a drizzling rain at the football game in the evening and saw the Marauders _____ the Gunners 7-0. More action and comedy in the stands as some of the Gunner boys got some “pop” bottles and proceed to get quite high. One conversation between a RA and a US (colored boys) was really funny and had most of the crowd in laughter. Some of the colored boys have a mannerism all their own, and when 8-10 of them get together and begin talking, some of the expressions are priceless.

        While getting a sandwich at the Kue Restaurant, one of the SP boys came in all “s_used” up. He made a lot of noise and asked anyone to fight him outside. No one paid any attention so he grabbed a middle aged Filipino man by the coat collar and began dragging him. About 8 of the 8105 boys stepped in and separated them, and took Wally to jail so as to sober up for his 2 AM - 8 AM shift. I doubt if he makes it.

NOV 12

        The second day of our 3 day holiday, and the 2nd day that it has rained. It rained all day today and made it gloomy and somewhat miserable. In the morning I hopped a bus and went to the Plaza area in order to take my visa applications to PAA, as they said they would fly them to Japan for me. The man in the office had a brief change of mind and at first said that he wouldn’t be able to do it unless I bought a ticket. I told him that I would probably try and get military rides for part of the way, and then ride commercial the rest of the way. After a few minutes, during which he called the Air Force to see if they had any means of getting my visas, and upon finding out that there wasn’t, he said he would do it for me. I thanked him and said that I hoped that no difficulties developed.

        From PAA I went to the Plaza House where I bought a pair of earrings to match the bracelet that I had sent Carolyn. Took a bus to the Gift Shop and bought a pillow for my “reading chair.” The chair has an iron bar supporting the seat and it gets uncomfortable when I sit in the chair for any period of time. Bought some more Christmas cards and that finished my shopping – for some time I hope.

        One of the fellows in the hut had some films that he was going to show some of the Okinawan laborers, and he decided to show them to the boys so as to pass a rainy afternoon. One of the movies was about Hiroshima, another showed shots of the last war, and one was an American safety movie with Japanese words. The war movie had shots of the Okinawan battle and it was interesting to see the tremendous struggle for this “The Rock.”

NOV 13 (SUNDAY - WEEK 47)

        Listened to the Iowa – Ohio State football game for awhile and was sorry to hear Iowa go down to a 20-10 defeat. Missouri also lost, and consequently I am worried about the 3rd member of the Trio – Washington U. They have around a 500% for the year and I am anxious to see them do a little better.

        Journeyed up to Kadena and spent about 2 ½ hours watching the All-Okinawa track meet along with approximately 20,000 other Okinawans. The participants represented various villages on islands (Naha, Nago, Itoman, Miyako, etc.) and they were accompanied by many clapping and cheering well wishers. The races were in meters and I finally figured out the distances they were running. Some of the athletes looked quite fast, particularly in the longer distances. In these long races, the runners competed in their bare feet, the track being a clay mixture. In the 10,000 meter (approximately 7 miles) the winner paced himself nicely over the 25 lap grind, and even lapped a couple of the tail enders.

        Part of my time was spent watching the Okinawans, since this was the largest group that I have seen in one place. The people on the whole seemed health, although they wore uniformist and somewhat tattered clothing. They were about 5’4” – 5’5” in height and almost all had coal black hair. The men wore their hair very long, the women having a fancy for curls once they break from the strictness of the school girlish straight hair. Some of the older women had tattoos on their knuckles an old time sign of beauty. The children were the ever-cute rascles that they are.

        One interesting thing is that many Okinawans have bad complexions. Interesting that such a large group of people would be so affected. Perhaps it is their dirt or daily living habits although I really have no idea what it is being caused by.

NOV 14

        Was asked by Air Force Construction to sit in on a negotiation meeting with Kokuba Gumi concerning the Government’s proposal for the additional work and modifications for the Maintenance Hangar in Naha. Kokuba originally proposed $69,000.00 but revised it when the Government wrote them a letter saying that it was far too much. They lowered it to $62,000.00 and said that that was their rock bottom price.

        The meeting was held in order to determine the difference in the $62,000 price and the Government Estimate of $29,000. As we progressed down the items, it became apparent that their estimate had many mistakes, errors in multiplication, quantitative and price wise. They gave little thought to the transportation, misc. Materials and labor and quoted huge figures for all of them whether they were 100% correct or 1000% over. Many of their multiplications were against them and it was ludicrous to see a huge company make mistakes such as these. Kokuba has got about 8-9 million dollars worth of Government work, and it appears that whereas they could make a killing, they probably end up with small profits owing to the inefficiency and poor engineering help.

        Eviedentally Kokuba lost money on the Maintenance Hangar job and is attempting to pad this modification so as to recap some of their loses. However, they did it in such a sloppy way and with poor bargaining men to help them that they probably won’t get much more than the 20% allowed for overhead, profit and contingencies. After pa__ing off a couple thousand dollars, the contractor said they would resubmit a new proposal on Friday.

NOV 15

        In the afternoon I went on a field trip to a project near Kue where a guard house was is being built. I had an estimate to make of some rip rapping on the sides of a ditch, and thought it would be a good idea to check the field conditions; ahem, and excuse to leave the office. One of the fellows in the hut was is the inspector on the job and he and I walked around the jobsite for about 2 ½ hours, observing the construction and remarking about Engineering design and Okinawan construction practices. It was very enlightening to me as I have very little background in practical construction and welcome such opportunities as this.

        Read my Time magazine, and went to the office to write a few letters. I received during the day a letter from the Missouri Board of Bar Examiners in which they stated that the credits from Melbourne are acceptable to them provided the University wherefrom I receive my LLB accepts the credits. Consequently, I wrote to St. Louis University and George Washington University to find out what their official policy is on foreign schools. Also wrote home some prices of things and objects that are noted buys in the Orient, to see if anybody is interested. I mentioned jade, ivory, raw silk, pearls, china, etc. for unless they desire something, I don’t think I will send anything just to be sending it. Morton has said that he might be interested in jade and ivory so perhaps this information will help him decide.

NOV 16

        Today the one and only New York Yankees came in on the morning airplane to play 2 ballgames here on the Rock. The early morning weather was great and the sun beamed as it hasn’t done in many a day. Around 10:30 – 11:00 it began to cloud up, and at approximately 11:15 it began to rain. At first it was just a drizzle, but by 12 noon it began to pour. The rain came in bucketfulls, and by 1 PM it became apparent that it would be impossible to play a game. Since those that had tickets were excused for the game, most of the fellows decided to stay away from work and take it easy.

        I read a magazine, joked around with Junko and watched some movies that Ted had gotten and was showing in his room. The one movie was about the war in the Pacific, and showed scenes of our country fighting back and eventually whipping Japan. There were a couple of instances were close up shots showed dying Japanese soldiers, and it was somewhat disgusting to see fresh flowing blood, rigor mortis setting in and recently burned bodies. Junko watched the boys movies but didn’t have much to say. I asked her later about the movies but all she said was “I understand.” It must be sort of rough on her since most Okinawans consider themselves part Japanese, and they have a tendency to look up at to the Japanese people; their education and higher standard of living.

NOV 17

        The weather was bad all morning long and it caused postponed of the 1st game of the proposed double header with the New York Yankees. In the afternoon it died town to a drizzle and Pepsi Cola, sponsors of the game, decided to go ahead and play 1 game so that refunds had would not have to be made.

        Intense preparations went into the readying of the field for play, even though the end result was still a muddy mire. The men poured gasoline on the infield and ignited it in an effort to vaporize some of the water. Tons of earth were brought in and spread on the infield so that there would be at least a couple inches of dry dirt. The Okinawan laborers then raked the dirt and packed it in an effort to eliminate unequal levels of earth.

        By 2 PM the field was in as good as shape as possible under the conditions, and since there was only a slight drizzle, the game was on, – the NY Yankees versus the Okinawan All-Stars. The Yankees came to bat first and produced 4 runs on 3 hits, one of which was a booming home run by Carey into left field. The All-Stars were out, one, error, two-three and the score was 4-0. The Yankees got another homer in the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 7th for a total of 9 runs. The All-Stars scored one run on a homer by their right fielder.  The game was boring and too lopsided.

        Perhaps in the future, major league all star teams should accompany the team so as to furnish good competition and make for interesting games. Games like this point out the fact that baseball has a tendency to be boring.

NOV 18

        Well the (excuse me) THE New York Yankees have come and gone and life settled down to the same drab existence on Okinawa Shi_a, lovingly called “the Rock.” The contractors came back with a new proposal, and presented an estimate of $50,000; $12,000 under the 2nd, and $19,000 under the first. Still this was about $24,000 more than the comparable work in the Government estimate, and it was decided to discuss each major item, and the listed work under each item.

        For 7 hours we discussed the mechanical work, which consisted of about $3000 (Gov’t) work including partitions, piping, construction of a transformer house, and miscellaneous work. The Contractor (4 men) came down from $8,000 to about $3,500 for the work. The Gov’t [Air Force Const. (2) and Construction Branch (2)] were anxious to complete the work today even though the Contractor’s proposal had lump sum figures which the Government had asked them to breakdown. Around 4 PM col Colonel Miller came in and put a blast to the committee for the slow progress and said the “negotiation would have to be done finished today.” Not only did he scare the contractor, but he scared his 2 men, also. Mr. Jackson who was conducting the meeting then proposed to split the difference between the Government and Contractor on the electrical work #23,000 vs. 41,000. The Contractor wouldn’t listen and so Jackson proposed a compromise at $36,000. The contractors agree ahd thus ended the negotiation. Thus, we talked 7 hours on $3,000 worth of work, and 15 minutes on $23,000 worth of work of electrical goods. I said that the Construction Branch would not go along with such a compromise, but all I could do was voice our disapproval since we were only in the meeting for consultation as to our quantities and prices in the estimate.

        I returned to our section and voiced my disgusted opinion to Mr. Kent. He said that the agreed price, if over the allotted 15% increase, has to come back to him and he then can ask for Colonel Miller’s justification of the settlement. On the way to the chow hall I passed Colonel Miller’s office, and I stuck my head in the window and voiced my disapproval of the last bit of work of the negotiation, – the electrical compromise. What followed was about 15 minutes of good natured discussion and argument concerning the negotiation, the “bending over backward on the part of the Gov’t to make up for the Contractor’s inefficiency,” relative merit between Japanese and American Contractors on Okinawa, and estimating in general. I was glad to get my thoughts off my chest and it seems that the Colonel is such a guy that he doesn’t mind such backtalk from EM. I hope so! (Incidentally he was a Lt. Colonel at the age of 27 and is now waiting for his full bird (age 38)

NOV 19

        Not much doing today. I went to work in the morning instead of training, and will probably have to get a flu shot next week. Also missed character guidance, but that didn’t phase me as it is generally quite lousy. The rest of the day was a typical Saturday; – eat lunch, read, shoot the bull, tease the maids, play basketball, eat supper, read, write in the diary, go to the Castle Terrace and finally go to bed. There are no Big Saturday Nite dates over here.

NOV 20 (SUNDAY - WEEK 48)

        Fifth straight day of rain and the cool air made the weather quite uncomfortable. Consequently the day fell into the typical Sunday mold; listened to the football game of the day (UCLA - Southern Cal.), tuned in on a report of the football scores (lost the pool for the 8th straight week), read, ate and goofed around.

        In the evening I went to Naha and in particular, the Orion Theater. I purchased the tickets and then we (Junko) went upstairs where the most comfortable seats are located (also 10¥ more per seat). The show was jammed and we decided to wait until the break hoping to get a seat at that time. The break came, but still too many people for the empty seats that were available. We wound our way up on one of the aisles, and partly sat, strained and did everything in an effort to see some of the screen. Luckily after 15 minutes of this ritual, 2 people nearby left and we were able to grab the seats.

        People were everywhere, and I daresay they sold 3 tickets for every 2 seats. The people did not pay heed to the No Smoking signs and it was very stuffy in the theater. I gave one thought of what would happen if there was a fire, but quickly dispelled it from my mind as we were sure goners.

        The movies were individually good but combined were too long, and after 4 hours I was lucky only to come out with a slight headache. Along with the movie they had commercial shorts, a news, and about 4 or 5 teasers of coming movies. Altogether it was too much movie, even for the ¥40 price.

NOV 21

        Blue Monday, and not only did the weather continue to be uncomfortable, but I was tired and I had a hard time keeping awake. I had to go to the water fountain a couple of times during the afternoon in order to put cold water in my eyes.

        Near the end of the day I saw Jackson, and he informed me that the electric prices we had for the maintenance hangar job were much too low, and did not represent the true cost from 1955 catalogs. Consequently, he said that the $41,000.00 price that was agreed on, was just exactly what the price should be. I said that I was interested in the fact that our prices were low, and expressed the opinion that perhaps he was justifying the end and not the means to the end. I still am of the opinion that the bargaining that went on was a bad policy and that irrespective of the fact that he latter proved his actions to be justified, still when he compromised he wasn’t aware of the cost figures.

        The discussion continued and he expressed his thoughts concerning Estimating and the Construction Branch’s method of preparing estimates. From the conversation it was apparent that he had had considerable experience in estimating and knew what he was talking about. (He also embarrassed me somewhat by showing up my inexperience in this field, but although feeling somewhat awkward at the time, it only furthered my interest in learning more about estimating. He loaned me an estimating handbook which seems to be quite good and perhaps I can get something out of it.

NOV 22

        At last the sun came out, and it was a brilliant sunlight that sweeps away the bad taste caused by 6 straight days of rain. Chapman and I decided to play tennis, so we left work about 3:30. As luck has it, the sun went down, but nevertheless we got in 2 good sets of tennis before it became too chilly and too dark. Al is a better than average player and makes a good opponent; – even too good for he whipped me 6-1 in the 1st set. I won the 2nd set 6-3, but not without a struggle.

        Tried something during the day but it didn’t work. I had the Company Clerk make out a 3 day pass for next week and I took it in to Mr. Kent for his signature. First, I asked him if he it would be possible to get placed on TDY orders so that I could visit Formosa for 3 or so days. I said that I would much rather take the 3 days there instead of in Hut #725, Camp Kue. Mr. Kent obliged by called Capt. Stillwagon to see if any courier service was needed to Formosa, but Stillwagon said there was noting at present. Sooo – no dice, however, Kent signed the pass and consequently, I will have a 3 day vacation next week. Heres hoping that it doesn’t rain.

        Dicker, my vociferous neighbor across the hall, has been staying at another fellows house for the past 4 or 5 days, and there has been wonderful silence in the hut in the evening. Consequently, I got some reading done (without having to put cotton in my ears) before being talked into going to the Castle Terrace for something to eat. (The evening meal was terrible.)

NOV 23

        I wish something exciting would happen so that my daily writing in the diary wouldn’t be as dull and uninteresting. Not nearly as exciting or revealing as some of the other pages in this red water sploched book.

        Completed an estimate in the morning and killed time reading until noon. Had hoped to receive some mail as I am expecting some papers and information from the States (Draft Board and Law Schools) and from Australia. However, I only received a note from Mom together with some clippings she sent. One clipping concerned Korea and the other was an account of N_rty’s wedding in Memphis. Sounded like quite a shi-bang, and I am sorry that I wasn’t in the states and thus able to attend.

        Received my flu shot in the afternoon and decided to follow the advice of one of the fellows by exercising my arm in order to allow the vaccine to enter my whole system and not lump up in my arm. Whether this worked (along with the aspirin I took) I am not positive but thank goodness I had little or no after effects. My arm didn’t pain me and I didn’t get any headache or throbbing, so I was quite happy. Was supposed to take training but they forgot to put my name on the list, so I didn’t go. Could never think I doing something that I didn’t have to!

        Typical evening; – read, went to the movie (terrible) and went to the Castle Terrace. Also looked at some slides that Chapman and Terry had taken in Japan. They were quite good and brought back some good memories of my travels to Japan. Fine land with fascinating people.

NOV 24 - THANKSGIVING DAY

        The day was beautiful and was ideal for outside activities. A couple of the boys got together and played some doubles, both in the morning and afternoon. The sun was beaming and the air crisp and delightful and we got in about 3 ½ hours of “fair” tennis. I had to borrow a racket as mine is broken, but they have some pretty good ones (SPECIAL SERVICE) and in fact the one I used was better than mine was before it broke.

        Came back to #725 in the morning and washed up for the big Thanksgiving meal. It was still early so I journeyed over to Kue Stadium to watch the football game between the Marines and the Army. The game was quite good, but the Marines won, which sort of spoiled it. )I haven’t much love for the jarheads.) Had my camera along and tried to get some action shots. Also took some pictures of the jarhead band during halftime activities.

        The noon meal was in the mess hall, but they had decorated it with pumpkins and corn stalks, and had table cloths on the tables. The meal was really great deli delicious and the meal consisted of turkey, dressing, cranberries, corn, potatoes, rolls, olives, ice tea, ice cream and pumpkin pie. Everything was really great and I stuffed myself with as much as possible. Actually I ate too much, and felt sluggish for part of the afternoon.

        Where will I be next Thanksgiving? St. Louis, Washington, D.C, Sydney, Melbourne, ……?

NOV 25

        It is always hard going to work on Monday or the day after a holiday, and today was no exception. At first I thought that I wouldn’t have anything to do, but about 8:30, Jackson of the Air Force Division came in and said that the recent estimation of the Housing Projects in Naha and Kadena were to be negotiated shortly and he thought that there were some errors in the quantity of some items and also the prices. The major items concerned the elimination of the metal latching; but instead of throughout the house as the Major had said, it would be only effective in the living room. He mentioned a couple of other places and I then returned to our section to do some checking. This took some time and I didn’t revise it until around 3:30, with only the cost of the latching still to be agreed upon. Engineering estimating said cost plus labor and overhead was about $.15/SF, while Jackson thought that to be too high. We decided to call one of the Jobbers on the island and see what he would want for the material. The jobber we called said he would call back, as he was busy, so I returned to my desk to await the final information. Goofed around until 5:00 and headed for the mess hall.

        Went to the movie in the evening and saw  British film on World War II, and in particular, a concentration camp in Germany, and how an escape procedure was devised to get out of the camp. The picture was quite interesting and provided a couple hours of delightful character study and comedy.

NOV 26

        Another Saturday and training once again. We “fell out” around 7:30 with Carbine, fatigue, canteen and pistol belt. “Attention, Right Face, Forward March, “ and we were on our way, that is, we were marching on our first hike at Kue. We marched about 45 minutes, rested ½ hour and then returned to camp. The hike wasn’t bad as we went along a route in back of Kue, and one upon which I had never travelled. The weather was great, and the walk was good exercise, and I really didn’t mind it. However, when we arrived back in camp we were marched straight to the 1200 block and given a 1 ½ hour lecture about squad tactics. Boring, to say the least, and I nearly fell asleep ten times. At 11:00 we went back to the company area, and had police call and an inspection. Sooo the morning dragged on, and was a bad plum that I was glad to get rid of.

        One of the fellows in the hut has checked out a 16mm movie projector and some films from USCAR. Lately he has been showing them to some of the Okinawans at his job site and today he invited the waitresses and maids to see the 4 films. I didn’t see the 1st 3, but did see part of the last one. It was in Japanese and concerned an artist (American) who visits a Japanese artists who explains (and actually does some sketching) some of the typical Oriental Art. The subject matter in these instances was nature, and the work interesting although not too exciting by my standards. Everyone seemed to enjoy the movies, and Ted should be complemented for he giving of his time and energy.

NOV 27 (SUNDAY - WEEK 49)

        Spent the morning in Naha, looking at some perspective items, and in general, observing the people. I have come to the conclusion that no matter where I am, with a doubt the most fascinating and interesting feature is the human being that inhabits the particular area that I am in. It was this way in Korea, Hong Kong and Japan. Japan was the country where I arrived at this conclusion since even though there is much to see and do in Japan, I felt that my most enjoyable times were when I just stood and watched the people, – such as Heian Park and on the Shinsaibashi in Osaka. I soon realized that the shrines and temples were very similar to the ones built 100 years earlier and maybe 600 years later. Not so with the people, – for there were the peasants, the finely dressed, the handsome ones, the artists etc.

        If it weren’t for this same interest on Okinawa I long ago would have stopped going to the villages, for everything of interest, or a good portion of it, was destroyed during the war. The people remain, though, and I spend much time observing the Okinawans trying to paint a picture of them in my mind so that I won’t forget. In doing this I subconsciously try to compare them with the Japanese, Koreans, Chinese, etc and try to visualize how they compare are similar and how they differ. The Okinawans seem to be a mixture of Chinese and Japanese, both in features and culture. Some of their oldest habits and customs come from China, but the more recent influence is from Japan, the language is Japanese and differs from Tokyo Japanese only in the same manner that Southern English differs from good old Yankee speak.

        Okinawans are about the same size as the Japanese and wear the kimono, although being a poor country, one doesn’t see many people wearing them. Also, there being so many Americans (percentage wise) I am sure that the Western styles influence the populace. I haven’t seen too many good looking women, and the men wear their hair too long, which seems to be typical of the Japanese people. The complexions are even worse than the Japanese and the hair seems to be a little coarser although I am not too sure of the later. The kids are cuter, I believe, but one sees many children with sores on their head. One also sees more children carried on the backs of other children. Unlike Korea where the legs of the carried child are wrapped around the waist, the legs are allowed to dangle.

NOV 28

        Takes a knack to spend a day doing nothing, but I believe I am getting to be a master at it. From 9-9:20 I wasted time in the Personnel Office waiting to sign my rotation papers but they weren’t ready. 10-11:00 was spent in Capt. Schlag’s office along with other Sgts getting the poop on the new reveille policy. 1:00-2:00 was spent waiting for the 1st Sgt and from 3:30-4:30 was taken up by leave problems and how to circumvent “Little God” Sergeants. This left ½ hour to do work, but instead I caught up on my mail. Oh well, no sense getting started on anything with a leave coming up.

NOV 29

        I got tangled in the stupid Army Red Tape today and was somewhat bitter over the whole thing. It all started on Monday when I found that I could get my leave orders without having all the letters of permission from the Military Attaches. Tuesday morning I attached the 2 letters that I had received and took the works to Personnel (and another Little God RA Sgt, Juong) so as to obtain the Captains signature that I needed. The captain was sick so I took it in to Major Hash’s office for his signature. He looked over the Request and said that not only would he not sign it, but that if it were him to decide, he wouldn’t of issued it in the first place. He said that I didn’t have enough time between leaves (it will be 3 ½ months) and that I had initiated the action too early. Not wanting to get in an argument, I saluted him and went back to Personnel. Juang said he would ask the Captain to sign it tomorrow if he comes in.

        The afternoon was spent in talking to Juang and in checking on Army regulations. I found that in order to get discharged I have to apply not later than 90 days before the date I want to be discharged. Since this means Novemb Nov. 30th for the school early release, it appears that this is out of the question. Oh well, when I finally get the acceptance, if I do I will still put it in.

        Sam Upson, the other NG SP1, told me of a possibility of getting out early by having been in the Reserve and Army a total of 6 years. His 6 years were just completed and he put in for a release from active duty. Don’t have any idea whether it will work, but it sure rates a chance. My 6 years will come along Mar 31st, and you can bet your dollar that if he gets out, I will sure apply.

NOV 30

        Another payday and also one lest less month in the Army. As of today I have 6 months to do in the Army. Too long in one sense, yet getting shorter all the time. Well, as I figured on my 3 day pass – it rained all day. Consequently, no golf, no tennis, not much more than moving and a little reading. As I figured, the Army finally got to me and insisted at breakfast this morning that I move into the Sergeant’s hut. Up to now there had been RA Sgts and Upson (NG SP1), but the Sgts all left the unit and all only Sam Upson remained. The 1st Sgt thought I should move in and promised that I would not have to move if the other Sgts come into the unit. (my objection up to now).

        My maid and the other maids in the hut gathered together my junk – I never realized I had so much – and in about 1 ½ hours I was moved and settled again. The new hut is nice in that it has an inside latrine and shower, and the rooms are about 50% larger. Sooo it should be pretty good, at least I don’t have any noisy neighbors across the way.

        Captain Stillwagon signed my leave and I hand carried it down to Rycom. The Sgt there said that I should get the orders shortly and so it looks as if I might “choggy” out of here in the first part of January. There are other things to get lined up before I can head for Southwest Asia, such as visas and letters of permission to enter the individual countries, but I am working on these obstacles now.

DEC 01

        The weather was cold and damp, consequently I didn’t have an opportunity to play any golf or tennis. Stayed in the hut in the morning reading and trying to keep out of the way of the maid who was trying to clean up.

        In the afternoon I went with Bill Chinstry to Shuri where he is helping two Catholic fathers build a church. Actually the church is being built by a contractor, but Bill and a couple of fellows from Engineering did the designing and blueprint work. The structure is of reinforced concrete and will cost in the neighborhood of $30,000. The contractor wanted to pour concrete today, but he was still a little behind with his work and the placement of some steep rods, so it was decided to put off the pour until Friday.

        Bill, the Father and I then adjourned to the house where we had a beer and talked about the job and things in general. I was interested in their setup and he explained that the Catholic order that he was in was responsible for the missionary work on the Ryukyus Islands. On Okinawa there were 5 parishes and a 6th would be officially opened in a couple of weeks. This particular Father was the Religious Superior of the Fathers and was in charge of the general existance of the men, their vocations etc; although, there was another father in charge of the missionary facet. He explained of the extended schooling that he had, and of the languages he spoke or could understand. He impressed me with his genial personality and intelligence and I believe he makes a good “teacher.” (Versus a descendant of the Pope!)

DEC 02

        Poor me, still lousy weather. At first I thought I would be able to get in a little golf in the afternoon but I got tied up at work for an hour or so and it was about quarter past one when I got away which made it too late to go for the course. Instead I went to the tennis courts with Chapman, but we weren’t there 15 minutes when it began to rain. Consequently, my first 3 day pass was somewhat of a failure.

        Spent some time today on my leave and I am still quite unsettled as to what I want to do, how to go, and where to stop. I guess the plans call for me to try and get a hop on the embassy flight in order to save some money. If I get the ride I will probably go all the way to India and spend a couple of weeks there. If I don’t get the hop I might either spend the time in the Philippines and Japan; or I might fly commercial to Indonesia, Singapore and Bangkok. Doing the later will entail a couple hundred dollars worth of air flights and I am not sure whether I want to spend the money that way. Oh well, have to give it more thought.

        Man some guys are really ignorant. Went with Terry to the Chinaman’s restaurant and joined a table of 4. One fellow was making remarks about the Jews and although the other tried to hint to him about me, he was too ploughed plowed to pay heed. His condition didn’t warrant any verbal blast on my part, for I am sure nothing would have sunk in. Shame to see guys get so instion_l and make asses of themselves.

DEC 03

        Training this morning was much better than usual although I had to do more than I generally like to. I conducted cl_se order drill for about 15 minutes and also had to read a 8 page brochure on American-Okinawan relations. The rest of training consisted of 2 films concerning “Escape” and Patrolling and a talk from Captain Shlag concerning the obligation of the American G.I. as a prisoner of war. (He is not the greatest of speakers!) One of the films – the one on Patrolling was a British produced film and was quite good, much better than the typical American training film.

        Played tennis in the afternoon and had 3 fine sets of tennis with Chapman. Lost the first two and tied the 3rd, but no matter what the outcome, the brand of tennis was better than usual and the games fast and interesting. Looks as if I will have to get on the ball to be able to beat him once again.

        Continued to read Spinoza, and I must admit that I am not getting much out of it. Haven’t the patience to parse over each paragraph to grasp the content so I am missing much that he has written. This is the second book on my “100 most important book” list that I have decided to put down after reading ⅓ - ½ of the book. (Moby Dick) I think I will concentrate a little more on my law, and possibly some lighter reading.

DEC 04 (SUNDAY - WEEK 50)

        Today was a dull day one of the worst that I have had on Okinawa. It was fairly nice in the morning, but Brian (the tennis court attendant) had said all the available time was signed for, so I resorted to reading to pass the time. Read the Morning Star newspaper, Stars and Stripes, and a little more of Spinoza. One portion concerned Man’s Emotions, and some intangible subjects such as good, bad, virtue, etc. A little of what he wrote sunk in but my heart wasn’t in it so I decided to put it down once and for all.

        The afternoon was equally uninteresting as I played a little tennis, read and took a shower. The evening consisted of a movie “Strategic Air Command”. I hope there aren’t many more days such as this.

        Yesterday while waiting for a friend I began meditating about Okinawa & what affect the United States has on the island, and the people. There is no question that with all the money that is being spent here that the United States intends to maintain control of the Ryukyuan Islands for many years to come – perhaps permanently. Defense-wise the island is being built into a Rock of Gibraltar and will be a formidable fortress in the Far East; the end result, I hope, being a deterrent to the Chinese war machine. I believe that once the defense program is completed, over 500 million dollars will have been spent here – mainly in the Sohe-Naha area.

        The actual benefit to the Okinawan economy has been discussed in many places and by many people but it can be boiled down to construction and sanitation. Many Okinawans work on the construction projects and for the U.S. Government and sponsored by USCAR. Also, some private Okinawan firms are rebuilding the war devastated economy. The water septim has been improved, roads installed, malaria wiped out and schools rebuilt. Concerning the later, the Univ. of the Ryukyus is the first University on the “Rock” and in time should be a fairly decent educational institution.

        In some places the Okinawans are attempting to go too far in too short a period of time, but I think that is mainly growing pains. The people seem to be more healthy and aware of what science and technological improvement can do to a country. Perhaps, like America, scientific gain has outgrown our the social standards for the Americans have brought some bad along with the good. This experiment on Okinawa is an ideal social study and much can be learned from the outcome.

DEC 05

        Well, I guess I am getting a little closer to my leave – besides the passing of time. Got my orders today (after hounding Personnel) and took a couple copies of to my PAA so that they could send them to Japan in order to get my visa to India. The man also informed me that my visa to the Philippines had been obtained so it looks as if only lady luck and MATS remains. Guess I will start crossing my fingers now as to build up a huge backlog luck.

DEC 06

        Things continue to be slow at work, and consequently I don’t feel too bad about doing personal work during work hours. Today I went to the library and got some more data concerning transportation rights that I have if I get my discharge over here. It appears that I am entitled to pay /mile from the port of debarkation to my home of record even if I don’t actually take the trip. HOwever, I will not get any money for not taking the boat trip home nor allowance to be able to ship my baggage.

        In the afternoon I journeyed to the hospital and got a Yellow Fever shot and a Cholera booster.
