The Wac thought that the Yellow Fever shot would hurt, but it was the other way around as the Cholera in the right arm caused some pain and bothered me during the night and the next day. The Wac completed my International Shot Record card, and so it appears that I am all set with this problem. Will have to get a medical clearance 48 hours before I leave.

        Didn’t do much in the evening, – read played a little basketball (to exercise my arm) and had a sandwich at the Chinaman’s. The Chinaman’s is a PX concessionaire restaurant located near the football field, and many times I get something to eat here instead of walking up to the Terrace. The food isn’t the greatest, but, I try to get around it by just ordering a grilled cheese for I figure that they can hardly ruin that. One of the waitresses is a cute thing that I like to kid, and I was really surprised when she started talking to me about the church she went to, how she enjoyed it, and what church did I go to. I was sorry to say that I didn’t go to church very often. I tried to explain to her that it wasn't necessary to go to a church to pray, but it was impossible to get her to understand, so I told her I went now and then and plan to go more often. I am somewhat surprised at the interest shown in religion by many of the younger Okinawans, however, they seem to be in the in-between stage, not too sure what to do. One of the girls in Air Force attends a Saturday night meeting, and she said that she enjoys the “message.” One of the draftsmen that use to work in our department had some Christian religious brochures (Japanese) which he said he had been reading. I borrowed them for Junko and she read them one weekend. She said that she is interested in learning more about Christianity, but I don’t think she has done much about it. She did say she wasn’t a Buddhist or Shinto, perhaps, she is like me – an in-between.

DEC 07

        Finally got a request for an estimate, and spent most of the day working on it. It concerned installing some roof ladders at the new 1000 man theater in Sukiran. The Sukiran shopping area is getting to be a huge project, and already is part completed. The Post Office, Branch Commissary are finished, the PX nearly done, and the theater, gift shop and bowling alleys in the immediate future stage. Okinawa will be a lush assignment when all the construction is completed.

DEC 08

        Sort of wish today was Friday and thus ending the week, but it isn’t and thus there is still one day to go. Finished up one estimate today, and did personal stuff the rest of the time. After given it a lot of thought I decided to put in my request for separation in the Far East Command. I talked to Quar_ and some of the boys, and decided that even though it is quite early that it is the safest thing to do. In this way, by pre-dating it 29 November 1955, I might be able to use it if I decide to try and get out early and go to school. The AR says that the request for separation must be in not later than 90 days prior to ETS. THe 29 Nov. date will be within the 90 day stipulation since the earliest that I could get out would be 29 Feb 56. Oh well, time will tell.

        Didn’t do much in the evening; – reading and a brief splurge at the Chinaman’s for a cheese sandwich. Also took a couple minutes to amble over to the Kue football field and watched some flag football being played. Wasn’t very interesting so I returned to the hut. I have a couple booklets on Thailand that PAA in Bangkok sent me, and I read one and started the other in order to orientate me on this city. The town appears to be quite interesting and colorful and I am looking forward to visit it and my leave. Got some delaying news, though, as Kadena Air Base told me that I probably won’t be able to get to Manila until after New Years on account of the holidays. Will put in my request anyways and hope to get a flight.

DEC 09

        I got two interesting letters today, – one from Trip and the other from Manse Hall. Trip’s letter was well written (by the misspelled words I could tell that he wrote it himself) and he seems to be growing up fast. He appears that he is quite active in sports and speaks of a football team that he plays on, and also a little basketball now and then. He sure is big and seems to be well proportioned for ports.

        Manse writes from Pusan, and Hialeah in particular. He is still a clerk in the NNIT Compound, and while the work is somewhat dull, it sure beats the Infantry work that he would be doing as he is connected with the 7th Inf. Regt. He mentions that he is quite active in teaching, in fact he spends about sch every night teaching at the Korean schools. Not only this, but he has gotten 6 other G.I’s to assist in teaching some type of course to the Koreans. The classes are held in a High School in downtown Pusan.

        Manse had started teaching a English class last April 3 times a week, and the present set up is an outgrowth of this initial action. Everything is self initiated and I feel that of anybody he has gotten the most out of his overseas tour, and Korea, in particular. He mentions that he goes to Korean movies, has received invitations from some of the Koreans and purchased all his Christmas gifts on the Korean market. (not easy as there isn’t much of a selection)

        He ended the letter with the thought that he would teach school next year, and maybe sometime in the future come back to Korea to teach a year. What a guy – great I think!

DEC 10

        I was wondering when Chanukah was this year and when I turned to this page I found out. Seems to be a little late this year, but then again, I really don’t know much about these things. Maybe I should think about going to religious retreat in Japan!

        Saturday training wasn’t as bad as I thought it would be. Had an hour march to the same spot outside Kue we went to 2 weeks ago, and then marched back. The RA tendency of our generally US’ish 1st Sgt blossomed forth as he set a to__d pace coming back. Must admit that I went no faster, and the thinking and expression of same provided time killing thoughts. Cleaned our weapons (no inspection as planned) and then went through the Physical Proficiency Test in a haphazard manner. No one exerted themselves and we are all sure we will have to do it over again, perhaps until we pass it.

        Played a little tennis in the afternoon, finally beat Chapman 5-3, and saw the second half of the Rycom All Stars – I Corps football game. The RYcom team was 14-7 in a fairly interesting game. I Corp (Korea) had a fairly good passer, but they seemed to have fumble-itis plus some pour ends. The weather was ideal, perhaps a little too warm. I wore a short sleeve shirt for the first time in many weeks.

DEC 11 (SUNDAY - WEEK 51)

        Hardly much sense in mentioning Sundays as they are almost all the same. Read, write, play tennis, eat and shoot the breeze. (Todays discussion was on semantics) This Sunday was no exception to the above.

        Junko asked me yesterday to take her dancing, and I said that I would. Couldn’t decide where to go, as there aren’t many decent places on Okinawa. Decided to go to the Ryukyuan Hotel near Naha, and so I told her to meet me at the bus stop at 7:45. The bus ride took about ½ hour and the hotel is a little ways from the highway. It is a huge hotel (for Okinawa) and Oriental in design, at the least the tile roof was. Didn’t see much of the decorations although the things in the lobby indicated that it was fairly much Western in nature.

        Upon entering the “Night Club” we found that this was a private party, which occupied most of the space. We first sat on the outside, but decided to mingle with the crowd as the atmosphere was better. (My idea, as Junko was bashful and scared of the whole idea). They had about 2 hours of dancing and we did the Fox Trot, Rhumba and a little Jitterbug. Since I am her teacher, for me to criticize would mean to criticize myself, so I shan’t say anything – except that she is a pretty good dancer, sometimes not stepping back far enough. We are both trying to dance fast but not having much luck at all.

        The crowd was 9/10 Okinawan, even though an American firm was giving the party. I guess some of the girls were employees, the others being hostess at the Club for lovesick G.I’s and “horny” old American civilians. As the party progressed the Tempo increased, and in fact, got quite loud at the end. It appears that Okinawans can’t hold their liquor the same as Americans can’t, even though they say they can. Many of them were falling all over themselves on the dance floor.

        The band was fair, and played both Oriental and Western tunes. They played some Japanese and Okinawan songs which the people danced to about the same as they do the bunny hop. They got quite excited by the game and enjoyed it a lot.

        Since the economic level is low, one can’t expect to find many interesting and smart clothes, – and one didn’t. The dress was mainly quite plain, with one or two men having nicely cut suits. Junko had bought a new dress and looked quite nice. She was beaming in her new dress and hairdo and enjoyed the party once she got rid of her bashfulness. In all I had a pleasant evening.

DEC 12

        Blue Monday – as usual. The weather has turned quite warm and makes the O.D. uniform very uncomfortable. Wished I was wearing the short sleeve khaki shirt. My request for discharge in the FEC finally went through the Orderly Room, so I guess all I can do now is sit back and see what happens. Don’t expect too much trouble, but the Army is bound to come up with something.

DEC 13

        The day started off with a chance for me to visit Miyako on a little estimating job. The job was the destruction of the present pump house and the construction of a new one. Mrs Kirk and Mrs. Gay, the 2 secretaries in the office, joked about my going and everything was all set for a quick one day trip down there and back via an airplane. But….. Mr. Sauer thought that the job was such a small one (about $3,000) that it wasn’t worth the trip down there. So, it looks as if I will spend Friday on Okinawa.

        I feel that I should be doing something about my leave coming up, but other than reading books and pl pamphlets on the various countries, I am more or less stymied. Am presently waiting for my passport and visas from PAA, and of course there is nothing that I can do about the airplane ride. Just have to wait until a day or two before the time I want to leave (Dec. 29th) and see if I can get a hop. Kadena Air Base had told me that it would be a little difficult to get a flight to Manila between Christmas and New Years since MATS was using up their plane allocation before Christmas so that as many people as possible will be able to spend Christmas where they want.

DEC 14

        Decided to not say anything about the Miyako trip and see if my boss decides I might as well go there for a one day trip. Didn’t seem to work as he stopped by the desk and said that the job was too small to warrant a trip down there, so once again I have been foiled on my off shore trips. Oh well, one of these days!

        More boat mail and packages came in, and while I didn’t get any, still there were an awful lot that arrived off the boats. I understand 3 boats come in next week, so the poor mail clerk will be really running around sorting and delivering the mail. Actually the mail clerk job is one of the best in the Army, and outside of a minor splurge at Christmas time, there isn’t much to do. As it is at Kue, the mail room has a very efficient Okinawan _a_san who does all the work, and all Heiger does is get the mail and sell stamps.

        Went to the Camp Kue movie for the first time in a while, and saw a fairly good movie, “Footsteps in the Fog.” The screen has been converted to Cinemascope and outside of a big gash up the left side, and poor focusing, the movies are much better than the 16 mm job we use to see. Many more people are now attending the movie, as the shows are better, and they only have 1 show a night, 5 nights a week. Actually had to look for a seat now whereas before one could have shot a cannon through the theater and not hit anybody.

DEC 15

        Very typical day on the Rock, – that is, very little out of the ordinary happened. Did go to the hospital to get some medicine for my face (my neck has broken out a little) and while I was there I decided to visit Jake Fox and Jacobs, two fellows from 8105th in the hospital. Jake Fox had a minor operation, and operation, and he said everything turned out fine. He didn’t know how long he would be there, but it was a good rest; especially since he had just come back from a 28 day leave to Hong Kong, and Manila, and Formosa.

        The other Jake is a colored fellow and a real credit to his race, the human race that is. I believe he has only a year or so of college behind him, but he has done a lot of outside education studying and building up of his body. He learned Japanese from a YMCA school back in San Francisco, and learned it so e proficiently that they “kicked” him out out of the language school for there wasn’t any more that they could teach him. He is an interpreter over here, and consequently constantly uses and improves his Japanese. After he gets out, he think he will come back to Japan and go to school here.

        Besides his Japanese he does weight lifting and judo. Judo is his present hobby, and he goes 5-6 nights a week to the judo school, practising and helping some of the other students. He thinks that by the next tests, around summer time, he should be a “black belt,” the highest grouping that one can go, although there are 10 degrees in the black belt. Quite a friendly fellow on top of it all.

DEC 16

        While reading the Sunday Post Dispatch over the past 3 or 4 months I have run across a couple of ads concerning job openings. One was for a Labor Relations man, and the other 2 for Sales Engineers. I decided to drop them a letter asking for more information. Not that I am really interested nor they interested in one who has 5-6 months left to go in the Army, but I have the time (worlds of it) and I will be waiting to hear what they have to say.

        Here it is 5 months before I get out (plus 3 months for traveling) and I haven’t decided what I want to do. Got some general ideas of what I want to do, but nothing definite and I am beginning to think that it is about time that I come to some decision. If it be law, well it isn’t too much of a problem as I will try and get a related day job and continue studying at night time. If it be something else, I should be really writing to various companies, inquiring of job possibilities and answering ads. Yet, how can one write when he is not sure what he wants to do? I know I have said it before but I really have to sit down and give it a lot of thought.

        Went to the movie (again) this evening and saw a really lousy show. It was about bull fighting but there was only 10, or so, minutes of bull fighting in the whole film. Even though it only cost 25¢ it was a wasted quarter. Cinemascope makes a good show better, and likewise makes a poor show worse. Tonights show was an example of the latter.

DEC 17

        We had character guidance this morning during training, and I must admit that it was the worst that I have yet sat through. Rabbi Waldman gave the talk and his analogies and thoughts were very confusing and non unconnected. Luckily I had a newspaper with me, and it helped me pass the time. Didn’t even go to sleep – for a change.

        The next portion of training was taken up with picture taking. The C.O. and 1st Sgt had decided to have some group pictures taken of the 8105th unit so we all got dolled up in our clean O.D.’s and paraded to the area set aside for the picture taking. At first the unit was assembled together for one all exclusive shot. Then the unit was divided into sections, such as Engineers, SP’s and Overhead. At first I didn’t think I would buy any, but perhaps I will get an Engineer picture. Might as well, since I will have spent about 1 year with the boys by the time I leave the Rock.

        A typhoon was supposed to steer this way, but at the last moment the big blow veered away and headed for Iwo Jima. No rain hit Okinawa, however 30-40 mile per hour winds blasted the Rock all day. We tried to play some tennis but it was a big joke. Good balls curved out bad, and bad balls ere blown on to the court. We gave up after an hour of playing.

DEC 18 (SUNDAY - WEEK 52)

        The weather finally cleared and consequently a couple of us got in a couple sets of tennis in the morning. Later 4 of us took a taxi and went to Mr. Kent’s house in the Machinato Housing Area. He had invited us to lunch, - together with another couple - and an opportunity to help trim a Christmas tree if we liked. The food was great and was one of the best meals that I have had since coming overseas. We had ham, potatoes, rolls, corn on the cob, cherry pie and milk. The corn on the cob was particularly good, and I helped myself to 2 ears of the fabulous product from the Golden Mid West.

        Played with the 2 kids during part of the afternoon and then we all adjourned to the living room where we helped put lights, Christmas decorations and tinsle on the tree. I still haven’t learned – or at least restrained myself – to placing the tinsle on one at a time; so the young son and I threw the tinsle when the other peoples backs were turned. Not nice, but we had a lot of fun.

        The Christmas spirit is spreading throughout the Americanized portions of the Rock and one sees trees, lights and decorating everywhere. One place even has records blasting out the trite over loud speakers and makes me think of the department stores back home. I still haven’t gotten the Xmas bug and I doubt if I will.

DEC 19

        Well, this should be the beginning of the general holiday season, with shortened weeks, parties, and perhaps the beginning of my leave. Found out that my passport still hasn’t arrived, but probably would be in that the afternoon. Learned from OKED’s transportation office that all flights are cancelled between 21 Dec and 2 Jan, so it appears that I will either have to wait in order to get a hop to Manila, or pay my way by commercial airlift. Couldn’t see the latter, so I shall wait.

        Basically not much is new both in the company or at OKED. Am working on a new estimate dealing with facilities of at Yozadahi and Ki___, but are such that I can’t worm a trip out of them. Couple of fellows are due to leave Kue this week, and from what I understand we are to get 2 new Engineers, on the boat docking the 20th. Happens all the time in the Army, – once you are just getting to know a fellow, either he leaves, you leave, or something else comes up. This stretch on the Rock is the longest tour in one spot and offers an opportunity to get to know some of the boys quite well. It is somewhat unusual in that outside of a group that left in September, the bulk of the Engineers came during the summer, and will probably leave in spring or summer. Most of the fellows, in fact all of them, are from 23-29 years of age. Consequently, they are fairly intelligent and provide a welcome change from the people I knew in basic and Korea.

DEC 20

         It is sure becoming more difficult to think of things to write about in this little book. Sure had better go on leave soon or the days will consist of getting up, working, eating and going to bed. Speaking of my leave, I went to PAA this afternoon and picked up my passport plus visas to India and the Philippines. India had also included a Tourist Introductory card. The lady wasn’t there so I will have to go back to pay them what I owe. Then I took the jeep to T_ttle’s Book Store to see if they had any books on Asia but they didn’t other than what I have already read. Did buy one book to read while I am flying (optimistic)

        Back at OKED I got word to see Qua_eg, and upon entering his office he told me that my request for discharge in the Fast East had been turned down. I noticed something pegular peculiar and asked to see the sheet. He then smiled and showed me the Request and the spot where CWO Dodge had okayed my discharge as of 30 May 55. Somewhat good news for now if I do apply for a school discharge I probably can get it, even though it would be within the 90 day period. However, I haven’t heard anything further from Melbourne nor anything from Sydney, so it appears that I shall be on the Rock for 5 months and 10 more days.

DEC 21

        In the mornin I asked Searge Sauer if I could have the afternoon off (I actually told him I wouldn’t be in during the afternoon) Read for awhile and gave Junko some lessons in conversational English. Actually she is improving very well, and takes her studies seriously. Many times when I come back to the room I find her there, copying and re-copying her lessons from school the previous evening. She goes to school 3 evenings a week, two hours each of the nights. The school is quite reasonable – 200 ¥ a month – and I have been giving her the money for the tuition and letting her pay bus fare there and back.

        Around 3 O’clock and I headed for the highway to catch a bus to Naha. The ride took about 45 minutes (it was raining) and featured quite a humorous event. At one of the stops one of the passengers got off and told the conductor to wait a moment. He then walked over to a nearby fence and proceed to take a piss. It seemed like 5-10 minutes, but I guess it was little more than a minute of actual time. Everybody on the bus started laughing, and when the bus driver honked, even he burst out laughing. Soon the young fellow was finished and still buttoning his plants he climbed on board the bus. Quite an experience, more typical of the Orient than anything else.

        In Naha I did a little shopping and looking, but didn’t buy anything in particular except a little Christmas present for Junko. Most of the fellows are getting something for their maids so I decided to buy a little something also. Stopped in the USCAR building and inquired about the necessary steps needed in sending an Okinawan to school in Japan. The man said that it was very difficult (about 1 in 5 that apply are accepted, the space being limited) and that if accepted she or he would cost about $300 to support for a 10 month school year. He suggested the University of the Ryukyus, which was steadily improving each year. The cost was from ½ - ⅓ cheaper and a little easier to get in, although the rate is still about 1 to 3. He said tests would be in February and that applicants should take the test before any more is done. I thanked him for the information and left.

        Next I got a bite to eat at an approved restaurant which consisted of 2 sandwiches and a 7 up. Not very good but filling. Decided to go to the new theater that just opened in Naha. It is a huge theater with many seats, and geared for Cinemascope. I had seen one of the pictures, but the 2nd feature, “The Land of the Pharaohs” was a tremendous production that employed many a Egyptians to provide the labor to build the imaginary pyramid.

DEC 22

        After an afternoon I decided to settle down and do a little work for a change. Am working on a big estimate for the revered Kume Pier which should keep me busy for a while.

        Well, got my slides back this morning and upon looking at them I found them to be correct as far as exposure goes but lacking in subject matter. Also I had experimented in action shots and a couple of them came out okay. My exposures were generally correct which is all I was worried about.

DEC 23

        Saw my former boss Joe Alfonsi in the morning and talked to him about Formosa and his job. He seems to be liking it more than he did when he was last here in October. On my way to lunch I bumped in to him again, and I asked him to have lunch with me at the Castle Terrace. He said “Sure” and we walked up to the Club. The meals are quite good and reasonable and so the lunch was very enjoyable.

        Joe also spoke some of OKED (on Formosa) and things in general. He said there were 3 civilians and a Lt Colonel who had just arrived on Formosa to head the Sub-Office. He was given (Joe, that is) a home and a 20% (I believe) pay bonus for being in Formosa. He had a male cook and a housemaid to do the cleaning and laundering. His opinion of the Nationalists wasn’t too high, and he thought that if the 7th Fleet even left, that the Communists would overrun the Island. The Formosan people are living no better that than they were under the Japanese, and in some respects worse. Many of the Formosan boys are now being drafted into Chang’s army to replace aging Nationalist soldiers. The Chinese women on the island are all taken by the Nationalists and the Americans have to be satisfied with the Formosans or divorced Chinese women. Joe said that it was interesting how it is an accepted fact that rich men can have more than one wife. When the man dies, children of this mistress will receive something, although after the legal wife and children have gotten their share. It was quite an interesting conversation.

        In the afternoon I took off around 2 PM and returned to the hut to clean up for the Christmas parties to be held from 3-5. The Operations Division Party was at the Castle Terrace and I got there - promptly at 3 PM I believe. There were free drinks, hor d'oeuvres, and shrimp chips and I partook of them all. I think I must of had 4-6 scotches and water, and while I didn’t get drunk I did feel a little woozy when I returned to the hut about 5:30. The Operations party and the one downstairs at for Air Force Construction were very enjoyable and a good time was had by all. I had to laugh at Mr. Ishu, a Japanese Engineer in our office. He is a short fellow, about 55-60 years old and he proceded to take quite a few drinks. He (along with me) went around to all the waitresses, kidding with them and telling them, “Watashi wa anata ga direhi desu” which means, “I love you the most!”

        After an a lousy show, 4 of us adjourned to the Terrace again where we “joined” another party, and also celebrated Arnold Pinado’s Sayonara.

DEC 24

        The morning after wasn’t as bad as I thought it might be. Did have a bad taste in my mouth but not much more. Played some tennis in the morning and then took the bus to Rycom Plaza to get some things that I need. Had to buy a small gift for a girl at the PX who had said she was getting a gift for me. Read in the afternoon and took in an at a movie “Not as a Stranger” in the evening. It wasn’t too good.

DEC 25 (SUNDAY - WEEK 53)                CHRISTMAS

        Christmas 1955! Really can’t say that this day was any different from the rest. There was no snow or big shibangs, and in many ways it was a typical Sunday. Played a little tennis, and read in the morning. Then adjourned to the Mess Hall where we had a really fine Christmas dinner. The selection was the same as that on Thanksgiving and was just as appreciated. The turkey was fine and the dressing tops. All the other food was cooked just right and I really stuffed myself.

        Didn’t do much in the afternoon, just laid around and read. It rained a little which put a damper on things to do. It really poured in the evening and made mud of many side roads. Samo-samo everywhere in the Orient.

        It is somewhat interesting to see how Christmas is celebrated in the Orient. The Americans and Filipinos celebrate it as if they were in the USA or the Philippines. Christmas trees and stars are exhibited everywhere and everybody exchanges or gives presents. The Okinawans are also influenced, and many hum and sing Christmas carols. They, I am sure, enjoy Christmas, for many of them receive presents from their employers. I even read an article about Japan in which it said that many department stores have a Santa Claus and Christmas decorations. Seems funny to me, but I just can’t see a Buddhist or Shinto celebrating Christmas. Must be the “Season of Happiness and Giving!”

DEC 26

        Twas a quiet day, all day. After breakfast I went to the office and typed about 7 or 8 overdue letters. Finally my arm got tired and I decided to quit. Went back to the hut, wrote some in the diary and finally gave up and headed for the mess hall. After chow I went to the Sukiran Library where I read magazines and listened to classical music.

        Later in the afternoon I played some basketball – got all sweated up – and had to take a shower before supper. Charlie Terry and I had decided to see Madame Butterfly at the Orion Movie down in Naha and so we caught the 5:30 Okinawan bus. After a long ride we found out that they changed movies the night before so there was no sense in staying in Naha (We had seen all the other movies or they were Japanese ones that we weren’t too interested in seeing). However, we did decide to get a beer so we went to the Bar Simbasha where we had a beer. One of the bar maids sat down to talk to us, but she didn’t know much English. The bar is one of the most popular in Naha and we saw quite a few G.I’s.

        Many girls worked in this bar, most of whom were dressed quite nicely in Western dress. The girl at our table had a nice figure, but looked a little sluttish. She didn’t press us to buy her a drink and so we sat and talked or kidded with her. After an hour or so we left and went back to Kue and the Castle Terrace.

DEC 27

        Even though Monday was a holiday, Tuesday was a typical Monday in that I had a rough time getting into the swing of work. I am still working on the revised pier for Kume and it is giving me a little trouble. Hope to finish it this week, though, since I will probably have only 1 working day next week. (That is if I go on my leave next week) I checked at Kadena in the morning and they said there were no flights to Manila this week, and that I wouldn’t leave until the following week. Actually, I am not disappointed since it allows me to enjoy the New Years weekend. However, if I don’t get away next week, I will have to have my orders changed as it will be more than 1 week past 2 January, the date I was supposed to leave.

        Yesterday I got a letter from Melbourne University and it had an application blank inside. Haven’t decided what to do about going to school in Australia – even if they let me go – however I decided the best thing would be to spent the £2.25 application fee and apply. In this way I can give it more thought, and not have to reach a decision until the 1st part of February. Also, it will afford me a chance to write a few more engineering letters; and consequently in the evening I wrote letters to the VA, Morton, Univ. of Michigan and the Institute of International Education. Included a self addressed envelope inside of each one, and so if they do me the favor of an early reply I should hear before I have to make my decision. If I leave on my trip 5 January I will have to be back the 3rd of February which will give me sufficient time to apply. I plan to send the application tomorrow.

DEC 28

        Didn’t know how to send the necessary applications fee to the University of Melbourne. At first I thought I would just enclose $5 in the envelope to cover the £2.25 fee. Later, decided to go to the American Express and see if I could get some kind of check or demand note. Checked out a jeep and went to Sukiran and talked to the lady about getting a check. She said that the only way they could send money through the mail, was for me to pay them and they in turn would advise their offices in Australia to credit the account of the University. After thinking it over I decided to do it this way, even though this was a possibility of a foul-up along the way. Lets hope not.

        Took off around 3:30 to clean my rifle and then to play a little tennis. My serve was the best that it has ever been on the island, and I hope it is an indication of things to come. We played a couple sets of doubles before one of the guys had to quit.

        Went to the Kue movie in the evening and saw a pretty fair movie – “The Violent Man.” The movie theater, as of late, was quite crowded and we had to look around for seats that were together. Somehow the screen has ripped and in order to repair it, they put on a long patch on the outside facing the audience. Consequently, whenever there are scenes in which the color in light, this long, jagged scar shows its ugly face. Guess one can’t be too choosy in an Army theater.

DEC 29

        Put in a complete day at the office without doing any personal work. It was not that I couldn’t or didn’t want to do any it was just that I had nothing to do. Am trying to complete the Kume estimate before I leave, and consequently I have done more concentrated work than usual.

        I have been trying to read up on India lately, and have found that there isn’t too much in these parts concerning the Indian sub-continent. I have an article from LIFE MAGAZINE on Hinduism and it explains much of the Hindu religion and the curious customs of that religion. Many Hindu terms are explained which I think will help in understanding the people and their daily doings. For instance they explain: Brahman-Atman… ultimate reality, and through knowledge of the identity of the individual self with Brahman-Atman that moksha (salvation) is attained. Karma is the endless reincarnation that a Hindu is a part of unless he achieves MOKSHA. The main Gods are Vishnu the preserver (worship through ceremony) and Shiva the destroyed (worship through knowledge). From Vishnu through 10 reincarnations have evolved other major deities, the main two being Roma and Kushna. Kushna is the main character in Bhagavad Gita, the most popular and best loved book of duration in India. Roma is the man who with the help of monkeys rescued his wife who had been carried to Ceylon.

        Everything about India seems fascinating, particularly the people and I hope that I will be able to visit that country. Since that part of Asia is noted for its June-July monsoons, I thought that I would try and see the Northern part of India while the weather is favorable.

DEC 30

        This year is getting short, and I am afraid that I am not sad. Just means that I have that much less time to do in the Army. Completed my estimate on Kue today and consequently I shouldn’t have much to do next week if I go on leave. Still early to get definite dates for air hops, and will have to check Tuesday. I hope to leave next Wednesday or Thursday.

        There was a little party in our office this afternoon in honor of Colonel Vivian’s leaving the Operations Division. Actually it is the present Operations Division that is changing, with Mr. Kent becoming head of the “to be called” Construction Divisions. This is a promotion of Kent from a 13 to a 15 and I am glad to see it, for he is a hard worker & respected by all. We will be the Construction Service Branch of the Construction Division, but as yet have no new head man to replace Kent. Mr. Kent said that either Lewis or Alfonsi have the inside track since both of them are familiar with the operations of the section. Will mean a promotion to whomever gets it.

        Didn’t do much in the evening. Talked to a couple of guys about what camera to buy, and I am still of the opinion that if I buy a camera it will probably be a NIKON S2. They seem to be a fine camera with an ever increasing public.

        Spent the rest of the evening reveiwing reviewing some law that I think I have been reading for a couple of months. Anyway it is about the time that I finished this particular section. Maybe I will do better when I come back off leave. Have sort of decided to sell the books before I leave the “Rock”. I don’t think they make much of a refresher course.

DEC 31

        It is indeed a pleasure to write in this diary on this day, – the last one of many of the year 1955. 1955 was a big year, for it marks the only complete year that I will spend in the Army. Now that it is over, I can breathe a sigh and look forward to 5 months of 1956. Actually 55 wasn’t such a bad year, considering that I had to be in the Army. First of all, thank goodness, there was no fighting and I wasn’t someplace testing my courage. Second, I saw quite a bit of the world, and the Western part of the U.S. that I have never seen before. It has truly been an experience, one that I shall not ever forget. Third, I think I have learned quite a bit from my job in the Army, particularly the part spent at the Okinawa Engineer District.

        Today was a long day, but the time past quite fast. Played a couple hours of tennis in the morning, and a little in the afternoon. Went to Rycom Plaza and bought some birthday cards and empty bottles. Went to see “Eddie Foy and the 7 Little Foys” starring Bob Hope in the evening.

        Came back to Kue, put on my sport coat and headed for the Castle Terrace with 5 of the boys. The Club was really crowded tonight and there were hats, noise makers and other junk in abundance. The people were in a festive mood, and everyone joined in for a loud and merry New Years plus singing Auld Lang Syne. I left the party around 1:30 and after doing a little talking finally hit the sack around 2:15.

Route as of December 31st, 1955 – end of Chapter 9.

CHAPTER 10 - LOST LEAVE

January 1st, 1956 - January 31st, 1956

No record exists for the month of January, 1956. It is unclear what other notebook is mentioned.  The journal containing entries from January 1956 has finally been found. Its contents are written in pale green, matching its exterior.

JAN 01 1956 (SUNDAY - WEEK 54)

        (See other notebook for 1 Jan - 31 Jan)

JAN 01 1956 (SUNDAY - WEEK 54)

        Thought at first that I would get up for breakfast and consequently I set the alarm for 7:50. Awoke with a start, and managed to get up to go to the bathroom. Then I decided – no go – and hurried back to bed. Slept until 10:30 at which time I thought it best to get out of the sack. Read a little until chow, and then hastened to the mess hall for a pretty good New Years Day meal.

        The sun was beaming and so a couple of the boys went outside to take a good old fashioned sun bath. The sun felt good on the face and body, however, I don’t think I got any tan. Discussed about every topic, but most of the discussions ended in kidding or joking.

        Yesterday I promised Junko that I would take her to a show in Naha, and arranged to meet her in front of the Taiko Theater. When I got there I found her talking to another maid – Kuniko, and one of Kuniko’s friends. Both of these two girls were dressed in kimonos as were many women and girls on this New Years Day. (Biggest holiday in Japan and Okinawa). I asked them if they would like to join us at the movie, and they said yes. We went to the new theater, Grand Onion, which was really crowded on this holiday occasion.

        After the movie I asked Junko if she would like to go to the Teahouse of the August Moon, the well known teahouse on Okinawa named after the Broadway Hit. When she said, “Sure”, we got in a taxi and drove to the teahouse located on the Western side of Naha. The private rooms were all occupied so we had to go into the main room. There were many Americans in the room, and kimono dressed Geishas to wait on them and to entertain them with song and little tricks. One group of Americans were so obnoxious and loud that I decided to leave, and so Junko and I left the “fabulous?” Teahouse for a small, American approved restaurant. Ordered the rice curry main dish, which I found to be lousy. I really can’t say that I enjoy Oriental food, with the possible exception of tempra (fried shrimp). Caught a bus back to our respective village and compound, and thus concluded the first and most likely last Oriental New Years.

JAN 02

        Today was a holiday, and another day closer to my leave. Since I am hoping to to catch a plane on Wednesday, my mind is occupied with only thoughts of the trip and any last minute arrangements that have to be made.

        The weather clouded up, and soon a great deal of rain fell on this little Rock. This was the first bad weather that we have had in the last 2-3 weeks, and so we couldn’t do too much criping. Only hope that it doesn’t linger on and cancel all flights. If I miss the Wednesday flight, I have to wait until Saturday before another plane leaves for Manila.

        Spent much of the day catching up on some unanswered letters. Figured that I would probably get some mail; while I was gone, and consequently, I didn’t want too large of backlog facing me when I returned. Having a private room makes all the difference in the world, for one can shut himself off from the rest of the Army and pretend he is something else.

JAN 03

        Was supposed to work today, but I didn’t do very much as I had some personal things to attend to. Checked out a jeep in the morning and went to Naha to put my name in for a flight the next day. From Naha I went to the hospital to get my medical clearance. Checked out “McKay’s Guide to the Far East” at the library and stopped by PAA to see if they had received word from Tokyo as to how much I owed for the visas. (Still no word)

        In the afternoon I received work from Air Force Construction Division that they were going to negotiate the Kume Estimate at 2 PM, so I stopped what I was doing and got my papers together. The estimates were far apart regarding the breds pier repair (161,000 vs. $105,000) but they were $3000 under my estimate concerning the bridge repair. We accepted the latter estimate but told Kokuba that they would have to reconsider their pier estimate. In discussion of the pier estimate we found that they had done little thinking on the matter, and were way off base on some points. They asked for a postponement so as to review their estimate and it was granted. I am sorry that I won’t be here when the negotiations are resumed.

        Got my junk together in the evening and packed my two hand bag. Thought at first I might have trouble in carrying all the stuff, but things fitted in the bag with not any extra effort. So it looks as if I am all set!

JAN 04

        Well, today was the big day. The torrential rains of yesterday subsided around 10 A.M. and the sun began to poke its fiery head over the black clouds. The winds continued, but were not as bad as during the previous day. Gathered my gear together, arranged for Junko to get in a typing class at OKED, and signed out – for 30 days.

        Got a ride down to Naha Air Base and checked in at Navy Air Operations. The seaman told me to report back at 1:30 PM, so I went to the PX, ate lunch with Ed Lyons, and walked around the Air Base. Upon arriving back at the desk, the officer said that he didn’t think there would be room for me on the plane. I decided to wait anyway, and luck was with me, as 5 minutes later he said that there would probably be a space available.

        About 2:45 we boarded the C-54 and took off for Tainan, Formosa. The flight was smooth and I read most of the way. We settled down at Tainan (about 200 miles south of Taipei) at 6 PM and reloaded some baggage and men. During the hours we stopped I walked around the airfield and couldn’t help noticing the many jets on the runway, and the protective mounds of earth around other planes. It looks as if they are prepared to meet any sudden attack by the Communists.

        We re-boarded the plane at 7 PM and flew to Sangley Point, across Manila Bay from Manila. I caught a ride across the Bay in a LSC and which docked near the Manila Hotel. I was too late for the USO dance at the Hotel, so I decided to call it an evening and checked in the Military Port Area. Thought I might find Estreich there, but evidentally some female must have caught his eye.

JAN 05

        Awoke about 7 AM, and ate breakfast at the mess hall. Hailed a cap, and rode to Warner, Barnes Ltd, where I obtained a 76 Pesos refund owed me from the Manila – Hong Kong return flight that I did not take last May.

        After finishing my business, I decided to spend the day sight seeing. First place I visited was Malacanan Palace, the home of President Magsaysay. Adjacent to the building was the Executive Offices which were crowded with people working and waiting to see somebody. Was able to take a tour through the President’s home, and was impressed with the beautiful furnishings and grounds.

        Next I went to the University of the Philippines in Quezon City. The campus and buildings are less than 10 years old, consequently the architecture is quite modern and clean. Part of the campus is still in the planning stage, consequently, the buildings are spread out making long walks from building to building. There are about 10,000 students here, and this is considered one of the best schools in the Philippines. I toured the Engineering Bldg, and was amazed at the well equipped labs.

For the remainder of the day I walked around Manila, and in particular, Escolta Avenue (many banks and fine shops) and the Intramuros section. Visited the Post Office and Jai-Alai Building although there are no games going on in the latter building. Luckily I was able to exchange my money (Pesos) into MPC as I didn’t want the Pesos. (Could have used them later though)

        Took a bus to Clark Field, and signed up for Flight 291 – The Embassy Flights. Have my doubts about getting on the flight tomorrow, as there appear to be many people wanting this flight. (My second nervous stomach begins now). Checked in the transient barracks, showered, and had a good meal at the NCO Club.

JAN 06

        Today turned out to be quite a hectic day. Found out early in the morning that I wouldn’t be able to get on the Embassy Flight. (Drat the luck, however, there were people with priority who weren’t able to get on the flight.) Now came the moment of decision, – wait around, go to Baguio, and try again Monday, or pay my own way to Bangkok. The man at the desk didn’t point a very promising picture of my chances of getting a hop Monday, so I decided to catch a commercial flight, provided I couldn’t catch the plane going to Saigon at 11 AM.

        As my luck continued, (!) – the Major said he had too much weight as it was, so no dice on the Saigon Flight. Hopped in a cab and rode to the main gate. Here I boarded a jeepney for Angeles, where I caught the “Rabbit” bus to Manila. In Manila I took a taxi and arrived at the airport with ½ hour to spare. Bought my ticket ($126 – Ugh) and flew via KLM to Bangkok.

        The flight was smooth and comfortable, and I had a fine time talking to 3 Australian students on the plane. They gave me all kinds of information concerning school in Australia, living conditions and other pertinent data. They made me quite interested in going to school in Australia, however, the problem of money looms its ugly head. The “chaps” were friendly and extremely nice and helpful and I enjoyed traveling with them.

        We landed in hot Bangkok at 3 PM and I got a lift to the Princess Hotel were the MATS personnel were staying. I checked in and then contacted the MATS liaison officer about getting a ride to Calcutta, tomorrow. No problem about the flight so I decided to do a little sightseeing.

        Left the hotel at 8 PM and began walking along New Street towards the main section of town. The streets were crowded, and business continued even at this hour. There were many little stalls where one could eat, drink, buy a raffle ticket or do almost anything. These stalls are typical of the Orient, and perhaps many countries in the world.

        About ½ mile from the hotel, a young man said hello to me and asked where I was going. I answered but kept on walking figuring him to be a salesman of some sort. He kept following me and came alongside, still talking, and being friendly. Decided to slow down, and engaged in conversation, that is, to the extent that he understood. It turned out that he was a Thai, a freshman in the Engineering School, and interested in talking to people and improving his English. We walked quite a ways, and he pointed out many interesting things concerning life in Bangkok, the Chinese population, sights to see, etc.

        Near the end of the evening, we had a beer at one of the night clubs which also featured Thai Classical Dancing. He explained some of the hand and leg movements, but also remarked that he didn’t think the girls were very good. He left about 10:30, as he said he had some homework, and I left soon after for I had to get up early in the morning.

JAN 07

        Up at 4:45 AM, packed my belongings, ate breakfast, checked in with the Major, and boarded the bus for the airport. The airport wasn’t too crowded at this early hour, but we were able to get a good look around. It is a huge airport, quite modern, and the center of flights for Southeast Asia. The plane left at 7 AM and we had a smooth – 4 hour – flight to Calcutta, India. I was am finally here!

        Before we could disembark the plane, some passport difficulties had to be ironed out. In due time everything was all right, and we (Pete Olin from Tokyo & Boston) went to customs. Not much trouble here, and after a 30 minute wait, we got a lift into downtown Calcutta with a representative of the U.S. Consul. He recommended the Continental Hotel, and we checked in for 15 rupees (about $3.25) a day. What a headache the money is – rupees, annas, pice (India); ticals, byat (Thailand); pesos and centavos (Philippines); yen (Okinawa) and American Dollars and Travelers Checks.

        After getting settled, we took a walk along Chowringhee Street, the main thoroughfare. From here we went to the Maiden, a huge, green park located in the middle of Calcutta. The park is quite nice, and we saw many forms of activities being carried on, ie, – cricket, field hockey, softball, walking the dog, flying model airplanes, mounted police, etc. Cows and monkeys were everywhere, particularly cows. Nearby was a museum which had a Modern Art exhibit which we walked through.

        The people we saw were interesting. On the whole they looked dirty and ill fed, and had no qualms about begging. Many times we were approached for money or to buy some little gadgit. Most of the people on the streets were men, the women we presumed to be in the home. The women we did see all wore the sari, the Indian national dress, with the flowing silk shirt and the sash over the shoulder and sometimes head. Some had jewelry in their noses, on their ankles and ears, around their necks and on their head. Others had red marriage spots on their forehead. The hair was black and straight and no lip-stick is worn.

        The men wore either western clothes, baggy pants which exposed part of one leg, trousers with ¾ coats or tight leggings with ¾ coat and Ghandi Gandhi cap. Many had mustaches, some had beards, and others were shaven except for the Hindu hair lick at the back of the head. Their skin was all shades of brown and their hair was black.

JAN 08 (SUNDAY - WEEK 55)

        Today didn’t seem like Sunday, however, everyday on a vacation seems the same as the previous day. I heard yesterday of a parade to be held in the park, and arose about 7:30 AM, in order to get there in time. As it turned out, the Pass and Review was finished by the time I got there, but I did see the latter half which consisted of a presentation of medals to outstanding Calcutta policemen. There were about 2000 policemen on the parade field and in the stands, and it affected me like a page out of the history book.

        There were a troop of Bengel Lancers, white dressed policemen with red tasseled hats, and khaki dressed men with rifles and bayonets. The crowd was composed of many wealthy Indians and I got my first good taste of rich, colored saris and male costumes. I couldn’t differentiate the (many) caste system, but perhaps it will be more noticeable later on. The bagpipes were playing, the men marched briefly – with the arm swinging style typical of the British – and I stood (and took pictures) in awe. I noticed many of the top officers were British, similar to Hong Kong.

After the parade was over I visited Victoria Memorial, a beautiful marble palace dedicated in the memory of Queen Victoria. It had many beautiful paintings and statues, plus well kept gardens on the outside. From here I cut across the Maidan and headed for the Hughli River and the poorer sections of Calcutta. Many cricket games were in progress as I walked across the Maidan)

        The Howarah Bridge across the river is an engineering masterpiece and is one of the largest steel girder bridges that I have ever seen. On each side of the bridge are my docks, small and large boats, and men working in the hot sun. Near the docks are poor houses and equally destitute men walk, lie, bathe, sit, eat, and exist in the streets (I would venture that one sees 90-95% males on the streets, the women supposedly being at home)

        At the bridge I noticed some music, noise and a curious crowd. I debated about getting very close, but then decided to go ahead and perhaps risk it a little. The excitement contained a group of “Saduhs” (religious men) who had come to Calcutta on a pilgramage. They had only loin cloths on, rubbed ashes on their skin, let their hair grow long, put mud in their hair, and smoked strong cigarettes to endure the cold nights. The men were disciples of a sage – an old man who accompanied the pilgramage – and existed only to pray. They performed no work, and were charity receivers. They spent the day praying and chanting.

        A man next to me spoke to me, and offered to explain the goings on. He told me who the people were and what they were doing here. He went on to explain other facts of Indian culture, such as the red dot on a woman’s head, the giving of money to these Saduhs, begging, etc. He spoke of Kruschev and Bulganin, and that he thought Communism could help India. I said that I disagreed, and felt Capitalism or Socialism would accomplish the same thing, and one would not lose his freedoms, such as speech, press, etc. I said that America was interested in helping India help themselves.

        I had told Pete that I would meet him at Firpo’s (famous restaurant) and asked the gentleman to join us. He accepted and we took a cab to the restaurant. Over lunch we talked some more, and we learned that he was a tax worker for the Indian Government. He said that he makes 500 rupy rupees a month ($100), and gives about 300 rupees a month to charity. He is not married – feels a woman would want to tie him down, and know always where he was going. He mentioned that he was a Brahman and that he was proud of the Bengalese People whom he felt more educated than others in India.

        Around 4 PM we left him, and returned to the hotel where we checked out. It was a big joke – every employee in the hotel had his hand out, and I soon got quite tired of giving to the waiter, the head waiter, the shoe shine boy, the bell boy, etc. From now on I only tip those services I ask for.

        We toured Calcutta, walking to Dalhousie Square, the financial section, back to the River and miscellaneous streets. Calcutta is a very crowded city with many refugees who have no place to go. In the evening we went to the All India Modern Music Show, but since it didn’t start until after our train was to leave, we didn’t go in. Stood outside and listened to the music, at the same time talking to a group of from 10-15 young men and boys who were asking us questions. Enjoyed conversing with them until we had to go. Took a taxi to Howrah Station, boarded the train – 2 man compartment – and then froze (no blankets) on the way to Benaras.

JAN 09        

        The night train to Benaras was quite an experience. We accidentally left 2 windows open, and consequently froze as the night air was extremely chilly. The cold air didn’t help my cold any, and it developed into an unpleasant cough. The train wasn’t too bad, although it was mighty slow. It was an English type train with compartments that opened on the side of the car. Our compartment had 2 bunks, a small table and a bathroom which had a sink, toilet and shower.

        Generally we would leave the car at each stop, and stretch our legs. The man in the adjacent car did the same thing and we naturally struck up a conversation. His name was Mr. Seth, and he was the publisher of the Lucknow Pioneer newspaper. He was quite an educated man and spoke excellent English. We discussed many topics, such as religion, India-US relations, 5 year plan, Nehru, Goa, Atom Bombs & Kashmir. He wasn’t anti nor pro American, but disagreed with Dulles on Goa. He said Dulles statement had an extremely bad affect on Indian-US relations. Concerning Kashmir, he said that the people weren’t interested in returning to Pakistan, as economically India has much more to offer. He said that there wasn’t anything to the talk about India refusing a plebiscite, as he said they could vote any time the UN so decides (not what I understand). Pete and I enjoyed our conversation with him very much.

        We arrived in Benaras around 10:30, checked into a nice hotel, and proceded to fall into a trap – the hiring of a guide and taxi. The whole shebang cost $6 a piece, far too expensive for my bloods, – and totally unnecessary. Before lunch we visited Sarnath, the spot near Benaras where Buddha first made his doctrines known to the world. In the general area, we saw Dhamek Stupa, where Buddha first preached to his 5 disciples and a Tibetian church – Mulaghandikuti Vikia. Nearby we visited a local museum which houses some of the ruins in the area, including the Asoka Pillar, – Indias National Emblem. (Asoka was the ruler who spread Buddhism throughout India. A later ruler outlawed it, and there aren’t many Buddhists in India today.)

        After lunch we continued our tour, and visited the University of Benaras – the largest in India, a temple where foul smelling monkies ran wild, and the section near the river where there were many beggars, people lying in the streets and people with leprosy. Rented a boat and went up and down the Ganges River. On the Benaras side are many mansions where the rich come to spend their last minutes on the earth. (The other bank is void of buildings). Also saw the bathing ghats where the pilgrams came to wash themselves in the holy Ganges. Passed a couple crematory pyres where bodies were being burned. All Indians (Hindus) are cremated except people with small pox, leprosy, children under 5 and priests. These latter groups, along with dead cows, are dumped in the River. Women are clothed in red, men in white.

        On the way back to the hotel we visited the Golden Temple (Vishwanath) and saw the people bringing the holy water from the River to the temple. Passed through some very narrow shopping streets with its beggers, shop keepers and miscellaneous human beings. (plus cows and cow dung) We spent a few minutes at a silk store, and Pete conversed with the proprietor about prospective business. I bought a sari for Carolyn.

        In the evening we ate – unusually good meals at the hotel – and talked to some guests. One of the ladies, a Canadian, was married to an Indian who she met back in school. He is in the Insurance business in Calcutta.

JAN 10        

        We were awakened at 6 AM – had tea, dressed and were off to the river to see the sunrise over the Ganges. Actually, there wasn’t much that we hadn’t seen the previous night, except that many more pilgrams were bathing in the river. I am afraid that we fell for the “typical American tourist sucker” bait, as I think we saw only one or two things on the tour that were any good. (Sarnath and the River trip in the morning). One learns by experience I guess, and old “watash” has chilled fast to the tipping, tours and other traveling handouts.

        Took the morning train for Lucknow, as we thought we would stop and visit the Mr. Seth who we met on the way to Benaras. We went 2nd class, and were crowded into a compartment full of people and sleeping bags. We met two interesting persons on the train whom we spoke to most of the journey. One was a coal mine wonder who made about $20,000/year. (1 lakh rupee – 100,00) He was not dressed to represent the upper class that he was in, and preferred 2nd class instead of 1st class. He spoke good English and we discussed and argued many points such as Goa, Atomic Bomb, Russia, etc. We noticed that whenever we thought we had him cornered he always came back on the subject of Goa and/or the Atomic Bomb. He was extremely anti-british (they had put him in jail) and justified Hitler’s attack in World War II as being Britains due reward for their evil deeds of the past. We also compared Communism and Democracy and the goals of Russia, India and the US. We had an enjoyable conversation.

        The second gentleman was a semi-retired shoe company owner who was quite prosperous. He didn’t discuss his political views and was content to sit back and listen. He had just come from Singapore where he has a couple of shop. He, like the other man, is quite rich by Indian standards. They both said they had big families to feed, but Pete and I felt they were just tight with their money. Perhaps they exemplify a group of people who are satisfied with hoarding money and not improving their standard of money living.

        Arrived in Lucknow around 2 PM and had lunch at the Carlton Hotel. Called Mr. Seth and after waiting 2 hours, his son-in-law plus the latter’s brother picked us up in their car. They said Mrs. Seth was ill and could not see us, which we were sorry to hear. They drove us around the town for an hour or so, and pointed out – in the dark – some of the outstanding sights of the town. We thanked them for their hospitality and left them around 8 PM so as to eat before boarding the train for Agra.

        The women are the most interesting sight in the country. All are dressed in saris, of course some saris being much prettier and costlier than others. Some wear the sari over the shoulder, others swing it over the head. The married women have the red dot in the middle of the forehead, and sometimes a red line at the crease in the hair at the middle of the head. (Some wear trinkets there also) The hair is black, straight and generally parted in the middle. Many have small precious stones in the left nostril, others wear sandals. Many are fat and unattractive, although I did see a couple of real beauties. Some accentuate the eyes with black powder or chalk under the eye although this is more common on children. The women don’t generally carry their young on the back like the Orientals do.

JAN 11        

        Arrived in Agra after another cold night, and rented a couple tongas [horse drawn cart (2 wheels)] to take us to the Laurie Hotel. We then ate breakfast and checked the Government Tourist Bureau for information. (The outcome of the talk was that I have pretty well decided to go North once we get to Delhi and Pete thinks he will go South).

        We rented a car and went to the mausoleums of Itimad-ud-Daulah and Abkor (the great Mogul King). Both edifices were tremendous structures with incredible inlaid stone. The art of inlaying stones came from Persia to India and the Itimad-ud-Daulah building is said to be one of the best examples of inlaid stone in India. Abkor’s tomb is an unusual structure as it is a cross between Christianity, Hindu and Moslem. Abkor had 3 wif wives, each of whom belonged to one of these three religions. Consequently, we have Moslem “onion towers”, crosses and Hindu sculptures intermingled in the temple.

        After lunch we visited Agra Fort, a huge fort (1 ½ miles in circumference) built by Abkor and improved upon by Shah Jahan. Its walls are 70 feet high and enclose many buildings, religious halls and gardens (plus the harem apartments). From the Fort we went to the Taj Mahal, which we had seen in the distance from the Fort. one cannot see the Taj until he emerges from the entrance building, and then he becomes face to face with perhaps the most beautiful building in the world.

        The Taj Mahal is simple, yet elaborate; colorless, yet a color contrast against the blue sky, and to the above must be added the beautiful garden, fountains and elaborate marble carvings and inlaid stone. We just stood at one end of the enclosure and gazed at the building, hardly able to contain ourselves. Of course we took pictures, and I am sure they will be pretty but they will not have the wonderful feeling one has in the presence of such a magnificent building.

        The Taj Mahal is of white marble with 4 minarets at each corner – (separate from the building) The walls have elaborate carvings and inlaid stones, and the Koran is inlaid in the wall in black stone. One can enter the building (with pads on his shoes) and when he does he sees the tombs surrounded by marble screens. Downstairs, directly under these false tombs, the real graves are laid; and one can also enter here via a tunnel. Down below one smells incense which burns constantly and adds mystery to the surroundings. We stayed to see the building at sunset, but didn’t notice any added beuty beauty. Sorry that there isn’t a full moon tonight as we understand that that is quite a sight to see.

JAN 12        

        We decided to stay in Agra today so that we would be able to go to Fatehpur Sikri, a deserted city located about 25 miles from Agra. The city was a huge fortress, approximately 7 ½ miles in circumference, and surrounded on 3 sides by huge walls, and the other side by an artificial lake. The city was built in the 1570’s by Akbar, as a monument to the area where his wife gave birth to a baby boy.

        The main entrance is called Victory Gate and is 176 feet high – the highest gate in India. Inside the walls are many well preserved buildings which are an indication of the solid manner in which they were built almost 400 years ago. Like the other Mohgul (Mogul) buildings in Agra, this city also had many fine designs, inlaid stones, gardens, etc. While the whole affair was a little repeticious of Agra Fort, still it was worth the trip out here.

        We caught the afternoon bus back to Agra and had an interesting – but bumpy – ride. We dodged cows, carts, horses and humans on the one way street into Agra. The country was flat, and much of the land was under cultivation. (still not nearly as much as in Japan). One unusual feature of the trip was the many peacocks we saw near the roads. Never have I seen so many peacocks, even if I counted all the peacocks that I have seen every time I went to the St. Louis Zoo. Also I saw water cranes and other brightly colored birds.

        After lunch – which as in Banaras, was quite good and sufficient in quantity – I set out to buy a blanket of some sort to ward off the cold on the train. Went to the old section of Agra and shopped around before finally getting 2 cotton blankets. The wool blankets were too expensive and I didn’t want to make the investment. After my film ran out (which occurred too soon) I found a busy corner and stood there for about 45 minutes, observing the Indian customs, habits and dress.

        The little kids were as playful as any other small child, and had fun playing with sticks, ropes (horse and driver) and anything they could get their hands on. Few had scalp disorders that I have noticed in the Orient, but they were thinner and much more shabbily dressed. Saw some kids gathering cow manure for the cow “pancakes” and others buying food from vendors on the street. One such vendor opened shop next to me, and he stood there while people would occasionally come up to purchase the concoction. They paid ¼ of an anna (about ½ ¢) for a loaf full of vegetable slop and 3 or 4 kids of seasoning. Others sold oranges, and other forms of food.

        Many people walked by, some of them young looking mothers with infants, old men, and many others shopping or working. Whenever a oxen cart came by all traffic was held up until it passed. Many men pushed and pulled carts loaded with heavy sacks and bundles.

        Once a young boy, (with not much apparent intelligence) who had been watching me, came running across the street brandishing a metal pole. He made noises and motions as if he was going to hit me, but and I tried to ignore him and keep calm. A few minutes later a man walked up, slapped the kid in the face and I guess told him off. Anyway, the kid retired to his store and I kept on standing and observing although a little upset.

JAN 13        

        On the way to the station last night we had an argument with the cab driver. (unmetered cab). We paid him 2 rupees and he wanted 5 for the identical distance we had come in the afternoon and for which the driver wanted 2 rupees. He showed his hand in a few minutes by offering to settle for 3 rupees. We were adamant and walked away from him and boarded the train. The driver called his honcho plus a policeman and told us that we still owed him 3 rupees. We laughed with him and the policeman and refused to pay. As the train started to move he finally gave up, but I must admit he had put up a good battle.

        The cap drivers, beggers, guides and everybody who does something for the tourist is never satisfied with what one gives him. Consequently I have become quite hardened by it all and laugh off most of these moochers.

        The night ride was as cold as before and the blankets didn’t help very much. We met a Finnish UN worker and we decided to spend the day in Jaipur together. At the Circuit House we rented a car and driver for 45 rupees and spent the day sightseeing. The problem of transportation betweensights confronts the tourist every day and takes a big bite out of the budget.

        The first stop was the deserted palace (and surrounding grounds) of Amber. It was wonderfully situated in the hills, and in fact, one could ride an elephant up the road to the palace if he so desired. The buildings and contents are well preserved, and it was fascinating walking in and out of the rooms and passageways. Much of the design is floral, and inlaid, but there are other beautiful things such as glasswork and carved ivory. From the top of the palace one can get a fine view of the surrounding area.

        From here we road to various places in and around the city.  Stopped to look at and take pictures of such places as the Hawa Mahal (a unique 9 storied building with curved roofs), Museum, Park and the Cenotaphs at Gaitor. Jaipur is a very picturesque city, with well laid out streets, clean (relatively) appearance, pink-stoned buildings, camels, peacocks and other interesting sights. It is the capital of the province of Rajasthan and one of the most interesting cities in India.

        In the afternoon we went to the City Palace of the Maharaja. He has some fine Mugal paintings and prints, plus an unused weapons room. We walked around the palace and even laid in the Maj Maharaja’s thick carpet in his bedroom (No pictures allowed while he still lives.) His garden was huge and well kept and the green contrasted with the brown of the mountains.

        Next to the City Palace was the Astronomical Observatory built in the 1700’s. There were many stone and iron sun dials and other instruments used in astronomy. Pete bought some pointed shoes common to this area and which had the mysterious Oriental appearance.

        Caught the night train for New Delhi and once again we froze. Met the Under Secretary for Food and Agriculture on the train and enjoyed discussing the agriculture problem and other problems facing India today. He like the others that we talked to, were well educated

JAN 14        

        The train ride was not only cold, it was also quite crowded and slow. Mr. Hillman, the Finnish UN worker, suggested we try his hotel, since we had heard it was difficult to obtain rooms in New Delhi. After considerable talking, we got one for 30 rupees a piece, which included meals and a suite of rooms. (Far too luxurious for our pocketbooks). The American Plan is firmly established in all the major (and minor) hotels and in some cases is a blessing – such as small towns where food accommodations are limited – but in the big cities it ties one down too much to the hotel.

        We showered, shaved, ate and then we to to Connaught Circle where the MATS office was located. He (MATS officer) said we shouldn’t have much trouble with getting a flight back, so that relieved a little pressure from our minds. Next we went to American Express and the Indian tourist Bureau; plus stopping at the YMCA to inquire about rooms and charges (10 rupees for room & board). Back to the hotel for lunch – the pain in the neck of American plan setups – and then out for the afternoon.

        I had heard of a Polo Match being played this afternoon and decided to see it. On the way, I passed the Parliament and Secretariat Buildings, in front of which were many lancers and soldiers. I got out of the cab and inquired of the occasion dn found it to be a practice for the Independence Day parade (26 January). I stuck around for 2 hours, watching the lancers, 3 bands (including the bagpipes) and observing the Indian people and the uniforms of the soldiers. Everything was extremely colorful and I enjoyed myself very much. Some of the band members had leopard skins over their uniforms, other men had socks and many medals, and the lancers looked great – out of the storybook – on top of their identical colored horses. Nothing beats bagpipe music and I was enthralled with the strains that issued forth from the clumsy looking musical instruments.

        In the evening I met Pete at an English-speaking version of an old Sanskrit Play. I thought it only fair and was bored at various times during the play. The only redeeming feature was that Prime Minister Nehru was in the audience, in fact 1 row in front and 9 seats to the right of me. He looked just like his picture, with the ¾ length coat, tight leggings and Gandhi cap. Many other important Indian officials were in the audience and the clothes of the women were quite attractive. I can’t imagine why they come here, although perhaps they enjoyed it more since they had a background in Sanskrit.

        After the show we had dinner (at the Hotel) and then went to a couple of hotels for night life. Found absolutely nothing so we went back to hit the sack.

JAN 15 (SUNDAY - WEEK 56)

        At long last – a good night of sleep. We got up about 9, and decided to check out of the hotel. We then took a taxi to the YMCA, where we registered, and then cleaned up. At the Y we met two Americans who had just completed 2 years of missionary work in Australia for the Mormon Church. They were taking the long way back to the US, before returning to college life at Brigham Young University.

        The four of us rented a taxi for 12 rupees and spent the afternoon sight-seeing in Old Delhi. We went first to Raj Ghat, the simple monument where Mahatma Gandhi was cremated. I am glad that they decided to mark the spot with a simple without any elaborate structures for it wouldn’t have fitted in with the memory of this great leader. One pleasure was the fact that there were no tip seeking guides to bother the people who came to the Ghat.

        Next on the list was Juma Masjid (built in 1658), said to be the largest mosque in the world. We arrived at 2 PM which was prayer time, so we weren’t able to do much looking around. No foreigners are allowed in the temple when the worshipping is taking place.

        One of the outstanding sights in the Delhi area is the Birla Temple, built in 1938, and dedicated to all the religions of India. The architecture was interesting, and blended in with the idea behind the construction of this unique structure. It is encouraging to see a temple, erected for all religions, and in sections of which, all people can pray to the religion of their choosing. In the back was a park where people could rest and children could play. We were sorry when we left, but since we had rented the car for the afternoon as we thought we had best use the time to see some of the other sights.

        The Red Fort was interesting but did not compare to the other forts that I have seen in India. We then rode around the city, and thence back to the Y. In the evening we went to the theater to see the English-speaking version of the visit by the Russian leaders.

        The movie was good and gave a good rundown on the accomplishments of the 5 year plan, plus many of the tourist attractions in India. The welcome given to the Russians was the greatest I have ever seen, and in Calcutta it was so tremendous that it was unbelievable. In Calcutta over 4 million curious people crowded the Maidan to see and hear, if the could, the speeches. The Indian government went out of its way to make the visit a great show and it was just that. Some say the visit helped the Communist Party in India; others say that the visit cut the ground from under the Party since the Russians by their visit put their mark of approval on Nehru. I guess only time will tell.

        Ate at Gaylords after the show and had a fine Indian meal – chicken tandori. The chicken was baked in a barBQ (similar) sauce and was very tasty. Best meal I have had in India.

JAN 16

        Ted Johnson and Bob Steck (the two American boys that I met at the Y) decided to go to Lahore, Pakistan on the evening train, and I decided to join them. (Pete had decided to go South to Bombay.) In the morning I went to the U.S. Embassy to obtain some information regarding passports. Frankly, I wasn’t very much impressed with our representative in the Embassy that talked to me, but maybe I didn’t impress him. As it is, I am somewhat stymied with my temporary passport which prevents me from getting any visas while I am in Delhi.

        From the Embassy I walked to the Technical Corporation Mission (Foreign Aid) where I was introduced to a Mr. Luderheim. He arranged a visit to Batala Community Project located North of Amritsar. I hope the visit will give me an opportunity to see some of the work being carried out under the 5 year plan. Had an opportunity to talk to a young college graduate in the Industrial Section, and he gave me the low-down on life in Delhi for a young bachelor — with a good looking auto. He said life was a little boring, but there were women available for dates if a person wanted one. One could date Embassy workers, Anglo-Indians and Foreign workers; however, it was extremely difficult, if not impossible to date an Indian girl. I haven’t seen a single Indian girl out by herself in a night club or restaurant.

        From TCM I went to the Pakistan Embassy where I obtained the necessary visa. They were quite nice to me, I guess because I am an American. Then had lunch at the Alp Club, and it was very enjoyable.

        In the afternoon I didn’t do much. Walked around New Delhi, looking in show windows, watching people; and in general, passing the time and at the same time learning more about the Indian customs, habits and dress. Didn’t buy anything but some stamps and a pair of long underwear. Had to laugh at the man from whom I bought the long underwear. He asked 4-8, then 4-8. I came up from 3-0 to 3-8.
