He then said, “Lets flip for the difference?” We flipped and I lost, but I didn’t mind paying the extra ½ rupee.

        Thought we would be able to buy sleeping bags at the station but no luck. However, it was a modern train, similar to those in the states, so it wasn’t too bad of a ride. Met a rich silk man from Banaras and talked to him awhile. He seemed to be like all the other rich men that I have met – let the Government do something for the poor. They couldn’t be bothered with the less unfortunate. I think this is a bad frame of mind which will eventually have to be overcome for India to get ahead.

JAN 17

        The last 2 days haven’t been very eventful, although here and there were a couple of interesting moments. Around 7 AM we were awakened by a lot of shouting at one of the stops on the way to Amritsar. It developed that a large crowd of laborers had come to the train station to welcome one two of their leaders. They were shouting the names of the leaders, plus throwing in the word Comrade, etc, and the fellow I talked to assumed they were Communists. Had to chuckle when the men emerged from the air conditioned cars and proceded up the line receiving garlands around their necks. “Pep leaders” kept the crowd spirited and yelling constantly.

        Began talking to a couple of men in the next car and they invited me into their car for tea. At first I thought they were Indians but they told me they were Pakistanis working for the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi. There were about 6 or 7 in the car and they were quite friendly and seemingly intelligent. One of the fellows spoke of Kashmir and the unsettled state it has been in for 9 years. He said that the ruler is Hindu and wants to belong to India, whereas, most of the inhabitants are Moslems. India refuses to have a plebiscite so the issue has remained unsettled and a thorn for the UN to remove – if it can. I asked him what would happen if the UN ruled in favor of India?— “War” he said, “Why Not!”

        We arrived in Amritsar at 8:30 and took a bumpy bus to the check point. Then we proceded through immigration, customs and othe much paperwork before being allowed to cross no-mans land and into Pakistan. In Pakistan we did the same, and were finished about 11 AM. Took the bus for Lahore (2nd largest city) and arrived there around noon. We were unable to check in Flatti’s hotel, so had to settle for a dive called the Princess Hotel.

        After lunch I had “takusan” trouble trying to get my Re-entry visa into India. Was taken to the wrong place, then had to go all the way across town only to find that I needed 4 photographs. Will have to return in the morning. Took a tonga to Shalamar Gardens, a supposedly beautiful garden built by Shah Jahan. I wasn’t too impressed, however, and felt it wasn’t worth the much publicity given to it. The tonga ride to the garden was quite enjoyable, though, as we went quite a distance in and around Lahore. The town seems to be quite nice with quite a few Universities. Everywhere one sees women with veils over their face, and it reminded me of the biblical past. Some of the veils are quite neat and distinctive while the peasant’s outfit looks more or less like a white tent. Didn’t see any monkeys or cows running wild nor many beggers. Did see some poor hovels on the outside of town. The people look the same as Indians and their dress is quite similar, too. Some wear fezs and grow “Rabbi looking” beards, but the majority of men wear the loosely draped pants or Western clothes. The women wear the veil so it is difficult to see how they are dressed. The way I understand the veil;– a woman wears a veil on the street and in public if the man she sees is younger than her husband. Don’t know how true this is, but I did see a lot of old women with no veils.

JAN 18

        This was quite a hectic day. Had a good nights sleep and woke up refreshed at 6 AM. Ate and then bid farewell to Ted and Bob who were going to Karachi. First, I went to the Police Station and Registered. Then I hopped a bus and road rode to the India High Commission Office. Filled out a blank and was anticipating only a short delay, when the man said that he didn’t know how to treat my case because I was in the U.S. Army. I told him that they knew this in Tokyo when I got my visa previously, but he said that he would have to get the approval of the First Secretary.

        I waited and waited and waited some more and all the time getting more and more upset. My blood began to boil and all kinds of thoughts ran in my head (like banging in on the First Secretary or Press Officer and telling them what I think of their organization) but other than getting ashamed at the way I got upset, I did nothing but sit on the front porch. Finally, after 3 hours of waiting I got my visa and went on my way.

        It was so late that I had no time for more sightseeing, so I caught the bus and rode to the check point. Here I had a little trouble for the India Commission had refused to clarify me as a tourist and thus made it so that I would have to register in each town that I visited. Luckily I met a pretty decent immigration officer who said that since I hadn’t been out of India for over 2 weeks that my former tourist visa would still be in effect.

        Met 2 Pakistani men on the way to Amritsar and spent some time talking to them. We discussed many Indian-Pakistan and US-Pakistan problems and I think I am beginning to get the other side of the picture concerning Indian-Pakistan problems. We went to an Indian movie in the evening which was quite good, and I enjoyed the dancing very much. The movie was quite long, but the color and acting were very good.

        – Two last thoughts on Pakistan. One concerns the buses which are segregated as in the U.S. (South). The women sit in front and the men in the rear, and neither sit in the other section if theirs is full. The women enter first and leave first and generally raise their veils when on the buses.

        The Pakistanis are quite aroused about Kashmir and will fight if it is given to India. However, some say they would be satisfied if Kashmir is made an Independent Nation. One of the main problems concerning Kashmir is the fact that most of the rivers that flow through Pakistan, originate in India. Thus the Pakistanis feel that their lives depend upon the use of the water.

JAN 19

        Today turned out to be a much better day than the past few days. I met Mr. Haiden (Pakistani) and his friend at 9 AM. We went to the Golden Temple which is the Holy shrine of the Sikh people, an offshoot or slightly different phase of the Hindu religion. The Sikhs believe in one God (with no name), they never cut their hair, and pledge their life to this religion.

        A guide showed us around the temple grounds and also the inside of the Golden Temple. Singing is carried on 18 hours a day inside the temple where priests constantly read from the holy book. The temple is surrounded by a big pool of water and is connected to the side of the pool by a causeway. The top of the temple is Gold Sheet, from which the temple gets its name. The work in the temple, and on new construction is all voluntary labor. Even the women offer their services by preparing free food for the many pilgrams. The Sikhs want either their freedom from India or at least a majority in the Punjab Provence Government. (Population-wise, it is Sikh 30%, others 70%).

        In the afternoon I took the bus to Batala, where I planned to visit a Community Development Project. I was introduced to some of the officials – they had thought I was arriving on Wednesday and thus had given me up as not coming. (An official in New Delhi had written to them telling them I was coming). One of the officials drove me around the countryside and pointed out some of the many projects being carried on. He mentioned that recent floods had washed away many of their accomplishments. In one village I was shown a house where an American College boy had spent about 1 month on an exchange basis. They all said how much they enjoyed the work and help given by this fellow, and wished more Americans would come. Also, met an Indian who had spent some time in the U.S., and I enjoyed hearing his comments

        From 4-6 PM we had tea and sandwiches at the Executive Officers house, and talked about India, America, the 5 year plan, etc. I really enjoyed myself, first of all since the food was Indian and quite excellent; and second, I think we all got to understand each other better. Some of their comments: “India would never go Communistic”, “Pakistan is a shallow-nation full of fanatics”, “Chester Barnes is tops”, “Gandhi is like Washington, Nehru similar to Lincoln”, “A. Mayer and Slocum were two fine Engineers helping India,” etc. I caught a late bus and went back to Amritsar.

        The Community Project scheme is a project of Chester Bowles (TCM, ECA, ICA, Marshal Plan, etc.) whereby we help India help themselves. Most of the aid is in technical assistance or in the giving of funds for the cost of roads if the village put up ½ the cost and do the labor. Main prospect of the Community Development Project are the increase in schools, self better use of land (Agriculture has risen), sanitation, roads, health and a general raising of the standard of living. Each project has about 400 villages and by the end of the 2nd 5 year plan – 1961 – it is hoped that all of the villages will be covered by these projects.

        It is interesting to compare China and India, for whereas China is doing everything under the lash, India is attempting to do it democratically. China has concentrated first on industry, India on the villages. Both nations are trying to accomplish much in a short period of time.

JAN 20

        Again, – a cold night on the train. I have finally decided to take no more night train rides while I am in India. I guess it has saved me time and money, however, if I hadn’t tried to arrange it so that I had a good nights sleep in between these trips I am afraid fatigue would have overcome me. Arrived in Chandigarh, the Capital of the Punjab, around 7 AM and took a tonga bus and pedacab to the hotel. I decided to stay the day and night in Chandigarh, so I checked in the hotel. (First on the agenda was a good shower – I hadn’t taken a shower for the past 4 days!)

        My day in Chandigarh was very interesting. I literally walked my foolish feet off as I attempted to see all of this new city plus take in the gorgeous sunshine. Chandigarh is the first new Indian city after the Independence and the Indians are quite proud of it. Everything is modern and functional, and they have kept out all mud hovels and broken down shacks. Everything is modern and it is as if a new city was born from the tactless waste upon which it stands.  Chapman had said that Le Corbusier of France had design a couple of the buildings, so I went to see them first.

        The High Court building was a good example of Le Corbusier’s functional architecture. Dramatic lines, unfinished concrete, etc made it a very “different” but pleasing building. Some of the apartment houses seemed a little outlandish, with too much white zig zag designs, but on the other hand I liked the judges homes very much. All of Chandigarh has been pre-planned and there are wide streets and ample space between the buildings. In the background one can see some high mountains which add to the beauty of this new city.

        The town – commercial section – is also modern, however, the shops while new, still do not live up to the examples set up by the apartment houses and office buildings. Most of the shops are one room affairs with no merchandising to speak of. I really haven’t seen any big stores, or department stores in India, and in fact, Okinawa has bigger and better shops.

        Today was the birthday of the 10th Gaur, one of the founders of the Sikh religion. Consequently, it was a holiday in the Punjab and people were milling around here and there. In the afternoon there was a small parade, with a couple of vehicles, a band, marching boys and girls and some of old “warriors” of the Sikh people who devote their lives to go from temple to temple. Took some pictures of the goings on and I hope they turn out o.k.

        One of the fellows that I met at Batela had just come from Chandigarh and he said that he sure hated to have the modern convenience and come to the small town of Batala. I sure understand why!

JAN 21

        Got up early, ate a small breakfast and caught the bus to New Delhi. The trip took 7 hours and I was quite happy when the bus arrived in the Capital City. Some aspects of the trip were interesting such as the small towns we passed and those we stopped in, the farms, and I guess most of all, the fellow passengers on the bus. One of the passengers was an Army Captain who spoke fine English and who was quite a jolly chap. He was friendly and we generally spent a few minutes talking at each spot stop. I had to laugh when he said that I must be an American. I asked him way, and he said a Britisher would never have asked him – sitting 3-4 rows ahead on the bus – what time it was.

        From Old Delhi I took a tonga to the YMCA, and checked in around 2 PM. Ate lunch and went to the Imperial Hotel for a haircut. (The lunches and dinners at the Y are quite hot and spicy and not very good. Some of the stuff isn’t bad however, I never leave feeling satisfied.) Was treated to a rich man’s haircut, but can’t say I appreciated it. Should have seen the look on the barber’s face when I didn’t give him a tip!

        Happened to see Pete in the hotel lobby and found that he had decided to check in the Imperial Hotel (45 rupees a day) so as to impress a girl he had met in Bombay. Joined him in his room and spent a couple hours discussing our trips. In the evening I went to see “To Hell and Back” the story of Audie Murphy the most decorated US soldier of World War II. Then had a bad supper and went back to the Y.

        At the Y I met 2 Pakistan boys who were touring India. We talked for about a hour concerning India, US, Pakistan and life in general. It was interesting to hear them praise Nehru (the last Pakistan I had talked to thought him a sneak) and to say what a good job he is doing for India. They felt that the relations between Pakistan and India will continue to be strained and perhaps there might be a war over the Kashmir problem.

        The boys felt that Pakistan was beset with many major problems;– such as Kashmir, economic conditions and the separation of the country in 2 parts. East Pakistan they said was quite different that West Pakistan in people (east were more Oriental), language, customs etc. They wished they had a man like Nehru to lead them, and they also said that they thought Nehru was pro-West.

        One of the main features on the trip has been the meeting of many different people. Of course there has been the Ph Filipinos and Indians, but also there were the 2 New Zealand women I talked to on the bus, the Canadian and Argentine fellow at the Y, the Sudanese student and hosts of other people. Each are interesting and offer much to broaden my outlook.

JAN 22 (SUNDAY - WEEK 57)

        Monson and Amer, the Pakistani boys, and I went to Quitb Qutb Minar in the morning. The tower was built in 1126 and is 280 feet high. It is made out of sandstone and is said to be the most beautiful example of a perfect tower known anywhere in the world. From each of its five stories one can see a great deal of the surrounding land. At the foot of the tower is the Quwwatul-Islam mosque, the first mosque to be built on the plinth of a destroyed Hindu temple.

        Near the tower is the Iron Pillar which is said to have been made in 375 A.D. Neither time nor elements have harmed the Pillar and it is said to be from a meteorite. (99% Iron). The tower and pillar, particularly the former, are the outstanding spots in New Delhi.

        Had lunch at the Imperial Hotel with Pete and found it to be quite reasonable (⅝). In the afternoon we rented bikes and along with the Canadian fellow, we biked around the mall and visited Parliament, Secretariat, and the President’s House. In the latter building we saw some of the gifts given to Nehru on his visits to Yugoslavia and Russia. Also saw some of the extreme preparations for the big Independence Day coming up.

        I went to a movie in the evening and then met Pete at the Alps Restaurant. The food was quite good but the floor show was very bad. We bumped into the SFC from the Consulate and he joined our table for a drink or two. He invited us to his apartment tomorrow for a few drinks.

        New Delhi is quite a decent city, with its wide streets, big parks, nice homes with their yards, and in general, the modern atmosphere. Much construction is going on and this includes housing, for in the outskirts of the city I saw section and after section of new housing projects.

        Old Delhi, however, is typical of the India as we think of India. It has narrow, crowded streets, teems of people, cows and people everywhere, small shops and open stalls, and filth and poverty everywhere. The difference between New and Old Delhi is dramatic and exemplifies what India is attempting to change from and to.

JAN 23

        Today begins the 3rd week, and the time is beginning to pass quite rapidly. I called a man at TCAA who had told me that he could arrange a visit to a factory, and he said that he would check into it. Stopped by the Imperial Hotel to say hello to a fellow St. Louisan who was PAA’s India manager.. As it turned out, he was to leave for the U.S. in a couple of hours and he said he would call Mom if he got to the US St. Louis.

        Rented a bike and decided to ride around town. Near the Mall (Maidan or whatever you call the park) I heard a lot of noise and decided to investigate. It turned out to be a full dress rehearsal of the Independence Day Parade and I stayed a couple of hours to watch it. Everybody had on colorful uniforms, and in addition to the bands that I saw the other day, this time there were troops, school children, elephants, cavalry, camel corp troops, mechanized equipment, and other things, such as overhead jets and fire equipment. I am glad that I saw the parade and now don’t feel too bad about missing the celebration Thursday.

        Went to old Delhi in the afternoon and took some pictures of typical scenes. Felt a little funny about taking the pictures as I didn’t want to embarrass anybody. Sort of stood on the background and took a couple shots of people as they walked by.

        In the evening, Pete and I went to hear a Russian writer – Ehrenberg – speak on “The Folly of Armed Peace.” He spoke in Russian and it was crudely translated into English. His speech was witty, interesting and naturally slanted. Nevertheless it was interesting to see the people who attended (Pro-Russian newspaper sold in front) and to hear first hand how the Communists twist the truth to show themselves in good light. I guess many people eat up what he and others like him have to say, but there are many more who think of it as two-face talk, particularly if they have all the facts.

        Went to SFC Palmers house after the meeting and had a couple of beers. Around 9 PM we went to Gaylords Restaurant where we had a good dinner and saw a fine floor show. Met 2 fellows from the Russian Embassy and invited them to our table. (Even though Palmer objected) They joined us in a couple of beers and I – and Pete – had an enjoyable time discussing things in general. The fellow I talked to was about 30 years old, I would guess, and was political chief in the Embassy. He spoke pretty good English – was also learning Hindu (our Embassy personnel do not have to learn Hindu). His wife worked in the Embassy on the evening shift. We discussed the talk we had heard, schooling in the USSR & US, and good Russian authors such as Dostoyevsky. (He thought Crime and Punishment to have some social faults). They left after about 45 minutes and I think we both enjoyed the evening. It is a shame that such friendliness can’t exist everywhere in the world.

JAN 24

        Didn’t do much today, – my last in India until perhaps next June. In the morning I went to American express and cashed a traveller’s check, and also obtained some visa applications. Once again I saw the parade and as before I enjoyed the colorful processions.

        In the afternoon I rented a bicycle and started out for Old Delhi. Didn’t know where I was going and consequently ended up in the same place I had been the previous afternoon. The streets were crowded with bikes, tongas, cows, cabs etc. and a couple of times I narrowly escaped getting hit. After a couple of hours I headed back to New Delhi.

        In the evening I read Time, wrote in the Diary and talked to the two Pakistan boys. One of them worked in Saudi Arabia for a US Oil company and I enjoyed hearing his comments on American food – he didn’t like – and American life in general. He said that he considered the Oriental habit toilet habit as being more sanitary particularly the washing il instead of wiping.

        Old Delhi is a typical overcrowded Indian city, – and one that is similar to most of Calcutta, Banaras, Agra and Amritsar. The streets are crowded with people, animals and equipment. The people are very poor and most of them have on rags. The women do much work – if they are on the streets, such as sweeping horse cow & horse manure and creating clouds of dust, and carrying heavy objects. The men, with their Hindu wisp of hair in the back, squat in the stores and shops and wait until somebody either comes to buy or to talk. India is quite the country and I am looking forward to returning sometime in the near future.

JAN 25

        With much effort I got up at 3:30 AM and gathered my things together. Called a taxi and drove to Palam Airport where we waited for the MATS personnel to arrive. Didn’t have too much difficulty in going through customs, and it wasn’t long before we boarded. The flight to Bangkok took 6 ½ hours, probably my largest flight up to now, and I occupied most of the time by reading.

        In Bangkok – they have a fine, new airport – we went through customs and were then driven to the Princess Hotel. Rooms were difficult to obtain so we had a pedacab boy take us to the Hotel.  We checked in the Loy Hotel for 80 ticals ($4 – 2 people) and found it to be relatively clean place – except for the hordes of mosquitos.

        We didn’t do much in the afternoon – just bathed, ate and walked around town. Looked in a couple shops, and did some pricing however we didn’t do any buying. In the evening we went to the Hoi Thian Lao restaurant which is noted for its Chinese food. We had egg young foo, shark fin fish soup, chicken and noodles and another form of food that I forgot the name of. Can’t say that I enjoyed the food, as it seemed awful starchy and greasy. (wasn’t very cheap, either)

        After dinner we went upstairs to a dance hall. It was a huge place, quite nice and had many “fair” dancers. I had a couple of dances but Pete didn’t like the place so we left for better grounds.

        After a couple dead ends we ended up at the Lido, a modern dance hall somewhat near the American Embassy. They had a nice band, singer and again, plenty of women. (mostly Thai girls, and older than the other girls). Danced some at this club and had a couple of beers. Actually, I was somewhat surprised at the large number of Thai and Chinese at the club and paying, what I think, high price – $.80/small bottle of beer)

        Near the end of the evening I asked a girl to dance, and she said “OK.” When we finished, I returned her to walked her to the bar, where she had been sitting before, and said I enjoyed the dance. A man sitting 2 seats down called me over and told me to give him 15 ticals for the beer he had bought her. I said that it was no concern of mine and started to turn away. All of sudden he grabbed my arms and began talking louder and louder, about paying the money. I repeated what I said before and tried to move away but he had a strong hold on my arms. Actually he was very drunk and I decided that it wasn’t worth a fight as he might get a couple of good punches in and break some teeth or tear my clothes. He continued to yell and call me names, but I just stood there, nervous, and not exactly knowing what to do, except not to look worried. Finally I sort of shoved him away, and backed off, he all the time calling me names. (Everybody had gathered around, but no one stepped in to help – except Pete) Fi He soon was attracted to some other direction and so I left – my pride having suffered, but I could see no advantage in fighting.

JAN 26

        Well, the beginning of 5 full days in Bangkok, and it appears that I will have time to spare. Pete isn’t too much interested in the sights and tends to rush through the places of interest. We had lined up a rickshaw man to take us around town, but he never showed up so we hit the road ourselves.

        First place we visited was Saovapa Institute which is a snake farm where cobras and other poisonous snakes are bred and milked. We watched them feed the snakes and milk them, and of course, take pictures of the events. Enjoyed seeing the cobra and the way he arches his body as if to strike. Also was amazed at the amount of venom that they get from the snakes.

        Next we went to the Public Relations Department and inquired about visiting the palace. However, we learned that the palace was closed for 100 days on account of the death of the King’s grandmother. From here we visited the National Museum in which many old relics were kept. Next we walked along the streets, visiting a Buddhist temple, passing the ultra modern lottery building and observing the people, their habits and customs and jobs.

        After lunch we visited the Chapel of the Emerald Buddha which was one of the highlights thus far. The Chapel is full of figures, Thai architecture and rich colors. This is the most sacred chapel in Thailand and is where the Royal Family worships. Near the Chappl Chapel is the Wat Po where the reclining Buddha – 150 foot long – is housed.

In the evening we went to Thai Boxing which is quite unique and brutal. The men wear boxing gloves, but no shoes, and anything is allowed. Feet and arms fly through-out the bout and most generally one of the the two are counted out before the 5 rounds are completed. Only 1 fight went the 3 rounds that it was supposed to last. The feet movements are very fast, and the blows to the head are reverb reverberated throughout the area. Near the end of the show they had a 8 round Western style match and it was interesting to compare the style of boxing.

JAN 27

        We got up early so that we would be able to get an early start on our canal boat ride. Six of us hired a boat and spent approximately 3 hours on the canal taking many pictures of life on the canals of Bangkok. It is fascinating to see the houses which are built adjacent to the water’s edge and surrounded on the other side by jungle growth. Boats are the only means of transportation and everything and everybody are sold, carried, transported and almost ma__ed in the canoes or larger water boats. Children go to schools, men to go their work and women shop in the boats. Bathing and washing is likewise carried on in the canal. The people seemed to be quite friendly and waved to us as we rode by.

        We stopped at Wat Arun, Temple of Dawn, from which we obtained a fine view of the city. It is a huge stupa with the steepest stairs that I have ever climbed. Was fortunate in observing some Buddhists in the act of praying and I hope a couple pictures that I took through a crack in the door turn out okay.

        Went to a Thai restaurant for lunch, and had some Thai Food. Also had some fried rice which was quite good. The Thai food is even hotter than Indian food which likewise is hotter than American food. After lunch I went to ICA and lined up a visit to the Agriculture Research Mission on Monday.

        From here I visited a couple of temples, took a picture of the Monument of Democracy, and spent some time at the Marble Temple. At the temple I met a 20 year old Buddhist priest whom I conversed with for about 1 ½ hours. He explained some of the features of being a priest and also explained some of the objects in the temple. He accompanied me as I walked back from the temple, and finally said “Goodbye” as he left for his evening prayers. I would have enjoyed the meeting more if he had a better command of the English language.

        Went to see the movie “Trial” in the evening, but found that it had changed theaters. Instead of seeing what was there, I just walked around Chinatown, watching the people, and observing the night activities. Watched a Chinese musical side show for about 10 minutes and sort of enjoyed it although the acting and singing wasn’t very much good. Much of the singing was in the form of screeching intermingled with drum beats and other crude instruments.

        Talked a cabbie in to taking us to an Opium Den located in Chinatown. It was a huge building occupied by about 100-150 stalls of 3-6 men each. (I presume these Opium dens are legal and police controlled). The police were in under-clothes and were laying on their side with their head resting on a hard block. Some were sleeping, some eating and others smoking. Most of them were thin and had a dazed look in their eyes.

        The Opium pipes were about 2’ long and an with to 1 ½ inches in to 2 inches in diameter. They filled the pipe and then placed the open end over a heroine lamp. They would then inhale the opium fumes. I was offered a pipe and/or a massage, but declined both. A couple of times some of the Chinese yelled at me but I didn’t understand what they were talking about. It was an interesting experience, which I shall remember.

JAN 28

        Had a good nights sleep and got up around 9 AM. Ate and then did some checking on the cost of flying from Manila to Cairo. It seems that one can buy Pesos in Hong Kong at a premium which I could then use to buy the airplane tickets. Probably would be a little risky but not too much (Be just my luck to get caught)

        Spent the day shopping – and enjoyed the arguing and trading. I bought 2 bracelets and a star sapphire, but not without a lot of haggling. The bracelets were particularly rough but I think I got good values. The man wanted 82 ticals a piece for them but I got them both for 87.50 ticals.

        I went to a couple of places for the sapphire and did some pricing. Ended up buying the first one that I looked at. It cost $15 and had a nice star in it. Don’t really know if I got a good bargain, but anyway I think it is a pretty nice stone.

        Pete and I went to a Thai Classical Dance program in the evening. It was excellent and we saw fine examples of Thai costuming, dance steps, acting and hand and foot movements. The Thai costumes are quite gaudy and heavy looking, and consist of gold metal pieces topped of cloth and a pointed cap or crown with ear flaps. The audience consisted of well dressed Thai families as it was held in the Ministry of Culture auditorium. The whole atmosphere was so much better than that which we had seen at the night club. Tried to take some pictures but I didn’t have a flash attachment.

JAN 29 (SUNDAY - WEEK 58)

        Today was a spare day, as I didn’t have anything in particular to do. Wished that it could have been spent elsewhere, but there wasn’t much that I could do about it. (Anyway one can’t kick a gift horse in the face!)

        Said goodbye to Pete, as he left for Hong Kong in the morning. Things worked out fine on our joint travels, and outside of having an intelligent companion, we both saved money by sharing costs. There were a couple of disagreements, but generally everything worked out quite well. The way we worked it, was to do the sightseeing together, and then split up for any other personal interests.

        I spent most of the morning wandering around Chinatown. The streets were crowded (even though it was Sunday) and I tried to be inconspicuous so as to get some good pictures. The Chinese people are very industrious and life in Chinatown is one “hustle and bustle”. The shops are a little more modern than we saw in India but the basic principles are the same – single room, no merchandising, children and animals all around the shop, shop in front, live in back; street stalls and people squatting and talking everywhere. I don’t think the Chinese are as attractive as the Thai but are more industrious and control the economy. The Thai seem to be more interested in Government work. Didn’t see any slit dresses, but did see a lot of black skirts and pajama-like pants. The Thai women wear tight skirts – either blue or brown – which tend to wrinkle in front. Some of them are quite good looking.

        Went to the horse races in the afternoon, but didn’t win a thing. Most of the races are small horses, and it was funny to see the races with men the jockeys on their backs, edging their horses on. Didn’t understand the para-mutual board so bet at the windows and hoped I picked a good one. – I didn’t, and lost the 4 times I bet.

JAN 30

        After some confusion with my cab driver, I finally arrived at USOM where I met Dr. Middleton. We then got in a Government Car and drove to the Agriculture University. At the University he took me in the fields and showed me how the rice experimentation program was being carried on. He said that the men were working with the University in attempting to create better types of rice so as to obtain larger yields per acre. The work has been going on for 5 years and many new hybrids have been developed. (I didn’t t know that there are two kinds of rice, one that is planted and is covered by a couple inches of water, and the other that is sowed on the top of 4-5 feet of water. The latter is grown in the Northern Part of Indo-China).

        Mr Dr. Middleton showed me a thrashing machine, mill, rice polishing equipment, laboratories and other features of the school. The school has about 600 students and is the only Agriculture School in Thailand. They have a 5 year curriculum and, surprising enough, a well equipped school. He said that the big problem is student interest, and that the students – mostly Thais – were mainly interested in getting a degree and then working for the Government.

        Later he (Dr. Middleton) introduced me to Mr. Yoder a young man who was a member of the 7 man Oregon State Faculty which was assisting the school in setting up a sound program. Mr. Yoder is connected with the Agriculture Engineering section, and showed me around the shop, library (Well stocked but not too often used – can bring a horse to water but you can’t force him to drink!) and the student gardens. He pointed out a pump that he was working on and which would be of help to the small farmer in his irrigation problems.

        Mr. Yoder invited me to lunch at his house where I met his wife and young son. We had a nice lunch plus some enjoyable conversations concerning Thailand, the Americans in Thailand, the Army, Okinawa (he was here in 1945) and even politics. The lunch was very enjoyable and my day was a success on account of my visit to the school.

Got a lift back to the heart of Bangkok from a couple Thai girls that Mr. Yoder knew. One had just come back from the states and the other two were soon to go. Oh yes, last Friday I was in the office of USOM and the man said that his secretary had been to Stephens College in Columbia, MO. — What a doll I am sorry I didn’t follow it up, but se was seated in his office and it was difficult or at least embarrassing to be too forward.

        Bought a luncheon set for Mom and took it easy the rest of the day. Hit the sack early for I had to get up early in order to catch the MATS plane.

JAN 31

        Awakened early in the morning and slowly dragged myself to the Princess Hotel. Had breakfast and then caught the bus for the airport — my leave was fast in drawing to a close. We cleared customs and then boarded the plane bound for Manila via Saigo.

        We stopped an hour and one half in Saigon and had a chance to get out and stretch our feet. I cashed a dollar for some Viet Nam money and bought a cheese sandwich at the restaurant ($.75, and lousy at that) The women wore pajama like pants covered in front and back (with long sleeves also) by an ankle length piece of cloth with small slits on the sides. The collars had were high and typically Chinese. Saw one stunning woman.

        The plane ride to Manila was smooth and we arrived around 4 PM. Went immediately to Operations and was told that the next flight was the following Monday. Called Sanglie and they said they might have a flight on Friday and that I should call back. Commercial flights left on Tues, Thurs and Sat but I didn’t want to spend the money. So it looked like my best bet would be to sit around the airport and see if I couldn’t talk some pilot into taking me with him.

        Checked in the transit barracks, ate, reported back to the terminal just in case. Found that there was to be a flight the next morning so I decided to get to bed early and see if I couldn’t get on the plane. Went to the Service Club, then to a movie and back to the barracks where I prayed for a hop the next day.

Route as of January 31st, 1956 – end of Chapter 10.

CHAPTER 11 - SPRINGTIME ON THE ROCK

February 1st, 1956 - April 22nd, 1956

FEB 01

        I got up early, cleaned up and then went to the mess hall for some breakfast. Loaded up with my two AWOL bags and headed for the Operations building. Parked myself near the pilots desk and waited for the pilot of the C-54 that was scheduled to depart for Kadena. The O.D. saw me and asked if I was heading for Hong Kong as were some others in the building. I said no and told him that I wanted to go to Okinawa. He said “Just a moment” and then said “Come with me.” We talked to the pilot and he said that he would carry me if he had space and was not over weight. I thanked the O.D. and waited for more information from the pilot.

        About an hour later he came over and said that he could take me – along with 2 officers – if he could round up some parachutes and mae Wests. Well, we got 3 parachutes and only 2 Mae Wests. It looked as if fate was against me, but it turned out not to be, since 4 men that were supposed to go cancelled out at the last moment. Thus, there was ample room and equipment for me.

        The ride was uneventful and somewhat cramped. However, I was thankful for the hop for it saved me 2 days of leave time which I can add to the 7 I have left and perhaps I can take a trip to Japan in the Spring. We landed at Kadena – amidst rain – around 3:30 PM and a ½ hour later I was back at Kue. It was sure an odd feeling to be back and I am sorry my trip is over. It was a great trip and I enjoyed almost every minute. The weather was perfect and things worked out all the way around.

FEB 02

        Have to admit that I had a pretty good nights sleep. The old frame must be use to the curves and bumps of my army cot. After breakfast I came back to the hut and saw Junko, who was happy to see me. Spent an hour talking to her and finding out what was up. She told me that she was able to get in the the typing school and consequently she takes 2 hours of typing a day. Second, she has decided to take the entrance exam for the University of Ryukyus and has been doing some studying for it. Third, Lennon fired her in January and thus she has only one boy to work for. This latter fact might make it necessary to pay her a little more, at least while she is going to school and studying for the entrance exam. If she doesn’t pass the exam, then perhaps she can get a typing job in the administration building and quit being a maid.

        Went on sick call and had the doctor look at the rash on my back. He said it wasn’t much and gave me a bottle of medicine which he said would clean it up.

        Finished reading my mail that had accumulated. Also opened some Christmas packages that had arrived after I had left for my trip. Christmas in February!

FEB 03

        Actually I stopped by the office last night, but tonight was my first complete day of work since returning from my leave. Received an assignment in the morning which was replaced by another one in the afternoon. Had to check with Mr. McDonald concerning the latter estimate and since he wasn’t in his office I didn’t get much accomplished.

        Read some of the newspapers and magazines that had accumulated and around 9 PM I journeyed up to the familiar club on the hill – the Castle Terrace Club. Felt good to be back as I think this is one of the nicer clubs in Asia; however, I had the feeling that I was re-entering the old routine mighty fast.

        About 5 of the old boys in the unit went home in January, and in their place we got 2 new Engineers and about 12 new SP’s. Interesting to observe how the place where the Engineer is assigned determines the clique or group with whom he associates.

FEB 04

        Most of us thought that Thursday nights training would take the place of Saturday’s training. However, we were mistaken as the Captain decided to have an inspection. Soooo we checked out our carbines, cleaned same, and then stood at attention while “the old man” stumbled up and down the ranks chewing the men out for having colored name plates. By 10 AM it was all over and I returned to my hut.

        Cleaned up a few things, and after lunch I went to the office to do some letter writing. Got quite a bit done, although most of the stuff I did concerning concerned firms, schools, etc with little work on the letter angle. Will see what I can do concerning this tomorrow.

        Came back from a show in Naha around 11:30 PM and while passing the laterne I heard female voices. Had to check so I decided to use the facilities and see what was up. It turned out that 4 of the boys had girls in their hut, and at this instant all concerned were taking showers. One sees almost everything while in the Army and particularly so at Camp Kue. While this doesn’t occur too often, it happens enough so that life is interesting in and around the company area.

FEB 05 (SUNDAY - WEEK 59)

        Awakened in time to see the 4 girls of the previous nights escapade leave Hut 720 and get into a taxi cab. Didn’t have a very good look, however, one of the girls appeared to be quite cute. Hard to believe that this is the Army although there are many other things to remind me of this miserable fact.

        Borrowed Estreich’s new portable Swiss typewriter that he purchased in Hong Kong. It is a compact little gadget and does a nice job. I decided to catch up on some of my letter writing, and consequently, spent the day writing letters and listening to the radio. Actually I didn’t get too much done, but the pile of letters is slowly dwindling.

        Played some basketball in the afternoon and it felt good to run around and now and then make a basket. This is probably the first real exercise that I have gotten in over a month, however, one can’t chalk off the many miles that I walked while on leave.

FEB 06

        The beginning of my first work week since returning from leave. I am finding it extremely difficult getting back to work and into the “rut” again. The weather continues to be lousy, as we have had a lot of rain plus some mighty cool evenings. A Mr. Hands is taking over the reins of the Construction Service Branch, and as an indication of the new order, SP1 Werner had to move his desk to make room for some bookcases and other belongings of the new “honcho”.

        I received a letter from Herf Blake (my former boss at Dow Chemical Company – that is, until he got fired in Dec 53) today and I was interested in what he had to say. After he left Dow, he went to work for a consulting firm, then did some consulting work on his own; and recently he went to work for Kay Williams Personnel Service. He said that Dow has undergone some chaotic personnel changes in the last few years, – and Mr. mcNutty, Wat___, Honey Do__ and Dietrich are no longer there. Even Mr. Mansfield is rumored on the outs because of an affair he has been having with Rita. Funny world! I guess that if I went back it would almost be like beginning anew.

        I always liked Herf and think that he got a raw deal from Dow when they canned him. I guess he has some personality faults, but at dow he was just unlucky and became the scapegoat of a misfiled job evaluation program. It will be interesting to look him up when I get back to St. Louie, and maybe it can give me some help in settling down to civilian life. If nothing else, he knows my capabilities and faults.

FEB 07

        My rash hasn’t cleared up, so I went back to the Sukiran Dispensary to see what the trouble is. The doctor gave me some pills, and said to continue the ointment for the next 3 days. If at that time it hasn’t cleared up, then I should return for further treatment. Must be some Indian – or Thai – crud that I picked up!

        Work is coming along all right, however, there isn’t a very big backlog of estimate requests. Can’t say that I am sorry, for the less work there is, the better I feel about goofing off. Haven’t had a talk with the new boss as yet, so I don’t know what his ideas are concerning military personnel. Really not worried about it; however, it is best to know how one stands.

        Wrote some more letters in the evening and have whittled away a major portion of the unanswered letters. Still have about 10 letters to go, but most of them can be taken care of in the normal manner. Have decided to answer some newspaper ads, so as to get use to the procedure again and to acquire information of available jobs. Most companies send the application blanks, but always state they would like face to face interviews. Consequently nothing definite can be accomplished, however, one can never tell when something might turn up. As it is, I can quite particular about which ads I answer. Generally they are about sales engineering or industrial relations work.

FEB 08

        Well, I have been home a week now and I can say with sorrow that I have fallen into the Rock Rut quite rapidly. During the past week I caught up with some over-due projects, so it appears now that I can begin new projects postponed because of my trip. The two big projects on the orizon are: one, plans for my trip this coming summer; and two, thoughts concerning what I want to do when I get home, such as type of work, school and where to live. This latter problem is first on my list with my trip plans scheduled for spring.

        Did a little work on some estimates, and tried to keep busy. Renewed my membership to the NCO club, mailed the presents home, and visited the new Kadena PX. Saw a fair movie, ate some of the cheese that Gladys sent, and had a beer from Hut 722’s bar. Thus a typical day on the Rock.

FEB 09

        The weather turned sunny today and I was sure glad as we have the afternoon off on Thursday for organized sports. (That’s a laugh!) Thought that I would play tennis, but participated in a volleyball game instead. Actually we didn’t have enough men, so we recruited some of the maids to fill in the vacant positions. Played about 2 hours and it was great getting some long needed exercise. Actually my legs are in good shape as a result of the trip, however, my arms are quite weak and I am sure I will see some soreness in them tomorrow.

        Had training in the evening, and it consisted of 4 movies. THree of them weren’t too bad – not good either – but the 4th was a typical Army training film. I guess the films aren’t too bad in what they are attempting to explain, yet since I have no interest in learning about Riot Control, MP work, etc, I find the films quite dull and boring. Still it is better than PT or close order drill.

FEB 10

        The weather turned rainy and it was an unpleasant day. Really don’t mind too much, as I have used up my sightseeing interest during the last trip, and it will take a couple of months to develop again. Also I have some backlog things that I want to catch up on.

        Had a breather at work and decided to go through some recent bill of mt’ls that were turned in by Contractors to the District, and thus acquire a storehouse of price information. Too often I am unsure of my prices, and the source of information; consequently having my own data from actual cost figures I won’t have this problem anymore. It is quite a tedious task, though, and one that is tiring on the hands as I have to thumb through many pages of invoices.

        Left work early in the afternoon and went to the Sukiran Dispensary to let the Doctor check my rash. It seems to be going away and I hope that it won’t leave any permanent marks. Also went to the Dentist section and had a small cavity filled. He worked so fast that I can’t help but wonder whether he did a good job or not.

FEB 11

        I must admit that the time is passing quite rapidly. Not too far off when CAW will be leaving Okinawa for the last time. Oh, perhaps some day I will come back – as a civilian – but I doubt if it will be for many years. Will be interesting to see Okinawa, both militarily and with respects to the indigenous population in 5-10 years. At that time most of the boom construction will have passed and life will probably have settled down to a steady pace. Also, I would like to see Junko in say 5-10 years and see who she married, whether she finished school, her family, etc.

        It rained all day and it was quite miserable outside. For training we had 3 ½ hours of movies, some of which weren’t too bad. One, concerning sports (training!) was a late issue and had some fine scenes. Didn’t do much in the afternoon – read, watched premieres of slide showing, and goofed around. Just another day!

FEB 12 (SUNDAY - WEEK 60)

        My visit to India has increased my interest in that country 100%. Now when I see a book or magazine with material about India, I top to give it closer attention. Actually I have found this true concerning all of the countries that I have visited – from Korea to India.

        I guess of all the countries, only Korea has left a bad taste in my mouth. In Korea, unlike the other countries, the people do not seem to appreciate what help is being given to them; and they just seem to want more. When aid is not coming, or at least slow, the government is quite outspoken against the U.S. They try all angles, such as getting the US to use the 180 hwan exchange rate and not the market value of 500 hwan to the dollar.

        India seems to have used our aid to the most advantage – at least in building up their country. Japan, Thailand and Pakistan use it mainly to balance their economy. I keep on thinking of the Agriculture School in Bangkok where they have very modern and expensive equipment, yet there is no driving desire on the part of the students to learn, nor of the administration to improve the curriculum. I guess all we can do is throw the halfback the ball, and he has to do the running.

FEB 13

        The weather continued to be miserable, however, it doesn’t make much difference on weekdays. Spent the day compiling pricing data which I and the other boys will be able to use on the estimates. I got some of the Contractor’s Bills of Loading and Invoices, and from these sheets I make alphabetical listing of the various materials that have been used and are still being used in construction. I am sure that the figures will help me, for there are many times where I am not sure about the latest prices.

        The continual typing and thumbing wore me out and my arms and thumbs became mighty tired. To top it off, I must have eaten something the other day which didn’t agree with my stomach for I have had a slight stomach ache the past couple of days. Guess the hypochondriac in me blossoms forth every now and then. On my travels, when there were 3-4 days in a row where I couldn’t take a shower, I didn’t give it much thought. O Guess I just have too much time to think.

FEB 14

        Still more rain, but today it wasn’t as cold as it has been lately. Finished the work that I had been doing lately, and got an estimate to do which will be a good check on my new pricing data. Electrical prices have been my biggest headache up to now, because of rising prices and only an adequate electrical estimator in our department.

        My upset stomach of the previous couple days has vanished and likewise I have felt a lot more like joking and kidding around. Joking and teasing has been one of my saviors overseas as it relieves ones mind from worrying. Actually almost everybody in the District are is quite pleasant and generally they have a smile and hello for each other. This makes a much nicer atmosphere and is far better than a complete GI atmosphere that I have been in before with its habitual griping and bitching.

FEB 15

        Can’t really complain about anything except the weather – as it poured all night and morning. Around noon it finally cleared up and it became quite pleasant later in the afternoon. No estimates at work consequently a legitimate excuse to do personal work.

        In the afternoon I borrowed a jeep and went to the American Counsel Consul at Naha and applied for a permanent passport. Filled out the necessary papers but didn’t have a letter stating that I will be discharged on Okinawa. Thus, I will have to get same and return to the Consul’s office.

        From here I went to USCAR where I met Junko. We went to the Education Section where we talked to a Mr. Evans. Discussed Junko’s application and the $150 fund Poole, Campbell and Whitmire have established for Junko if she gets accepted to the University. I am hoping that she passes and thus is accepted for I think she will be a good student and in turn a credit to Okinawa. Sending her to school has been one of my projects while on Okinawa, and I have given her money for books and application fees. Also arranged for her to go to typing school so she can improve her ability to read English.

FEB 16

        While I was on leave one of the Sergeants in Engineering arranged to have a weekly “Organized Athletic” afternoon. Thursday was the day agreed upon, and consequently every Thursday afternoon we get off from work. Last Thursday we played volleyball, but today there weren’t many fellows around so I decided to join a couple of fellows on a trip to Moon Beach in order to take some pictures. (Haven’t completed the roll I began in Bangkok.)

        The weather wasn’t too nice though, as it was cloudy and there were ominous signs of rain. There was also a cold, brisk wind which prevailed during the 2 ½ hours. The walk was refreshing and we strolled up and down the seashore; observing the rock formations, sand, and the sea inhabitants on or near the shore. The ocean had worn down various places and had formed secluded little coves with sand bottoms.

        Chapman remarked that he and another fellow had asked one of the maids to pose in the nude for them in such an alcove, but at the last minute she chickened out. Got to give him “A” for effort though.

        On the way back a Air Force captain stopped his jeep and gave us a ride as far as Kadena. First time on Okinawa an officer has been so considerate.

FEB 17

        More rain, but the worry of rain was for the weekend and not today as there is not much I can do during the week with regard to athletics. In the morning I got a sedan from the motor pool and rode to Naha to visit the American Consul for the express purpose of giving Mr. McLaughlin a copy of my AFFE RyCom approved FEC discharge. Had to wait about 45 minutes, but finally was able to talk to the gentleman, and in turn give him the papers. Upon completing the necessary forms, I took my oath and gave him the necessary $1. He said that it would take approximately 45-60 days before word is received from Washington. I hope it doesn’t take much longer as I am planning hoping to visit Japan at the end of April and would like to have my passport with me in order to get some visas.

        Today I worked on a Finding of Fact which is a change from the estimating that I have been doing up to now. Actually it isn’t too interesting but it does give me an insight into the complicated paper work comprising contracts, – particularly with the Government, U_ use set form, phrases and procedures, consequently the work isn’t very enlightening, in fact quite dull if done over a period of time.

FEB 18

        Saturday morning training – the farce of the Army. Today we had Character Guidance, so we all piled into buses and were taken into to the Sukiran Theater. There we were subjected to the ignorant tirades of a real hick preacher. His message is ludicrous and tends to drive me further from having an outward religion. His analogies are poor, and he talks as if we are all babies. Maybe I am all wet, and the others obtain something from his talk, but I can’t see how. Don’t know whom I think worse – this preacher are or the Young Rabbi. I guess I want to hear wise, broad-minded men or none at all. Ridiculous for someone to say all liquor is bad, etc; for under I am sure few people, even the ministers, actually believe this statement. Moderation seems to me to be the only right course for them to preach, and consequently since orthodox religions are against this, I am against orthodox religions.

        I have to laugh at a couple Filipinos I know in our office. Saturday night they go out, “shack up” all night and morning, take a 2-3 hour breather for church, and then return to their honeys. Just doesn’t make sense.

FEB 19 (SUNDAY - WEEK 61)

        Read in the local newspaper of a benefit Judo match that was to be held in Shimabuku in the afternoon. Four of us decided to go, and we left around 1 PM. We got pretty good seats in the balcony (on mats) and had a good view of the stage. First, the boys – both Americans and Okinawans – did some practiced throws which were somewhat interesting. About 45 minutes of boring speeches followed and we were almost ready to g leave when the matches began.

        The matches consisted of 2 sides and 2 men would engage in combat, and the winner would keep on fighting until he lost. Consequently some of the men would fight 2-3 times in a row, which seemed a disadvantage, for undoubtedly they would become tired. Also, there were no weight classes and thus there were a g couple of matches where 120 pound Okinawans would have to fight 230 pound Americans. Everytime such a fight would come up, the audience, including me, was for the underdog.

        The object of the match was for one of the 2 men to use a clean throw on his opponent and to throw him to the mat. Also, a winner would be declared if one would hold another on the mat for 30 seconds.

        One of our men in the unit participated – Jake – and had to fight a huge 230 pound American. The match was interesting but neither could get a clean throw on the other. Finally the other fellow was on a ½ point advantage.

FEB 20

        Got back the remaining 5 boxes of slides from the processing plant in Hawaii. Got a kick out of looking at them and as a whole they came out pretty good. Sorry that a couple of my Taj Mahals were a little off centered, but I don’t think it will make too much difference. Without a doubt, the Taj Mahal is the most beautiful building that I have ever seen.

        Spent a couple of hours at work preparing letters that I plan to send to Senator Hennings, Jeri Lumsd_n and Lou Washa_er. I plan to ask the Senator about job possibilities in his office; Jeri, how things are at Dow and where I fit in the overall picture; and Lou – his thoughts on Dow, now that he has worked there about 1 ¾ years. Hope to get some of these things cleared up now so that I can devote most of my time later on with respect to my trip.

FEB 21

        More rain – this time it started around noon and lasted all afternoon and part of the evening. Started to work on my new estimate, but had to put it aside and wait for additional references. Spent part of the afternoon at the Dental Clinic, as my filling is still sore and I thought perhaps it had come out or was loose. He told me to rinse my mouth with salt water and if it continued to hurt, to come back later on in the week.

        Have been helping Junko with her Algebra lately in preparation for the entrance exam. I find that I have forgotten many of the basic principles, but once I do a problem or two, much of it comes back to me. Tried to do a calculus problem, but got all fouled up. Sure haven’t made much use of my College math. I think that I have used my higher mathematics only a couple of times over the past couple years. One thing for sure and that is I am certainly glad that I have no need for differential equations. I can still remember that submarine problem that threw me for a loop.

FEB 22                         WASHINGTON’S BIRTHDAY

        Today was Washington’s Birthday, and with it came a 1 day holiday. The weather in the morning was its usual cold self but it became sunny in the afternoon and we played basketball.

        In the evening a bunch of the boys got together and went to the All Club, a teahouse in Naha. We were ushered into a second floor room in which there was nothing but the traditional low table. The floor consisted of tatomis, the traditional doors were sliding panels and the ceiling and majority of the room was wood construction.

        We ordered sake and spent about 3 ½ hours drinking, flirting, shooting the breeze and having a good time. The girls were dressed in kimonos and they sat at our table, pouring our drinks, playing match games and trying to get us interested in them. They alternated; all the time there were some girls coming and going. Some of the girls were cute, but most of them were too made up and weren’t very good looking.

        One of the girls played a samiseri and the other girls sang in the typical high, squeeky, voiced Japanese style. Some of the girls did some Japanese dances and a couple of the more daring boys joined them. As the evening wore on, the sake began to take effect and a progressively “forward” time was had carried on by all. We disappointed them as we said Good-bye and took off for Kue. It was a fine evening.

FEB 23

        Journeyed down to Machinato (South end of the Island) and spent about 2 hours being orientated and shown the work that has to be done to complete the Quartermaster Building, before it is turned over to the Army Post Engineers. Three contractors accompanied the tour and will enter bids as to how much they will charge to complete the job. The estimate has to be completed by next Tuesday so it appears that I have my work cut out for me.

        Once again – organized athletics – or at least an afternoon off. Since it rained most of the afternoon I stayed in the hut doing miscellaneous work. I spent most of the afternoon checking algebra problems that Junko had done. Boy, one surely forgets his formal education in a hurry.

        Took Charlie Terry to the Castle Terrace for a final Sayonara dinner. Had a fine charcoaled broiled steak that sure made me forget our Army mess. Some of the other boys joined our party in the later part of the evening, and we had a fine time “sending” old Charlie on his way.

FEB 24

        Worked all day today – for a change. Again, we had a lot of rain and it appears that it will never cease. If this is the dry season, I hate to think what the rainy season will be like. Today, Terry, Estrich, Cornell and 2 others departed for the US. By the time I leave this post I will have seen almost a complete change-over in the Engineer staff.

        The Army is the same story over and over – make a friend, learn to like and understand him, and then most likely, never see him again. After Basic training – where I met few people I wanted to go out of my way to meet again – I lived through a complete change-over at Leonard Wood’s Training Aid section. Now, the same thing is happening again on Okinawa. I have met many fellows, but probably won’t see but a couple of them again.

        Lets see – at Leonard Wood there was Anderson, Batterton and Hoza. At Pusan, I guess Manse Hall were was the only fellow I really liked. And finally at OKED probably Terry, Chapman and Poole complete the picture, although there are a few others I would like to have a couple of beers with.

        The Army has certainly been an eye-opener. I have met different and unusual people, – people from all walks of life. Some have been educated and others had little formal education. Some were considerate, others loud-mouthed and malicious. Must admit that I believe I have benefited from this experience.

FEB 25

        Worked in the morning in order to finish an estimate that I have completed in a few days. Also, I heard that training was going to be messy today, so I thought this would be a fine time to miss the sloshing away around in the mud.

        The sun came out and in the afternoon and I played a couple games of basketball. Later I joined Chapman and Lichius in a bus ride – hike to a beach north of Kue. We got off the bus at Yamada and walked to a small peninsula nearby. The cliffs were quite steep and somewhat eaten away at the base my continual action of the waves. We walked along the tops of the rocks and took pictures in various positions. The weather was fine, and it was a pleasure to be outside. The breeze came over the seashore and refreshed all those in its path. On the way back we stopped in a small village and took some pictures of some little children. Some of the kids run just at the sight of Americans while others will pose for you, especially if you have candy. I always get a kick out of the “Harlo” that the girls and boys uutter instead of hello. The children are very friendly, unlike the Okinawan Korean kids, however for the latters sake, the Okinawans haven’t had a war in their country recently, like the Korean people have.

FEB 26 (SUNDAY - WEEK 62)

        Luck continued today as it turned out to be a beautiful day. Yesterday I had promised to take Junko on a picnic if the day was nice, so around noon time I went to the mess hall and got a couple box lunches. I also brought along a can of beans that I had purchased in the PX yesterday.

I met Junko at Moon Beach, and we walked aways to a small sandy spot which was somewhat sheltered in case of rain. There wasn't much wood around, so I had to use dry grass for the fire fuel. In good boy scout fashion I attempted to build the fire with no matches but had no success. With the aid of paper I got a blaze going and used it to heat the beans.

The sandwiches were fairly good and consequently we both enjoyed the meal. We spent the afternoon walking along the beach picking up seashells, and even doing a little waiting. Junko pointed out edible stuff – stuff that I think I would rather starve than eat. Around 4 PM we gathered our belongings and returned to Kue.

FEB 27

         Another week  – but at least this is the last week in February. Had some violent storms last night, perhaps the most powerful ones that I have seen or heard since I have been on the Rock. The wind shook the hut so violently that I was awakened and couldn't get back to a restful sleep.

In summarizing the weather on Okinawa, I guess one can say that it has been somewhat pleasant. It never gets too cold nor too hot, although the high humidity accentuates each of the weather types. The last couple of months have been quite wet, however, the 3 or 4 months prior to it were seemingly wonderful.

If there wasn't quite as much rain, I think this climate would be tops, as it eliminates extremes that are common in the US. I believe, after living on Okinawa for about 8 months, that I lean toward toward warmer climate. I found this noticeable in India when I nearly froze many nights, yet didn't mind the heat of Calcutta.

FEB 28

        Completed the estimate that I was working on, and spent the rest of the day reading a pipe fitters book and doing a little personal work. Actually, the office is out of estimating requests so I did not feel too bad about doing the personal work on Army time (Ahem!) I decided to put an ad in the Ryukyuan Review newspaper and see if I can get offers for my LaSalle law books. Later on in week I will see if I can get an announcement over the radio for the sale of my equity in the course. If I can get a decent offer I will sell the books and use the money for my trip this summer.

In the evening I went to the office to type a couple of letters and to type some paragraphs about my slides. Mr. Hands (my boss) was in the office and suggested that we show each other our slide some nights at his house. Couldn't say anything else but "sure, I would be glad to!" so I can see an evening for the (boring) cut out for me sometime in the near future. Also talked to Adams and enjoyed vicariously the trip he just took to Hong Kong.

FEB 29

        Another month – 3 to go and then I will write finis to my Army career ( least I hope it will be so). Had to attend training today as I had missed it on Saturday but I must admit that I really didn’t mind it too much. It lasted only 2 hours and wasn’t like Saturday morning training when we generally kill time in order to spend a minimum of 4 hours in training.

        Today we were supposed to simulate an attack on a hill near the Jaguar Gate. Thirteen of the boys gathered on the top of the hill overlooking Kue where we were supposed to get our “briefing”. At 2:30 we pushed off (amidst rain) and weaved our way through rain soaked shoulder-high grass. At 2:50 we were at the base of the hill and ready for the “final push”. We received the word and all of us would-be soldiers charged through huts and across open areas until we reached the bottom of the final hill.

        By 3 PM we were finished besides being worn out, and took a briefer. Had a good time looking back at our assault and laughing at the way the “_ais_ns” were flushed out of the huts. I had a laugh on myself for when I went to push one door open with the butt of my rifle I slipped and fell on my rump – very un-soldier like.

MAR 01

        My knee was a little sore from the “war games” held yesterday afternoon, which only goes to prove that I am not in very good physical shape. (Soft life). Had the afternoon off – organized athletics, and since it neglected to rain, I was able to complete some things that I had planned. Played some basketball, read and ate dinner early, so that I could spend some time in Naha.

        Did a little shopping around, and finally talked a sales girl into selling me a doll for Carolyn, for 300 yen instead of the 350 yen that she first wanted. Don’t know if she will like it – it is a geisha doll – however she asked for it, and I shall oblige. Still don’t know what to send Morton for his birthday. I hope he answers shortly telling me whether he likes the ivory carving that I sent him.

        Saw the movie, “The Fighting Leathernecks” in Naha and felt a little funny viewing this American-Japanese war movie in an Okinawan movie house. I am sure the Okinawans had mixed feelings on it all, mainly because their culture is still Japanese, whereas the Americans are superimposing a Western materialistic society on their own. Don’t think such movies should be banned, however, they do tend to bring back the war hatred of 1941-45, and make everybody race and color conscious.

MAR 02

        For the past few days I have been getting requests for informed estimates, which appeal to me since they don’t take much time yet they are items accomplished and thus it tends to give an impression that I am doing some work. Today was no exception and I worked on a small estimate for placing additional supporting brackets on the floodlight poles in the motor pool area. After completing the estimate, I went to the Quartermaster, Far Eastern Network (about an ad for selling my Law Course) and to Kadena to renew my membership at the NCO club.

        Back at the office I completed the write up of the finished estimate and was thinking of getting something to do when my former boss Joe Alfonsi came in. We talked about Formosa and how he liked his job. (He isn’t too hot on the job, but the long legged Chinese women are nice!) His belt line is constantly getting longer, so it isn’t too hard physically although he says entertainment isn’t too good, and whats there is crowded. Most of his work presently is with KMAG (the equivalent Formosan version) and soon that is to cease, which will reduce the work load to almost zero.

        He said one can get a good price for American dollars and perhaps I will be able to buy my airplane ticket in Taiwan and not have to bother about Hong Kong and Manila. I figure it would save about ⅓ of the price by getting it in Taiwan. ANyway, it is worth looking into

MAR 03

        Whereas I didn’t think training was bad Wednesday, and actually was a little fun, today’s farce was quite different. The main difference was the stupid RA squad leader that insisted we traverse up the hill via the woods and not through the waist high grass. Consequently, we pushed through the Kue jungle and it was quite an ordeal.

        The briars were everywhere one grabbed and my hands, legs and arms were loaded with briars and scratches. I was constantly getting my legs caught in the livine vines, and stumbling while trying to keep my carbine on my back. In some places the grass was 12 feet high and we were almost hidden from sight as we marched under these grass “archways.” Once we had to slide down an embarkment and only were able to do so by holding on to some vines. Near the end of the fight, we walked over some grass that was matted together so tightly it seemed that we were walking on air.

        The water tank at the top of the hill was a welcome sight and the cool water nearby served as a good cleansing spot for our sore hands. Can’t say that I go for this jungle warfare – either in wartime or peacetime.

MAR 04 (SUNDAY - WEEK 63)

        Very quiet Sunday. It sprinkled a lot around breakfast time, but then ceased completely around 9 AM. The sky remained cloudy, and the wind was strong and cold, so I decided to go to the office. Typed 2 ½ boxes of slide descriptions, plus a couple postcards and a letter to travel bureaus.

        At the office I found this diary plus a January 8th issue of the St. Louis Post Dispatch, so I had a couple things to do in the afternoon. Had a hard time keeping awake, as I felt groggy all afternoon – for what reason I do not know. Ate dinner at the Castle Terrace with some of the boys, but was disappointed in the club steak. The steak wasn’t nearly as good as the one I had a couple weeks ago, but it was still better than the food in the mess hall. Saw Joe Alfonsi at the club and stopped to chat as he proceded to lose many a quarter in the one armed bandits.

        Came back to the hut around 7, and talked to Chapman and Lic_ius for an hour or so – same topics, women, school, Army, and Kue. Decided it was about time to do some thinking on what I plan to do when I get out so I took out some paper and jotted down some pros and cons of various possibilities. Will continue this project in the near future as I would like to examine all facets of job type and what I would like to be or do 20-30 years from now. The more I think of what I want to do, the more confused I get, however, I think and hope things will begin to clear up after a while.

MAR 05

        Maybe the weather – the bad weather, that is, has finally cracked, and Okinawa might get some nice weather for a change. The sun came out in the afternoon and it made everybody wish they could discard the heavy O.D’s which all are still wearing.

Didn’t do much in the evening, nor, for that matter, the whole day. Received the weekly Time magazine in the morning, and finished reading it in the evening. Also began reading Chester Bowles’, “The New Dimensions of Peace,” the author’s latest book. Of the chapters that I have read, I have found them very interesting and well written. Mr. Bowles is one of the most enlightened Americans, particularly in Foreign Affairs. I think he has a fine understanding of people in Asia, and this seems to be a fact, since when in India I found many Indians who thought very highly of him, and wished he were still American ambassador to India. I personally think he would be an ideal Secretary of State.

MAR 06

        Sometimes I kick myself for starting this diary for I find that I have less and less to say. Work continues the same from day to day and even if it weren’t it would be still uninteresting to write about. Also, my living at the same compound where I work does not provide many daily interesting occurrences as there were in Korea. If it weren’t for the leaves I would have given this up long ago. I am sure I will not continue it after I get home.

        One feature of the Army that I have found interesting is the mingling (even though forced) of the men in one unit which is a common basis and the main tie among them. Living at Kue is like living in a college dormitory, with the individual rooms, mess hall, and common job. I think I have learned much of human nature since being in the Army, some good and some bad. Perhaps my biggest disappointment is in the average college graduate that I have come across. Many of them are very narrow, and know only the field that they have studied. Besides that their personalities are just fair.

        Kue is unusual owing to the mixing of the Engineers and the SP’s in one compound. Most, if not all, of the SP’s show me little and I hope they aren’t the backbone of the nation. I do think that this group is perhaps below average, both in initiative and intelligence. Maybe it is me, for there are really few of the Engineers that I think to have much on the ball, and those that I would want to continue to know after I leave the Army. I think it boils down that I am a snob – both intellectually and personality-wise. Sometimes I think this is good, sometimes bad.

MAR 07

        Today was a day of good and bad news. The good news concerned the sale of my Law Books. And had mentioned that Mr. Christian of the Hospital Division was interested, so I journeyed over there in the morning and talked to him about the purchase of my equity in the course. He said he was very much interested, and stopped at the hut at noon to look over the books and pamphets. That night he came again and paid me $100 for the books and my equity in the course. Sooo I am now $100 closer to my trip, although the sale represents a loss of $90 minus the subjects that I have taken.

        The bad news concerned Junko. Today was supposed to be the day she was to take the entrance exam. Around 4:15 I got a phone call from one of the boys and he said Junko wanted to see me back at the hut. I arrived at 722 a few minutes later and found Junko curled up on my bed crying and quite upset. It seems that when she reported to the school in the morning, she found that her name wasn’t on the list and thus not able to take the test. She said that her transcripts never arrived from her high school in Miyako and thus her application wasn’t complete.
