Caught the local to the Ueno Station where I had about 2 hours to kill before the train was to leave.

        I packed my bags near a post and stood for about 1 ½ hours observing the people, their mannerisms, dress and habits. The time passed quite rapidly and I enjoyed the time spent watching the people hurrying by. Of those I saw, I saw very few attractive girls, and but perhaps better looking men than one sees on Okinawa. Almost all the people were wearing Western style clothing, although occasionally one would see some older women in kimonos. The people were hurrying to and fro as in the big cities of the US, and few even took a second glance at me.

        The children were cute, with their long stockings and colorful clothes. The grownups as a rule wear darker colors, with little design work. The clothes on the whole are not fitted very well, particularly the footwear. All in all, I enjoyed the 2 hours, and the subsequent 2 ½ hours on the train to Nikko.  

        Arrived in Nikko about 3:15 PM and took a bus to the Hotel. The hotel is located near Yumoto and the bus has to go up a mountain to get to it. The ride is quite spectacular as it involves overcoming 32 sharp, steep curves to get to Chuzenji. From here it is a level ride to the hotel, which is located on Lake Chuzenji. Met Jerry Turnquiest (Branch 600_ at the Nikko Kanko Hotel  and had a fine time talking over old times with him.

MAY 07

        Sure froze last night. When I got in bed I kicked aside 2 of the four blankets for I couldn’t believe it got cold enough to use that many blankets. In the middle of the night I found out soon enough for the temperature dropped quite low for this time of year, and I was too sleepy to get the other blankets. Thus I froze.

        Said goodbye to Jerry after breakfast and told him to stop in St. Louis sometime and say hello. I took the Army bus to a spot nearby where a cable car went to the top of a mountain peak. From here one could see for miles and in particular, it afforded a great view of Lake Chuzenji and Kegon Falls. I looked at the falls through a high powered telescope and it brought the foaming spray almost in my grasp.

        I then took take the cable car down the mountain and thence a street car to Nikko Park. I spent about 2 hours wandering around the grounds and looking at the various temples and gates. The wood work was excellent and the coloring quite brilliant, but still I was somewhat disappointed. The buildings are the same that I have seen all over Japan and consequently do not strike me like they did at the beginning. I was impressed with the magnificant old and large trees which were in abundance. The trees furnished a most beautiful setting for the various buildings. It is also interesting to notice the thousands of school children who visit this and other shrines throughout Japan. It is a great way for them to learn and love their country and its heritage.

        Took the noon train back to Tokyo where I decided to remain instead of going on to Hakone. I checked back in the Hardy Barracks (economy reasons) and got cleaned up. In the evening I went to see “the Rose tatoo” (great) plus walking on the Ginza and Z avenues. Stopped in one of the fine Tea Shops for tea and passed the rest of the time listening to the music – Great City!

MAY 08

        I decided that I would spend my time shopping, so I got up relatively early and visited the Imperial Hotel Arcades. Didn’t find much here, but since it was too early for the PX, I visited an interesting industrial show in Hibiya Park The show was similar to equipment shows in the US, and contained many of the products of present-day industrial Japan.

        Took the Army bus back to Hardy Barracks and ate lunch at the mess hall. (Really tight with my money this trip). Near the mess hall is the Tokyo PX so I didn’t have to walk very far to spend the money I have saved. Bought some perfume, film, flash attachment and priced some other articles. Didn’t have any raw silk or ivory carvings so I adjourned to metropolitan Tokyo to see what I could find. Walked up and down 10th, Z, and the Ginza and only bought a couple wood block prints. Did visit an ivory shop but didn’t have enough ¥ with me to buy anything.

        From here I took a street car to the Tokyo Sub-Office of OKED where I met Ed Campbell whom I had known at Kue before he went to Tokyo. We talked about things in common, and then he drove me back to Hardy Barracks where H he also lived. In the evening we visited another tea house which is as great as the one I visited the night before. This place was in Chinese furnishing and had three floors serviced by Japanese girls in slit skirts. The great feature was the band stand which was on a track and went up and down like an elevator, playing a few minutes at each of the floors. Unusual to say the least.

        Next we visited a small bar which is frequented almost entirely by Japanese men (no Americans to spoil it.) We sat here for about 2 hours conversing with the bartender, mamasan, hostesses and customers. All in all it was another good day.

MAY 09

        I had heard so much concerning difficulty getting a hop back to the Rock – and since I didn’t want to pay my way – I decided to wind up my shopping and take the 7:45 PM bus to Tachikawa. Thus, I checked out of Hardy Barracks in the morning and headed for the Nikkatsu Arcade to price some ivory. On the way I passed the Sanshin Building and decided to stop and visit the Dow Chemical Office for a few minutes.

        The few minutes turned out to be 2 ½ hours as I met a fine young man – assistant manager – who was as friendly as I could ever imagine. We talked about everything – from Dow to Madison to Japan to living in the Far East and even working in the Far East. I really enjoyed the talk for I am interested in perhaps a job such as he has, and the various difficulties and advantages that go with it. He spoke of the young organization that Dow has in the International Field and likewise the bright future that lies ahead. I will have to look into this when I get back to the USA.

        Spent a great part of the afternoon buying 4 ivory statues that I thought to be quite nice. Did a lot of bargaining – over few dollars – but enjoyed the hassle with the sales people. Bought one warrior that I think to be exceptionally nice. Also, stood on street corners taking pictures but I am a little too much embarrassed to be very daring so as to get good shots.

        Then ah yes – I spent an hour at the Tokyo Onsen. Paid my 800 ¥ and had some josan give me a bath, steam cabinet treatment plus a massage. I was a little embarrassed but she wasn’t so I soon forgot my inhibitions. Actually the bath and steam cabinet weren’t too good, but the massage was fine. Particularly liked it when she walked up and down my back. Hate to leave the Orient, for it does offer things one can’t get anywhere else.

MAY 10

        Up at the awful hour of 4:30. Went to the Operations Terminal and checked in at 5:30. We boarded the C-124 at 7:30, but didn’t take off until 8:30 as we had to add additional fuel. The trip took a long 5 ½ hours, and the time passed slowly as we were crowded and there wasn’t any leg room to stretch out. The plane is enormous and must hold about 120 men plus a lot of freight. Incidentally the runways of Tachikawa were loaded with these planes, – I imagine there must have been 20-30 of them.

        Adjacent to my seat on the plane was a Marine Doctor by the name of Mel Post who had gone to Washington University undergraduate work school before getting his PHD at Chicago. He knew Don Kramer and some of the other 47-49 ers and so we had a pleasant chat. The chat developed into a rather heated discussion – at least on his part – when I asked him whether he thought doctors were more materially inclined than before. He issued forth a loud and long tirade about the medical profession, how much the public misunderstands, malpractice, clinics, salaries etc. Actually, I was a little embarrassed, but since he continued for an hour or so, I threw in a couple thoughts and questions whenever I could.

        My conclusion to the talk is that he is a little bitter about the long education and training and lack of salary during this time. (sure seems that most Jewish doctors that I know feel the same way.) Also, he is quite defensive of his profession and tends to blame most of the misunderstanding on the public who wants but does not wish to pay for good health. In a sense I agree with him but feel that the AMA has not done the selling job it could.

MAY 11

        Somewhat of an anti-climax, but each day that passes is one less in the Army. I went to work in the morning but didn’t do anything as there is a lull in the work backlog at this time. So, I spent the time on personal matters, such as haircut, checking at AG and Recruiting concerning my discharge, and talking to Northwest concerning the flight. I am interested in getting a through flight to Hong Kong so I don’t have to get a visa, but the man says that this may not be possible. If I have to get a visa it will mean an extra 4-5 days on the Rock – something I am not looking forward to. Will have to wait and see what he finds out from the Northwest office in Taipei.

        It rained all day and made things quite miserable. From what the guys say, it was great for a couple of days before I came back, but it will be just my luck to be gone while the sun was here, and then to come back for a lot of rain. Didn’t do much in the evening, – saw a really lousy movie, read my Time magazine, and then fell asleep during a “reading break.” Awoke later in the night, a cold and “lost” man.

MAY 12

        My next to last training class wasn’t too bad, as there weren’t many people present so class was dismissed at 9:00. It was raining so I returned to the hut where I dissipated the rest of the day. I don’t know why, but I sure find myself not interested in doing much except passing the time. I guess I have those short term jitters.

        In the evening I went to the Mercy Area where I saw a pretty good movie, “The View from Pompey’s Head.” It is a relief to see a good movie every now and then, for we have our share of lousy pictures on the Rock.

        I went to the PX in the afternoon and priced a “B-4” bag, and I think I will buy it for the trip. It isn’t very good looking – and I might not use it very much when I get home – still it is roomy, light and convenient. I might have a little difficulty with it if I did much hiking or I cycling in Europe, but I will have to worry about that when I get there. Actually, probably the B-4 bag will hold everything, however, I will take my AWOL bag with me for carrying stuff on side trips or guide books, etc. And so my time shortens – 

MAY 13 (SUNDAY - WEEK 73)

        I feel a little guilty about only sending Mom a card, but it seemed silly to buy expensive flowers, or to get something that she wouldn’t need. I will go to the PX and/or Bembo in the next few days and see if I can’t find anything nice for her.

        Took some pictures in Naha in the morning and completed my last roll of film on the Rock. Tried out my new pocket flash attachment and it seems to work o.k. So I guess the $380 wasn’t wasted. I don’t think I will buy any more film, and wait till Europe to replenish my stock; for Okinawa’s prices are too great. Maybe I will ask Lichius to check in Hong Kong for me.

        Again I dissapated the morning and afternoon as I was quite tired from the previous night. However, I finally settled down after dinner and did a little work on my trip. Later I went to the Castle Terrace for a sandwich and beer.

MAY 14

        The weather turned nice and I hope that it will stay this way until I leave the Rock. Started the day off by not doing much, but I was surprised to receive two small estimate requests about 10:30. I spent the rest of the day working on them, and completed them by the end of the day.

        I am sure getting listless lately and I find it more and more difficult to get much done. I came back to the hut after supper and found Junko there sewing cuffs on the khaki pants that I plan to take. After she finished I helped her with some typing homework that she had. Next I took a shower and sat down at the desk to read some more from the travel books that I have collected. However, In saxophone music – and a poor quality at that – blared forth from a nearby hut and I couldn’t do much concentrating.

        Sooo – I went outside and sad and talked to Ted Sjoberg (leaves Wednesday) and a couple of the other boys. We shot the breeze for an hour or so, and also talked to a fellow stationed in Korea about life up there. We were shaken to the core when he said that if he had 6 more months in Korea that he would probably have married his “moose”. (Even though one day he caught another guy sleeping with the wench.) I guess there are many young fellows who have not experienced such devotion and sex life before and consequently forget about anything else. Maybe there are a few Orientals that can speak and understand English well enough to provide varied conversations. For the others, when the physical attraction wears off, – then what?

MAY 15

        Not much new today. Did some personal work at the office, checked an estimate for O’Campo, and just passed time. Received some bad news from Northwest Airlines, as they said that I wouldn’t be able to exchange my airplane ticket for a through ticket; consequently it appears that I will have to get a visa for Taipei. This, of course, emans 4-5 extra days on the Rock, but there isn’t much that I can do. Called the COnsulate again, and this time talked to the Consul, – but still no soap about getting my passport until after I get out of the Army.

        Went to the Kadena Rocker Four Club in the evening after taking in a movie on Kadena Base, but I really didn’t care for the club very much. It was too crowded and noisy for my money, so I shall by-pass it from now on, which won’t be much of a struggle these last 15-20 days!

MAY 16

        Actually I don’t know why I told Adams yesterday that I would go fishing with him this morning, but I did; consequently I was awakened around 4:15 AM. Having nothing more than slits for eyes, I stumbled out of the hut, told Sjoberg good-bye and climbed into the ¾ T truck. There were six other fellows in the truck and all were as tired as I, but curious about “this deep-sea fishing” routine.

        Adams had called Special Service on Monday and thus signed for the morning cruise on a chartered cabin cruiser which took groups of soldiers out for 7 hour fishing trips. The boat was quite nice and we were relatively secure going during the 15-20 mile journey each way to the fishing areas. We trolled to and from the spot, but didn’t get nary a nibble. Around 9 AM we dropped anchor and poles and bait were issued to everyone to try their luck and I guess skill.

        For two horus I waited, re-wound, placed new bait on the hook, tangled my line, etc, but didn’t get even a bite. A couple of the fellows got fish, one guy catching 2 pretty good size fish. One was an unusual fish with speckled coloring and 4 or 5 good size teeth at the front of his mouth.

        We returned to Naha Port around noon and headed for the highway so as to catch a bus back to Kue. On the way we passed a schooner anchored at the basin, and we stopped a few minutes to gaze for this ship had just crossed the Pacific. We were overwhelmed because it was so small and seemed actually puny, but the shipper asked us below and we found quite a nice set up under-neath the water line. We then continued on to Kue and the routine of Army life.

MAY 17

        Completed my last estimate and did some personal work at the office. Went to the Jacona mooring site and watched, along with Willie Yu, a welding demonstration. He had said that it takes 1 pound of rod for ¾ ‘ of weld. I said that he should be able to get 4 feet per pound. The test showed 2’ and we both agree that we would let the inspector decide if the welding was adequate.

        Since I had the jeeps, I decided to take a ride to Awase and talk to the CAT people about exchanging my ticket for a through ticket to Hong Kong. I was amazed when the fellow said that it could be done. He then figured out the difference in cost – $25 – and after I paid the amount I received my ticket which entitles me to leave the rock on the 1st of June. I guess I am a little pessimistic, for the ticket still has to be endorsed by Northwest and I am afraid that they might balk. Guess I will just have to wait and see.

        Went to Naha in the afternoon and bought a blue B-4 bag. The price – $12.25 – isn’t too bad and I think it will be sufficient to hold all my junk. Getting short!

MAY 18

        Last day of work – great feeling. It’s been a long wait, but the big day has finally arrived. Now, the next big days are May 30th (my last in the Army) and June 1st (the day when I leave the Rock). I didn’t do much at work today, mainly completing a few odds and ends. I cleaned out my desk and checked in all the odds and ends equipment that I had been assigned.

        At lunch time I received a rude shock, – the 1st Sgt accompanied by Copeland and King as onlookers informed me that I would have to move to hut 714 after lunch so that Sgt Morris can begin spicing up his hut 2 rooms. I thought it was a big joke and told Veometh so, but I he was adamant and said that he would give me help to get moved. I still couldn’t believe it, especially since I have only 2 weeks more, but Veometh showed me his true colors and said “Best get started, now.” I laughed the whole time I moved the junk, but must admit that when I came to my sense later on, I will missed the conveniences of Hut 722.

        Got to work at 2:30 and joked about my moving. Mrs Kirk gave me an envelope and when I opened it I found a “Good-bye” card plus $32 and 400 ¥ from the people in the office. It was really too much, and I was overwhelmed at the kindness of the 24 people who chipped in. I went around to all of them and thanked them for their best wishes.

        Took Junko her sister-in-law and 2 year old niece to the movies at Naha in the evening. One of the features was a talent show plus some singing by some of Japan’s top singers. I can’t say that I thoroughly enjoyed the show but Junko and her sister-in-law seemed to have a good time.

MAY 19                ARMED FORCES DAY

        Looking back to yesterday’s page in the diary, I didn’t realize how many mistakes I made. Guess I was just too excited about it being my last day of work. From now until – say November – I will be on the longest actual vacation thus far in my life; that is, unless one wants to count the 2 years in the Army.

        Today being Armed Forces Day, we had a holiday, and I didn’t do much of anything. I read a little, played some basketball, had my picture taking for some passport and visa photos, and in general, dissipated the day. My new hut is much nosier than the other, and I doubt if I will be able to do any sleeping in the morning.

MAY 20 (SUNDAY - WEEK 74)

        I had promised Junko that I would take her swimming and so we arrived at Moon Beach around 10 AM. It wasn’t a very sunny day, but she said that she still wanted to go so we both changed into our swim suits. I tested the water and it was quite cold, so we decided to wait and hope that the sun comes out. About this time it began to rain and so we retreated to an overhanging ledge for shelter.

        Junko spotted a plant high up on a cliff and said that she was going to get it. She climbed over the jagged coral rocks and returned in a couple minutes with 2 small plants with 6-8 inch stalks. I couldn’t figure out what she was going to do with them and thus watched as she patiently removed the outer covering and then peeled off a thin layer of membrane. She wetted the stalk and then rolled off a translucent membrane, which when tied at one end, could be blown up. I had to laugh at her Miyako-trained “genius” and soon found myself climbing over sharp rocks to get the plants. In this manner we killed about an hours wait while it rained.

        The sun peeped out and we both scampered into the water to enjoy the sun. After splashing around for an hour or so, I tired and we both adjourned to the beach. We dried ourself ourselves and then caught the bus for our respective homes. A fine time was had by both of us, and perhaps we will do it once more before I leave this Rock for other parts of the world

MAY 21

        I reported in to the Military Personnel section in the morning and received my clearing papers. Began to get the initials that I need from the various sections, and also picked up the passport pictures I had made.

        Had some questions concerning my orders, shipping of my footlocker, authority to leave the Rock, etc; consequently I went to Recruiting to get the answers. I was told that I could probably get my orders in a couple of days, and also that I would have to pay to ship my footlocker home. Concerning the authority to leave, and even to remain on the island until I get my passport & visa, Recruiting couldn’t answer. We called Immigration and when the situation to the USCAR Immigration officer was explained, he got all excited. He said that this was the first case that of this kind that he had heard of, and said he would call back at the end of the afternoon. I went to the Library to wait, and around 4 PM returned to Recruiting. Mr. Brown called and said that I would have to write a letter addressed to the Deputy Governor and ask permission to stay on Okinawa for a few days. – More blasted technicalities and paperwork, but there is nothing I can do.

        Went I Went to the Castle Terrace in the evening and introduced some of the new fellows to “our” club. Most of the boys seem pretty decent and I sort of wish they had been here while I was here. And so I drowned my sorrows.

MAY 22

        Spent the day doing 2 things – taking my separation physical exam in the afternoon, and hand carrying the necessary letter to Mr. Brown at the Immigration Office. Concerning the former, the physical took about 2 ½ hours and was a fairly thorough check. I guess the Army wants to find out exactly your state of health when you get out of the Army; however, the incoming physical was not nearly as complete.

        Had to get Captain Hatcher, Major Mayer and Rycom to approve the letter, and then go to USCAR to give it to Mr. Brown. How people can be so shook over little problems such as this is beyond me. One really wonders about the civil servants of our great country when they get upset over any irregularities, no matter how small.

MAY 23

        One week to go – this morning I showed one of the new Engineers where RTS-RCA was located and also took him with me when I went to the Plaza House area. I we stopped in at the CAT office and had an hour and one-half talk with the gentleman there and Mr. Devantier of Northwest Airlines.

        We discussed every angle and phase of my problem and how I can get off this Island and satisfy all concerned. Naturally, I don’t want to have to wait for my visa and would like to go straight through to Hong Kong. Northwest wants me to originate in taipei so they can get their remittance in dollars. CAT just wanted me to return the ticket they had sold me last Thursday.

        The meeting finally broke up around 11 and Mr. Devantier was to write a letter to the Taipei office and see if I couldn’t come down on Friday and switch planes in Taipei so that I could be on the Northwest manifest as originating from there. If that won’t work perhaps I can buy a through ticket and get a refund of my $70 ticket from Taipei to Hong Kong. Anyway things look a little better for me, as Mr D_vantier thinks the best thing is to forget about the dollar remittance and chalk it up to “lessons learned.” I really don’t want to cause any trouble, however, I don’t relish the idea of waiting 4-5 additional days and still not be sure of leaving at the end of that time. Anyway, I will have to wait a little longer.

        Played some tennis in the afternoon and found myself to be back where I was before I came. My backhand is getting worse, and I regret I didn’t concentrate more on my game while I was here.

MAY 24

        Didn’t do much today. Got my clearance papers initiated and turned them into Personnel. Consequently I have finished most of the preliminary work and all I have to do now is wait.

        Went to see Herzik, Chief of Engineering, concerning a job for Junko and I think things might develop. She went back in the afternoon and took some typing and English tests and apparently passed, so now all we have to do is hope there is a vacancy. She is to return at 10 AM tomorrow for some additional interviews.

        Packed my footlocker in the morning and mailed same in the afternoon. Hated to spend the money, but the Army refuses to send the box home for me. Also packed some of my books and will mail them tomorrow when I got to the Hospital.

        Had dinner at the Castle Terrace with my former boss – George Sauer – and had an interesting time talking about my proposed trip. He gave me some good pointers on what to see and how to travel. He along with many others have been mighty helpful in planning my trip.

MAY 25

        I thought that I would be able to get some time off during my processing, but it appears that there are too many little things to take care of. I stopped by Military Personnel and found that I had to pick up my IT&E card, plus stopping by Rycom to get information about insurance.

        Around noon I went to the hospital where I had a small cavity filled along with having some X-Rays taken. Mailed my packages of books and then waited to see Colonel Rice concerning my scalp and face. He gave me some more medicine and wished me bon voyage on my forth coming trip.

        At dinner I talked to Oscar and he said that his office had OKEYED a position for Junko in the Engineering Division and so it appears that she finally has secured a job. Needless to say I am quite please. When I returned to the hut Junko was waiting for me, and was extremely happy about the job. She said that she is to report to work on Monday morning and so unless something goes wrong, little Junko will graduate from the maid status to that of an office worker.

        Didn’t do much in the evening. Cleared up some things concerning my trip. Also spent an hour and ½ at the Terrace, watching TV and talking to Bill Bonner.

MAY 26

        Dashed down to Mercy Hospital and picked up some scalp lotion and my x-rays that were taken yesterday. Back at Kue I messed around with odds and ends and tried to get myself set up a little better for the forthcoming trip.

        In the afternoon I played a little tennis and took it easy. (The trip is sure going to shake me out of the routine I am presently in. Also, will have to be a little careful at first so as not to over-exert myself.) The Los Angeles Symphony played at the Sukiran Field House in the evening and I went to hear them play Bhr Brahms (sp?) 1st Symphony in C minor plus 4 other selections. Although the acoustics weren’t too good, the concert was quite good and applauded with enthusiasm by the 7000-8000 persons who attended.

        Had an interesting experience later on in the evening. Five of us went to the Castle Terrace where we had a sandwich and drink. Then some decided to go to Jagaru and soon a party of 13 was formed which headed for our neighboring villa in 3 taxis. We descended on one of the geisha houses were we all plopped on the floor. Only one naisan came out to entertain “the boys” so same decided to go across the street for more girls. The rest of us stayed, and were entertained by 1-3 girls, who drank with us, teased and completed frustrated me. The atmosphere was quite casual and everybody let themselves go and had a fine time. Around 3 AM we gathered in the streets, hailed 3 more taxis and headed for Kue – without the girls. Lucky no M.P’s frequent Jagaru or our “rear ends” would be hurting on Monday.

MAY 27 (SUNDAY - WEEK 75)

        Since I didn’t get to bed until after 3 last night – or early this morning – I slept most of Sunday morning, finally getting out of bed at 10:30. Ate chow and then got my gear together for an afternoon at the beach.

        About 8 of us went by bus Ishikawa beach, the best beach on the island. The only trouble with it (besides the hour ride to and from the beach_ is that the water is mucky and unclear, with many sand particles suspended in the water. The beach is huge and is divided into an EM and Officers section. There is a lot of sand on the beach, and the bottom is sand all the way to the buoy. The water isn’t too deep most of the way to the buoy, although there are areas where the area water is about 6 feet deep.

        Besides swimming, there are other facilities such as prams (small, square boats), volleyball, restrooms and showers., and eating and beer joints. The sun didn’t come out, but most of us had a fine time. The distance to and from the beach makes it a little inconvenient, and probably I prefer moon beach or one of the swimming pools.

MAY 28

        Another day of nothing doing very little. Checked on a couple things at us Military Personnel and Finance, and I am hoping that I do not have any trouble concerning the latter office. We have a wise-ass corporal in Finance and he gives the EM more trouble than any 5 officers. All I can say that if I am not paid by Thursday I shall go all the way to Colonel Finley and see if something can’t be done so that I can leave the island Friday.

        Played some lousy tennis in the afternoon and figure it is about time to lay down my racket for awhile and take up another sport. Back in the company area I was told to call Sgt. Benson at Recruiting, and to give him some answers about my Army career. Upon completing that I caught the bus for Naha where I saw the movie “Daddy Long Legs.” Both Fred Astaire and Leslie Caron were quite good and I enjoyed the movie very much.

MAY 29

        Time is passing somewhat slow. Didn’t do much in the morning, sort of stayed in or around my hut trying to keep out of trouble. Talked to Junko in the morning concerning her new job in the Engineering Division. At the present time she is processing and will probably begin work on the 1st of June. If nothing goes wrong, she will begin work at the same time that I leave – couldn’t have been timed more perfectly. I am sure grateful to Mr. Herzik for giving her the job, and I believe that she will do a creditable job.

        Went to recruiting in the afternoon and completed my processing. They gave me my separation papers a day early and upon presentation of these papers Thursday I will receive my final pay. – Getting close – Called Northwest and still no word concerning my flight. I am pretty sure that I will leave on Friday, but I wish things were more definite.

        Took Junko to the movies in the evening and we saw a pretty fair picture – “Meet me in Las Vegas.” I guess she is a little sorry to see me go, but the prospect of the new job is compensating and her spirits are pretty high. I don’t know if I have helped her (Yes, with respect to the job and typing school) by all my “so called lectures;” or if I have hurt her by taking her to movies and occasionally dancing, for once I leave I doubt if she will do much of the latter. Her sister-in-law living with her will help to pass the evenings and with the new job I think she will readjust quite rapidly. I have enjoyed her friendship and hope to continue same via letters, for I feel that she is a better than average person.

MAY 30

        Todays the day! After 2 long years in the Army, my Army career is finally coming to a close. (At least I hope it is finalizing). Didn’t feel much different, but the civilian attraction is rapidly approaching and no longer will I be bothered by 1st Sergeants.

        Didn’t do much during the day, except unload some of my belongings. Sold my chair and fan, and in the process of selling my lamp and radio. Am a little undecided about the radio for I thought I might give it to Junko, but I gave her a lot of my clothes and stuff, and I really don’t want to overwhelm her.

        Went to the Castle Terrace in the evening for the last time. Have spent many enjoyable evenings at the Club and in many ways it has been a life saver. Sort of wish one could dance with club sponsored girls, but such a practice was not done at our “high brow” club. Had my typical egg salad sandwich garlic bread, beer and coffee and listened to old man Cowan speak Sayonara.

        Back to Kue, Hut 716 (my new home the last 2 weeks) and to bed – the last time as a soldier!

Route as of May 31st, 1956 – end of Chapter 12.

CHAPTER 13 - SAYONARA, OKINAWA

May 31st, 1956 - July 7th, 1956

MAY 31

        My next to last day, and it was a busy one. I was extremely lucky to get a ride to the American Consul to pick up my passport. (Finally) at OKED I got paid – in checks – and had a long argument with a Finance officer about not getting US dollars. Fortunately I was able to get traveller’s checks so it isn’t too bad. Spent a little time at Kue saying good bye and packing my clothes.

        No word from Taipei, and so Northwest and I didn’t know what to do. Decided to wait until tonight and see if any cables come in, and if not I would fly direct to HK in the morning and cash in my $70 Taipei-HK ticket. At 9:30 PM I got a phone call and I was to buy a $32 OKI - Taipei ticket at the Airport in the morning. So, this was all set.

        Saw Junko in the evening and said good-bye. I guess I didn’t think I would feel bad in leaving her, but for I was wrong. Sort of felt a twang as I walked away from her, as most likely I will never see her again in my life. Oh well, not much else can be done.

        Went to the Terrace – again – and was treated to champagne. Perhaps drank too much, but this time was surely to be my last with “the boys.” Back to Hut 714 and finally to sleep.

JUN 01                SAYONARA OKINAWA

        I had a rough time opening my eyes at 3:30 AM. Stumbled around the room, gathered my things together and walked to the police station. Sgt. Mack was kind enough to furnish a ¾ jeep in which I and my baggage could be transported to the Naha Commercial Airport.

        The Northwest plane was 15 minutes late but made up the time on our flight to Taipei. At Taipei I dashed to immigration, presented my problem to the Immigration officers and Northwest officials, and was fortunate in being allowed to leave immediately. I rode the same plane to Hong Kong and landed at 11:30 AM. Took the Airport bus to the BOAC office and got a shock when the lady said that my reservation had been cancelled by CAT. Consequently, I am not sure if I will be able to leave until Monday.

        Decided to get some visas while I had time – I also was required to get a Hong Kong visa as I would be here more than the allowed 48 hour transient privilege. At the Hong Kong Police building I got my Hong Kong, Pakistan and Ceylon visas. Also went to the Indian High Commissioner and filled out the forms for that visa. So it appears that the visa problem won’t be too difficult, although I might have some trouble in the Middle East.

        Came back to the Y and took a shower – they only allow showers 2 ½ hours a day because of a water shortage. Meant to eat supper but when I laid down to “rest” I fell asleep and slept until 11 PM. Dressed and went to the Princess Ballroom where I ordered shrimp and fried noodles. Didn’t enjoy the food very much, although enjoyed drinking and dancing.

        Good to be away from the Army routine, and on my own again. Can’t say that I miss Okinawa very much, although I did have a good time there, plus Junko’s friendship and schooling problems helped pass the time.

JUN 02

        Today was about the same as yesterday – at least weatherwise. It rained for a few minutes, then was cloudy, and the rest of the time the sun shone brightly. I got up early, and had a lousy breakfast at the Y. Went to the Peninsula and found that I would be able to get on their flight bound for Singapore at 3 PM. Consequently I headed for the Hong Kong side to get my passport and I hoped my Indian visa. Had to wait a while, but finally received the visa. Thus I now have visas up to and including Pakistan.

        I spent about an hour walking around Hong Kong and inquiring at the money exchanges as to the exchange rates on rupees, malayan dollars and other currency. Bought $20 worth of straits dollars, but decided to hold up on the other currency, as I didn’t know whether I would go to Ceylon or not, and there wasn’t much savings on Indian rupees.

        Hong Kong is much the same as I remembered it from my visit of a year ago. Much construction is going on and I see the completion of buildings in the process of being built a year ago. The transportation is great and law and order seem to be prevalent throughout. Water is scarce and one can only take a bath during a 2 ½ hour period at night. Recent rains have helped alleviate the critical shortage.

        The Chinese, not the British, give the flavor to Hong Kong, and it is a bewitching feeling to experience. The slit skirts are the greatest and makes beauties out of ugly wenches. The people are industrious and forced to work hard as the city is terribly overcrowded. Saw more women dressed in the pajama dress, but I resume it to be their working clothes.

        Met some interesting people on the flight. One chap Australian had just spent 30 days in China and was somewhat of a queer duck. Sat next to an American who had finished a construction job in Korea and was on his way home.

JUN 03 (SUNDAY - WEEK 76)

        Slept a little late as I didn’t get to bed until 2:30 AM. Took a shower and walked through Chinatown to the Raffles Hotel. On the way I stopped at the Raffles Museum which has many old ethnological exhibits of the Malayan people. Some of the objects were quite interesting and things one doesn’t see in museums back in the states – such as animals, fish, etc of this area.

        Met Mr. Shellan (man who sat next to me on the plane) and we walked around the city together. The city is quite modern and there is a great deal of construction going on. There were quite a few boats and ships in the harbor although the HK and Yokohama harbors appear larger. Most of the people appear to be Chinese or of Chinese discent, but they tell me the language is Malayan. I have never seen such a cosmopolitan town, with Chinese, Malayan, Indian and English all in the same melting pot. In the evening I passed a Catholic Church and was amazed at the mixture of people inside. Astonishing to see Indians, dressed in saris, cross themselves.

        We went to the top of the Cathay Hotel where we got a fine view of the city. In one direction was the downtown area where we had just come from, and away from it was the Government House with its pretty lawns, and the Botanical Gardens. I visited the latter place, but didn’t see much except people feeding monkeys and people dressed in varied native dress. The heat and strain on my feet began to tell so I headed back to the hotel.

        Had a fine dinner at the Adelphi Grill and then went for a walk down some of the streets. (ACtually a little scared because of the tension that is mounting in this town composed of 80% Chinese and 50% youths under 21 years of age.) Passed a Chinese theater and decided to see the movie, which had English sub-titles. The picture was a Chinese fairytale and somewhat interesting. The Chinese seem to sing a lot, and use a lot of percussion instruments in their shows. The place was jammed and the people seemed to enjoy the film very much. Sure different from most of the American films that get overseas.

JUN 04

        Checked in with BOAC in the morning and found that my reservation for Tuesday’s flight had been confirmed. Not much to see in Singapore so I decided to go to Johore. Took a bus to this – the Southern most Malay State – and enjoyed the scenery as we rode across Singapore Island, the causeway and into Johore. Sections along the highway were almost like jungles, with many trees and thick underbrush. Other parts of the countryside were composed of modern houses, schools and factories and made one think of a highway scene back home.

        Johore isn’t a very big town, nor is it much different from the other sections of Singapore. The people are quite cosmopolitan, although it appears that there is a greater percentage of Malayans. An information office got in touch with a rubber estate, and I asked the manager if I could come out and have a look around. He said “Yes” so I caught a bus and rode the 11 miles or so to the estate. The manager was a Dutch fellow (Malaya – American Rubber Co.) and was quite pleasant and hospitable.

        He had his driver drive us around the 2500 acre holding and we stopped a various places so that he could point out different points about the rubber process. He said it takes about 6 years for the tire to mature, and after that would produce dry latex for 20-40 years depending upon the point of diminishing return. The majority of the estate has been replanted, but there were a couple acres where they had mature trees and where he could show me how they collect the latex.

        With his knife he cut the tree and I was amazed to see latex come out and flow down the cut to a small cup. The latex is then collected every other day (or at least the tree is tapped then) and the latex collect brought to a control tank for transportation to a factory. They pay the men M#3.05 a day which isn’t much, but and he said that the Union is presently asking for M$6 a day. Such a wage would surely equalize the price of rubber of synthetic rubber and perhaps price natural rubber out of the market.

        I noticed that he carried a 38 pistol with him and he said all Europeans do as protection against terrorists. Lately the situation has been pretty good and the British seem to have the Communists on the run. However, one has to be safe, for instance, only last week they found a bandit camp only 3 miles from the estate.

        The situation in Singapore isn’t very good, though, as the population is 80% Chinese and 50% of the people are under 21. Recent talks with England broke down, and some are afraid that there might be trouble ahead. Today they changed chief ministers, and time will only tell what will happen.

JUN 05

        The plane left for Colombo at 7:30 and we had a pleasant trip there. Passed over some interesting land, some of it appearing to be impenetrable jungle. Lake Toba was bright blue and quite beautiful and I guess this will be as close to Indonesia as I will come during this trip. We landed at Colombo about 1 PM Colombo time, and spent an hour going through customs. Finally we were done and we got in a bus which took us to the city.

        On the way in – actually near my hotel – I noticed a large gathering of people around some Government Buildings. The driver said that these were Sinhalese people and that they were agitating for a passage of a “Sinhalese Only” law which had just been introduced in Parliament. About 80% of the Ceylonese people are Sinhalese and they want their language to be the one which replaces English as the official tongue. The Tamil minority (about 15%) want their language to be on an equal level, and consequently in the morning about 200 of them gathered outside Parliament in a peaceful satyagrahi.

        This aroused the Sinhalese and thousands came looking for a fight. (All Tamilese had closed shop anticipating trouble). Minor fights broke out and the police had all they could do to keep order. A couple men were beaten up, some thrown in the lake and others stoned. When I got there – about 3:30 the crowd was milling about, and everyone felt the tense atmosphere. The police had tear gas, water hoses and rock shields ready for any action that developed. One fellow got blood on his arm and he went around waving the arm and trying to stir up trouble. It was something to see how the people followed this man and cheered him on. The crowd appeared to be composed of low intelligence Sinhalese as English speaking ones near me condemned such actions.

On occasions a portion of the huge mob would run a certain way, and like frightened animals everyone would run in that direction to see what was what. No more action took place and the mob dispersed about sun down, primarily since the bill will be in Parliament a couple more days. It was quite an experience to witness this mob action today.

JUN 06

        Got up early and took the train to Kandy, the old Capitol located 70 miles from Colombo. There was a derailment and thus the train took 5 ½ hours going and 3 hours returning. I only was in Kandy 2 hours and had time to visit an uninteresting Buddhist temple, view the lake and head for the bus since the monsoon rain intervened and there wasn’t much point in staying.

        The trip was interesting, though, as I met an educated Ceylonese on the train who spoke fine English. He discussed the language issue and felt that there was too much concern over nothing (I think the 4 year transition period is too short, though.) We also talked about the US and he was interested in segregation and the Lucy case. I explained as best as I could how segregation was gradually being eliminated even in the die-hard Southern states No Trouble and I came back in the evening from Kandy. Saw many armed police but still no trouble. Lets hope there isn’t any although my curiosity is presently aroused.

JUN 07

Decided to stay in Colombo today and do some sightseeing – plus arrange passage to India. Perhaps I am foolish in not flying on my ticket to Bombay, still the trip will afford me the chance to see some of South India. At the shopping lines I paid 25 rupees for a tourist passage aboard the “Malim”. Might be making a mistake taking tourist, but he said the trip would take 20 hours of which 8 should be during the night.

Colombo hasn’t many unusual sights for the visitor. The walk along the sea is nice, and so is the park called Galle Face Green. The buildings are old, and there didn’t appear to be much construction going on in the downtown area. In the afternoon I visited the park – nothing much, and walked through a typical museum. Consequently by 3 PM I was ready to leave.

I went back to the hotel, gathered my stuff together and headed for the dock. Customs wasn’t much and so I breezed through it and into a small boat by which 2 oarmen would row me out to the Malim for 2 rupees. The trip out to the boat took a long time, and was because the Malim was at dock, on the far side of the pier, unloading her cargo. The ship was quite small – 400 tons – and my hopes fell quite a bit.

Since they wouldn’t be ready till morning I decided to sleep on the boat, but got chow at the hotel. On the way to the hotel 3 men – pimps I thought – talked, begged, showed me pictures and managed to have their arms all over me. Suddenly they left, and equally suddenly I thought of my 4 rupees in my shirt pocket. Sure enough the rupees were gone, but so were the men. Next time they shan’t get so intimate. This time I just didn’t want to fight or hit them to get away from me.

JUN 08

        I awakened around 7 AM and felt the boat pitching and rocking, even though the Captain said it wasn’t very “rough”. I went out on deck but soon retired to my bunks in the Chief Officers cabin. I soon became quite ill and didn’t feel like doing anything but sleep. (2 cups of tea, nothing to eat – all day).

        Sleep is what I did all day, but I wasn’t tired in the evening and had a miserable night. I would doze off for 15-30 minutes and then wake up to check the clock. The night dragged out and I thought it would never end

        Oh what a sick guy I was. And to think for 7 more dollars I could have flown. Even found out that it was somewhat difficult to get to Cochin and even if I got there I would probably see nothing but rain as this was monsoon time. Soo I decided to head first to Madurai and then decide where to go next.

JUN 09

        The day started out as bad as yesterday. The ship – if you can call it that – had stopped pitching and consequently I felt well enough to go out on eck. By 9:30 we sighted Tooticorn but since the tide was out we had to wait until 12:30 before we could proceed. The inept handling of the crew and captain made it 1:30 before we landed – thus in the last 40 hours I have only had 4 cups of tea and 2 pieces of bread.

        Then the fun began; – at customs they took my passport and I had to come back later to fill out the Police registration form. At that time 2 Indian Government officials argued among themselves as to how to fill out the form. Next since I had no rupees I went to the bank to obtain some for my dollars. The man said they were closed and to come back Monday morning – Joke! A Famished and thirsty American then went to an English spinning firm and asked to see one of the Englishmen (there were 9). I presented my problem and the gentleman was extremely kind in getting me some rupees. Another fellow then offered to get me some food and asked his wife to fix me a cold buffet. I was next to starvation – at least it seemed so.

        Words couldn’t express my appreciation for I was a beaten man at that time. The town of Tooticorn is beyond description and handfuls of dust and disease blow everywhere in the hot wind. The poverty is greater here than up North and I was somewhat glad to leave on the 5:50 train for Madurai. I decided not to go to Cochin because they are experiencing heavy monsoons at this time of the year.

        The extremely kind Britishmen fixed me some sandwiches and I was off. (I don’t think I would like their jobs here. The company is huge and is carried on in the 1900’ style with beavers at each elbow) On the train I began talking to a wise old gentleman who turned out to be a member of Parliament (Upper House) from Madurai’s district. He was very much anti-Communist, in opposition to Nehru’s party and a believer of Capitalism. He talked for about 4 hours and I enjoyed listening to him.

JUN 10 (SUNDAY - WEEK 77)

        Today was quite a fine day. The sky was clear and the sun extremely bright – 101, but I really didn’t mind the heat too much. In the morning I visited Meenakshi Temple, one of the foremost examples of Dravidian and Tamil architecture. The temple is huge and has great sculpting, both on the pillars (such as the hall of 1000 pillars, or on the majestic “gopurams” which surround the temple on the 4 sides. Four of these gopurams rise 8-10 stories high and have great works of stone sculpturing on all sides.

        The inside of the temple was similar to other Hindu temples except on a grandeur scale. Today being Sunday, perhaps more Hindus than usually were present were in the temple. Everywhere there were people sitting, lying, walking, staring, sleeping, praying etc. Some had marks and ashes on their foreheads, others touched stone, some walked around the Gods and Goddess statues 2 or 3 times, and some fell prostrate on the ground in front of the statues. I am still amazed at the Hindu religion and can’t fathom how educated people can tolerate it (or any other orthodox religion for that matter)

        Spent some time in the town which is a good size city of around 500,000. Madurai is entirely Hindu with little Western influence. The town had its “million” of beggars, unemployed and others that stared at me with my white sun cap. The women are somewhat pretty, but still have the figures which we generally don’t like in the West – at least I don’t. Some had on pretty saris and with their white teeth, dark eyes, and jewelry they made a pleasant sight. On the way back to the hotel I was shocked to see a woman lying in the street, presumably dead of starvation. Many stared and passed her, but none bothered to see if she was still alive.

        At lunch time I spoke to an English lady in the train station and she asked me to visit her at the mission house. Well, I went to the temple after lunch, but since it was closed, I decided to look her up. It developed that she was a Sister Long, from the Prince Memorial Hospital, a part of the American Missionary Hospital. She was Australian, had been in India 28 years and was extremely nice to me for the 3 hours that I was with her. We talked, walked around the hospital – 220 beds – and she even drove me about town. We then had tea and I left at 5:30 PM. (Fine time, extremely friendly and hospitable)

        Visited Tirumala Palace and then returned to the Railway Station.

JUN 11

        Shades of agravation. The man at Madurai didn’t tell me I had to switch trains before Pamban, consequently I didn’t get to Rameswaram until 10:45. No time to see the temple as the express was to leave shortly – and without it I would have no food – so I decided to forge on to Madras.

        Did spend an hour or so at Pamban walking through the 2-3 inch dust roads and trying not to be too obvious, yet interested in seeing the village. The area is desolate and the people seem to only eak out a living that is next to starvation. I saw some of the men repairing their sails, and I guess were going out to fish. Also stopped at the school house and took a peek inside – disrupting school to say the least. The kids – say from 6-10 – were sitting on the floor, signing words after the teacher. They all stared at me and my cap.

        The train ride to Madras was long and boring. For a portion of the way it was empty, and I was able to give some thought to my plans when I get home. For another portion of the trip I spoke to an educated Indian man, and we discussed many subjects, ie, Hindu being national language, Kashmir and the fanatical Pakistanis, Nehru and whether there was anybody to replace him, the Tamil people & their sarongs, etc.

JUN 12

        Oh what a lousy nite the past nite was. June is a favorable month for marriage and so it seems everybody is either coming or going to a wedding. My compartment was jammed, and I had to spend the night sitting up. Got only a few hours sleep, and was quite uncomfortable sitting through the dark hours.

        Arrived in Madras and checked in at the Ambassador Hotel. Went to the Museum and Art Gallery in the morning, and rode along the Marina Drive, a 4 mile road along a wonderful beach. The only trouble is the shark which tends to come in close, otherwise this would be an ideal place to swim. Took care of some odds and ends, such as arranging a flight to Bombay, typing a letter at the Consulate (to Mom) and buying a thermos jug.

        Madras is a huge, modern city, and seemingly quite a nice place. It sure is hot, though, and it makes me wonder what things are like back in St. Louie. I have been lost, these past couple of weeks concerning news from home.

        India – fascinating place. It sure is a land of extreme and is the most different country that I have ever visited. Extreme poverty, yet many wealthy people who do d nothing for the poor. No wonder Nationalization and Socialism is here or at least imminent. The people are friendly (English speaking ones) and curious. They stare at the foreigner and tend to make him feel self-conscious. The people in the South seem poorer, more Indian or at least not as affected by the West, better looking (women) and more distinct in costume. The men wear a sarong like affair which seems clumsy, but still it is their national dress. The language is varied, but Tamil seems strong. (future trouble when Hindi becomes national tongue). The women in the South appear more primitive, with much costume jewelry everywhere on their body. Even saw some with huge ea ear rings in the lobes of their ears.

JUN 13

        Twas a lousy and hot day today. I got up early and went to catch the bus to Mahabalipuram, ruins of a by-gone era located 50 miles from Madras. The ride was uncomfortable – but cheap and consumed 3 hours each way. The scenery on the way was typical of most of South India, that is, barren, desolate country badly in need of water. From what I understand the NE monsoons come in December and January, and then the rice crop is planted. There were some areas of rice, but the water came from wells.

        It was interesting to see how the wells operated and how the INdians filled the irrigation ditches. Some used oxen to hall up buckets of water; others had men pulling by hand; whereas a third way was to have a man walk up and down on a pulley like affair which raised the water. Surprising enough I saw a lot of goats and cattle and even hogs, although the later looked much fiercer than our domesticated hog. Not many trees, nor even grass, but there was scrub plants here and there. A couple of varieties of trees in the villages are quite pretty, particularly a red flower tree – called Flame Tree.

        Mahabalipuram was a fascinating place, and I spent 3 hours – in the boiling sun – viewing the stone temples, caves, and sculptural scenes on rock hill sides. The artists were great (600 AD) and the proportions, likeness and ability are nearly the best I have seen. The men of a bygone era took huge, single rocks, and from these rocks carved the caves or temples standing today. One particularly interesting carving was on a hillside (100’ x 50’) and depicted a scene from Hindu lore. I am glad I took the time to visit the city.

        Tipping and begging is getting on my nerves in India and I will have to be careful I don’t explode. One rascle followed me for at least 2 miles, begging and asking for money at least every 5 seconds. The worst part about it, is that if you give them something, they are never satisfied and want more.

JUN 14

        We had a delayed connection at Nagpur, consequently the plane didn’t arrive in Bombay until around 7:30. The bus ride into town was quite interesting as we drove in-and-out of the streets, down alleys along the coast and covered a great portion of the city. Bombay is a huge city, swollen with refugees from Pakistan. I believe there are almost 4 million in the city at the present time.

        The buildings are quite big and many of them are modern. The atmosphere is “more Western” than the other Indian cities including Calcutta. One thing that surprised me were the many women that I saw in Western dress. Coming from the South the change was dramatic, and I believe I saw more women in Western clothes than during my whole stay in India.

        My day was occupied with many smaller things as I wanted to leave on the night train for Ajanta. Checked in at BOAC and KLM about future flights, and temporarily arranged a schedule to Cairo. Obtained my visa for Egypt and thus eliminated that problem. Did some odds and ends at American Express plus checking on any mail that might have come – there was none, but I left a forwarding address.

        I visited the Museum – typical (my last) and walked around the city. There were the beggars and unfortunates but I didn’t see any ricksas or pedicabs to harass the tourist. As in Calcutta, there were many street vendors peddling their trade. The city was hot, and sticky (like St. Louis) but I believe of all the Indian cities I would rather live here.

        In the evening I saw a fair movie – “the littlest Outlaw” and then took the train for Ajanta.

JUN 15

        Arrived in Ajanta at 7 AM after a fairly decent night of sleep. I was told that the bust to Ajanta left from a spot near the station, so I packed my junk and began to wait. Two Americans strolled by and when they asked me where the Ajanta bus was I told them that I was also waiting for the bus. Struck up a conversation and soon discovered that we had the same plan, so we decided to join each other (Mr. & Mrs Kohler, Des Moines – just finished 3 year stay at a Mission school in Korea.)

        During the day we were joined at separate intervals by 2 other Hindu persons who were also viewing the caves. One of them was a journalist, and plied me with all kinds of political questions. I answered them and also asked him a couple about India. In this manner I passed an enjoyable bus ride to the caves.

        We were at the caves about 4 hours and enjoyed them immensely. There are 29 caves hewed out of solid rock, from a crescent shaped hill. For about 1000 years, pious Buddhist monks chiseled out the caves, and sculpting beatified beautiful statues (Buddhas), columns, and other decorations. In addition, they added a cow-dung, plaster base to the walls, and upon this painted some exciting and colorful frescoes. Many of these frescoes are still existing, and with the aid of 500 or 1000 watt bulbs, one can study the work of almost 2000 years ago. Almost everything was Buddhist in nature, and it was interesting to compare the work with that from other Buddhist countries.

        The ride to Aurangabad was long and hot and my poor old seat suffered again. Much of the land was packed as this is not the rainy season here. The countryside was poor and reflected much the same pattern as seen in South India. Got a bed for 2 rupees (.40¢) for the night.

JUN 16

        The night wasn’t too bad even though the bed was like a wooden board. In the morning I had a fine breakfast at the Railway Hotel and felt capable of carrying on another long day. Four of us (the Kohls) and an Indian fellow had decided to rent a taxi to visit all of the places in and around Aurangabad.

        The first place on the agenda was Daulatabad Fort located just outside the city. The fort stands on a rock about 2250 feet above sea level and is one of the most outstanding forts that I have ever seen. The workers chiseled down the sides of the mountain, and formed invaluable cliffs which ended abruptly in a moat, also chiseled out of rock. There was only one route to the top of the hill, and many of the passages zig-zaged in and out and made it extremely easy to defend. One of the astonishing features of the fort was the passages chiseled out of sheer rock, and which served as a means to get from the top to the bottom. It was indeed a fabulous fortress. In the adjoining grounds was the Chand Minor or Pillar of Victor created in the 13th century. It wa about 4 stories high and had fine proportions together with an attractive pale pink color.

        From here we drove to Ellora Caves, a wonderful collection of 35 caves cut into the side of a hill. The general scope was similar to Ajanta although none of the caves at Ellora had any paintings in them. The caves are divided into 3 groups – Buddhist, Bramhan and Jain, with the figures of Gods and animals pertain to the respective religions in the different caves. The outstanding cave (or rock cut temple) was the Kailasa Temple cut and chiseled from the hill. The area was about 250’ deep and 150’ broad, and the main temple stood in the middle, a beautiful temple with symmetrical sculpting on all sides. The process must have been from top to bottom, and took hundreds of years to complete. There were other caves, some 2 or 3 stories high, and with spacious halls and massive figures. There was so much that it overwhelms a person, and as he progresses expects to see equivalent or better in succeeding caves. There are many fascinating and almost unbelievable buildings in India, perhaps unrivaled in the world. I am anxious to get to Egypt and compare the pyramids and other structures with what I have seen in India.

        We stayed - the Kohls and I – at the Railway Hotel for supper and then proceded on to the railway station and to Bombay. Hard to believe that I have only 1 more day in India, but I feel that my 4 weeks (including my January trip) has provided me some with an excellent introduction to an unusual, vibrant country.

 JUN 17 (SUNDAY - WEEK 78)

        The train right from Aurangabad was fair – that is, I was able to sleep from Arangabad to Manmad, but not from there in to Bombay. I was quite tired when I reached Bombay, consequently, I decided to check check in at the Red Shield House (Salvation Army.) The cost was extremely low ($1.30 for room & board) and I wish that I could find similar clean-inexpensive places to stay.

        I slept most of the morning, but did go to the Airlines to check on my reservation. In the afternoon I took a bus to Malabar Hill, from which I could get an excellent view of the city. The day was rainy and cloudy however, so I didn't take any pictures. Nearby were the famous hanging gardens but I wasn’t very impressed. It continued to pour, so I went back to the hotel where I stayed until I left to catch the plane at 11 PM. One nice feature of such places as the Red Shield house, is the fact that many students and interesting people stay here. At the house were the Kohls, a German student and newspaper man, a French boy, 2 American students, 2 Canadian girls and some elderly American and English women. Most of them were interested in living at cheap but clean places, and consequently had heard of this hotel.

JUN 18

        Arrived early in the morning, and was taken to the Metropole Hotel. Since it was 4:30 AM I decided not to get a room, and consequently sat or dozed in the lobby of the hotel until 7:30. Had a good and filling breakfast and then started out to see the city and get a little business done. I had my brown AWOL bag with me and it sure got heavy after awhile. First shock was at KLM who said that I might not be able to get out this evening, nor get to Baghdad as the spaces were all taken. He did put my name on the waiting list and told me to come back.

        I then headed for the IRAQ Legation to get a visa, and persisted in getting lost. Finally got there – a really hot and hand-sore man – and obtained the visa. It was too hot to walk so I got a taxi to take me to the Jordan and Syrian Legations and obtain visas for those countries. The travelling to and from these places afforded me any opportunity to see quite a bit of Karachi.

        The town is huge, modern and somewhat crowded with refugees. The shacks or so-called homes of the refugees are quite pitiful and are as bad as I have seen in India. Much new construction is going up, and this small seaport – now Pakistan’s capital – will be a huge metropolis in a few years. The climate is warm, and from what I hear, not very healthful. Didn’t see much begging, nor cows in the street as in India, however the rickola and “helping hands” were present in numbers.

        The country being Muslim, the women wear veils or sheet like things over their heads (most of the time quite filthy). I did see many without veils and some in Western dress, so I guess Karachi is to Pakistan as Bombay is to India. Didn’t see very many women on the streets and there were only a handful occupying the front rows of the buses and street cars.

        The men dress in Western, Indian type, and Muslim form of dress. Many men wear the fez and surprisingly great numbers have full beards. Had to look twice and the ones that had full red beards, something one doesn’t see in India. One thing I liked was the many camel drawn carts & wagons.

        I don’t know why I feel it, but I don’t think as much of this country as I do of India. The people seem to be less intelligent and by religion, quite more fanatical – this religion enters into their everyday life and rules it completely. I truly wonder what would have happened if we hadn’t given any aid, and likewise wonder what will happen when we stop the assistance. It doesn’t appear if basic steps are being taken to support the economy.

JUN 19

        I went to the airport at midnite and found that I was not on the manifest for Baghdad. I then went to BOAC, and in discussing the matter with him, he suggested that I take the flight to Beruit which would leave in 15 minutes. I could then go on to Cairo from Beruit. Quick decision – but I decided to go.

        The flight was pleasant and we arrived in Beruit at about 9:30 AM. Aboard the plane were 25 members of a British ship which had just been sold to a Hong Kong interest for over $1,000,000. (Probably end up in Communist hands). I talked to the Captain most of the trip.

        I had decided to stay at the YMCA and had the BOAC taxi take me there. When I got there I found that they do not have beds and I would have to get other accommodations. I saw two boys standing nearby and asked them where I should stay. They said they knew of a place near the center of town and would take me there. Not only did they help immediately but they spent the greater portion of the next 8 hours, showing me around the modern, extremely–cosmopolitan city of Beruit. We visited the huge American University, walked near the ocean where many were frolicking in the surf, and ambled through the residential sections with their modern apartment houses. It was a fine day.

JUN 20

        Rode from Beruit to Cairo in a smooth Viscount turbo-prop. The flight was short and enjoyable. Took quite awhile to get through customs and get into town, but we finally made it around 11 AM. I dumped my stuff at American Express and dashed to see the military parade which is a part of a week-long celebration honoring the removal of the last British troops from Egypt. I missed the marching part, but did see hundreds of huge tanks, jets overhead and artillery pieces.

        The people cheered and clapped and appeared to have a lot of pride in this their army. Talked to a few and as in India they said how they use to be slaves, and were nou now a free and up an coming nation. As in Beruit, they liked Nasser and the prestige that he has given the Arab world.

        The city is huge and like the previous 3 towns, quite modern with much construction going on. I would say that they are many fine places to live. An English speaking Egyptian told me of a cheap, clean pension and so I checked it and then moved in ($2.90/room & board). The people are both dark and light and speak mainly Arabic. Some of the educated speak also English and French.

        It appears to be a very cosmopolitan taw town, and I saw all sizes and shapes in the park. People were everywhere since this was a holiday. In the evening 2 Fullbright people that I met at the pension – the advantage of living at such a place – went with me out into the deeply highly lighted streets. Lights were strung everywhere and fireworks went off occasionally overhead. People were milling around everywhere and there was a lot of noise. One of the fellows is studying Arabic and read many of the Nationalistic problems posters and signs that were about.

JUN 21

        First thing was a visit to the American Embassy to sign the register and to pick up my mail. Correspondents back home were good to me and I got 7 letters, which I eagerly read. Not much news except that Mom & Carolyn are going to Mexico for the summer, – sounds good.

        I walked to the front of the American University and caught the bus to the Pyramids. The ride through the city was interesting, and as yesterday, I was impressed with the modern buildings and construction going on. Also, over seas the green national flag; red-white-black revolutionary flag and Nasser’s picture everywhere. Evacuation week lasts until Saturday at which time there will be national elections. I don’t think there will be any question who will win.

        Arrived at the Pyramids about 9:30 and I had to fight off all the “official guides” and “watchmen”. I read a good book I had bought yesterday concerning the Pyramids and decided not to use the services of a guide. (they don’t say anything as it is). I did rent the services of a horse to ride around the area of the 3 Pyramids and the Sphinx. Needless to say the Pyramids (the 3 I saw at Giza) are overwhelming and as great as I have imagined. They are not beautiful, and as one gets close it is possible to see all the weather-worn rock and spots where vandalism has taken place. The impressive things about the Pyramids are the Engineering feats and skill it took to build it. The granite and limestone rocks are huge and weigh from 2 ½ - 15 tons. On the inside it is almost impossible to discern where the rocks touch, the craftsmanship of chiseling had been so accurate.

        The Great Pyramid is the 1st that one comes to, and is about 450 feet high. It is supposed to contain about 2,300,000 blocks and a total volume of 83,000,000 CF. One is able to enter this Pyramid and inspect the chambers and Ascending and Descending Corridors. Fabulous! From here I viewed and marveled at the one and only Sphinx and the other 2 Pyramids located at Giza. It is quite thrilling to be able to see such things as the Pyramids and the Taj Mahal; – all are as great as imagined.

        Waited 2 hours for a flower parade but it never materialized. Even on the way to the train station (3 hours after it was to begin) the parade hadn’t passed. I did see Nasser, though, and was impressed.

JUN 22

        The train ride to Luxor wasn’t too bad, although it was quite expensive. I think when I return on Saturday nite, that I shall forgo the sleeper and see if I can’t manage O.K. On the train I met an American fellow and his mother, and we decided to go together so as to share expenses. We found a cheap hotel, and unloaded our bags and stuff preparatory to doing some sight-seeing. The lady was quite fussy and couldn’t decide whether to stay here or not. Finally it was arranged to see this side of the river today, and go to Thebes tomorrow.

        We took a short carriage ride along the Nile and gazed in wonderment at the river which is the complete life blood of a nation of 20,000,000 people. Without this river, and the fertile land it deposits, Egypt would be a barren desert. There wasn’t much activity on the river, just a couple of sailboats plying black and forth. The sight was quite picturesque, with the Nile, blue sky, sailboats, and fertile, green fields on either side of the river.

        The object of our carriage trips was Karnack Temple, a whole city of temples showing traces of building covering some 15 centuries. This was my first real introduction to Egyptian history and I was fascinated by the huge, massive columns, the wonderful obelisks carved from granite, and the hieroglyphics that covered the walls, monuments and obelisks. It is interesting to see the writing as it is composed of many symbols, such as birds, flowers, animals, lines, circles and other pictures which I imagine represent works or phrases. Whole walls and gates were covered with the writing and I found out later that each King wrote his history in such fashion so as to please the Gods with a fruitful life on the earth.

        Some of the statues were huge, and quite attractively sculptured. The proportions used are as to the physical body, but always in a fine, trim form (Likewise the women). One fabulous hall consisted of 135 huge columns, and is said to have been the largest temple hall in the world. The obelisks rose 50-60 feet in the air and were are almost in perfect condition. Such columns, pillars, statues and obelisks were also at the Luxor Temple, another grand Temple located near the hotel.

JUN 23

        My American friends backed out on me, and decided to go back to Cario on the night train. Consequently, I had to visit all the hotels to see if I couldn’t round up a person or two to share expenses as it is very expensive to visit Thebes. I got in touch with an American woman and we arranged the trip (for 3 £E. – $7.50 each) to visit the sights starting at 6 AM.

         In the morning we took a sailboat ride across the Nile (the men actually rowed most of the way) and reached the other side in 15 minutes. There we were met by a car (we had a guide) and began the 6 hour visit. The sun in Luxor is unmerciful and we tried to see as much as possible before the 110º temperature came upon us. The first step was the Memnon Colossus, which were actually 2 huge (60’) figures of King Amenophis III. Here as in other places we saw how the various Egyptologists had done a remarkable job of putting the pieces back together again.

        Next was the temple of Medinet Habu, a fine example of columns, walls and hieroglyphics. Many of the ceilings had coloring on them, and the blue, red and yellow paint could be seen, even though it had been exposed for at least 3500 years to all the ravages of the weather. The guide was quite good, and pointed out in the hieroglyphics scenes in Ramses III life, for whom the temple was build. He pointed out scenes of the battles, the prisoners, the cutting off of the hands and removing tongues, etc. It was quite interesting. From here we visited the Temple of Deir-El-Bahari, a remarkable temple built about 1500 BC into the side of a cliff. It is the most graceful and delicate of the Egyptian temples that I have seen, most of them being huge, massive monuments, capable of lasting thousands of years. The queen was not liked by her brother and when she died, he chiseled out her picture in all the hieroglyphics on this temple.

        Perhaps the most interesting sights were found in the Valley of the Kings and the 4 tombs that we visited. The tombs were cut out of sheer rock (like Ajanta and Ellora) and extended down into the ground, sometimes for hundreds of feet. The pathways were slanting and afforded easy passage for the burial of the king. Since the Egyptians believed in afterlife, the tombs had big halls, places to store precious goods, boats (to travel), beds, food and wearing apparel. (all having been previously robbed) The walls and ceilings had fabulously preserved paint on them, and in some cases perfect paintings from 3500 years back. The paintings depicted many historical scenes, pictures of the King giving offerings to the Gods, and other characters which the people of that time believed in. (Visited King Tut-Ankh-Aman, which was the only one not robbed, the pious king in the Egyptian museum, except the mummy which is in the Tomb) at one point a watchman lighted our visit to a tomb by holding mirrors which reflect the sunlight. In this matter, the workman of past years lighted their work to be done.

JUN 24 (SUNDAY - WEEK 79)

        I think that if anything gets me down, it will be the sleepless nights on the trains. The train last night also had the distinction of being the dirties train that I have ever been on. I was completely covered with soot when I arrived in Cairo. I dumped my stuff at the room, took a bath, and then spent the rest of the morning at the Egyptian museum. The museum is jammed full of mummies, tombs, statues and many other interesting objects from the early times. Of particular interest were the objects found in the tomb of King Tut-Ankh-Amen at the Valley of the Kings (which I saw yesterday.) This was the only tomb that has been found which had not previously been robbed; consequently, there were many treasures and priceless pieces of antiques to be examined so as to shed additional light on life 3500 years ago. The only things that remain at Thebes are the mummy, 3rd casket and original sarcophagus, all the rest having been brought to the museum. It was amazing to view the treasures, closets, beds, vases, caskets, jewelry and hundreds of other objects that were jammed in the Tomb.
