        In the afternoon I visited the Citadel, a fortress like affair built on a hill, and from which one can get a good view of the city. Included in the grounds is the Mohamed Aly Mosque, perhaps the most impressive Mosque that I have seen thus far. (All Mosques tend to be huge affairs, yet barren of any furniture as they pray on mats). The coupola caupola was particularly beautiful with one center dome, and 4 smaller, surrounding domes. From here I went to El-Moosky Bazar, but most of the shops were closed.

JUN 25

        By prior arrangement I had scheduled myself to take the Foreign Service Test at the American Embassy in Cairo. I really don’t know why I did, for I did no studying and am not sure if I am really interested in the Foreign Service. However, it was only a 1 day test – versus the 3 ½ day previous test – and I felt that I couldn’t go wrong. The test was in 3 parts, and quite difficult. The only consolation I got was the fact that those that pass must be quite intelligent people. (Still, why do we have such lack of ingenuity in the State Department and such an inept foreign policy?)

        I completed the test about 4:30 and then went to American Express to make some last minute arrangements for leaving this town. As it stands now, I should pull out on the afternoon of the 27th bound for Beruit. Let’s hope I don’t get as seasick as before.

Egypt is quite a nice country and has many interesting things to see. The climate in the North isn’t too bad, and Cairo seems to be quite a decent city with various attractions and Western places to interest the foreigner. The men wear the pants and shirt in Cairo, but in the villages they wear the nightshirt and fez. The women also dress Western in Cairo, but in the village and to some extent in Cairo they wear black shawls and veils. Some wear interesting trinkets that dangle on their forehead.

        Unlike the beautiful women’s figures seen in the Egyptian relics, I see nothing but fat and unattractive women on the streets. This country has regressed in more ways than one. There are many soldiers in Cairo, and they dress quite snapily. Their leader – Col Nasser – was just elected President (on Saturday) by a 99% plurality. He will serve for 6 years unless he gets shot or thrown out.

        Some of the people in Cairo are fair skinned and have European features. Others are quite dark and have negroid features. It is interesting to see some of the men with tribal scars on their faces, generally 3 slashes on each side. Most of the men have mustaches and appear to be quite gay and happy. As a rule they are kind, but there are too many that want the tip.

JUN 26

        Have to give a few men lines to the outdoor theater that I and 2 other fellows went to last night. We were all hyped up about seeing some belly dancer, so we went to a place called Safia Hilmy where we paid $.60 to get in. The show started in a few minutes and we sat through 2 hours of the dancing and “so called Arabic” music. I was quite disappointed with the dancing as all of the girls were real fat wenches that weren’t even pretty. One of the fellows said that the Arabs liked fat women, but I sure don’t; consequently, I dozed thru most of the show. The dancing is nothing more than a lousy burlesque, with a little more accent on shaking the tummy and rear end. The women certainly were no copies of the fine figures seen on the ancient tombs. My how Egypt has regressed.

        In the morning - tuesday – Bob and Dave, two Fulbright fellows staying at the Pension where I am boarding, went with me to the Sakharah, a city of the Dead located about 12 miles from Cairo. Dave had been here before and took us around to the various tombs and old temples from the 1st to the 30th Dynasty. Predominating the scene was a steep pyramid erected by Zoser in the 3rd Dynasty. This is the first of the Pyramid type burial places, and precedes the Pyramids of Giza. In this Pyramid, the Egyptians had not acquired their skill with rock, and tended to build the Pyramid as if the stones were lumber.

        There were some very interesting tombs, some belonging to Kings and one to a powerful nobleman. As in Luxor, there were beautiful hieroglyphics on the wall, all chiseled out, and some in fine colors. The scene depicted the daily life of the people and were very detailed. For instance, one scene was of a boat on the Red Sea, NILE and the fish in the river have all been identified today as being Nile River fish. Other pictures were of growing, measuring, reaping grain; offerings to the Gods; dancing girls and people playing musical instruments, and almost every form of daily living. The most curious tomb was the Serapeum, dedicated to Apis, the ox; a deity worshipped and mummified in exactly the same ceremonial fashion as human beings. The tomb was quite intensive and was cut out of solid rock in the ground. There were 25 sarcophagus (caskets) and some of them were huge 10’ x 8’ x 15’ blocks of solid granite. Quite an interesting place. In the afternoon I visited the El-Moosky bazaar and walked around the various side streets. One can buy most anything here, and even watch the craftsman work with the silver or whatever object it might be. Didn’t seem to be too different from other bazaars – perhaps larger – even though it is supposed to be the most famous in the Orient.

JUN 27

        Left early in the morning for Alexandria, and arrived about 10:30. I checked my bags at the station and spent a couple of hours walking around the city. Alexandria is quite modern and seems to be a halfway decent city. Not much to see in the city, so I just gazed in the shops, observed the people and their dress, and just passed the time. Had lunch and then walked back to the railroad station to get my junk.

        Took a cab to the Port and checked through customs. After arguing with the porter about a tip (he really got violent, but I was almost sure that the Customs fee included his tip_ I boarded the ship – the ENOTRIA. The ship was quite large, and I had my hopes that I wouldn’t get seasick. Deck passage included nothing except a deck to sleep on, plus food; however, the food for dinner couldn’t accurately be called supper. Met 2 American girls and 2 American fellows, and had a fairly enjoyable evening talking about all kinds of subjects. I was quite tired, though, and finally excused myself to get some sleep. I found a bench in the room set aside for Deck Passage personnel, and curled up on it and fortunately fell asleep. Awakened once in the night, but again fell asleep, so in all I got about 6 hours of “sore” sleeping. THus far the trip hasn’t been bad at all.

JUN 28

        I awakened quite early, and could only get about another hour or so of restless sleep. The bench that I was lying on was getting harder by the minute, so at about 5:30 I finally got up and attempted to keep awake. Breakfast consisted of rolls and tea – like a prison – however lunch wasn’t too bad. The five of us spent the morning talking and gazing out over the blue waters. Land was sighted about 11 and almost at 12 noon sharp the boat pulled into the harbor.

        It was quite humorous to see the humans act like animals as the crowded and pushed into the immigration office in order to save 5-15 minutes. One lady used her crying baby as an excuse to get through the line even though she could quite easily have sat and waited until we were all done.

        George went to the Eden Roe Hotel, but the four of us checked into the Metropole Hotel. There being not much to see in Beruit, and since I had already visited the University and walked around town, we spent the rest of the afternoon walking around and buying some food for tomorrow’s breakfast and lunch. George invited us out to his hotel in the evening and we had a fine meal plus drinks. He is staying at a nice, resort hotel, and we all drolled when we saw the swimming pool. I also cashed some money in order to get some Turkey and Yugoslav money.

        Lebanon is a nice country, and seems to be the most modern of the Arab nations. Beruit in particular is modern, and one thinks he is in Europe, particularly since a lot of French is spoken here. The shops are clean and merchandise is displayed the best of the countries since I was in Japan. Many of the women are attractive and most of them wear Western style clothing. The taxis are madmen, though, and one has to be on the look-out so as not to get run over. I think I could live in Beruit and enjoy myself.

JUN 29

        We arranged to have a taxi take us to Baalbeck, Lebanon and then go on to Damascus Syria. Consequently, promptly at 7 AM the drive drove us to our hotel, and 15 minutes later we were on our way. The drive to Baalbeck was very enjoyable as we passed over the Lebanese mountains that surround Beruit (quite high), drove through some of the resort towns where the people go to escape the heat in the summer, and then down into some plains which seemed to have very fertile soil.

        Baalbeck is a group of old Roman ruins and is supposed to have been one of the most ancient cities of the world. The Phoenicians built a temple in the city in honor of their god, Baal, and to this day the old name survives. Later the Romans built their temples here and Emperor Augustus established a Roman colony. In later periods Christia churches and Moslem mosques were built in the area, but the main attractions today are the Temples of Jupiter, Bacchus and Venus. The Temple of Jupiter is built on an artificial platform and was at one time surrounded by 54 huge stone columns, 20 meters high. Six of these columns exist today and strike a grand pose as they look over the ruins. The Temple of Bacchus is still in a fairly well-preserved state and one can see beautiful panels decorated with portraits of various Roman gods and goddesses. The main gate is considered to be one of the finest examples of ancient architecture and is elaborately decorated with engraved pearls, interlaced vine branches and ivy leaves and ears of corn and poppies. (The emblems of life and death)

        We viewed the ruins for about 1 ½ hours and then headed for the border and Damascus. Didn’t have too much trouble at the border and soon passed into Syria. From the border to the capital we drove by some of the most desolate plains and hillsides that I have ever seen. Absolutely nothing grew in the rocky soil, and one could not see a tree for miles. Damascus is quite modern in sections, and this surprised me quite a bit. Everything was closed today –Moslim Holy Day – so we just walked about the town.

JUN 30

        I decided to spent the day in Damascus and then continue on to Jerusalem tomorrow, since the others wanted to do some shopping here. In the morning we devoted our time to sight-seeing, and visited the Omayad Mosque, built in the 4th Century as a Christian Church and later converted into a Moslem basilica. Supposedly the tomb of St. John the Baptist is contained in this church. (so what!) Next we visited Azem Palace, which is a quaint little palace, in which scenes of ancient events are portrayed by mannequins in Moslem dress, and old rugs, guns, chairs, vases etc. Inside the courtyard was a beautiful garden with flowers and orange trees.

        The rest of the things we saw were mostly Biblical  (for Mo_’s sake) such as the home of Aranias, the place at the city gate where Paul was lowered in a basket to escape the Roman soldiers (!!) and the ancient wall of Damascus. We walked through the BAzaar and I think it is the nicest that I have seen in the Middle East. It is covered from sun and rain, and is quite extensive in length. I think one could buy almost anything, – from staple goods to tourist prizes such as inlaid boxes. (I bought one for $1.40)

        We had kabab in the afternoon – a delicious Arabic dish – and toyed with the idea of more shopping. The stores were closed so the others went back to the hotel, however, I walked around and stood on a street corner for about an hour and a half. I took a couple of pictures of women and men in their dress and just observed the people as they walked by. The costumes varied from Western dress – to fezes – to Arabian head gears – to things I would call night sheets. Some of the women had tattoos on and around their mouth, and the majority of them were veiled. I saw an unusually large number of men in soldier uniforms, however, they did not impress me as looking like good, intelligent fighting men. I am interested in seeing the Israeli soldier.

JUL 01 (SUNDAY - WEEK 80)

        We had good intentions of leaving Damascus at 8 AM, but our driver had some stuff to do, so we didn’t pull out until almost 9 o’clock. The ride to Jerusalem was long and tiring, yet in some respects, quite interesting. It took us about 6 1’2 hours to make the journey, including the brief stop at the Dead Sea. I tasted the water and found it to be extremely alkaline. (Hope I don’t have any bad aftereffects). We also whipped through Jericho, but at such great speed that we didn’t see a thing.

        Contrary to the Northwest portion of Syria, the Southern part looked somewhat fertile. It appears that there must have been a good wheat crop this year, for one sees wheat in all stages of processing; and quite a lot of it. The thrashing, separation of the husks (?) and other processes are done in the old manner of a thousand years ago. In the former they toss the wheat into the air and let the wind carry away the lighter portion, and in the latter they have donkeys pull women or children on sleds over the wheat. They then pile the wheat on the backs of camels, horses or humans and take it to the next stage. At one place it was interesting to see a caravan of camels, 16 in a row, walking in at their slow, idiotic appearing gait.

        We crossed the border into Jordan, and came upon some really desolate country. The ground was barren and extremely hilly, and the road zig zagged in and out. Can’t really see why anyone would want this country. The Jordan headdress is interesting, and consists of a white or colored shawl over the head, and kept in place by a thick, braided cord. The Army men were particularly impressive, and I imagine are quite good fighters.

        Spent a couple of hours walking through the streets of the old city, and enjoyed the narrow streets, crowds and atmosphere. Even stopped at the wailing wall for a few minutes, but of course none of the Jews were present to add atmosphere.

JUL 02

        Today was sight seeing day in the Holy City and it turned out quite nice. There are very few tourists in Jerusalem at the present, consequently, one doesn’t find the horrific clamor that there would be on Easter or Christmas. Jerusalem – the Old City – is very picturesque, with its narrow streets, stone pavements, Roman archways, and hundreds of people. It reminded me of an Oriental city, with its numerous little shops and street vendors, however, it seems to be much cleaner than the Oriental towns.

        The first place we visited – the 2 girls, Mac and I, was El Harem, better known as the Dome of the Rock. This is the most religious site in Jerusalem to the Moslems, and one of the top 3 in their religion. The Mosque is exquisite, and consists of a beautifully proportional dome abound with colorful mosaics and golden paint, over a rock which is believed to be the site of Mount Moriah, where Abraham was to sacrifice his son. There is also a legend concerning Mohammed and this rock. The Mosque is built on land believed to be the site of Solomon’s Temple, and we visited the area under the temple where he brought the stone to build the temple. The Romans (or Crusaders) later used these vast underground areas to stable their horses.

        Next we visited a convent where Christ is supposed to have walked on his way to Calvary. We followed this path – Via Dolorosa – for about 7 of the 14 stations but then turned off to go to the market before going to the Church of the Holy Sepulcher. This church is generally considered the most important site in Jerusalem for the Christians, as it is the accepted site of the Crucifixion of Christ and his Sepulcher. The Church is old and not very pretty, but it is interesting to see the many Orthodox sects in the church and the interesting costumes they wear. A boy pointed out the tomb of Christ, where the cross was, etc, however, it seems like a lot of rubbish to me.

        Talked to a Jordan soldier and was interested in his comments about the last war. He said the Jews make lousy soldiers, and turn their heads when they fire. He went on to say that their Army was pushing the Jews out of Jerusalem when the cease fire came and they had to stop. He thought that if there would be war, that the Jordan army would split Israel and then Egypt would attack the South and Syria and Iraq the North. He also said that it is America that is preventing this war. Interesting comments – 

        Visited the Garden of Gethsemane, Church of All Nations and Mount of Olives in the afternoon. Also applied to go into Israel tomorrow but I may have to wait a little while.

JUL 03

        The four of us got up really early and took the bus to Bethlehem via a long winding road. I understand that there is an easier route, but it is in Israeli territory. Bethlehem didn’t show me much, and the orthodox churches, as in Jerusalem, seem to have built up many traditions and stories concerning the Church of the Nativity. The Church is quite old and is divided into various sections, for the Greek, Roman, Armenian, etc churches. We had a souvenir shop salesman show us around, so naturally he rushed things as to drag us into his shop. I went back to the Church, although the others bought a couple small items.

        Back in Jerusalem I obtained my exit permit from the Jordan Government, and then picked up my military pass (Israeli) at the American Consul. Around 1:30 I trudged – carrying my 2 bags – up to the border, and then across. Actually I was surprised with the narrow “No Mans Land” that separates the countries, and also the plainness of the so called gates MANDELBAUM GATE – actually no more than a road block. I went first to the Tourist Bureau and obtained some information, plus the name of a Hotel.

        I walked around the town – New Jerusalem is just that, a modern, clean looking city – and saw more long noses, and Jews than ever before. The people seemed happy and well fed, and there wasn’t much tenseness in the air. Went to the YMCA in the evening and heard a fine concert. Also had an opportunity to talk to some Americans who had lived in Israel for a year.

JUL 04                INDEPENDENCE DAY

        Had a fine hot water shower, and then began my sightseeing for the day. Actually I had to get some travel information first, and the news that I obtained was disheartening. The only boat to Athens is all filled, and the boat to Istanbul takes 4-5 days and cost $51 w/o bed and $64 with bed. Consequently, I have decided to fly to Istanbul ($80) either on the 8th or 10th. I then headed for Prof. Klausner’s house in the country so as to say hello to him for the Klausners back home, and perhaps to speak to this intellectual gentleman. He couldn’t speak English so I soon departed.

        Took the bus to the YMCA and dined went to the top of the tower from which one can obtain a fine view of New & Old Jerusalem. The tension and bitter feelings that exist are such a shame, as both people need each other to exist. Also visited the Knesseth Building and observed the Legislators in action. There weren’t many people on the floor or in the galleries and I guess this was a quiet day. Couldn’t understand the Hebrew so I returned to my hotel for a Werner prepared bread, cheese and orange juice lunch. (Orange juice is very cheap here.) In the afternoon I viewed Meah Shearin, the orthodox quarter where the men wear ¾ coats (even in this hot climate), hats, beards, curls on each side of their forehead, and long socks. The boys wear short pants and it is as if one was on a time table sent back to the 17th & 18th centuries in Europe. I tried to take a few pictures, but wasn’t too successful as everybody stared at me and my camera.

        At 3:15 I took a bus to Kiryat Anavim Kibbutzim located near Jerusalem. It is one of the older Kibbutzim and was founded in 1920 by a bunch of Russian immigrants. The colony is composed of around 400, which includes members, children, applicants and people who live but are not members. The colony is collective, and is a part of around 70,000 people who live and work on similar projects in Israel. There are also co-operated and private farmers in the economy and I had a fine talk with the Dentist (member, not married, German & Swiss trained, lived here for 20 years) and he explained much concerning the collective status of the Kibbutzim. We also discussed many other Israeli problems – questions with respect to the jewish Nation, the Arab and other problems facing Israel today and in the future.

 JUL 05

        My stay at the Kibbutzim was very enjoyable. I got up at 6:30 and went to the orchard to pick plums for 2 hours. I didn’t mind the work, and sort of enjoyed pitching in and sort of “paying” for my free room and board. Later the secretary took me around the settlement and pointed out its main features. Poultry and baby chicks are their main source of income, and they add to it by selling milk, honey and fruit. They also have a Rest House for people from the cities. This settlement is perhaps richer than most others as it has been in existence 36 years. The people appear quite happy and satisfied with their life. The Jews have made the most of the land, and there are green crops everywhere. Haifa is somewhat picturesque being located on a side of a mountain, and the view of the harbor from above is quite good. Somehow, though, I don’t care for the city and will leave for Tel Aviv tomorrow.

I really don’t know what to think of the Kibbutzim. I believe that in the beginning, as in wilderness or desolation of any kind, such as the Negev, that a collective life is perhaps the quickest way to raising food, maintaining protection and the standard of living. However, once this initial phase is over (as in much of Israel) I think I would prefer to see the collective life turned into a co-operative life. I don’t like the idea of the elimination of distinct family entities. Nor do I think I would like to see a settlement tell me how much education my children should get, or raising of my child for the first 3 years, or having allowing people to have no capital. Perhaps the first generation is idealistic enough, but the 2nd and so on loses the ideals with which the early struggles were conquered. Perhaps I have been brought up wrong, but I would think that a collective life tends to kill initiative, cover up the slackers and tend to make people “get by”. A co-operative life would be economical as doctors, schools, sanitation etc could be pooled, but the family tie would be retained and one gets directly as much as he puts out.

 JUL 06

        I don’t know exactly what it was, something I ate or drank (Haifa had the worst water I have ever tasted in a big city), but I got up in the morning with a belly ache. Sort of put the damper on things all day, for a case of diarrhea accompanied the pain. First order of business was to check the airlines, and then buy a ticket to Istanbul via Athens for $90. I was glad to find this out, for it will save me money –deck passage to Istanbul is $51 and to Athens is $36. Besides 6 nights sleeping on a deck, one has additional costs which would boost the figure over $90. For one time air transportation is cheapest. The Athens route is heavily booked, though, and I might not get out on Sunday, perhaps Tuesday.

        Didn’t do much in Haifa, really didn’t feel like it. Took a bus to Mount Carmel, from which I got a good view of the city and port below. Haifa is quite a pretty and modern city, but the lousy water and food have dampened my spirits here. I also stopped in at a tomb to some Moslem, the name of which I never did get. The gardens were well kept and a new gold dome shone brilliantly in the sunlight. Back in the dock area, I mailed some books home, and checked my films at the censor office. Then I took the express (bus) for Tel Aviv.

        Everything closes in Israel after sundown – and earlier – on Friday and most of the offices are also closed on Saturday. Consequently, when I arrived in Tel Aviv, I had to get a hotel and then hurry back to the bus station to get my bags before it closed. I got a reasonably cheap hotel near the beach, and perhaps if there isn’t too big of a crowd tomorrow, I might go swimming. In the evening I went to a tourist Oneg Shabbat at the 20A house. It was strictly a tourist affair, but I enjoyed the dancing and singing of the young ones that were putting on the entertainment. Met Bob Willis (I had previously met him in Cairo) and he told me that he has been in Israel for about 10 days waiting for money from home. He is a nice fellow, (black, bushy beard and all) who taught for 1 ½ years in Japan. Also met an interesting NY stockbroker who was quite friendly.

        Getting back to the Israeli people, I think they are hard working, conscientious people who have done a lot in a short time. (with the $50,000,000 a year from the USA) the children are healthy looking, and I like to hear them sing, or do one of the Israeli folk dances.

 JUL 07

        In the morning I took my blue baseball cap and went around the corner to an orthodox synagogue. I felt a little funny, but picked up a book – in Hebrew – from a table, opened it, and made as if I was praying. For the next 30-40 minutes, I was an observer, and tried to see and hear all that I could. The men sat downstairs and the women upstairs. The men wore hats, naturally, and most of them had on a tallis. There didn’t seem to be an organized services, as various people went to the central stand and proceded to read and chant, the others more or less following along. Each man – and they were mostly middle aged or older, read the entire service out loud to himself. Sort of general confusion prevailed, as some were chanting, others reading, some talking and some trying to sing out as if to show off their voices.

        I really felt like a foreigner here; both the languages and customs mystifying me completely. The men bobbed and as they read the Hebrew which is as foreign as Arabic was. Like the Hindus they went forward, kissed the robe in front of the altar, then their tallis, and finally covered their heads with the tallis and did I don’t know what. Anyway it was a good show.

        Also visited the beach and the museum in the morning, the beach being very crowded and noisy (Coney Island). I met one of the fellows in the hotel and he, his friend and I had lunch together. We had some good discussions concerning Israel, USA and the Arabs. They are sure Israel would win a war against the Arabs, for the other alternative is being driven it into the sea. They feel, however, that the US has let them down concerning the Arms problem, and soon Egypt will have a much more powerful Army. They, as do all the Israelis, expressed their desire and need for peace, and wish the UN would force the Arabs to sit down to a peace table. I tried to explain the US’s role in the world today, and her desire to have the UN handle this question. I said that if Israel is attacked, the world will be on their side.

        Later in the afternoon I went to Accadia Beach where I enjoyed the waves and salt water for a couple of hours.

Route as of July 7th, 1956 – end of Chapter 13.

CHAPTER 14 - EUROPEAN ENTRANCE

July 8th, 1956 - August 8th, 1956

JUL 08 (SUNDAY - WEEK 81)

        I am not very crazy about the Sabbath as everything shuts down in Israel; buses ,stores, offices, etc. Consequently, the only way I could contact LAI Airlines was to go to the office at 8 AM and check on the 10 AM flight. This I did and they informed me that I would be able to get on if I got to the Airport in time. (TWA still had me on standby). I hailed a cap, picked up my luggage and paid through-the-nose ($2.75) to get to the Airport. I made it in time and cleared customs, and soon was flying toward Greece.

        We landed about 1 PM, were greeted by 2 charming Greek Airline hostesses, and soon were then driven into the town. Through the Tourist Agency where they left us, I managed to get a half way decent, cheap hotel. A writer for the National Jewish Post – Charlie Roth – came along to the hotel, and so we spent the rest of the day together. (He leaves tomorrow for the USA). I enjoyed his company, for he is friendly and intelligent and we had some good discussions concerning Judaism, the American Jew, Israel and the Arab situation. Although he is a Zionist, he says one can be a good American Jew, if he does not need a black and white definition, nor needs to look any further than what Judaism means to oneself personally. That which he likes he should use in the religion, and vice versa. Food for thought.

        Most of the time was spent in walking around Athens. We watched the changing of the guard at the Palace, and I took a shot of the guard in his ruffled shirt, high socks, and shoes with big balls on the end. Viewed the Olympic Stadium, and even visited a church bazaar by mistake. Actually, we stayed there about an hour, as the people were very friendly, and we were interesting in seeing such typical Greek atmosphere. In the evening we saw 2 acts of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” which was given in an open air theater in the National Gardens. The background and lighting were beautiful, and the trees and shrubbery reminded me of the Municipal Opera in St. Louis. It was in Greek, and thus “Greek” to us, so we left after an hour and one-half. Had 2 fine meals in Greek restaurants, the supper consisting of veal, tomatoes and egg plant.

JUL 09

        The more I see of Athens, the more I like. The people are friendly, kind, proud and they dress quite nicely, at least those in and around Constitution Square. The main difficulty is that they do not speak much English and sometimes it is hard to order a meal or ask directions. (Also, they the women do not shave under their arms, and their being quite hairy makes it look quite bad, – at least in my standards)

        Met Rolf Fladt in the morning – Brazilian Doctor I had met at Luxor – and he advised me to take a bus tour plus going to Rhodes. The first is a little expensive, but I decided to go on a 2 tour day tour, and then go to Rhodes on my own. Ate at a Greek restaurant and had a Greek dish called “mousaka.” It consists of eggplant, ground meat, flour and milk, and was very good.

        Later in the afternoon I walked around town, and then headed for the Acropolis, which is situated on a rock mountain near the center of the city. As one approaches, he climbs a relatively steep hill on the west side of the hill, and enters through the Propylaea or entrance buildings. Much work (debatable whether it is good or bad) has been done in restoring some of the old buildings and columns, and one can visualize how the arrangement must have been. The Parthenon is the most beautiful of the buildings and is one of the most perfect examples of ancient art. Many of the columns still stand, and the grace and effect of the tapering columns are quite impressive. The roof has fallen, but one can get an idea of the frieze that went around the top of the building. Also visited the Eretheum (dedicated to Athena Polias), the Odeon of Herodes Atticus (theater), and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.

        In the evening I went back to the theater to hear a symphony concert, but it was all sold out. I and about 300 others went up the hill and sat and listened awhile to the music. The theater was started in 6th century BC but completed in 2nd Century AD. The Roman facade in front adds indescribable atmosphere to the concerts.

JUL 10

        Today was tour day, and so I left my bags at the hotel and went to the designated spot to catch the bus. There weren’t many people on the trip, – 3 Japanese, 2 Belgians, 1 Frenchwoman, 1 American – but the American was an B a fellow I had met at the pension in Cairo. He is quite nice and knows a lot about this region, and consequently, makes a good traveling companion. Our guide is a decent one for a change, and she speaks English & French quite fluently. Since not all of the tourists speak KNOW English (or French) she has to repeat everything twice.

        The bus is quite modern and so everything seemed O.K. as we headed for the Monastery at Daphni. Actually it is a Byzantine church built during the time of Emperor Justinian, and doesn’t seem to be used today. The main feature at the monastery were the fine mosaics on the walls and ceilings. From here we journeyed to Eleusis and viewed the ancient Sanctuary of the Eleusinian Mysteries where people were initiated into problems of life, death, and the hereafter. The guide furnishes much relevant data, as much of the structures are greatly destroyed. Old Corinth, once the largest city in ancient Greece was interesting with respect to the Agora (old Roman marketplace). It also had some columns from the temple of Apollo. After a good lunch, we visited Mycenae, the stronghold of Agamemnon, who lived in 1400 BC and was remembered for his part in the Trojan Wars. The fortress is located on a hill which overlooks the valley of Argolis. Nearby was Agamemnon’s tomb, a fantastic bee-hive shaped structure with earth over it so it resembled a hill.

        We then drove to Nauplia where we had supper and spent the night. Before summer, Dave and one of the Frenchmen and I climbed the 1000 steps to the top of the nearby fortress. To say the least I was dead and ready to hit the sack after dinner. All in all, it has been a good day.

JUL 11

        I don’t think the second day of the 2 day tour was quite as interesting at as the first day since we only visited 2 places. The first place was Epidaurus, a health sanctuary, built around 5th Century BC. The buildings, dormitories, temple and circular rotunda are all in almost unrecognizable ruins; however, the stadium and theater are in faire shape. The theater was built by Polycletus the Younger, and has manby many rows of stone seats which extend up the hillside. For the past 4 years this theater has been used to present some of the old tragedies, and only last Sunday, the final 1956 performance was held. The orchestra is in the circular Greek fashion, and the acoustics are fantastic.

        We had 3 hours of the noon meal, so Dave, one of the French Fathers and I strolled about town for an hour or so. The village of Paulia is quite nice, being fairly large, located on the sea, the houses seem adequate and the people appear happy and contented. The Father likes to take pictures and it was amazing to see the people so eager to pose for him. I don’t believe I have ever seen people so willing to have their picture taken.

        Lunch was quite good – and filling – and at 3 PM we headed for Tiryns which is an ancient fortified city. As at Mycenae, the castle is built on top of the hill, with huge (20 foot thick) walls surrounding the structure. One of the amazing features of the wall is the fact that they built underground galleries within the wall which were used as storerooms during peacetime and shelters during wartime.

        The way back was a little long and tiring, but the countryside was interesting. The wheat has been harvested and people were in the act of processing it. Passed over the Corinthian Canal, a fantastic canal, 4 miles ling. Cut out of sheer rock mountain.

JUL 12

        My ship to Rhodes was to leave at 2 PM, so I thought that I would try and finish off some odds and ends, and if I had time, to do some sight-seeing. I got the rest of my food for the trip, bought some writing paper, exchanged 2000 Yugoslav money into 100’s, had my shoe fixed, bought a ticket to Monday night’s symphony performance at the Odeon of Herodes Atticus, and did a couple of other minor things.

        I finished the work about 10 AM so I decided to visit the Theseum, a well preserved temple near the old Greek and Roman marketplaces. (I lugged my bag there, and boy was it heavy) The excavation is being done by an American group, and they are even restoring the Roman marketplace (AGORA) into a replica of the original and it will serve as a museum for the objects found in the excavations.

On the way to Omonia Square –  where the subway to Piraeus begins – I stopped at the University for a few minutes to look around. There are some interesting statues on top of pedestals – and some murals of ancient Greeks. The guard wouldn’t let me in so I had to be content with walking around outside.

        Arriving in Piraeus I went to the dock where my ship was tied up. It was quite a large ship, and I don’t think I will have any trouble. Hundreds of students came aboard – also deck passage – and I soon found out that there was an outing from the University of Athens to Rhodes. I saw a fellow with an American college ring, and reading an English book so I began talking to him. His name is Phillip Chapalis and he is studying medicine at the University. (for the past 5 years, 2 of which was teaching chemistry) He speaks fluent Greek so I think I will go around with him. The voyage arm was quite smooth today, and the blue water brilliant. We passed many small islands which tend to break the monotony of the water.

JUL 13

        It was a long and somewhat chilly night, and I only got about 5 ½ hours sleep. I slept on my back on the top of a life preserver box, and was lucky that I didn’t roll off during the middle of the night. Naturally everybody awakens at the break of dawn, and we were surprised to see some fog around the ship. Didn’t think much about it at first, but it gradually got worst and soon we were standing still, afraid that if we continue that we would hit one of the many islands that we pass quite close to.

        Two hours later we began moving and soon were going at the regular speed. On our left we could see Turkey, as the Dodecanese Islands are very close to the Turkey mainland, much closer than to Greece. The remarkable thing about these Islands is that they were under foreign rule for 639 years, yet preserved their Greek customs, traditions and language. I had bought a Pelican pocket book called “The Greeks” and spent most of the morning in the sun reading this book. It is fairly good, and gives a general background of ancient Greece.

        The view of Rhodes as we came into the harbor was very beautiful. One could see the Palace of the Grand Master and the old walled city and its fortifications and moats. In the harbor was St. Nicolas Fort, built in about 100 B.C. and subsequently destroyed by an earthquake. We could also see many beautiful green vines and brightly colored flowers, and I later found out that Rhodes means Roses.

        We docked, and Phillip, Petros and I found a cheap hotel where we could stay. Phillip and I then walked around the city, and were amazed at the cleanliness and beauty of the city. The Italians, I am told, did a lot of construction and re-construction during the 31 years that they occupied the island. I am sure that I will enjoy my stay on Rhodes.

JUL 14

        Had a good nights sleep – had only about 5 restless hours the night before – and awakened ready to go out to see the ancient city of Rhodes. The city is really beautiful, with flowers everywhere, the streets clean, the people quiet and friendly, and of course the old walled city which adds so much charm. There are two huge moats around the old city and the walls are reinforced with earthwork which makes it quite formidable. I believe the fortifications were first built in the Byzantine era, added to by the Crusaders, and taken by subterfuge by the Turks in about 1500.

        I met another american in fact the 4th of the four fellows I had known at the pension in Cairo, that I had known; and we plus a young British couple (District Commissioner in Tanganikya) toured the old city in the morning. We first walked up the Street of the Knights where the ancient knights use to live, and we noticed their emblems and crests on the sides of the buildings. Next we visited the Palace of the Grand Master where we were taken on a tour. Mussolini was supposed to have rebuilt the palace for a summer home, when it was but he had never had a change to use it. The rest of the morning was spent walked around the old city, peeking ito homes (and noticing the immaculate cleanliness, and pretty colored floors and walls) and enjoying the old city and Rhodes in general.

In the afternoon Paul and I rented bicycles and rode to the ruins of the ancient Acropolis.  Nearby was located the ruins of the Temple of Apollo and a well preserved theater and statues. The view from this spot was wonderful, as one can see the town below, plus the brilliant blue waters of the Mediterranean Sea. Later in the afternoon I visited the Aquarium (fair) and joined a tour around the ramparts of the walls of the old city. The fortifications and moats are quite impressive, and I also enjoyed seeing some of the stone boulders thrown by catapults during wars of bygone years.

JUL 15 (SUNDAY - WEEK 82)

        I took a couple dramamine tablets after I saw the size of my ship, for I need everything in my favor for sea voyages. The ship is only around 1000 tons, and deck passage might not be so nice under stormy conditions. After packing I headed for the harbor, and since I had time I stopped for about 10 minutes at a Greek Orthodox Church. The church is one of the larger ones in Rhodes, and heavily decorated on the inside. Frankly I don’t care for the taste of this church, for the roof and a good portion of the walls always have pictures or paintings of Jesus and his disciples. Down the center of the church hang heavy chandeliers and lamps, either in gold or black silver.

        There weren’t many chairs in the church (except along either wall) and the people were standing up, – the men generally on one side and the women on the other. During the 10 minutes that I was there I only heard singing, most of it by the blue-robed, black-beared priest, who incidentally had a fine voice. The people bought candles as they came in, and lite them, and placed them in a big candle holder. The songs were quite nice and I was somewhat impressed by it all.

        I boarded the ship at 10:30, and a half hour later it departed. Paul was also aboard the ship and we conversed throughout much of the day and night. Surprising enough the ship sped along at a nice clip, and even smoother than the one that I had gone to Rhodes on. We were slightly cramped on the deck, but it was interesting to see the people, how they managed with their luggage and children, and to pick up any hints from the type of food they brought along. (There were some with live chicken, but I imagine they were for future use). I had brought some bread, cheese, aprocots, jam and canned corn beef. The latter was terrible and I had to throw it away. Thus the day passed, – quite rapidly and “smooth sailing.”

JUL 16

        I managed to get 4 hours of sleep on the top deck before the ship’s whistle awakened me. I then was too much awake, for I felt the cold air and couldn’t go back to sleep. Paul had a tourist ticket, and he didn’t like his 6 man cabin, so he offered his bunk to me. I readily accepted and proceded to doze off for about 3 ½ more hours. (Incidentally, he is a Fulbright student studying Arabic in Cairo). The sea was even smoother today and we had a fine journey into Piraeus. Docked at 10:15 and by 11:00 AM I was at my hotel in Athens.

        Both of us were starved so I we dropped our things and headed for a restaurant. Food is relatively cheap in Athens and I have enjoyed my meals during my stay here. After a haircut, and the purchase of a few items, I adjourned to the hotel where I proceded to do my washing. Spent 1 hour and 15 minutes of backbreaking work, and I doubt if they are very clean. Oh well, as long as no one sees them except me.

        In the later afternoon I walked up to Benaki Museum, in which are exhibited many fine pottery pieces, clothing and miscellaneous relics of ancient and modern Greece. Fortunately they have guide books in English which one may borrow to enable himself to understand the different displays. From here I went to the same restaurant where I had lunch, and had another fine meal for approximately $.60.

        Tonight was Symphony night and so I journeyed over to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus, which lies at the base of the Acropolis. The setting is tremendous and other than for the fact that the stone seats were quite hard, I don’t think I ever enjoyed a concert as much. The music sounded good to me (actually that is in basis though) and the semi-circular theater with the Roman stone staging, lent a great deal of atmosphere.

JUL 17

        In the morning, while having breakfast at the YWCA, who should walk in but Bob Willis; a fellow I had originally met in Cairo, but who I also bumped into in tel Aviv. Really is a small world. After a lousy breakfast, Bob and I walked to the Archaeological Museum. They had some fine statues and old pottery on display, and while we only stayed an hour – could stay all day or even longer – we were impressed with the craftsmanship of the ancient Greeks.

        It approached 11:00, so I headed for my hotel and departure from Athens. Checked in at TAE airlines at 12:15 and by 2 PM was heading for Istanbul. I sure have flown on a lot of airlines since I left “the Rock” six weeks ago – Northwest, HKA, CPA, BOAC, IAC, AI, BOAC, MEA, LAI, & TAE. We arrived in Istanbul at 4:15 and five minutes later were finished with the custom and currency men and riding into the city. I bought $10 worth of lira before I came, and I am hoping that it will last awhile, since Turkey is in the midst of a terrible inflation; which however, is to the benefit of the tourist.

        Checked into a hotel (will see if I can switch tomorrow) and had a Turkish meal of KABAB and salad. I headed for the Istanbul Hilton Hotel, but got sidetracked at a building near the hotel. It seems that the Harlem Globe Trotters were playing so I bought a cheap ticket & went inside. The house was crowded, although there were still a few vacant seats to be had. Pre-game entertainment consisted of a game between some small boys, an accordi accordion player, a unicycle man and a cowboy. (The crowd seemed to enjoy it all – I didn’t though) Then came the Globe Trotters and their opponents, an all-white team nick-named “Texans.” They put on some antics before the game and then proceded to play their fun-loving, crazy brand of ball. I am afraid I was bored and so I left at the half, however, I think the crowd enjoyed it all. The Globe Trotters miss Goose Tatum, for the man that replaced him is not very good.

        

JUL 18

Ran around like a chicken with his head cut off in the morning, but I managed to get a few things done. Obtained a transit visa from the Yugoslav Consulate, and I hope now that my visa-getting days are finished. I don’t think I will need anymore during my trip home. Stopped at American Express and received some information on trains and ships to and from Yugoslavia, with the result that I will probably leave Istanbul Friday nite.

After lunch I stayed by the Hilton Hotel and took in the view of Istanbul and the Bosphorus from the roof. The hotel is really magnificent and the landscaping superb. There are tennis courts, swimming pools, fountains, circular stoneways, and acres of land overlooking the Bosphorus. Someday I wouldn’t mind staying here awhile.

Decided to do a little sight-seeing, so I took the tram and headed for the European side which is on the other side of the Golden Horn. I visited in succession, the St. Sophia Museum, Mosque of Süleymaniye,  and the Blue Mosque. The architecture is basically the same, all huge structures, with domes at leat 150 feet above the floor, and huge stone columns decorated by paint or tile. The Blue Mosque has 6 minarets, the other having 4 of these slender “pencils” sticking into the sky. I guess the Blue Mosque with its tile interior is the most beautiful, however, the Mosque of Süleymaniye was quite interesting in that a large group of Moslems were praying while I was there. From what I understand tomorrow and the next few days are major Moslem holidays, and throughout Istanbul people were preparing for it by buying coffee and live sheep. Incidentally coffee is dear in inflation-rocked Istanbul, and I saw long lines (of mostly poorer people) waiting to buy a little ½ lb bag. One line got out of order and I saw a policeman use his bully club to restore order. (Pushing the women & hitting the men). Also visited the bazaar (fair), walked in the grounds of the University (nice) and Obelisk of Theodosius.

JUL 19

        At breakfast I met an American Fulbright student on his way to Japan for further study in Physics. Sort of decided to go around Istanbul together, first stop being a ride up the Bosphorus. Took a “Dolmus” (shared taxi) to the Galta bridge and bought a ticket to By Büyük Ada Island, one of the Princes’ Islands. Found out after we boarded the boat that we were going in the wrong direction as the Princes’ Islands were in the Marmaran Sea and not the Bosphorus. Decided to go anyway, and visit the Bosphorus tomorrow.

        The ship was a speedy little ferry boat and we made the journey in about an hour. Passed a couple of other islands on the way, and had a wonderful view of the Istanbul skyline from the Sea. The Island is near the Artistic side of Istanbul, and is a pleasant spot where Turks come to relax and swim. Elliott (Lieb) and I rented a carriage and took an hours ride around the Island which was enjoyable and relaxing, although nothing outstanding. After the ride we had some Turkish food – Dalmas and Su Böreği – which was pretty good. Took the 1:30 ferry back to Istanbul.

        Next we visited the Seraglio Museum, but it and the rest of the Museums were closed sin on account of the Religious Holiday (Bayrami). Not much else to do but walk around, and visit a couple of the Mosques, which we did for a couple of hours. Istanbul seems to be quite interesting, with its divided city, fabulous mosques and minarets, and pleasing sea views. The people dress strictly Western, and one sees very few women with veils. The language is Turkish and not Arabic although the majority of the people are Moslems. The economic condition of the country is quite bad, and inflation is per rampant. (Official rate $1 = 2.80; black market $1 = 10 liras)

        In the evening Elliott and I went to the Halk Oyunlari, a selection of Turkish folk dances. The dances were in colorful costumes and to the accompaniment of horn & drum, drum, drum & accordion & fiddle. They did both lively and slow steps, typical of their region. The dances were quite good and I felt fortunate to have seen them.

        

JUL 20

        I was determined to take the boat ride on the Bosphorus, so I got up early, took my suitcase to the station and arrived with Elliot at the boat pier at 10:00. The trip up the Bosphorus took 2 hours, and the boat was extremely crowded as there were many Turks who were taking advantage of Bayrami to do a little sight seeing of their own.

        Todays trip was much more interesting than yesterdays, as one the boat was close enough to the shore at all times so that one was able to see the people, houses, activities and landscape. We followed the European side of the Sea and stopped at numerous “places of call” in our journey to Saryer, a small port near the point where the Bosphorus meets the Black Sea. The scenery was green and picturesque, and I spent the whole 2 hours at the side railing viewing the old and new houses, people swimming from their front doors, fishing ships, etc. At the narrows, where the Black Sea can be seen, the Turks have a submarine net, and consequently our ship could go no further.

        We got off at Saryer and took a hike up a hill overlooking the countryside. The view was well worth the climb, as we could see for many miles in all directions. To the South could be seen the Bosphorus, and the zig-zag route it takes from Istanbul. To the East were the narrows, and an ideal spot to protect the entry of unwanted visitors. To the North was the Black Sea, and beyond that Russia, however, one could not actually see Russia through the haze. After lunch we took a bus and went back to Istanbul via the overland route; and on the way we saw quite a bit of new construction, – both housing and factories.

        Again everything was closed, owing to the holiday, so we killed a couple of hours walking around the city and visiting The New Mosque. The streets were crowded and it was interesting to observe the Turks and what they do during their holiday. (Nothing much, although the city recreational park was jammed). Saw thousands of Turkish soldiers, both on the streets and at the railroad station, an indication of their huge army.

JUL 21

        Today – all day – was spent on the famous? Orient Express. by no means. I boarded the train last night and was surprised to find the 2nd class (lowest) car quite empty and even had an 8 man compartment to myself. Consequently, I got a good – but sore – nights sleep stretched out on the narrow 4 man seat. Again my air pillow came in handy.

        On the tran were an odd assortment of people, for instance, 1 German news correspondent, 3 Iranians, 3 Iraqis, and 4 Turks. This comprised our car for the majority of the way to Salonika where we stopped for the night. A 100 kilometers or so before Salonika, quite a few Greeks got on the train, but they left when we reached Salonika, the last major stop before crossing the Yugoslav border.

        The train ride was extremely slow and made many steps. The time passed heavily, and it was hard to keep from getting quite bored. The countryside is hilly, and in places, mountainous, and our little steam engine had a hard time climbed climbing the steep grade. A major pest to contend with was the soot from the engine which poured into our car everytime we went through a tunnel. As in lower or Southern Greece, the people looked poor, but they appeared clean and happy, and of course we saw no begging. Many of the fields are strewed with rocks (as in Syria and Jordan) and it is no wonder the people have to work so hard to make a living.

        Talked to a Greek air force jet pilot for a couple of hours, and enjoyed his comments on Greece, the Communist war in 1945-48, Greek women, and his 1 ½ years in the United States. He is a happy go lucky, lady-killer, and is proud of what he is doing. It appears that the Greek people think higher of their Army positions, as the relative pay and privileges make it quite attractive relative to the rest of the economy.

        Since most of the people left the train at Salonika, I was able to stretch out once again, and consequently got a 2nd good nights sleep. I contemplate the worst, though, in Yugoslavia.

JUL 22 (SUNDAY - WEEK 83)

        Fortunately the train was not crowded last night again, and I got a good nights sleep in the 2nd class compartments. Was able to stretch out and “saw wood.” We stayed at the Salonika station all night and left in the morning when the Athens train came in. I met an American from Virginia who said he might go to Dubrovnik, so we stuck together all day. As it turned out, we found out that it is quite difficult to get to Dubrovnik unless one flies, and also, the Yugoslav Consul only gave me a 3 day transit visit. Not wanting to fight these problems, plus the language barriers I decided to go on to Zagreb and spend a day there.

        The whole day was spent on the train and most of it in Yugoslavia. Didn’t have much difficulty at the border (although the Iranian man did have a humorous experience with the conductor, police and a woman who wanted to change money but wasn’t supposed to). The train passes along a river and the general view one sees from the train is quite pretty. The farms are nice, the land cultivated and the people busy – even on Sunday. Was somewhat disappointed that I didn’t see more native costumes, though.

        The best part of the trip was the Yugoslav people that I met. All were friendly, and one even bought us drinks in the dining car. There were a couple of girls near our compartment and I and some of the others had a good time teasing them and being teased in the universal sign language together with a language book. They weren’t very pretty, but quite friendly, and I promised to send one of them a post card. Particularly enjoyed conversing with one gentleman in the next compartment. He is in the Export-Import business and could speak English. He told us that he was a member of the Communist party and a former Partisan Lieutenant. We discussed Yugoslavia, Tito, Russia, USA, Dulles and many other things including the Chetniks, and Tito’s friend who was recently expelled from the party. He appeared intelligent and somewhat liberal, although he said one could not believe in capitalism or religion and be in the party. He said that there was a much improvement in Yugoslavia, particularly in the last 5 years. He also said that he thought that Russia would have a higher standard of living than the USA in 10 years. I said I didn’t know, but that we thought it was better to not rise as fast, if to rise fast one has to do without freedom of speech, religion, press etc. (He didn’t say anything). He went on to say that Yugoslavs liked Americans, but many times couldn’t understand us. (Amen)

        With respect to Tito, he said he did not know him personally. He did say that he was popular as the poor like him (the rich don’t) and there are many poor people in Yugoslavia. The whole conversation was carried on in a friendly manner, and I enjoyed it very much. We all agreed that it would be disastrous to have war, and that a compromise between Communism, Socialism and Capitalism was looming in the future.

JUL 23

        The compartment was crowded and I didn’t get much sleep during the night. Ray (the fellow I had met from Virginia) and I got off the train at Zagreb to spend a day. Checked in a hotel and then decided to go out sightseeing even though we were both tired. Not much to see in Zagreb, so we just walked along the streets (wide, clean and free from Automobiles) and stopped at a few churches and at the market place. The market was just closing for the day – noon – so we didn’t get many pictures.

        Zagreb is the 2nd largest city in Yugoslavia, and the capital of Croatia. The buildings are old, but well kept, and the people seem not too bad off. We were surprised at the little activity that we saw on the streets, although, there were more near the shopping center of town. After a brief nap and writing we again went out. Stood on the corner of a busy intersection for awhile and just watched the people. Didn’t see many soldiers, nor pictures and slogans of Tito. Stopped at the USIS reading room, and as per usual, I think they are it was quite good. They seem to attract quite a few people a day, and are worth the taxpayers money. Ray got tangled up with a Hungarian whore, but I couldn’t see it and so ate supper and went back to the hotel to get some sleep.

JUL 24

        Up at the busk of dawn, lugged our luggate to the train station and (RAY AND I) were on our way at 6:30. The train was somewhat crowded but we managed to crowd our way into some compartments and get seats. The scenery was very nice and I am impressed with this part of Yugoslavia. We had an hour wait at the Yugoslav border, and switched locomotors from soot and steam to electric. (The soot is quite bad on these coal burning trains.) At Trieste we had a cursory customs check, and were then informed of a train strike. Piled out of the train and into buses which took us to Trieste where we switched buses to Venice.

        Venice, Venetzia, craddle of civilization and tourism. I don’t believe I have seen as many tourists on my whole previous trip as I have seen in the few hours tha I have been in venice. Had some difficulty in getting a room, but Ray had a smart idea to ask if there any rooms in private homes. The man at the Italian Tourist Bureau called and got one for us near St. Marks and for only 700 Lire. It appears as if Italy is going to be quite expensive, if hotels and our dinner price is any indication.

        Strolled about Venice at night time, along with all the other tourists. Spent most of the time in and AROUND Saint Marks Cathedral, a beautiful church, even at night time when it was lit up only by moon light. Thousands of people were in the Piazza, some standing and listening or talking and drinking. After the symphony finished, small groups of musicians played dinner music for rich tourists who paid high prices for food and drink. The city is quite charming and I think I will like it in spite of the tourists. Saw the gondollas gliding down the canals, the many islands, houses built right on the waters edge and the many eating & drinking establishments. The Piazza is quite beautiful, however, a new tower they built tends to spoil the symmetry of the architecture and building materials.

JUL 25

        Slept somewhat late, but finally got up and to a corner store for breakfast. A 3rd fellow joined us – Fred Ronte, works for oil company in Egypt – and he and I did sightseeing all day. I bought a pretty good guidebook, and I think it will help me on my visit. Bad luck – dropped my light meter, and took it to a Kodak place where a fellow said he could fix it. (Scared to get the bill).

        First stop, naturally, was Saint Mark’s cathedral and the “Piazza”, the number 1 spot in Venice. The square was jammed with people, of whom 90% were tourists or people trying to sell something to the tourists. Most of the people appear to be Europeans, however, the Americans seem to be the rich tourists with the money to spend “in tourist attractions.” The Cathedral is very impressive, both on the inside and out. The mosaics, statues and architecture tend to make this church the most interesting that I have seen. Near the Cathedral is the Campanile, a 322 foot bell tower, built in 1912 to replace one that had collapsed. From the top one can get a tremendous view of the city, the houses awith their red tile roof, the islands and the lagoons. At 12:00 the figures on the clock tower moved and gonged the bell announcing the hour.

        After lunch – cheese, fruit, beer, bread – Fred and I visited various places in Venice. Walked to and over the Rialto Bridge and gazed in the shops in the bridge. Past the Rialto Market and to the Canal where we got a view of old 15th Century Palace, Ca D’Oro. Hoped in a taxi – large motor launch – and took a trip down the Grand Canal, the main thoroughfare of the city. On each side of the canal are many old houses and palaces of a bygone Golden Era. There were many gondolas, motorboats and other boats carrying on their trade or service on this Canal and the smaller canals. Visited the Palazzo Duccale, but it was closed, so I went to a couple of the outstanding churches – Saint Salvatori and Saint Stefano – both interesting examples of the glory of the Renaissance and a couple centuries prior to that time.

        Just walked around in the evening, – not much doing.

JUL 26

        Fred, Ray and I left early in the morning for Murano, an island about 1 mile from Venice noted for its glass factories. We first visited the museum, but didn’t stay too long as Fred and Ray weren’t very interesting. Near the museum were some factories and we spent about 2 hours watching the men blow and I mold the glass to various patterns. One made a dog, another a woman with a vase (face is pressed into shape by a metal stamp) and a third was working on a swan. I was fascinated by the agility of the men, and the speed in which they made the product. Various colors of glass were used in the designs and each craftsman had 3 apprentices to help him. The equipment consisted of simple pieces, such as board, wood mold, iron plate, and a thing that looked like a huge forceps. Very enjoyable morning.

        I left the others at noon, and went back to Venice. Had a pizza pie for lunch – not as good as the ones in St. Louie – and then walked to St Marks where I picked up my repaired light meter. (Seems to work O.K.) Took the ferry to the Gardens where I spent 3 interesting hours viewing the 18th Biennial International Contemporary Art Exhibit.  Thousands of paintings, motifs and sculpturing was on display and I enjoyed comparing the modern day art with that of the bygone days. I can’t say that I understand much, but still there were some that I liked, with colorful impressions or splashes of paint, and likewise there were many that I did not care for. The mobiles were certainly varied, with some of metal, welded pieces, wood, plastics and almost everything imaginable. Art critic that I am (?) I still appreciated the exhibit.

        Took the ferry to Lido, an island about 7 ½ miles long, between the lagoon and the Adriatic. The Island is a very fashionable resort and I saw many chic women in abreviated swim suits. The beach is very long, with thousands of cabannas along the beach and if it is nice TOMORROW I will spend a day there, tomorrow. They had another concert in the Piazza and I spent some time in the evening listening to it.

JUL 27

        Spent the day on the Lido beach, soaking up the sun and gazing at the good looking women. Met a German boy and an American serviceman, and they, along with Fred and I, spent the 5 or 6 hours making comments about the women and trying to gather up guts to approach a couple of them. The beach seemed to be loaded with Americans in the afternoon, and from information we obtained from them, most of them are on tours of one kind or another. Most of these Americans are of the college age, and appear to have ample money.

        The average American tourist then jumps to the middle age school teacher type who are on fairly tight budgets. The next big batch is the old (50’s – 60’s) man and wife, or each separately, who have been successful in business and who follow American Express tours to the “T”. These are the suckers for which the tourist people grovel, and these are the ones that make Americans appear to have a lot of money, and spend it foolishly and fast. One doesn’t see many Americans going around Europe the hard way, however, I haven’t spent much time near hostels. Of course, the boat fare across the Atlantic is a big obstacle to surmount.

        Most of the tourists that I have seen in Greece, Turkey, Yugoslavia and Italy are Europeans, and many of them on tight budgets. They come in droves, with their short pants, leather pants, funny hats, knapsacks and other camping equipment. Many bring all members of their family and there are youngsters everywhere. Have seen many good-looking, healthy kids; the past World War seems to be “long forgotten” both in memories and standard of living.

        Italy, and or at least Venice, is fascinating and I have had a fine time the last 3 ½ days. Prices are high, though, and I won’t be able to live as cheaply as I did up to now. The Italians sure go for the tourist money and seem to do a good job at wringing it out of the people.

JUL 28

        Met 2 U. City boys on the train (“Mo” Orenstein and Gene Rosenfield) and spent the day sightseeing with them. We were lucky to get a nice room at the Student Hostel (400 Lire) and to find a cheap place to eat (about 300 Lire a meal) Consequently, living in Florence will be under $2 a day. However, entrance fees are quite expensive, and will eat up any savings we might create.

        Florence is the craddle of Renaissance Art, and has many fabulous galleries, museums and churches. My guide book on Italy is adequate and with it and a couple of other pamphlets, we began to visit the sights systematically. First stop was the Convent of San Marco, which houses some famous paintings and frescoes by Fra Angelico. Inside were many small cells of monks from years back, and we were able to walk around and see where they lived, paintings on the walls, and even some souvenirs of the monks. Nearby is the Gallery dell’Accademia which is noted for its Brussels tapestries and statues by Michelangelo. The most outstanding statue is that of “David”, finished in 1505, and declared to be one of his best works. I was quite impressed with the statue and think it to be one of the finest of I have ever seen.

        Down the street, and not too far from the Arno River, stands the Cathedral, one of the most beautiful in Italy and the 2nd largest. The building is about 600 years old and I think, extremely beautiful – particularly the outside. The exterior is faced with colored marble – white, pink and pale green – and has many mosaics, busts and bronze folding doors. The doors are particularly fine, with small, intricate details; raised or set back in the metal. The inside is somewhat bare, – yet has many beautiful stained-glass windows. Two outstanding features in the interior, are the capola cupola with its fresco “Universal Judgement” and statue by Michelangelo, “Descent from the Cross.” Near the Cathedral is the Campanile, a 270’ tower which has become the symbol of Florence. Across the street is the octagonal Baptistery, the origin of which goes back to the year 1000. Its outstanding feature is the “Door of Paradise” with its 10 panels, so delicate in execution that they resemble formal paintings. Also visited San Lorenzo and San Maria Novella, both fine churches.

JUL 29 (SUNDAY - WEEK 84)

        Busy day today, didn’t stop from 7 AM until 5:30 PM. First place we visited was the Church of the Santissima Annunziata  with its extremely decorated ceiling and walls. The work is well executed, but I think too ornate and rich. The more I see of the Catholic Religion and its ceremonies, the less I personally think of it. It all seems pagan and idol worship to me, with its statues of Jesus, Virgin Mary, the Saints and other objects to which one kneels and prays. In most of the Churches in Florence there is a life size figure of Jesus, with his wounds, and lying in the prone position. In many of the churches a father or assistant jingles a money box for contributions, and connected to the Church of San Croce is a leather shop (If that isn’t hypocritical!)

        Enough about the Catholics. Next stop was the Medici Chapels where members of the Medici family are buried. Most impressive thing was the wonderful inlaid marble mosaics so perfect that the colors blend into a picture or design that almost appears painted. The Venetian mosaics were mostly of colored glass, while the Florentine are of precious stones. Also quite good, was 8-10 statues by Michelangelo depicting Dawn, Dusk, Day, Night and various moods of the Medici Dukes.

        Everything is free on Sunday, so we tried to see as much as possible. Visited the National Art Museum which has many paintings, statues, and other objects of art of interest in the study of medieval and Renaissance Art. The Uffizi Museum was next and it occupied the whole afternoon. It is the most outstanding museum of Renaissance Art in the World. There were hundreds of paintings by painters such as Lippi, da Vinci, Boticelli, Raphael, & Giattino, and others. In addition there were fine statues and tapestries, the latter works of art being beyond ones imagination to the length of time it took to make and number of stitches they contained. Can’t say that I thoroughly enjoyed the paintings, as I don’t appreciate religious subjects nor understand the art techniques. I guess I enjoyed it “because one is supposed to enjoy such great art!”) (Enjoyed the Modern Art in Venice better). Also visited San Croce church and attended a symphony in the courtyard of Palazzo Pitti.

JUL 30

        Not nearly as busy today as yesterday, as I decided to see only the main sights. First stop was the Palazzo della Signoria (Palazzo Vecchio), perhaps the most important public building in Florence and the most important example of the “public palace” of the Middle Ages. It was built in 1298-1314 and through the years has housed members of the Medici family, and in later years, the Chamber of Deputies of Italy (1865 - 1871) and the Municipality of Florence. The most important room is the Salone di Cinquecento, an enormous room with elaborate paintings on the walls and ceiling. There is also a statue by Michelangelo, “Victory.” Upstairs are other rooms which have many fine paintings and statues. (One sees so much fine work, that he soon becomes a little unimpressed with “another statue by Michelangelo.”

        Took the route over the Arno River via the Ponte Vecchio Bridge, an enormous two story bridge which has shops on it. Sort of took my time, as I wanted to price some of the leather goods, however, I didn’t buy anything. Did see a lot of fine looking bags, purses, wallets and other leather objects. Not far from the River is the huge Palazzo Pitti (where the concert was held last nite) which was built buy a rival of the Medicis in the 15th Century. Today it houses two art galleries and a museum, the Galleria Palatina being one of the finest in the world. The paintings are displayed in the rooms of the palace, and both the paintings and ornate decorations add something to each other. I saw many Raphaels, Titians, Rubens, and works of other outstanding artists. The subject matter was not as religious as at Uffizi, nor were there as many paintings, and I believe I enjoyed this gallery more than the one I saw yesterday. Also visited the Modern Art Gallery and thought it “so-so”, the modern art not nearly as good as the work that I saw in Venice.

        Around 2 PM I left the Palace ands trolled around the Giardino (garden)di Bobolia which was quite nice. Then I followed the Arno River to the Piazzale Michelangelo, where one has a tremendous view of the city. Florence seems to lie in a valley, and is surrounded on most of its sides by mountains. Bought my train ticket to Rome, and went to bed early, as I plan to get up at 3:45 AM to catch the train.

JUL 31

        Got up early, and broke my back lugging my baggage to the train station. The ride to Rome was pleasant, and we passed through some pretty country. Arrived in Rome at 9 AM and again carried my bags to the Student Hostel. The distance was greater than I thought, and I think I pulled my shoulder out of joint. The hostel was filled and so they sent me to a lousy pension near by but I was too tired to look any further.

        First order of business was the American Embassy, where I picked up my mail – 13 letters in all. It was great hearing from home, and finding out that all are O.K. and ready to go on nice vacations. Also, received a letter from Junko, half in English and half in Japanese. Consequently, I had to go to the Japanese Embassy to have it translated. (Nothing in the letter, just small talk). My last task was to go to the Ministry of Culture and get a permit to visit the museums. If I would have had it in Florence it would have saved me a lot of money.

        Decided to rest awhile, and tow rite an overdue letter home. It seems that I am writing fewer and fewer letters, however, I just don’t seem to want to make more time available for letter writing. Also, it is quite expensive in Italy to mail things home. Around 5, I gathered my things together and went out to do a little sightseeing. Visited San Maria Maggiore Church, and as before, was interested in it because it is a huge, well-treasured church; and not because I like the decoration, figures and other garbage.

        From here I walked to the Colosseum, one of the most photographed sights in Rome. The Colosseum is a huge Ampitheater which can hold about 50,000 spectators. It was begun in 72 AD and is the largest edifice of Ancient Rome. Ones imagination leaps back to the early centuries, when game, combats and fights between men and animals were held here for the amusements of the spectators. After supper I went with a fellow I met at the pension (Bill Crutchfield) to see a performance of Aida at the Terme di Caracalla (old Roman baths). Enjoyed the setting, but too tired to enjoy the performance.

AUG 01

        Still tired from the day before, however, I pulled myself out of bed at 8:30 and dressed to go out and see Rome. Rome is a huge city, and one has to take trolley cars or buses to the various sights, otherwise he will walk himself to death. The city is clean, and quite modern, and there appears to be quite a few things to see and do. The weather is extremely hot, and Bill and I noticed it as we tramped around the city. Seems as if we could never get enough water.

        Took the trolley to Gianicolo Park, and walked through it on the way to the Vatican. There is a famous statue of Garibaldi here, and near by one can get a good view of the city. I had Bill take a picture of me with my 12 day old mustache. It is getting to be a nuisance, however, & I believe that I will soon shed it. We were quite impressed as we rounded a turn in the street, and came upon the Piazza San Pietro, the famous square and Colonnade that lies in front of the St. Peters Cathedral. The square is huge and one can understand now how so many people can jam in there to see and hear the Pope. (He is at his summer’s residence now).

        The Church is the largest in the Catholic world, and I think it has one of the most beautiful domes that I have seen. The architecture and decorations (done by Michelangelo) are superb, and make the rest of the garbage-strewn church look ridiculous. The Church has too much gold decorations and statues of saints and popes to suit my taste. One statue – however ”Pieta”, by Michelangelo, is great, and I spent quite a length of time gazing at it and the Virgin mary, for I think he has represented her as I would imagine her to be – simple, pure and universal looking.

        Nearby is the Vatican Museum and Sistine Chapel. The Chapel is quite famous, and has some celebrated celebrated paintings on the walls and ceiling by Michelangelo, Botticelli, Signorelli and Rosselli. The Museum has many fine statues plus some rooms with design and paintings of Raphael. From here we visited the Basilica San Angelo, an immense fortress overlooking the Tiber River.

AUG 02

        Got an early start and took the tram to the National Art Gallery. Didn’t see much that I liked (nor did Bill who accompanied me) and we headed for the Villa Borghese where there was an old house – now a museum – surrounded by beautiful gardens. I have begun to tire of museums, so I didn’t spend much time looking at the statues and paintings. The walk in the grounds was quite nice and peaceful, and for a change we weren’t dodging the deadly Italian traffic, – particularly the hordes of motor scooters.

        Progressing South we arrived at the Trinita Dei Monti, an old Spanish Church with many steps leading up to it.
