I guess it is most famous because Audrey Hepburn ran up the steps in “Roman Holiday.” Not too far from here was the Fontana Di Trevi, also famous for its part in Hollywood’s, “Three Coins in a Fountain.” Naturally, I had to throw in a coin, so that someday I can come back to Rome. It was interesting watching the people make their wishes, throw turn around, and then throw in their coins. The Pantheon or Rotunda, built in 27 B.C. is one of the most interesting engineering feats in Rome. The building is well preserved, and its magnificent dome is still intact. The dome is 141 feet wide and high, and is pierced by a hole which admits the only light in the building. In the building are located the tombs of Raphael and a few members of the House of Savoy.

        Next on the list was Piazza Navona (interesting fountain); Piazza del Campidoglio (once the political and religious center of the Roman Empire – and which now has a monument to King Victor Emmanuel II which is a huge marble structure dominating the scene); Colosseum; and San Pietri Vincoli (in which is located Michelangelo’s fabulous statue of Moses, so life-like, that it appears ready to move at any moment). It was a crowded but interesting day.

        In the evening, Bill and I put on suits and visited a night club. We found a cheap one! – and sipped a $1.25 beer for an hour while we watched the really attractive hostesses. Danced with one of them, but left before she could plant her expensive body and stomach at the table.

AUG 03

        Today was quite interesting. Visited the Catacombs of Saint Callixtus in the morning, and enjoyed wandering through the extensive passageways. Our guide – a priest – said that the early Christians used the Catacombs for burial of their dead and for secret meetings, and also that the Romans knew of the catacombs but generally left them alone because they were cemeteries. Took the bus to back along the Appian Way – narrow, but in good condition – and arrived at the thermae of Caracalla, – ruins of a huge bath built in 212-217. The ruins are immense and thousands must have been able to use it at the same time. In the summer evenings, operatic productions are given here among the natural ancient settings. Not far from the Baths is San Giovanni in Latin Church, another of the huge, outlandishly decorated Roman churches. It was a pleasure to visit San Paolo Church, one of the latest churches in the city. It is huge, but much simpler (in some respects) than the other Renaissance and 18th century “baroque decorated” churches. It did have 80 granite columns, but they were plain and quite attractive. Enjoyed the stained glass windows the most, as they were quite different from what one generally sees. (The glass seems to be faced depict_ in various patterns and yellowish-brown colors)

        Along with the Catacombs, the most interesting things were the Roman Forum and Palatine, situated near the center of Rome. Much of the ruins are in a fine state of preservation, and I got a thrill walking in the passageways, among the columns and near the broken columns, statues and structure. The hill where the Emperors built their residences was magnificent, and hard to believe that the basic materials – mud and brick – could last so long. Walked near the famous arches of Septimus and Titus, gazed at the spot where Julius Caesar was cremated, and stood next to the ruins of the Rostras, where orators harangued the crowds. It was really a page out of history.

AUG 04

        I wanted to get an earlier start to Naples, but the first available train got us in around 10:15. Checked our bags and then bought tickets to the excavations at Pompei where we spent the afternoon. The visit to the “unburied city” is one of the highlights of the trip to Italy. The buildings are in an excellent state of preservation, and one is able to see how the people were living in the year 79 AD when the eruption of Mount Vesuvius took place. The life seemed to be simple, yet rich, and there are many paintings and decorations on the insides of the houses.

        Some of the houses were of the wealthy and influential, and these houses had nice courtyards, gardens, and pools where rain water was collected from a hole in the roof. Everything about the houses seemed straight and geometric, and even functional in the sense we think of it today. The Romans or Pompeians of that era and previously to 79 AD, had been influenced by the Greeks, and there are Greek temples, paintings, and other influences from the Greek civilization. I can rightly say that I was very much impressed with the excavation and the manner in which the inhabitants lived almost 2000 years ago.

        Back in Naples, Bill and I just walked around town after getting a room in a cheap pension. Naples is a big, dirty, port city and full of pimps preying on the numerous US sailors that are on liberty. Sort of feel a little uneasy here, and I will watch my possessions quite closely. We continued to eat in relatively cheap joints, and I must say that it is strictly quantity and not quality. Generally speaking, we walk everywhere and try to economize as much as possible.

        The people in Italy don’t seem much different than those in the States. Perhaps they are more argumentative, but they are quite decent about helping us fiend our way. The people are poor as in Yugoslavia and Greece, an there are many more beggars. Can’t truthfully say that I would come here if it weren’t for their wonderful historic sights and spots like Venice.

        

AUG 05 (SUNDAY - WEEK 85)

        Bill and I took the early boat to Capri, and our luck continued as the weather was perfect. We decided to stay at a student pension – cheap but without many of the luxuries – and to see as much of the Island as we could before taking the boat to Sorento early in the morning. The Isle of Capri is very attractive, perhaps more outstanding as one approaches the island than when he is on it The cities of Capri and Anacapri are located high up the mountainsides, and one either has to take long, winding roads, or ride the funicular from the harbor to Capri.

        The island is solely for tourists and there were plenty of them – perhaps because it was Sunday. One can go walking, swimming (places didn’t appear too good), take a boat ride or many other diversions. We started to take a boat ride to the famous Blue Grotto, but were told that it was too rough to permit entry into the grotto. Decided to visit Mount Solaro (1935’) instead. One reaches the summit by an interesting chair-lift ride over houses and vineyards. The view from the top was fabulous as one can see the whole Island before him, including the peninsula on which are located Amalfi and Sorento. Even Naples and huge Vesuvius can be seen clearly as there was very little haze blocking ones view of the landscape. Perhaps the most interesting feature was the steep cliffs which plunged into the blue sa beneath our observation tower. We tried to figure how long it would take a rock to hit bottom, but some safety conscious people stopped us.

It was still early so we decided to walk to the Blue Grotto via Anacapri. The walk was interesting, at least thru the town, as it was a narrow, winding road which passed white, clean-looking houses. We were forewarned of our troubles coming back up, as the final ⅔ of the walk was over a steep rocky path. Finally got to the Grotto, but as we found out earlier, it was too rough to enter. We could see the blue water though, and imagine how it must appear in the inside. The route back up was torturous, and we didn’t think we would make it. We did, though, and returned to the pensions for supper and sleep.

 

AUG 06

        Our boat pulled away from Capri at 0645 and I really wasn’t sorry to leave except that I did not see the Blue Grotto from the inside. Personally I believe the Island to be over-rated, however, I guess I wasn’t there long enough to give it a fair shake. We landed at Sorento, a lovely, little town about an hour’s distance from Vesuvius. Walked about a bit before catching the train, and admired the clean, quiet streets. The train ride to Vesuvius passed through orchards and vineyards, and as near the coast as it could. There are many towns along Naples Bay, many of which are fishing villages.

        At Vesuvius Station we received a blow – 950 Lire to take a bus and then the chair lift to the crater. At first we were hesitant, but since we had come so far, we decided to go on. The chair-lift was interesting, and the view from the crater’s edge quite spectacular. One could see for hundreds of miles in all directions, and if if weren’t so hazy I would have taken a lot of pictures. The volcano was a little disappointing, as one could see no lava, only a gapping crater with little puffs of smoke coming out of various places. The last time the volcano went off was in 1944 and I was hoping it would do some KIND of performance today – no luck!

        Back the way we came up and thence in to Naples. It was still early so we visited the National Museum, perhaps one of the nicest that I have seen in Europe. It has nice paintings (Raphael, Titian, Breughel – ”The Blind Leading the Blind”, Lippi and others); a huge collection of statues, – both Greek and Roman; and many examples of objects found at Pompei. I guess the last exhibit interested me the most, as I enjoyed the simple, yet delicate paintings of the Pompei Era, the daily utensils, gold jewelry, gladiator helmets, and a scale mock up of the excavations. I think, though, that the objects would look better in their original setting.

        Visited the Naples Cathedral (fair) and walked in the courtyard of the Castel Nuovo. Stopped in at the USO and had a shave and 2 cups of real American (Brazilian) coffee for a change. Then took the night train to Pisa and didn’t get a wink of sleep.

AUG 07

        Bad night – no sleep. Pulled into Pisa at 5 AM and adjourned to the waiting room where I slept for about 1 ½ hours. Bill and I then headed for the Piazza del Duomo where the main buildings are situated. The Leaning Tower is just that – and it was interesting to frame it in an imaginary rectangle and notice how it deveates from the perpendicular. (Actually, 14 feet). The tower is quite nice, and aside from the fact that it leans, it is famous because Galileo used the tower for his experiments on the fall of solid objects.

        The A nearby Baptistery (1153) and Cathedral (1063) are very nice, and we spent some time walking there and then sitting to study further the objects and designs that appear the best to us. I still can’t seem to care for the gold-flowery roof, baroque lines and lavish decorations of the Renaissance Churches. I feel sure that I would like them better if they were simple, particularly the ones we saw today.

        Bill and I departed at 10 AM, as he now heads for Venice. A real nice fellow, even though he is too gullible. Small world though – bumped into Mo, Gene and Victor (fellows I knew in Florence) and we rode the train together, – at least to Santa Margherita where I got off. Had a little difficulty getting a room or bed, and managed to get one for the price of 1000 Lire. (too much). Got my bathing suit on and heading for the beach. Was quite shocked and disappointed to find a puny little rock beach, overcrowded with people. I was all set to leave tonight, but I decided to go to another place tomorrow and see if they have a sand beach. Can’t see how people like stone beaches, and how this place got such a famous name. Nothing about the swimming is good, and hotel and restaurant prices are high. Most admit that it is a pretty little cove with houses built on the hillside which comes almost too the water. The hills are all green and the light colored houses stand out quite nicely. Hit the sack early in the evening.

AUG 08

        Great night for sleeping, – and I got 10 long hours in. Washed some stuff in the morning, re-arranged some things and then gathered my swimming clothes together for a day at the beach. Took the bus to Paraggi, a small cove near Santa Margherita which has a sand beach (all 70 yards of it.) Still it was quite sufficient, and very beautiful, as there were many boats; umbrellas; homes near the shore and then green mountains rising abruptly; and the “air” that I thought I would find on the Riviera.

        Swam, sun-bathed and read for about 6 hours, and had a good rest. The sun was strong, and there weren’t too many people. Didn’t meet anyone, – in fact I saw no Americans and heard only a handful of British. Late in the afternoon I walked to a nearby resort – Portofino which is also picturesque and expensive (for what!). There were only boats here, and I do not know where the people go to swim, – perhaps Paraggi.

My stay in Italy is fast coming to an end. I will catch the morning train for Nice, and then Switzerland. I liked Italy as there was much to see and do. Venice was No. 1, and then followed Rome, Pompei and Florence. Somewhat disappointed in Capri and the Riviera, particularly the latter. (The beaches I saw were not very good.) The people were very friendly and helped me a lot in getting around. I didn’t care so much for the food, still I didn’t eat in the best places. However, one begins to wonder what the average person lives on, for I never got much even when I spent a dollar a meal.

Transportation is cheap and crowded, but quite sufficient. I didn’t notice much effect from the war, perhaps Pisa being the city I noticed the most ruins in. Tourists are a big business in Italy and the Italians are out to get as much as they can (I don’t blame them for that). Must admit that now that I have seen the main spots and sights, I don’t have any burning desire to return to Italy. It is not my idea of a country where one can relax and be carefree.

Route as of August 8th, 1956 – end of Chapter 14.

CHAPTER 15 - CONTINENTAL CROSSING

August 8th, 1956 - September 6th, 1956

AUG 09

        Up at 3:30 and on the way to the station by 4. My blue B-4 bag will be the end of me yet. I now carry it on my back, for if I attempt to carry it by hand, it nearly pulls my arm out of the socket after 10-15 minutes. It took 7 hours to get to Nice, but the train ride wasn’t too bad as we followed the coastline from Santa Margherita to the French Riviera. Passed thru Monaco, but I decided to come back later to visit the casino. The only unpleasant part of the trip was the fact that I noticed a small black spot in my right eye. I thought at first that it was a foreign particle but it wouldn’t wash out. Doesn’t hurt, nor does it look bad; yet one doesn’t like to see such a thing in his eye.

        Ran around quite a bit in Nice trying to locate a room, and get a bus ticket to Grenoble. Settled in a dormitory (crowded and dirty, yet cheap) and put on my bathing suit to sun bathe. The beach in Nice is all small stones, and not the type that I like. Certain parts are free and other parts are private; the latter such beaches having boards on which to lie. The bikini bathing suits are quite a sight – brief and exposing, and quite interesting to observe. I like the way the men and women wrap a towel about their bodies, and then proceed to change clothes. (I was waiting for one of them to fall, but no such luck) The Riviera is very crowded at this time of year, and prices are high. In the evening the streets were jammed with people walking here and there, or sitting watching the other people do the walking.

        My eye got redder – perhaps because I sat out in the sun – nevertheless I decided to visit the British-American Hospital and have them take a look. Walked at least 6 miles to the Hospital only to find that there wasn’t a doctor on duty. Decided to wait and see how it is in the morning to determine whether I should go to Grenoble and Geneva. If anything has to be done, I would prefer to have it done in Switzerland.

AUG 10

        My eye still had the black spot in it, however, since it wasn’t red, nor did it hurt, I decided to take the bus trip today. We had a full bus and it was a fairly modern one, although I had the misfortune to be seated over the rear wheels. The trip lasted 10 hours, including 5 stops, but it went quite fast and was very interesting. The bus followed “La Route Napoleon”, supposedly the same route NAPOLEON took when he returned from Exile in Elba.

        The scenery was extremely beautiful, for we passed through and over the portion of the French Alps between Nice and Grenoble. The mountains had many green trees on their slopes, and the rich pastures in the valleys added to the beauty. Here and there were lakes, waterfalls, snow on the tops of the mountains, holes in the mountain-side and many flowers which perfumed the air. The towns were small, but picturesque, and it was amusing to see the 2 story houses with hay in the second floor. Didn’t notice any particular costumes, and as a matter of fact I haven’t seen any unusual clothing since I arrived in Europe.

        Although the sun was bright, it wasn’t too uncomfortable when we were moving. Generally, whe we stopped for a few minutes of rest, I got out and walked about. We arrived in Grenoble about 7 PM and I made arrangements to leave tomorrow for Geneva. The air is much cooler here, and it appeared as if it had been, or was about to rain. I decided to go to the Youth Hostel, and after a long search, finally found the place. (questionable noun). One section – where I decided to sleep – was an a classroom, with 13 wooden bunks and straw-bedding mattresses,. No sheets, or anything – except one clean! Blanket – but I guess for 100 Francs one can’t be choosy. Anyway, I didn’t want to cash any more dollars, and I hadn’t tried the Youth Hostels before. Too old to use the hostels in Switzerland, so I guess I will have to pay a little more, and at the same time, enjoyed the luxuries, ice showers and sheets.

AUG 11

        Difficult to write with only one eye, as one can’t judge distance very well. I went to the Clinic in the afternoon, and one of the doctors used a needle to remove the foreign particle that was lodged in the eye. He then covered it with a bandage – Hathaway shirts – and asked me to come back tomorrow. So, it looks as if there isn’t anything serious.

        I left Grenoble in the morning and had a pleasant bus ride to Geneva. We didn’t pass over any mountains, yet there were mountains all around. The air was cool, and in some places it was raining, consequently I took out my blue jacket when we arrived in Geneva. The countryside appeared green and quite fertile, and the cultivated plots extended quite aways up the sides of the mountains. Wheat and hay seemed to be the major crops, plus quite a few cows and/or cattle.

        Geneva is a very pretty town, situated on the SW shores of Lake Leman. Today, and for the next couple of days, the “Fetes of Geneva” are taking place, with parades, fireworks, concerts and colorful costuming. Big, beautiful flags of the Swiss Federation were flying everywhere and added much color to the city. I didn’t do much, since I spent quite a bit of time at the clinic, however, I was able to see quite a bit of the city on my tram ride to and from the clinic. Everything is neat and clean; and the people appear healthy and friendly. The clothes were of a decent quality and fashion and it appears that the Swiss have a relatively high standard of living.

        In the evening I went to the Festival and watched an hour-long fireworks display over the lake. Then everybody bought confetti and walked around throwing it on everybody else. Later in the evening they had some Swiss folk dancing which was quite colorful and entertaining.

AUG 12 (SUNDAY - WEEK 86)

        The doctor at the clinic removed the bandage, and said it looks all right. From the Hospital I walked to some of the “listed” sights in Geneva that the tourist must see. In rapid order I saw the Reformation Monument (simple, adequately done yet not outstanding), Town Hall (not much) and the Cathedral. I sat thru 30 minutes of the service, and enjoyed the organ music but fell asleep when the minister preached the sermon – in French naturally. The church is quite different from the overly-decorated Italian churches and I thought its lack of ornaments or paintings added to the spiritual feeling that one sometimes finds in churches.

        Missed the boat on the UN building, as it was closed when I got there. Perhaps I will wait until tomorrow noon to leave, so that I will have a chance to see it. Had some time to kill before the matinee program of the Festivities, so I strolled through the Park and to the docks where there were many sailboats, motorboats and a couple large Lake boats. I took the time on the program, as the time at which the parade would start, however it wasn’t until 1 hour later before anything showed up.

        The Lake roads were jammed with thousands of people and I had a rough time getting a halfway decent spot. The parade was quite good, and lasted almost an hour. There were many floral displays, with pretty girls throwing flowers to the audience crowd. The various sections of Switzerland were represented by boys and girls in costumes of their part of the country. The groups danced, sang and strolled by as the people cheered and clapped in approval. In addition there were a couple of commercial displays, one of the best being Air India’s four elephants, and beautiful maiden on a flying carpet. Pey Perhaps the best float was one that had a girl on a cloud, and from the cloud dangled parachutes which held little boys and girls. The expressions on the faces of the kids were priceless, and I am sure they did not know what to make of it all.

        Went to the festivities in the evening, but was disappointed as they only had groups from the afternoon parade and more confetti.

AUG 13

        I was very glad that I stayed over to see the Old League of Nations Building (now the European Hqs for the UN). The Building is very beautiful, particularly the front which faces on the Lake. The grounds are well kept, and the Wilson monument is back quite unique with its rotating heaven of stars. A guide took us through the building and we saw the various chambers, plus one of the meeting rooms. The committee on Crime Prevention had its first meeting this morning and I sat in the public section for a few minutes; however, they were only getting organized (no murder or rape statistics!)

        Took the 12:37 train to Lausanne and went immediately to the Kodak shop. If all goes well, I can pick them up tomorrow nite at 5 PM, at which time I will be anxious to see if and how they turned out; for I am a little pessimistic about them since I have been carrying them for over 2 months. Decided to go to Montreux so I bought my ticket and then killed an hour walking about Lausanne. Not much to see – did visit the Cathedral and Art Museum – but the town appeared quite clean & pleasant. Something about these Swiss towns that I like.

        Montreux is a big resort on the Lake and my difficulty in getting a room proves the above fact. (13 Fr for room & Continental breakfast, which is a robbery.) The location of the city is perfect, – being on the edge of the Lake and at the opposite end from Geneva. All around are towering mountain peaks, some of them 8,000 -10,000 feet high and still with snow on their cap. Other mountains are green with trees, and sprinkled on their slopes are occasional homes or chateaus, which are quite impressive. Sports, hiking and enjoying the scenery are the main things to do here. One thing I noticed was the many Englishmen that I saw about town. This must be one of their favorite Swiss vacation spots. (It would be mine, too, if I had the money.)

AUG 14

        It looked like it would be a nice day, so I began to walk up to Glion and Caux, two cities on a mountain near Montreux. Decided to hitch-hike and was glad that I did because it began raining and continued all day. The rain and clouds took a great deal away from the beauty, but still the sight from Caux (3500’) overlooking Montreux, the Lake and the other Mountains was quite impressive. There are many trees on the slope, and their dark green, plus the lighter green of grass and the yellow of the pastures made a pretty picture to behold.

        As I stood near one of the buildings, and latter in garage, waiting for the rain to stop, I began reflecting on the points that I had jotted down in my little book. Questions such as “What is my purpose on earth?” and “Do I believe in fate or free will?” interested me and I jot thought of each and mate notes of same. I have decided to buy a book and began analyzing some of the question which up to now I have ignored. It is so much better to think on these lines, than on much of the Trivial that I have been thinking of up to now.

        On the way down the mountain, I stopped at what I thought was a hotel, but what turned out to be the Caux Mountain Haus, no one of the two International Conference Meeting Places (the other is at Mackinac Island) for Moral Rearmament.  I had heard of the organization in connection with the controversy over its play “The Vanishing Island” but did not know much about it. One thing led to another and I soon found myself staying all day, finally leaving at 9:53 PM. During this time I met some of the members (or workers, for no one joins or quits – there is no membership) and attended two meetings, a play and saw 2 movies.

        Basically MRA is based on thoughts from God to Man, which he obtains by listening during a half hour or so a day that he devotes to his “Quiet Time.” He practices world changes, a re-making of the world based on absolute honesty, unselfishness, purity and love. If there is no re-shaping of man, then man is doomed, for he is becoming more entangled every day. God’s work is the main basis of MRA

        Many of the people at Caux – about 700 – were vitally interested in MRA, some devoting all of their lives and material wealth. The organization exists from donations of people, and food and other services offered by people interested in MRA. The work seems to be directed to influencing bodies of the countries of the world to become enlightened, unsullied statesmen. Today, there was present Heads of the Universities of Zurich and Rangoon, President of the Finnish Parliament, and some influential African leaders. The people were from all over the world, and I guess I have never seen such a cosmopolitan group. The play, and the films were excellent and illustrate quite professionally the MRA has to make.

There was some very interesting entertainment – a Ceylonese folk singer, African Gold Coast drummers and an International choral group. It was quite a day.

AUG 15

        Visited the Castle of Chillon near Montreux and found it to be quite picturesque and interesting. The Castle (built in the 13th century and the subject of a poem by Lord Byron) is built on a rock that projects out into the Lake. it is complete in that it has the rooms one would imagine to be in a Castle of Old – dungeon, storeroom, towers, bedrooms, banquet halls, etc. One interesting room was the latrine, the first room of this nature that I have seen in an old medieval building. The crapper consisted of 2 boards and the crap falls down into the lake.

        Went to Lausanne in the afternoon and picked up my film. Glanced thru the boxes and nothing drastic appears to be wrong. Took the train to Bern and got situated in a pension. Had a fine evening meal and then went to the Kursaal, a Casino-Dance Hall-Bar place which seems to cater to the middle class. Quite enjoyable.

AUG 16

        I shared a room in a pension with Charlie Trinkham from Massachusetts. (Recent graduate of Duke). We toured Bern together, viewing the sights and getting into discussions concerning such things as segregation in the South, America’s foreign policy and the world today. The first sight we saw was the famous Clock tower with its ingenius mechanism which moves, gongs, or hits the bell. From here we visited the Cathedral, perhaps the nicest that I have seen thus far. When I say nice, i mean with respect to such things as spiritual structure and simplicity worthy of worship. The church is Gothic, and has fine spires and stain glass windows. The inside is bare, although the roof has on it some nice simple designs, and there is a beautiful organ in the front end of the church. I like to compare this church with the overly decorated, idol worshipping churches I saw in Italy.

        Not too far from the church – incidentally we climbed to the roof, where we had a great view of Bern, and the mountains in the distant – were the Bear Pits, the symbol of Bern. They have about 6 bears and 6 cubs, and the latter animals were full of fun and play, and provided the crowd with a lot of laughs. Bern has a beautiful garden – the Rose Garden – where we admired the flowers, and also sat a while, as the Gardens overlooked the city and the Aare River and provided a relaxing place to talk.

        In the afternoon we strolled by the Town Hall, and then went to the other side of the river to visit the Alpine and Postal Museum. The museum was interesting, as they it had many alpine pieces of equipment plus pictures and displays of the Alps. Downstairs in the Postal Mus section were relics of the past years concerning the mail and telegraph and telephone improvements. Next door was a well laid out historical museum. In general, I like Bern very much, as it is a clean town, has good food, interesting shops and a certain charm about it that is lacking in most cities.

AUG 17

        Didn’t have as much trouble as I thought I would in getting up, to the station, and on to Interlaken. I kept one eye peeled at the sky since I decided that if it wasn’t a good day, I would rather postpone my trip than pay $7.50 to see rain. The sky was blue and the sun bright, so I bought my ticket and headed up the mountain via railroad and railroad-cog cars to the Jungfrau.

        The view from the cars is spectacular, as one it climbs the steep grade to a point approximately 11,300 feet above sea level. The last 4,000 feet is covered thru a tunnel blasted out of solid rock. The engineering feats in building the railroad, tracks and tunnels is quite amazing. Saw some fine glaciers that were slowly making their way down the mountains; green pastures with cows (and their delightful bells); many colorful wild flowers, and of course the snow capped peaks that rise to heights up to 13,600 ft.

        The final tunnel is amazing as it gives on the feeling that he is underground, and not 11,000 feet in the air. Then to have it snow, and to walk in snow, when it is very hot back in Interlaken, is like coming in and out of a climate or time machine. During the first hour that I was on the observation plateau, the weather was clear, but it gradually turned cloudy and began to snow. Even when the sun was out, the wind was so cold that it hurt my ears. Visited an underground “palace” dug out of solid ice, and walked to the point where people were skiing on a slight slope.

        Took the train down to Kleine Scheidegg (6700 ft) and walked around there for an hour, breathing the thin air and admiring more and more, those mountain climbers that go up 28,000 feet or so. The ride down was as interesting as the ride up, and it certainly was an interesting day.

AUG 18

Took the early train to Brienz, a picturesque little woodcarving village on the eastern edge of Lake Brienz. I spent the whole morning, walking about, and stopping to observe various things that interested me. Woodcarving, like glass blowing, is a fascinating act, and when I passed a shop where an elderly man was carving an antelope from a block of wood, I stopped and watched him for about an hour. The block was first sawed into approximate shapes, and then roughed into form using a mallet and woodcarving tools. He then used finer tools, and an experienced eye to carve the shape into a realistic looking antelope. It was quite interesting to see him work, – and to mold the figure with such speed.

        The town isn’t very big, and consists of some tourist shops, hotels, etc on each side of the highway that ran thru the town. There is a woodcarving school in Brienz and I came in the back way, and observed some of the young boys doing some of their work. It appears to be a modern school as the building and equipment looks new, and they have many human and animal figures of anatomy for reference. From the school, I walked along the side streets and watched the people at work and the children at play. Most of the buildings are wooden, but quite large and “liveable”. As in Bern, all the houses had flowers in the windows, and the bright colors did much to liven up the dark lumber. The town is a stopping place for one of the Lake Boats, and so I journeyed to the Lake to watch the arrival of a boat, gaze at the scenery and observe some people feeding some swans.

        Took the afternoon train to Lucerne, and went to the Symphony Concert (part of the Lucerne Music Festival) in the evening. Isaac Stern was the soloist and he did a creditable job with the violin. The program was contemporary music, and the audience clapped quite enthusiastically at the end.

 AUG 19 (SUNDAY - WEEK 87)

        I met an American Girl at the concert last night (Clara Karl from Chicago) and we walked around Lucerne together. It was cloudy and misty in the morning, but turned out quite sunny in the afternoon. Lucerne is, very beautiful, as it is situated at the foot of the Lake of Lucerne on the river Reuss which issues from it. The buildings are somewhat old, and quite tall, and are built on the river and lake’s shores. There are two old, covered bridges across the river, each of which has religious paintings hanging on the rafters. Some of the outstanding sights in the city are the nine towers part of the largest fortification in Switzerland; a Lion Monument erected in memory of some brave Swiss defenders; and an old town Hall. In the afternoon, Clara and I strolled about town with all the other inhabitants, admiring the beauty of the lake, boats and mountains; and breathing in the pure air, scented with handfuls of flowers.

        Lucerne is a very picturesque town, and has all the great Swiss attributes of cleanliness, flowers, and friendliness. I wouldn’t mind living in any of the three large towns – Geneva, Bern, Lucerne – that I have visited. I guess I can say that Switzerland is as near to the USA as any country that I have visited; and in addition, has the good features of beautiful scenery and an a seemingly, unmaterialistic attitude.

        Took the evening train to Zug, a small little town situated on a lake. Thought I would be able to get a room with a shower (have been staying in dormitories for the last couple of nights) but still no “douche”. Strolled about town before supper, and liked the lack of tourists and tourist establishments. The streets are narrow, and of brick construction, and in typical European fashion, have very narrow sidewalks. Ate dinner in a typical little German-Swiss restaurant and had fun trying to order a meal. The waitress shook my hand at the beginning and when I left.

AUG 20

        Slept late, and it was a pleasure, as I was tired and the bed was quite comfortable. The sun was bright when I got up, but then disappeared and rain clouds drifted over. Had my usual breakfast of bread, cheese and some fruit. This morning I also purchased a bottle of milk which tasted quite good.

        Morton had met a Swiss girl when he was in Zug, so I decided to look her up and say hello. After a little difficulty, I located her at her office, and introduced myself as the brother of MW. She was a nice looking girl, well dressed and could speak good English. After some introductory remarks, she invited me (and la Clara) to accompany her and ride around Zug. She drove to a small lake cabin which her father had built, and there we talked for about an hour and a half. She poured drinks, and furnished pleasant conversation, consequently I had a very enjoyable time. The house is modern, but small, and situated right on the lake’s edge, so that one had a view of the lake, mountains and surrounding land. Zug is a very picturesque city, and is not overrun by tourists since the canton of Zug refuses to sell much of the land around the lake. In this manner, they intend to keep the surrounding land in woods and pasture, and to provide pleasing scenery. I think it would be nice to live here, and either commute to Zurich (25 minutes) or to live WORK in Zug itself as they have a number of industries here. The nicest thing about the city is that it is so close to lake, mountain and big city, so that one has many sports or things to choose from.

        Took the train to Zurich and arrived adi amidst much rain. The rain doesn’t bother me too much as Zurich is not a picturesque town, instead it is a big, modern city, the largest in Switzerland. It too is located on a lake, but the lake is not nearly as charming as that at Lucerne or Geneva. Got some mail at American express, and walked about town, stopping here and there to window shop or to visit a church or other listed sight. Saw a lousy movie, “Helen of Troy” in the evening.

AUG 21

        More rain, but like yesterday, the rain doesn’t bother me very much here in Zurich. Went to the Dow Chemical International and spoke to the manager, Ted Knapp, for about an hour. Sales work sounds good, and this branch of Dow is just beginning to grow. However, I think Sales work or work overseas is best for a family man, or for those who prefer the life and of a single man. Not easy to find mates overseas, and one is likely to get into a rut, dating foreign women, and playing around with same.

        I visited the National Historical Museum but didn’t care for it too much. It was loaded with objects, but the titles were in German and also, I think I am just getting a little sick of “average museums.” Had some time to kill before my train, so I began a couple letters – long overdue – to Mom and Carolyn & Morton. Took the 1342 train to Innsbruck, and had a pleasant ride (6 ½ hours), however, it rained all the way. Despite the rain, one could see the surrounding countryside and it was indeed the most outstanding view that I have seen riding on a train. The tracks ran in a valley, on each side of which were high, jagged mountains. The valley wasn’t very wide, and had a swift stream flowing down its center. Small streams of water flowed over the tops of the cliffs and splattered and sprayed down the mountainside. Everything was green, and the houses quaint, which added up to a picturesque ride thru the countryside between Zurich and Innsbruck.

Places were crowded in Innsbruck, so i got a room in a private house. Women stood at the station and tourists were assigned to them by the tourist bureau. I was supposed to go with a young girl, but since she s it was raining, she said get on the bus and she would follow to tell me where to get off. I rode and rode and never did see her, and was just about to go back to the station when she appeared. Sloshed with her to her house where I obtained a clean room, no running water, for 20 schillings.

AUG 22

        Today didn’t come off so well. First of all, I guess I am getting a little tired of mountain scenery, as I didn’t go “head over heels” over the Innsbruck scenery, and it is supposed to affect people that way. The town is loaded with tourists – mostly German, many English and French, and not too many Americans – and they seemed to get in the way and caused delays. Second, the published price for the cable car trips was wrong, I had to wait 2 hours to get to the top, and when I got there, the clouds obstructed the view. Another hour getting down, and a wasted afternoon, both in time and money. Third, it was raining when I returned from Hafelekar Mountain (7000’) and I was boarding too far away to get my raincoat and/or my blue jacket. Consequently, I froze and got soaked by the time I got back to the room. Fourth, I decided to go see some typical “Tyrolean Native Dancing” and killed 2 hours drinking a beer and reading waiting for the show to start. Then, – my fault – I found that it was all sold out, so I waited for naught. So be it.

        The good points are present, though, so it hasn’t been a complete waste. The sun was out in the morning and I enjoyed walking about town and visiting a few main attractions. The Hofkirche (Palace Church) where there is which houses the tomb of Maximilian I, is quite elaborate and not overly-done, except perhaps for the 16 bronze statues. Still it was somewhat impressive. Another nice thing was the City Tower from which one can get a good view of the city. The Goldenes Dachl (balcony with gold roof) and Palace were just “main sights” for tourists to see.

I enjoyed the Austrian costume that the peasant class wears – and I think the native dress is the best that I have seen in Europe. The women wear white blouses, somewhat fluffy and aprons. The men wear green hats, leather shorts, and a green jacket. Usually there is a little embroidery work on the jacket.

Maybe I will have better weather in Salzburg

.AUG 23

        I am glad that I decided to move on to Salzburg, as it was raining when I got up, and proceded to rain all day (also in Salzburg). I can’t say that I really enjoyed Innsbruck, however, if the weather had been nice, I am sure the perfect location of this city – nestled in the Alps – would have made me an Innsbruck convert. The ride to Salzburg took 6 5 hours, and was so-so. The rain frosted the windows, making it difficult for one to see out. Unlike the Swiss train (of which there are ample), and like to Italian trains, the train was jammed with people, and consequently many were standing and/or sitting in the aisle.

        I got a cheap room at the student dormitory and then went immediately to the ticket office to see what events I could purchase cheap tickets for. There was a big crowd, but I was able to push my way to the front and thus get the last cheap (!! $2) seat for the opera tomorrow night. The piano concert had seats for $3.60 (too expensive for me) and the opera tonight was sold out. Nevertheless, the opera and Marionette Show will hold me for this season.

        Had time on my hands, and even though it was drizzling, I walked about and visited a few of the sights. Visited Mozart’s birthplace and the museum on the top floor, (fair), & looked in on some of the churches, in particular the Cathedral which was damaged during the war. (at the end which was damaged they have built a plain white wall, and on it is a large gold cross adorned with the image of Jesus. This is the simplest and nicest altar I have seen in any Catholic church). Walked back to the dormitory (in a class room) and enjoyed the atmosphere and scenery on the way.

        In the evening I went to the Salzburg Marionette Theater where I saw some great puppet art. I was sitting quite far back (17th row) and consequently the strings seemed to be lost in the background. The figures were manipulated with great skill, and the costumes and scenery were excellent. The figures appeared almost life like, and I and the crowd got a bang out of the antics of some of the animals. Very enjoyable evening.

AUG 24

        Quite an enjoyable day, even though the rains came for the fifth straight day. In the morning I visited the Hohensalzburg Castle, built in 1077, and the oldest fortress erected on German soil. It has an excellent location, being situated on top of a hill overlooking Salzburg. The sun came out for a few minutes while I was at the castle, and I was able to get a good look at the surrounding area. An interesting feature of the castle is the cog-car that brings one up and down the hill. The cars (2 of them) operated by water only, and goes up and down at a rapid speed. The car at the top received a load of water in its tank, and the weight of the water moves the car downhill, at the same time raising the one on the bottom. When this car gets to the bottom it drains its water, and the car at the top now draws the head of water. Quite remarkable.

        Perhaps the best feature of Salzburg outside of the music festival, is Castle Hellbrunn, a Renaissance building with fine parks, gardens and ingenious fountains. The fountains are all water operated and little mechanical figures do all kinds of amazing things. One great exhibit consists of about 200 little figures which represent the daily happenings of a little town. All the figures either go in a circle, in and out of buildings, move their arms or any number of clever acts. While this is going on, an organ is playing, it too being operated by water. As the guide ushers the crowd here and there, he operated handles which spray water on the people from hidden water spouts. Everything is in fun, and the people get a big kick of getting sprayed with the water.

In the evening I went to the opera and saw Mozart’s “Idomeneo”,         an opera which I had never heard of until I came to Salzburg. I bought a program before the opera began, and thoroughly read the description of the story. Knowing the plot I enjoyed the opera very much, particularly the first act and part of the second. Near the end I tired of stretching my head, and wasn’t too enthused. People were dressed quite handsomely many of the women had on expensive looking gowns and furs.

AUG 25

        The men in the dormitory must have been a bunch of foremen, for they were up early and made a lot of noise. I didn’t mind as I had to get up early to catch the train for Linz, a main stopping point on the Danube for river boats to Vienna. I had an hour to kill, so I walked around Linz, and stopped in the Cathedral for a few minutes. The Church was huge, and quite nice, although there were too many spires and arches to suit my taste.

        The Austrian dress is quite nice and many of the men and women wear the so-called national dress. The men are interesting, as they wear the grey-green dress, with the green tie and huge green band on the hat. Actually it looks a little like a uniform, as some have wide green bands on their pants. A few of the men wear the leather shorts, however, mostly children wear this form of clothing. It is interesting to see the many men wear knickers, and many times in combination with a suit coat and tie. Its been a long time since I wore knickers, now I wouldn’t think of it.

        The boat was a fairly large one, at least for a river boat. It traveled at about 10-12 miles an hour and made about 10 stops on the way to Vienna. The Danube is very muddy, not too wide (about 50 yards or so) and winds its way through some beautiful country. There are very few large towns on the River bank, and one sees mainly trees and farm land. The houses that are near the river are quite old, and there are traces of old city walls, and fortress ruins. Some of the sights were quite spectacular, such as the abbeys and castles situated on the nearby hills. It was a pleasant trip, and perhaps it would have been even nicer if the sun had been out and it hadn’t drizzled and rained during part of the trip.

        Arrived in Vienna at 7:45 and finally got to the Student Place at 9:30. On the way I had a brief look at the city, and the section that I came through is quite modern. Anyway, I will find out tomorrow.

AUG 26 (SUNDAY - WEEK 88)

        The only way I could tell it was Sunday was that the stores were closed, – otherwise it seemed like any other day. I went first to Hofburg Palace to see a performance of the Spanish Riding School. However, I was only able to see the arena – actually a part of the Palace and quite fabulous – and the stables where the horses are kept. Most of the horses are white and quite attractive, and I wish I were able to take one out and ride it as they seem very tame. From here I visited some of the rooms in the Hofburg palace and one of the adjoining museums, but wasn’t too interested whe with either of them.

        One of the interesting sights in Vienna is St. Stephen’s Church, the main Catholic church in the city. It has two huge spires anda  tower that is quite high, but not worth the effort to climb. Other than the size and its age (consecrated in 1147), there weren’t many features that I liked about the church, both inside & outside as it is filled with too much crap – typical of Catholic churches. (at least those in Italy and Austria). Viewed the simple and attractive monument to the Russian dead, the Parliament Building (nice), the City Hall (many spires and attractive location) and the University building.

        Decided to go out to the Vienna Woods, so I took the street car to Grinzing, one of the famous suburbs of Vienna, noted for its wine gardens and rustic atmosphere. I am glad that it was a little chilly, for it made the walking a lot easier and more enjoyable. The woods are nothing special, still they are quite nice and I sat on a park bench for awhile, – lost in my thoughts! On the way back I stayed at one of the gardens, and had a stein of white wine. Don’t know if the wine was strong (this year’s wine, so they had a bundle of hay over the door to indicate same or I wasn’t use to it; but I noticed the effect on me after one stein. Some old ladies at a near-by table tried to get me to join them – they were drunk – but they couldn’t speak English so I declined regretfully. A violinist and an accordionist provided music for the customers. Enjoyable evening.

AUG 27

        Finally a nice day – after 8 straight days with some rain. I got up early and went to the American Consulate to get help on deciding whether to go to the Dental Clinic or to a private practitioner. Made arrangements to see a private dentist tomorrow even though it will cost a lot more. (Don’t have the guts that I did at Geneva) Re-visited the Spanish Riding School, but wasted 10 shillings as the training consisted only of riding the horses around the enclosure. Visited the National Library but didn’t appreciate it to the extent that I probably should as I could not read any of the German titles and descriptions. Still the building is quite elaborate and the wood paneling some of the nicest that I have seen.

        Enjoyed a visit to the Summer Palace of Shoënbrun, located on the outskirts of the city. The building is huge, although not extremely beautiful, and the gardens the nicest that I have ever seen. The grounds behind the palace are extensive; and after an area of flat ground which contains brightly colored flowers and plants, the ground runs into a medium size hill. On the tip of the hill is a large pavilion from which a great view of the palace grounds and Vienna can be had. All of the walk ways are bordered by trees, which have been pruned to a uniform height and a perpendicular front on the walk side. Where 🌳 WALK 🌳 the walkways cross or join, the tree branches have been cut into the shape of an archway. Very pleasing sight, especially when the sun is out, as the trees are of the same type, height, etc; yet, variations can be discerned in the color of the leaves.

        Headed back into Vienna and went to “Amerika Haus”, the name given to the USIS library. The library wasn’t jammed, yet there were quite a few people reading the American newspapers and magazines. I was in 7th heaven, and spent 2 ½ hours trying to catch up with the news. In one of the magazines there was a fine article on St. Louis and the progress that has been made in the last 4 years.

AUG 28

        Lugged my back-breaking baggage to the train station, and as usual, felt like pitching half of the contents. My handle broke in Linz and consequently when I passed a leather store, I stopped in to see what could be done. I bought a cheap plastic handle, and then wired it to the existing rings on the bag, and I hope that it will hold during the remainder of the trip.

        From the station I walked to the Museum of Fine Arts and Natural History, located on the Ring – a large street that circles the inner section of the city. Walked around the museum for a little more than an hour, and enjoyed sections of it; but like the other museums, I wasn’t able to get the full benefit since I can’t read the German titles. Not too far from the Museums was the American Express office, so I stopped by to get data and prices on a Vienna-Copenhagen ticket. Since I only get a discount if I buy the through ticket, I decided to go ahead and fork over the $30 for the trip. So, I am headed for Denmark – 

        My afternoon didn’t consist of things relative to Vienna, as I went to the dentist and then stopped by the USIS reading room again. The dentist spoke good English, and we had a little chat concerning the far east, since he had been in China from 1938-1952. I was relieved after he checked my mouth, for he said there wasn’t anything visibly wrong. Perhaps a seed had pressed against or lodged among one of my fillings. The bill was $1 – less than I had expect, and so I hope I have no more trouble with my teeth and/or rest of my body.

        Again I enjoyed the reading room, as I caught up on the latest knews, plus 3 copies of Business Week and the July issue of Fortune. I found another article on progress in St. Louis and enjoyed reading same, plus feeling a little hometown pride. As I read business and financial news, I am cognizant of my limited knowledge of such things, particularly finances, and will have to read up on them when I get home.

AUG 29

        Someday when I am rich (!) I am going to read this diary and get a big bang from it. Decided to take the night train to Munich, to conserve time and money, but I don’t know if it is worth it. Left Vienna at 0020 and arrived in Munich at 0745, sandwiched in there somewhere is about 3 hours sleep. Oh well, it is my choosing, and actually I don’t mind it so much.

        Got a room in a private home ($.75) and then set off for some sight-seeing. Visited Nymphenburg Castle and enjoyed the huge garden-park in the back. Decided not to see the rooms & museums, as I get so little out of the German speaking guides. Took the trolley to the main part of town and walked up and down the main streets, plus some of the important side streets. Enjoyed the Frauenkirche Cathedral very much, as its old brick frame now houses a very modern interior. Don’t know if the interior is completed yet, but the white walls and simply designed roof are great in my book. The pulpit was extremely modern as it had abstract figures of Saints and other objects made of Silver, bordered by red & blue tile, and featured to a combination finished and un-finished concrete circular pulpit. The altar was plain, the stained glass windows quite nice and the huge wooden cross only somewhat attrocious. Walked quickly in & out of some other churches, visited the spot where Hitler use to harangue the crowds, and spent 2 enjoyable hours at the Technical Museum, Germany’s largest. It is similar to the Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago, and one can see the equipment and things he reads of plus operate many of them by buttons. If I could read German it would have been the greatest.

        In the evening I went to the huge and well known beer hall – the Hofbraühaus. The place was jammed – all three floors – and the people were having a great time drinking beer from huge steins, swinging and forgetting their inhabitions. I stayed for about 3 hours and had a great time watching the people, making noise and trying to drink 2 large steins of beer. Must admit that it is the best beer hall that I have been in.

AUG 30

        Almost didn’t get up, as I went back to sleep after turning off the alarm clock. Awoke with a start, and “apniced”, but did manage to catch the 8:10 train. To get to Dinkelsbuhl, I had to take 4 trains, 2 of which were nothing more than buses that ran on rails. The changing of trains helped pass the time and before I knew it I had arrived in the old Bavarian town of Dinkelbühl, – population 7400. The sun came out, and after I had found a reasonable room, and did my washing, I strolled about the city.

        Most of the city is located within the old walls, and an air picture of the town shows many trees near the walls, and from then on, farmland, and occasional houses; thus making the city a quaint little oasis. The streets are cobblestone, and every house has a pitched roof, some of them almost 60’ angles. The houses are quite large, with 3 or 4 floors plus a small attic where the sides of the roof join. The houses are old and made of either wood or stone, primarily the latter. Some of them have designs on their walls, and all of the larger hotels have metal signs hanging near their front door.

        There isn’t much to see in the town, but I enjoyed walking about and enjoying breathing the peaceful atmosphere. Many of the houses had colorful plants in their windows, and everything was green in the fields and park. Most of the little boys had on the leather pants which are typical of Austria and Switzerland, and the girls wore long leggi stockings. The middle age and older women seem to prefer the color black, and even wore black stockings. The men wore either long pants or knickers. The Germans are quite friendly, and appear to be hard workers. The cities are clean and only occasionally can war rubble be seen. Now and then I look at a German and think of him as a soldier, but time seems to have wiped out many memories. I have noticed, though, that the Germans talk about their soldiers and the last war far more than the Japanese men did.

AUG 31

        Took the morning train to Rothenburg, and arrived about 10:00. The sun was blazing, the blue sky was woven with white clouds, and the quaint walled city of Rothenburg lent intself as a suitable spot to spend a carefree day. I walked around the city in the morning and climbed the tower of the city hall to get a birds eye view. The city is old, larget than Dinkelsbuhl (11,000), and more of a tourist center. In the market place – and square, there were sight-seeing buses and guides to point out – for a price – the outstanding sights to behold. I decided to just walk around and when they wanted to charge me to enter the church, I refused as I did yesterday.

        All of the houses have painted roofs, with red tile shingles on the outside. The streets are narrow, and generally made of cobblestones, however, the sidewalks are of concrete. There were too many tourist shops to suit me, but I guess that is the main vocation of the townspeople. The dress was about the same as in Dinkelsbuhl, and I guess, for that matter, in most of the rural towns in Southern Germany.

        Went walking in the afternoon, and spent the majority of the time outside the city walls. Sat on a bench for awhile and jotted down some things concerning “What I Plan To Do When (and if) I Get Home!” Also, watched the people stroll by, most of them pushing baby carriages of one sort. The view was great as there was a valley on the side of the city where I was, and I could see for miles. The land was green, and well cultivated and I noticed a lot of women helping the men in the fields. Later in the afternoon I walked away from the city, and got a great view of the city, its walls and towers, standing out against the blue sky background. The sun was in the right spot to give the picture the correct coloring.

        Went to see a play given by the townspeople in the evening, and while I didn’t let understand the German, I enjoyed the costumes, music & acting

SEP 01

        I had hoped that the weather would be nice today, but by the time I arrived in Wurzburg it was raining. I called Al Kohn from the Wurzburg RTO and made arrangements to see him and Joanne in the afternoon. The rain slackened, so I decided to see the sights of the city, which weren’t very much since the city had been bombed quite extremely during the war. Across the Main River is a famous bridge with religious statues on the sides, and from the bridge one can get a good view of Marienburg Castle, situated on a hill overlooking the city. Lugging my “heavy” small bag, I walked across town and spent some time at the Residence Castle,  which has some attractive frescoes and an outstanding staircase. Much of the Castle is fire gutted, probably from the war.

        The morning was still young, so I decided to try my luck at hitch-hiking. Stood along the highway for an hour, but only one car stopped and that wasn’t going to Bamberg. Went back to the station, and took the train to Bamberg arriving at 2 PM. Joanne and Al were at the station, and it was good to see familiar faces and to talk about things in common. They had a car, and so we did a little sight-seeing, visiting the Cathedral, Rose Garden and Convent. Bamberg is quite picturesque, and while it is more modern and less quaint than Rothenburg, still it has narrow streets, interesting homes and people, and a Bavarian atmosphere.

        Later in the afternoon we drove to the PX where I bought a few things, and then to their apartment – a 5 room, luxury, Army housing unit. Al is in ASA, and seems to have a good deal. They have participated in activities such as the local theater, visited German families, and have done a lot of sight-seeing in Europe. Consequently they have gotten quite a bit out of their tour over here. They had to attend a battalion party in the evening and asked me to come along. I hesitated at first, but decided to go when they said that it was quite informed. There were about 50 people present, and most of them were quite friendly – typical Army personnel (thought I had left the Army!) The food was fair, but the atmosphere congenial and I enjoyed myself.

SEP 02 (SUNDAY - WEEK 89)

        As my days pass in Germany, I sort of feel that I am not seeing much every day, or at least, new and different things. Still I have gone to some quaint and picturesque villages, but the wholesale sights in Italy, Egypt are not to be found in Germany. Many of the cities have had all their previous sights bombed to rubble and in their place are gleaming new buildings, not particularly interesting to see.

        I got up early at the Kohn house and read the paper and packed my bags while Al and Joanne slept. After they got up, I used Joanne’s t iron to press some things while she prepared breakfast. The breakfast consisted of waffles and I sure enjoyed them. Since they planned to go to Mainz, they drove me to Wurzburg where I caught the train for Stuttgart. Must say that they were very kind and couldn’t do enough for me.

        The train ride to Stuttgart wasn’t too different (from previous countryside landscapes) and so I read from the book I bought in Vienna,  – ”The Nature of the Universe”, by Lucretius. It is interesting, although I can’t say I am fascinated by it. While I can’t discern the effect the translator has changed the words, still the theories of this man of almost 2000 years ago are quite remarkable, and in some aspects, correct. Arriving in Stuttgart I had some difficulty in getting a cheap room, but finally got the name of a State Dormitory. The building is quite large, and one can get a bed for only 1 mark. Things seemed clean, and so I and the hundreds of others (mostly middle age Germans) settled down to a good nights sleep. (Will be interesting to see what the people look like in daylight)

        Before I went to the Dormitory, I stopped at two places to have a glass of beer. One was a GI hangout, and I was interested in seeing the type of German girls that went with the GI’s. (So-so). They must have a ruling that the GI’s wear ties for an MP asked me why I didn’t have one on. I got a great thrill in saying, “I’m not a member of the Army!” (Its these little things in life that make it so interesting from day to day.) Also visited the local Hobfraü House.

SEP 03                LABOR DAY

        Should be home this time next year to enjoy the Labor Day holiday. Today, it was just another sight-seeing day. A person came to our room at 5 AM, & again at 6 AM, and by 7 AM we were all supposed to be up and gone. I got up at 6:30 and by that time most of the fellows had gone, so I didn’t have a chance to see what they were like. Went to American Express and picked up 5 or 6 letters from the family. Nothing new, but it is good hearing from home. Decided to join the Youth Hostel (balked when I heard it was $4.50) but and so I visited the Stuttgart headquarters to get my card.

        The expected rain came as I left the Hostel place, and since I had some time to kill, I went to see a boy friend of Morton’s that he had met 4 years ago. After a struggle of finding his apartment, and fighting the rain, I found that he was out of town. Still I left him “Best Regards” from MW. Earlier in the day I found out that the Service Club was going on a tour of a brewery at 1:30 so I decided to join the group. (Again – back with the Army). The tour was quite interesting as the gentleman showed us all around the plant. He pointed out the malt mixing room, vats, yeast and fermentary vats, bottling plant and ended the tour by presenting everyone two glasses of beer. The people on the tour reminded me of the fellows in my basic platoon, and once again I can be thankful that I was able to get in with older fellows and to do engineering work.

        Took the afternoon train to Heidelberg – with half a load on – and arrived at 6 PM. Got mixed up in my directions, so I went downtown instead of to the Youth Hostel. Heidelberg is bigger than I thought, is quite modern in certain sections, and has many GI’s roaming the streets. Far from the station (my poor arms) I found the Red Ox Inn, one of the old student drinking places.I stopped by for a glass of beer and to enjoy the atmosphere. The trinkets, horns, pictures and other junk on the walls were very interesting, as they were from 70-100 years old. Some of the fellows in soldier uniforms reminded me of “The Student Prince.”

SEP 04

        At 6:45 music began to blare, and it was “Time to get up at the Hostel.” I obeyed Big Brother and paraded into the wash room where there must have been 2000 other fellows attempting to wash their faces. Later when I wanted to check out, I had to get the initials of the girl of my floor to ascertain that I had made my bed properly. (I hadn’t) Sooo, after a period worse than the Army I managed to get away and to the downtown section of Heidelberg. As one would know, it began to rain, but I had my raincoat and was thus ready for the miserable weather.

        I decided to take a tour ($1) as I wanted to leave at 1:30 and at the University they said that was the only way to see the old University. The people on the tour were middle age English speaking persons who I had little in common with. The first part wasn’t very interesting so we drove along the river and thence into old Heidelberg – and over there is so and so, and quick turn to your right to see the oldest house, and that black spot is … so be it. The University was interesting as the guide pointed out the old rooms which acted like prisons when the students fooled around. The students had painted pictures, printed their names and just covered the wall with all kinds of decorations, many of them fraternity emblems. I liked the “mess” and sort of wish I could have stayed longer to just amble about. Also visited an old lecture hall which is still in use. Heidelberg Castle, though in ruins, was interesting, and the facade decorations were quite nice. It also has the largest wine cash I have ever seen – about 50,000 gallon capacity.

        On to Rüdesheim via 3 changes by trains, one a close connection. I didn’t realize that it was such a tourist town, and consequently I had to pay dearly for room, meal and wine. The wine is supposed to be the best, but I couldn’t tell anything special about it. Must admit that I have sure drunk a lot of beer and wine lately! – getting to be a booze and wine kid. Went to a wine cellar in the evening and got a kick out of the clumsy Germans prancing about the floor. Still they sang and appeared to be having a good time.

SEP 05

        I was disappointed to awaken to cloudy skies and wet clothes, as my washing of the previous night had not dried. I debated about taking the 8:30 boat, but it was so cloudy and misty that I thought I best wait until 10:15. I walked about town for an hour, and discovered that in back of the tourist or main street, is a quaint, old village with countless acres of vineyards. The land is hilly and I guess grapes are one of the best crops for such soil and topography. I stopped in a winery for a few minutes, but didn’t get much out of my visit as the man who showed me around could not speak very good English.

        The boat ride to Coblenz turned out to be quite nice, as the sun came out and one could see the surrounding countryside. On both sides of the Rhine River are thousands of acres of vineyards; and the neat, green vines make a pretty picture against the hillsides. Here and there along the banks were old castles and forts, some destroyed, others in seemingly good condition; all of them situated on the tops of their respective hills. One of the interesting features was the heavy traffic on the river. We passed many boats and barges of coal, lumber, gravel and other material. Flags of German, France, Netherlands and Switzerland were seen on these boats. Some boats appeared to be quite old, as they had ½ - ⅔ of their bodies exposed and were propelled by water wheels. Much more traffic than on the Danube.

        I got off the boat at Coblenz and then took the train to Cologne. The train went adjacent to the river for part of the trip and one could also see much of the river activity and opposite bank. Cologne is noted for its Cathedral, supposedly the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. It is really huge, and very rich in spices and archwork on its exterior. The interior is quite simple, and I liked it for that quality. The altar was particularly plain, the only ornate decoration being the gold shine of the Three Holy Kings. From the Cathedral I walked to Amerika Haus, where I passed the time reading magazines. Cologne is very modern, as the once destroyed city has been rebuilt on and now has many modern, beautiful stores, set off by bright neon lights.

SEP 06

        Some day I will be able to sleep on trains, but up to now I haven’t had much luck. The train wasn’t very crowded, so I was able to stretch out at times, but I only managed a couple hours of sleep. Arrived in Hamburg at 6 AM, ate, and found a cheap room near the station. Other than the noted “Reeperbahn” sailor district, I hadn’t lined up much to do, so I decided to just amble about town. (almost died from exhaustion when I got back to the room at 4:30). Mailed some travel booklets home; bought a new band for my watch; inquired at the US Consul where a Jewish Temple was (didn’t get an answer on the phone so I didn’t go); inquired of some shipping lines about passage home (appears to be more difficult than I thought); and visited a few sights.

        Walked along the waterfront and spent some time watching the activity in the harbor. Visited St. Michael Church (so-so) and took a brief tour of the Rathaus (City Hall). The guide spoke German so I didn’t understand a word, however, the interior decorations were quite impressive, and I could appreciate it without knowing its history. In the afternoon I visited the zoo which was quite nice, though not as nice as the St. Louis Zoo (they cha charge to get in). The animals were kept in simulated natural surroundings, and wild birds roamed the lawns. They also had elephant rides and a monkey show, both of them also costing money. Still it was a very nice zoo.

        Went to the Reeperbahn in the evening and I guess I can say that I was somewhat disappointed. The area consisted of cheap cabarets and unexciting bars, and I was almost ready to go home when I came across the best part. Down one 50 yard street is the red light area; and unlike what I have ever seen, the women sit in windows and discuss terms thru the glass-like-doors. Most of the women were old and ugly, and I guess their pride and vanity had long since vanished. Still I am amazed can let themselves be bought and laughed and looked over in such a crude way.

Route as of September 6th, 1956 – end of Chapter 15.

CHAPTER 16 - ANGLO-SAXON ADVENTURE

September 7th, 1956 - October 1st, 1956

SEP 07

        Took the morning train to Copenhagen, and had a pleasant trip either reading or standing on the deck of the train ferry and gazing out over the water. The ferry was quite interesting as it was large enough to carry our 5-6 coach train plus other railway cars and many buses and automobiles. It took about 2 hours to cross Kiel Bay and to and arrive on the island upon which Copenhagen is situated.

        Decided to get first things done first, so I went to the Student Travel Association to inquire of any interesting trips; but their season was just about over and their wasn’t much to choose from. Next I went to the American Express and inquired about voyages, but other than obtaining a list of passages, I couldn’t get anything definite. Spent the rest of the afternoon walking about the city and viewing some of the merchandise for sale. One of the interesting buildings is the Permanent Exhibition of Arts and Crafts which has samples of the work of many of Danish craftsmen. I particularly liked their ceramics.

        Visited the fabulous Tivoli Gardens in the evening and enjoyed it immensely. It is a huge amusement park with thousands of colored lights illuminating the pavilions, concert halls, amusements and lakes. They have many free attractions and one only need follow his program to see pantomime to ballet, and to hear band music, and concert music. The restaurants are good, but expensive, and one can choose either a dinner or one of the many sandwiches on the menu. The amusements and rides are typical, although they seemed to be flavored with more environment than at the Forest Park Highlands. The park was jammed with people and I saw many, – many – good looking Danish girls. Great!

SEP 08

        I decided to see as many of the sights today as I could without rushing myself, and so headed for the main part of town right after a good, cheap breakfast. First, I headed for the waterfront where I saw the famous “Little Mermaid.” can’t say that it was very outstanding, still it is one of the symbols of Copenhagen and a must for a tourist. I did like a work of sculpture near the Mermaid called “Gefion Fountain.” It depicts a Goddess guiding 4 oxen and is quite impressive. Turbulent water sprays add to the tenseness of her task, and fine spray bellows forth from the nostrils of the oxen. Very interesting.

        Walked around the waterfront, and then across the city to Rosenborg Castle built by Christian IV. It was loaded with many relics of the past, but it was too much of a hodge-podge for my taste. I met a GI earlier in the day and we toured these sights together. From the Castle (and after a fair lunch) we visited the Stock Exchange (closed for the day, but still, one was able to take a quick stroll through the elaborate halls); Thorvaldsen’s Museum (Denmark’s most famous sculpture) – fairly good; and Christiansborg Palace,  the site of the Danish Parliament (very beautiful, modern, regal decorations) Mike (the GI) and I then departed separated, and I went back to the Hostel.

        In the evening 5 4 fellows from the Hostel (South Africa, Canadian, 2 Scots) and I went to the Tivoli where we listened to a concert and walked around the park. Later we went to a dance at the Student House, which was well attended by hansome Danes and fine looking, blond women. I danced one dance with a Danish girl, and when I left (had to be back at the Hostel at 12:30) I made a date to see her at 8 PM tomorrow. It will be interesting to see if she shows up.

SEP 09 (SUNDAY - WEEK 90)

        Was late in getting up and consequently getting to the train station. Took the 10:15 train to Elsinore, and had a pleasant trip to the small town about 30 miles North of Copenhagen. The town is famous for the Kronborg Castle, supposedly the setting for Shakespeare’s “Hamlet”. It was built in 1574-1585 and the exterior is one of the most interesting Renaissance structures in Scandinavia. I must admit, though, that I was disappointed with the interior. A fire destroyed much of the interior in the 1800’s, and while they have done a fairly good job of restoring it to its original decorations, it is too much like a museum to suit me.

        Took the train back to Copenhagen and upon arrival, I went to the Information Counter. As I was walking away, whom should I see but the Dore’s. I knew they were coming to Europe but never thought I would bump into them. They have been in Europe about 3 weeks, and it was funny to hear of their woes and problems in getting use to the European habits. I think I laughed to myself the whole time I was talking to them. They said Al was in New York, and gave me him address. It was coincidental in running into them and I enjoyed talking to them very much.

        Grabbed a quick bite, dashed back to the Hostel to change, and then went to the appointed designated spot to see if Lis would show up. Promptly at 8 she walked up, and said hello again. We spent the evening at the Tivoli and I had a very enjoyable time. We watched some amusements, listened to a concert, and danced awhile. She is quite intelligent, and can speak good English, so things worked out just fine. Even made a date for tomorrow afternoon.

SEP 10

        I was up early, but didn’t leave the house until almost 11 AM. After a good breakfast, I borrowed the typewriter and banged out a hurried letter to home. Then I packed, but spent quite a bit of time talking to a bunch of fellows also staying at the hostel. The nice thing about these hostels – besides the cheapness – is the fact that one meets many interesting people, mostly students. For instance, at this hostel I met an intelligent South African who had just finished working in England. Across the breakfast table was an Indian girl from Bombay with whom I conversed awhile. It seems that most of the students traveling in this area are English speaking, most of the others I guess having returned home.

        After checking on some train prices and schedules, I went to the Student house for a fairly good meal. From here I visited the famous “World Clock” of Jens Olsens, a fabulously complicated clock which tells time, sunrise & sunset, position of the planets, calendar days and months and many other facts such as these. It is supposedly the most accurate clock of its kind, and the mechanism – exposed in back – are is a mass of springs, gears, pulleys and wheels. It was really quite interesting.

        At 2 PM I met Lis, and spent the next 9 hours with her. We walked around the city, talking about a hundred different topics. Did a lot of window shopping and visited an art and furniture exposition. We ate dutch treats at the University (she is an English major) and then went to see an American movie that she was interested in. After the movie we walked and talked some more and finally I left her at 11 at the train station. She is a very nice girl, quite intelligent, has fine tastes and habits and was very enjoyable to be with.
