For awhile I thought of staying another day, but then I figured it was best to move on, especially if I was going to Stockholm & Oslo. I enjoyed my stay in Copenhagen and Denmark very much – a great little country.

SEP 11

        Got more sleep than usual, but still not very much. Still don’t know whether I should stayed another day (and gone to the Deer Park with Lis) or push on like I did. Oh well, can’t think of such things as that. The train was slow, and late, but the weather was very nice and I was able to get a good look at the scenery. The Southern tip of Sweden seems to be full of forests, as there were trees everywhere. The houses and farms weren’t much different from those that I have seen in the rest of Europe. During the night and early morning it was quite chilly, but when the sun came out it warmed things up so that the weather was perfect.

        In Stockholm the Youth Hostel is on a very luxurious yacht in the harbor and I was fortunate to get a berth (I think there are 132 berths). The rooms and the ship itself are very clean, and to top it off there are hot showers. One other nice feature is that it is anchored very near the center of things, – within easy walking distance.

Didn’t do too much today, just sort of got orientated with the town. Visited Riddarholm Church  (where many Swedish kings are buried) but wasn’t too interested. This was located in the old section of Stockholm, so I walked around awhile, side tracking now and then into one of the narrow, cobblestone streets. Actually the old and the newer parts of Stockholm is are quite attractively located on islands, or surrounded by water of one means. Perhaps it is one of the most beautiful large cities that I have ever seen. Many of the buildings are modern, things are clean looking, much construction is going on, and the women are real beauties. Don’t think they are better looking than the Danes, but perhaps better groomed, for Sweden is a wealthy nation. Costs are quite high here, but so is the standard of living. I took the modern subway to a new section of town – Vällingby and was quite impressed with the attractive apartments & shopping center.

SEP 12

        Awakened to a torrential downpour, – how discouraging. Nevertheless, we had to be out by 9 and anyway I wanted to visit the City Hall. As it appears thus far, the City Hall is the most impressive sight in Stockholm. (However, I can’t do an adequate job of describing the beauty of the city itself, – located on the water. Very beautiful). It was inaugurated in 1923 and contains some beautiful mosaics, wood ceilings, brickwork and general appearance. The architect of this so called “monument” was Ragnar Ostberg.

        I was drenched by the time I got to the City Hall and stayed wet all morning. After a brief tour of the Parliament Building (Swedish guide) I watched the changing of the guard (in the rain) at the Royal Palace. The uniforms were the typical Swedish soldier uniform, however, the interesting feature is the fact that they all carry burp guns instead of rifles. (It reminds me of “the Rock” which incidentally just finished undergoing a typhoon blast which caused an estimate $20,000,000 damage) the Royal Apartments were so-so, and I left before seeing them all. One sight that I liked in Stockholm, was the home and garden of Sweden’s greatest sculptor CARL MILLES (He did the work on the fountains in front of Union Station in St. Louis). His work is quite interesting as his statues all portray movement, most of them on one leg or on thin supports. He had 2 nice fountains, plus some statues on the top of granite pedestals which I liked very much. (20-35 FEET HIGH) In addition, his home overlooks the water and part of Stockholm and thus commands a fine view.

        Went to the opera in the evening and saw a performance of  “La Traviata.” Had to leave shortly before it was over in order to get back by 11 o’clock, but on the whole I enjoyed what I heard. The female singers seemed to be quite good although the male lead was just so-so. Met a Swedish lad during the intermission and we discussed the forthcoming Swedish election & Swedish girls.

SEP 13

        Things turned out very nice today, – both the weather and my activities. The sun was out all day, and thus one didn’t feel the cool air unless he had a cold. And that is precisely what I had – a lousy, snuffling nose. Running nose or not, I still got in a busy day. In the morning I visited Skansen, the Stockholm version of Copenhagen’s Tivoli. I really can’t make a just comparison, as I was there in the morning where there was little or no activity, however, it just didn’t seem as nicely located in the center of town along with other nite life (although it had a nice view overlooking Stockholm), nor was it as elaborate or as well laid out. The Tivoli in Copenhagen is really great and saying that Skansen is not as good does not ruin this park, for it seems quite adequate. Later in the morning I visited the NK department store and found its merchandise and sales ladies to be top notch.

        Visited the Stockholm International Fair in the afternoon and enjoyed wandering around the exhibits. I must say that my pride was almost to the limit as I walked through the American display house. It was really great, and had hundreds of people packed in the aisles trying to get a good look at the television production. The television section and all the others had people demonstrating things and thus it aided in the presentation of typical American goods, hobbies & amusements. Other sections in the building were on wood working, “do it yourself kits”, model airlines & toys, a Navajo Indian doing some silver work, a library of trade magazines, television sets (including a portable one), phonographs and records and a Kodak display. This and the USIS are great sellers of the American way of life. There were many exhibits, equipment and goods from countries on both sides of the Iron Curtain. The kitchen products & samples were well attended, as was the fair in general. Very interesting.

        Later in the afternoon I stopped at a tea & sandwich open-air shop, and was amazed at the really beautiful and well groomed Swedish girls hanging around Italian & French fellows, most of whom were disheveled and looked like bums. I guess opposites attract!

SEP 14

        Last nite on the train wasn’t bad at all, in fact I got almost 6 hours sleep. The customs and passport men awakened me at 5 AM, but I soon fell asleep again. We arrived in Oslo at 8 (I met an English “bloke” on the train) and got the address of the student hostel. After a long subway ride, plus a back breaking walk, we found that there was no room, and thus had to head back to the station.

        It began to rain and appeared to be a miserable day, but I took my camera hoping that it would clear up. I checked on boat passage from Bergen and was told to come back latter (not very good prospects) and then went to the American Express Embassy to see if O could visit a Magnesium factory while I was in Norway. The lady called a firm and din’t get very good replies but they were to call back later and say if I would be O.K.

        Getting these things settled, Ray (the English man) and I decided to visit the sights in and around Oslo. We took a ferry across choppy waters and arrived at a spot across from Oslo where the boat museums were located. The first museum housed the Polar expiration ship “Fram”, and I enjoyed being able to go down into the hold and see the insides and deck of the ship which has been both to the North and South poles. The next museum housed the Kon-Tiki raft, and I was amazed at the crudeness of the raft. To think that 6 men spent 101 days floating in the Pacific to prove a theory on ocean currents, is almost beyond human capabilities. The raft was constructed of balsa logs from the jungles of Equador and is a replica of rafts until 5000 years ago Also visited the Viking ship museum (the vessels were quite sleek looking) and the Folk museum and old Norwegian houses (fair). At lunch time we saw some small boys and girls in national costumes doing folk dances. Quite nice and I hope the pictures turn out. Spent the night at the hostel.

SEP 15

        Good news and bad news this morning, – I guess I can’t complain of the so-so results. At the travel bureau I bought my ticket for the Bergen-Newcastle line on Wednesday (sitting up – but one must get across). The other news concerned my hoped for visit to a Magnesium plant. At first the man said that it would be okay, but then he said “No.” and gave the reason that I did not have a letter of introduction from Dow. No sense in arguing, so I said thanks and began thinking of what to do during the next 2 days. I visited the City Hall or House as it is called and was quite impressed with the decorations. The paintings, wood ceilings, and general interior decorations were quite nice and in a class with the fine one that I saw in Stockholm. While I was at the City House I saw 3 British submarines at the docks and took a visit down there to get a close-up view. Couldn’t really see much, except 2 be-medaled officers leaving the area for other parts. While Americans have campaign ribbons, the British have chestfuls of medals. The subs appeared to be modern ones.

        In the afternoon I visited the Cathedral (stopped for only a minute), passed the University and spent a couple of hours in Frogner Park. I enjoyed the park very much as it is quite huge; has beautiful, green, close, cropped grass; flowers are everywhere, and of course it contains the famous Vigeland sculptures. The statues – all nudes – of men, women and children and are supposed to represent the stages of life. There are quite a number of these statues – 58 on the bridge, 23 tr__rou__ around the fountain , and 36 large granite statues surrounding the Monolith. The Monolith is a huge granite obelisk, 56 feet high, and is made up of 121 figures shown in their struggle to reach the light. The other piece of work is the Life Wheel and portrays human forms in the form of a wheel. Quite interesting.

        Didn’t do much in the evening, – watched the people for awhile and then saw Charlie Chaplin in the “Gold Rush.”

SEP 16 (SUNDAY - WEEK 91)

        The Norwegians are noted for their big breakfasts, and the one at the hostel was no exception. For 2.75 ($.38) I had as much milk, cereal and tea as I wanted, plus 4 pieces of bread with a piece of meat and jam. Not having had much cereal for the past 4 months, I took 4 dishes and was quite filled by the time I left the table.

        The girls t the desk suggested that I visit Norefjell, so I packed my little bag and went to the docks where the buses also stop. Sat around the docks for an hour and watched the small sight-seeing boats, the larger ferries and also the 3 British subs which came in yesterday. The bus left at 12:10 and it took 3 ½ hours to get to Norefjell, a distance of about 100 Kilometers from Oslo. The trip was quite pleasant as there aren’t many towns between Oslo and Norefjell and consequently I was able to see a lot of evergreen trees, small lakes and a couple large ones, and numerous hills. Most of the houses were made out of wood, and reminded me of small farm homes back in the USA (Fruitland, Mo.) The evergreens were naturally green, but the grass was turning yellow, as were some of the small plants and other types of trees. Norefjell is on a  small mountain overlooking some lakes and at the top one can get a good view of the valley and of the mountains in the distance. The air was quite cool – 32° F – and after an hour I had to go inside to warm myself as I really don’t have sufficient clothing for this climate. I noticed a ski lift and I presume that there is a lot of skiing done here in the winter. The 2 ¼ hours on the mountain top were quite pleasant. Later I took the bus to Hamremoen where there was a Youth Hostel. There was only 1 other fellow there and I guess we will be able to scrounge together enough blankets to keep warm, for it is really cold. Had a huge dinner and I even had to turn away some of the food. The Norwegians sure feed one enough, and at a reasonable price.

 

SEP 17

        Great day today, – cool but with a warm sun; quiet and thought provoking; peaceful and beautiful – a well spent day. John (the English fellow at the hostel) and I slept late – 7:30, but it was a total of 9 hours of restful sleep. My 3 blankets kept my quite warm. I decided to try the breakfast to see if it was as complete as the supper of last night, – it sure was. For $.38 I had as much coffee as I wanted, bread and the choice of 4 meats, 3 cheese, 3 fish and butter and jam. I really prefer eggs and cereal, but I managed to fill my stomach on the above food.

        I spent most of the day doing nothing more than sitting, walking and thinking. Near the hostel is a beautiful wooded area, with occasional farm houses and farm land, and a wide lake. I ambled down the road awhile, cutting a twig with my knife, and stopping once to bury a dead squirrel. After awhile I headed for the lake and parked my camera on a rock and myself next to it. For the next two and one-half hours I just sat and thought, occasionally writing a couple notes in a little black book I have for such thoughts. Most of my thoughts concerned what I plan to do when I get home, and I think I have pretty well decided to get a production job for 6-8 months. At the same time I think I will continue my law education, for no matter what I decide to do, I think it will benefit me. By June of next year I hope that I will have decided on exactly what I want to do, – whether it be labor relations, sales or productions.

        Had a few hours to kill before the 4 PM bus arrived so I took my small bag to the roadside and attempted to hitch hike back to Oslo. About 15 cars passed in the 2 ¼ hours that I wired and only one gave me a nibble, but he wasn’t going my way. I really didn’t mind as I spent the time reading and thus didn’t mind the waiting for the bus. Didn’t do much in the evening – went back to the hostel and chatted with some fellows. (Dane, Indian, Amerian and a Hong Kong Indian.)

SEP 18

        I was pleased to see the sun out, because the train ride from Oslo to Bergen would be mighty boring if it rained the whole way. The train was crowded and I was lucky to get one of the last seats. I spent ½ of the ride in as a compartment with 3 elderly Australian women, a Norwegian couple and their 2 cute boys, and a Swede. The people were extremely nice and friendly and we had a pleasant conversation during the 5 hours we were together. Must admit that some of these cute blond headed Scandinavian children are almost as attractive as the oriental children.

        The scenery along the route was the best that I have seen thus far, and the brilliant sunshine added to the beauty. After we left Oslo, and before arriving in Bergen, we only passed through one medium-size town during the 11 hour trip. The stops that were made were at small whistle stops, where there were only a small number of wooden houses. The people were hardy looking farmers, dressed in plain but adequate clothes. The girls for the most part wear long leggings with their shirts.

        I doubt if I have ever seen such extensive wooded lands with millions of straight, green evergreens, blended with other forms of plant life, the latter beginning to turn yellow and red. Not too large a percentage of the land was cultivated, and when we got into the mountainous area, there were only a few farms. Many of the mountains had snow on their peaks, and at one stop we saw a glacier. The prettiest sights were the mountain streams, lakes and rivers. Many of the rivers and small streams had rapids which caused the water to churn, splash and foam white caps as it went on its way.We arrived in Bergen at night time, consequently, I wasn’t able to see any of the city. Went to the hostel – located on the mountain – and slept in a dirty bed, however it is cheap and only for 1 night.

SEP 19

        Can’t really say that this was a very interesting day. I left the hostel at 7:30 (as soon as I could) and went to the funicular which goes down from Floyen (where the hostel is) to Bergen. The view of the city is quite spectacular and the whole city and harbor is laid out, as if it were a map at ones feet. The day started off wrong as it drizzled all morning and I had fears of a rough trip. Had some time to kill before the 11:00 departure so I did a little food shopping plus some sight seeing. About the whole thing that interested me in the city was the fish market where the fishermen peddled their catch. I was “all eyes” as one of the men took a fish that a woman wanted and neatly cut its belly, removed the insides, chopped the fish into small steaks, removed the fins etc. Another stall introduced me as it consisted of huge hunks of red meat which I presumed to be whale meat. The time grew late so I headed for the boat, the long passport line and the boarding.

        The trip was quite uneventful. We passed hundreds of small rocky islands on the way to the sea, but after the first couple of hours there wasn’t much to be seen. The rain stopped, but it never got warm enough to spend much time out on deck. The sea was peaceful and outside of a little bumping by the motor, the trip was very smooth. I spent the time in the lounge reading my travel pamphlets and attempting to plan the rest of my trip. The trouble is that it seems to get longer and longer, and I doubt if I will ever get home. Oh well, my money will run out eventually. Began reading the play “Man and Superman” by Bernard Shaw and found it to be quite good, – better than I thought it would be. Just before I settled down for the night in the lounge, a vacant berth was given to me, so I slept in style after all.

SEP 20

        The steward came around early to awaken everybody, but it just meant that we had a long time to wait; since there was a thick fog in the harbor and the boat was unable to dock. I got my luggage together and got in line early, so that I could go through customs before the luggage from the ship got in and the customs officials thoroughly inspected the Britishers belongings. A boat train waited on the dock and took me (and the others!) to Newcastle where I switched trains for Durham.

        The thick fog and haze of the morning began to lift, and by the time I reached Durham, the sun was out, although it was not too brilliant, perhaps because of the smog over the city. Durham is a small town of 20,000, noted for its coal, castle and cathedral. I was particularly interested in the cathedral as my “Outline to European Architecture” had stated that it was a fine example of Romanesque style. I found that by referring to the book, I was far more interested in the cathedral, and for once the architecture and form of construction meant something to me. The church was built around 1100 AD and is noted for its rib vaults, pointed arches and simple yet elegant interior. I noted all the points brought out in the book, and also discovered that by seeing the technical construction mentioned in the book, that I was beginning to remember the terms and differences in architecture styles.

        I spent the rest of the afternoon walking about town, and visited the castle near the cathedral. (fair). I guess I expected all that I saw, but nevertheless I was all “eyes” as I looked in shop windows, observed the “bobbies”, watched the automobiles and the left hand driving, noticed the dirty faces of the coal miners and the heavy make-up on the faces of the English women, and in general, got my first tastle taste of everyday life in England.

        

SEP 21

        I was up quite early – the YMCA beds aren’t the most comfortable – and began a systemmatic tour of the city. My pamphlet listed 3 main sights, so I decided to see them first, and spend the remainder of the time on window-shopping and roaming the streets. First on the list was Edinburgh Castle located on a hill in the center of the city. Other than the strategic location and its age, there wasn’t much to the buildings. The view of the city was nice, and the items in the Scottish National War Memorial (located in the Castle) were fairly interesting. Not too far from the Castle is located St. Giles Church, the second item on the list. The outstanding feature of the Church was the “Chapel of the Most Ancient and Most Noble Order of the Thistle”, the highest order of Scottish chivalry. The chapel, 38’ x 18’, is elaborately decorated, and the wood carvings were some of the finest that I have seen. Between the canopies over the knights stalls (16 members) hang cute little bronze angels holding lights. The third sight was the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the official residence of Her Majesty the Queen when in Edinburgh. A guide ushered us around the building and pointed out interesting historical facts, most of them pertaining to Mary Queen of Scots.

        The city of Edinburgh is quite pretty and the huge hill in the center (Castle) and the one at East end divide the city so that it isn’t one mass of dark buildings. The main avenue is Princes Street which is a straight road across the center of the city, one side being a park and housing such things as the Scott Memorial, and the other side containing expensive store and banks. Saw some kilts, but not too many, (thank goodness as I don’t like them), and spent a lot of time getting use to the British Isles, its people and customs. Sort of smiled to myself when I passed a club with a rich looking man sitting in a big chair; or heard the accents; or watched the people using their World War II bags to carry things; and the many other generalities I think of when I think of England.

SEP 22

        The train ride to Callander was fairly interesting, but a haze seemed to keep the beauty of the countryside from appearing. On the way I read an article in Time magazine describing the damage that the typhoon did to Okinawa a couple of weeks ago. It said that there were 7000 Okinawan houses destroyed and $10 million damage to US installations alone. Whew it must have been a bad blow.

        I had a 2 hours wait in Callander, so I spent the time walking about this small country town. Seems to be pretty much of a resort town as there were many hotels and restaurants. The houses were mostly stone, and the majority of them had well kept flower gardens. The English seem to love flowers (and dogs) for everybody has them and/or discusses them. Overheard a priceless conversation on the train between 3 women concerning how the weather had effacted their flowers and vegetables this year. One woman had a “great” accent.

        The bus ride to the Trossachs and the subsequent ride on the boat on Loch Katrine was quite enjoyable. The Trossachs are a wooden area, noted for its wild beauty, and the connection (or mention of) that it and Loch Katrine (Ellen’s Isle) played in Scott’s “The Lady of the Lake.” The haze persisted all afternoon, and distracted from the trip, however, I was able to get a view of this part of Scotland. There were few houses around the lake, and I think that it would be an ideal spot for a summer house. However, since Glasgow gets its water from here, I doubt if it would be possible.

        Met a couple Americans on the train going back to Edinburgh, and after talking to them, I sort of changed my mind about American tourists, especially those in their 50’s and 60’s. It appears that this is their first, and most likely only trip to Europe, and these people are not interested in doing away with the comforts they are use to in the States. Most of them want to see as much as they can with not much effort, and consequently they go to agencies such as American Express. Time has been the big factor up to now as to the reason for not coming before. Also, they have had much responsibility in raising a family, and developing a decent standard of living. Also they buy many presents (1) because this is their only trip to Europe, and a they feel that they want to bring something back to their family. I think they miss a lot by traveling 1st class and going on guided tours, however, I don’t think they know better, nor what the inconvenience of same.

SEP 23 (SUNDAY - WEEK 92)

        Today was just “one of those days.” Things started off bad when the train to Birmingham was 2 ½ horus late, forcing me to miss my connection to Stratford-upon-Avon. Nevertheless, it afforded me an opportunity to spend 3 ½ hours in the dirty, industrial city of Birmingham. I spent the time wandering about the city, and although it is not right to judge a city in 3 ½ hours, I was glad to leave when the time came to catch my train. The city is dirty, there doesn’t appear to be much to see, and what public buildings that they have, are covered with black soot. One thing that interested me were the many negroes that I saw on the streets. I presume they are Jamaicans, and are beginning to present England with a color problem; for as the Scot told me last nite in the bar, “the darkies are ruining this place.” (Oh yes, I was invited to have a beer with 2 gregorious 50 year old Scots, who had been in the RAF, liked Americans, and felt sorry for me standing by myself!)

        Upon arriving in Stratford, I got a “bed and breakfast” for $1.75 (too much), but wanted to clean up and wash some clothes. Found out that there wasn’t any plays on Sunday nite, so I sort of feel that I came for nothing. Oh, Shakespeare’s birth place is a little interesting, together with some museum items, but they other houses, parks etc. left me flat. – A typical tourist attraction.

SEP 24

        Decided to visit Warwick and its famous castle while I was in the neighborhood; consequently I took the 9:30 bus to the town of Warwick, located 8 miles from Stratford. The Warwick Castle  is supposed to be the largest and most impressive of the old English baronial castles, and dates from the 13th and 14th centuries. One is able to take a guided tour of the premises, and see the collection of paintings, furniture and other objects collected over the years by the various Earl of Warwicks. I enjoyed seeing the castle, its collections and armor, but feel that if I saw too much of this sort of thing, I would tire of it quite quickly. The flowers in the garden are very nice.

        The remainder of the day was spent in a variety of activities. From the castle I visited St. Mary’s Church which has some interesting graves of the Warwick family. Walked around town a bit and then hitched a ride to Stratford with a woman truck driver who persisted in calling me “love.” She was very friendly and I enjoyed the ride with her to Stratford. I have no intention of returning in the future to Stratford so I thought I best go to the church and view his Shakespeare’s grave while I was here. The church is quite old, and somewhat interesting, and the tomb was worth seeing with respect to the inscription on the top. (Something like, – curse be he who moves my bones, bless he who leaves them alone – or something to this effect).

        I had time to kill before the next bus to Oxford, so I began hitching or at least motioning my thumb. After a half hour I secured a ride with a truck driver into oxford, and although it was bumpy I saved time and money. While looking for a room I saw a place labeled, “English-speaking Union” and asked them if they knew of a place to stay. The lady was extremely friendly and helpful, and suggested where to go (in student boarding house area) and arranged for me to have dinner at with an English family. The housewife was very nice, the dinner fair, and I enjoyed the evening very much. The 2 sons, Steve & Andy Hurst, and a french boy staying at their house, joined me in beer at a quaint, country pub situated on the River Thames. I have found the English to be very friendly.

SEP 25

        Today was one of those things when everything seemed to work out quite well. I spent the first part of the morning wandering around Oxford by myself. There was a thick fog so I couldn’t take pictures, still I could get an idea of the various (26) colleges. Oxford is somewhat different from most Universities and can be compared to the States-US National Government relationship. The students live, eat and study in the various colleges, but attend lectures or labs with other students from other colleges. The main difference is the tutor, who guides the student, and around whom the University is centered. The student must meet his tutor every week, however, he is not obliged to go to the lectures. Much of the work is done on by the student on his own.

        All of the colleges have long traditions; old, historic buildings, and an intangible feeling of “class.” Most of the colleges have their own libraries, great halls (eating and lectures) and rooms for the students. The layout of the buildings is generally in the form of a quadrangle, with the rooms of the students built in the quadrangle buildings, and usually a staircase for every 2-4 student quarters. (generally 2 rooms per student, although some share a sitting room.) The Lady at the English Speaking Union found a guide for me, and the young lady pointed out many of the interesting places and the history behind it. (Library, Divinity Building, etc.) All in all, I had a fine time in Oxford.

        Decided to hitch-hike and got a ride within 10 minutes after I began. Arrived in London at the same time my train would have, and then went to Earl’s Court where I was lucky to get a private room. It was great to unpack and know that I would be here awhile. Went straight to American Express, where I picked up some mail, and got nowhere on arranging passage home. Guess I will just have to wait until I either get to Rotterdam, or maybe Paris before lining up a last minute passage. Still don’t know what to do about Spain. Visited Piccadilly Circus later in the afternoon and again in the evening and enjoyed the teeming masses and neon lights.

SEP 26

        I saw many buildings, people and objects in general today, and enjoyed all that I saw and did. Westminster Abbey was one of the first places that I visited, and I think it is one of the finest places that I have been to in Europe. The building is a huge “perpendicular” Gothic type church, with rough-but-simple buttresses and arches, and tall towers and nave. While the construction might be of simple finish, the graves and monuments weren’t and some of them were very interesting works of art. One goes back in the pages of history when he sees the graves and/or memorials to Newton, Shelly, Henry VII, Elizabeth, etc.

        Near Westminster Abbey was the House of Parliament, but the only portion open today to visitors was the huge Westminster Hall, with its broad, unsupported timber roof. I believe the Royalty of England lie in State here upon their death. Not much to see at Buckingham Palace, although the Victoria Monument is well done, and I got a couple of laughs watching the ridiculous palace guards going through their show. Was very much impressed with St. James Park, as it is a very beautiful park, with extremely verdant grass and trees, a small lake with ducks, flowers and lawn chairs for people to sit in. It being a fine day (I have been very fortunate concerning the balmy weather England has had during the past week) there were many Londoners, – old and young alike, taking advantage of their park.

        Walked about town, passing famous buildings (No. 10 Downing Street, Scotland Yard, Treasury) and observing the passing parade on Whitehall Street, in Trafalgar Square and Piccadilly Circus. I love the men in their formal black clothes and derby hats. Near the end of the afternoon I visited Tate Galleries (modern art – good, but I wasn’t too interested) and Westminster Cathedral (huge Catholic church). Saw the play “No Time For Sergeants” in the evening and enjoyed it very much. Spent an hour drinking beer with a medical student from Malta.

SEP 27

        London is proofing to be a very enjoyable town. Even though rains came for the first time this afternoon, still I have found enough to do to be on the go from 11-12 hours a day. Today, I journeyed first to Buckingham Palace to see the changing of the guard. The whole “shenanigans” took 1 ½ hours, but I enjoyed the spectacle even though it would have been better were it a trifle shorter. The bands played, the pipers piped, the men strutted in their red and black uniforms and it was quite a production. Their slow-step hesitant marching and the piping were particularly pleasing for me to see and hear. I thought the other marching was sloppy relative to the fac that this was a show group which did nothing else.

        Next stop was the Tower of London which was interesting owing to the fact that many historical British personalities were imprisoned and/or beheaded here. I guess the thing I liked the most was the old Norman architecture in the Chapel of St. John. The short, heavy columnal & semispherical arches and ceiling fit the picture to a T of what I had read concerning this type of architecture. From the shore of the Thames I could see the To London Bridge quite clearly, and I was hoping that “maybe it would fall down!” (Poor sense of humor.) Speaking of humor, I did get a kick out of listening to the soap-box orators and watching a chain escape artist on Tower Hill. Two of the orators preached a fiery religion, another spoke on labor and a fourth did nothing much except provoke the crowd and then to outwit people who spoke up with a clever tongue ie. (“don’t bring your troubles to my table and vomit them in my food!”)

        St. Paul’s Cathedral was very interesting and I was impressed by the grandeur, yet beautiful simplicity of the architecture. The dome is quite outstanding and is on a par with the one on St. Peters in Rome. In the crypt below the church are tombs to great Englishmen in Nelson and Wellington.

        Saw a fine comedy in the evening. “The Chalk Garden.”

SEP 28

        Thought provoking day today, and I didn’t really resolve the problems by the time I went to bed. First thing in the morning I went to American Express to check on boat sailings, and was told that I could get a tourist berth on the S.S. Constitution sailing from Spain on October 29th. The main problem is the $208.00 cost, and the fact that I have to decide by tomorrow. I said that I would let them know, and started making the rounds of shipping lines, from Spain and England-France. Everyone said that they were booked solid until the middle of November, but they did admit that I would have a fair chance of getting a last minute cancellation if I wanted to hound the offices just before sailing. The matter gets more complicated by the Oct 20 summer season rates ($180-$190) and the fact that there aren’t many ships until the 24th or thereafter. Thus, I would have to prolong my Holland-Paris visit, while if I went South I would know exactly when I left and how to allot my time. I called the American Export Lines (SS Constitution) and the man said that the London office never charges cancellation fines – he didn’t know about the continent – and he added, “we would rather make a friend instead of an enemy.” Sooo – headaches, pocketaches, – I guess I will sign aboard.

        After I had exhausted the number of nearby shipping agencies, I decided to get some other small details attended to. Did a little shopping and bought Morton a scarf and Carolyn the white sweater that she wanted. Now all I need is a present for Mom and I will be finished. Walked to the British Museum and spent 2 hours wandering through the galleries and looking at the fabulous antiquities on display. The Egyptian mummies, statues and the Rosetta Stone; plus the Greek statues and the “stolen” work from the Parthenon were outstanding. Didn’t finish, so will have to return.

        In the evening I attended a ballet (Saddler's Wells Ballet) at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden. Must admit that I enjoyed it although the seats were extremely uncomfortable.

SEP 29

        Arrived at American Express quite early, and paid the ¼ fare down payment on the passage on the Constitution. The man said as did the one at the American Export lines, said that if I cancelled early enough I would most likely get my money back. Consequently, I shall check when I get to Rotterdam and Paris on freighters that might be headed to the States. Had an unpleasant experience with the railroad clerk at A.E. and decided to cancel the reservation after having him make it. Asked the mgr. (when I cashed my check) – without saying who the person was – whether he thought I was right (I wanted to pay for the ¼ fare and railroad ticket out of the 1 check and the man got mad that I couldn’t pay immediately) and he said certainly. Anyway, I decided that I wouldn’t harbor in my mind things such as this anymore and will deal for with them as they come up. Went to the British railway afterwards and saved 12 shilling by being able to buy 2nd class.

        I then spent another 1 ½ hours at the British Museum, and enjoyed my visit as much as the previous day. They certainly have a vast number of outstanding exhibits. The day was sunny and cool and I decided I best get to the Soccer match early to get a good “seat.” I arrived at 1 PM and immediately got in line for Standing Space. Waited 2 hours before the game and then stood another 1 ½ hours during the match. Actually, ¾ of the stadium is for standing, with occasional rails for the people to lean on. There were 66,000 people at the match and the excitement was tremendous, since one of the teams was the Manchester United Football Club, perhaps the best soccer club in Europe, – certainly England. The home team put up a valliant valiant fight but went down to defeat, 2-1. Although, I do not understand all the points of the game, the play was good, the game close, and soccer is the type of game where lucky bounces and rolls aid to equalize 2 teams. I can see why the Europeans find it so exciting.

        Saw Peter Ustinov in his own play, “Romanoff & Juliet,”but other than his performance I was disappointed. On leaving the theater I spent time in Piccadilly Circus and was amazed at the large number of prostitutes.

SEP 30 (SUNDAY - WEEK 93)

        I shall long remember this day, if not the date, surely the remarks and thoughts that it produced. Around 3:30 I went to Hyde Park to hear the soap box orators and I stayed nearly 6 hours listening to (and being involved in) to speeches concerning religion, communism, suez canal and other topics. Religion, Communism and Colonialism seemed to predominate; and in connection with colonialism, I heard a fine, intelligent colored man from the Gold Coast speak in favor of independence for his country and for all Africans. Many in his audience were negroes, and I presume that they were from Africa. The crowds varied from speaker to speaker, with many colored people and Communists in the audience. The speakers for the Communist Party were very poor and everybody had a lot of laughs at their poor reasoning. This further substantiates my belief that Communism should not be outlawed.

        Later in the afternoon I was listening to a small argument, and after I threw in a question, I found myself as a sole defender of American capitalism against 3 or 4 Communist thinkers. One of the fellows was quite reasonable and we discussed some basic philosophies. He left though, and I found myself discussing with 2 radicals, who speak spoke in idealisms and other distortions, and whenever I tried to make a point, ie against Stalin, they would say I was misinformed or ahead on the that I misinterpreted the facts. They got too senseless for me to continue so when another spoke up, I left, a wiser man than I had been before I came. For there is no question but that the Western World has many faults, ie Suez, Cyprus, tabloids, etc. and an ideal, preaching communist has attractive things to offer. It appears to me that there will have to be some form of compromise to the systems now practiced which is best for undeveloped countries of the world to use to raise their standard of living.

        Earlier in the day I visited Madame Tussaud’s wax works with its wonderful realistic statues of famous personalities, – living & dead. Also visited Pettycoat Lane (shops & stalls) but everything was closing up as it was around 2 PM, and no business of this sort can take place after that time.

OCT 01

        Awakened to a typically London day, at least the kind that I have been told about. It rained all day, and at times was extremely dark, however, I had seen most of the sights that i wanted to see in London so I took a side trip to Windsor. The rain spoiled much of the beauty of the old 15th century castle and the surrounding grounds, and I carried my camera for naught. Took a tour of the State Apartments (not too impressed although they had some valuable paintings); observed the miniature doll house (fair); and visited St. George’s Chapel. The Chapel is constructed in perpendicular architecture, and I enjoyed viewing it so as to compare it with what I had read of this style of architecture (new ball point pen). The ceiling in particular was beautifully carved stone, perhaps the most elaborate that I have seen – even including the one at Oxford. Just as I was leaving the sun came out, but not enough to take pictures.

        Strolled down to the other side of town to view Eaton College and the Eaton undergraduate. Sort of humorous to see these young fellows strolling about town in black-stripped pants, tails and white tie. Oh well. The British tradition must be preserved, even if it kills them to do it. This tradition is everywhere in England, particularly among the older people; but still preserved in certain places such as Eaton, Oxford and Cambridge. In London one sees many Englishmen with the black derby, gloves and umbrella. Tea is sold everywhere and it doesn’t appear that an Englishman could go a day without a cup of tea (like coffee in America). Even though I don’t think the people are extremely practical and hard working, still I like the tradition and the British people in general. Everybody was quite kind to me, and I received assistance whenever I asked somebody. The weather & people combined to make my 12 day visit an enjoyable one.

        Boarded the train and later the ship, and for once I didn’t have to worry about a berth as I had one reserved on my ticket. Oh yes, I bought Marx’s “Capital” today and hope to read it going home.

Route as of October 1st, 1956 – end of Chapter 16.

CHAPTER 17 - THE LAST LEG

October 2nd, 1956 - October 28th, 1956

OCT 02

        Quite a busy day today. The ship docked around 5:30 AM, but I didn’t get off until an hour later. Took the train to Rotterdam where I spent the morning visiting travel agencies and shipping lines in order to secure information of passage to the States. It appears that there are no cheap fares available until the end of November. I could of obtained booking on some freighters but it appears that freighters and cargo ships are more expensive than passenger ships. Consequently, it appears that I will be heading home via Spain aboard the Constitution. I didn’t spend a lot of time in Rotterdam as there didn’t seem to be much to see. Strolled about the harbor – huge in size – and explored the gigantic Wholesaler’s Building, supposed to be the largest building in Western Europe. About the only thing that fascinated me was an unusual brick decoration of the facade of a building near the station.

        Took the noon train to the Hague and spent the afternoon in this charming city. Took a tour through the Peace Palace which is the present site of the International Court of Justice. The guide that showed the group through the building was ever-so charming, but didn’t hardly mention what the Court did or the interesting cases that have been presented before the justices. Not too far from the Peace Palace in the miniature city, “Madurodam” by name. It is a reproduction, 1/25th to scale, of a typical Dutch city complete with harbor, moving ships and trains, lamp posts, flowers, buildings and even an airport. Although the individual objects aren’t outstanding, the city as a whole is a fascinating sight to behold, and one has a curious sensation as he, a giant, walks among the small buildings. Spent the rest of the afternoon walking about the city. Even though it is quite large, 550,000, it still has the charm of a large village.

        On to Amsterdam where I checked into the hostel. Morton’s friend, Else Byl, works at the Information counter of the railroad station, so I spent some time talking to her.

OCT 03

        I don’t think that there is a lot to see in Amsterdam; however I think it is a very nice town, with a lot of night life. The first thing that I did in the morning was to go to American Express where I picked up some overdue mail. Enclosed in Morton’s letter was a reply from the State Department saying that I passed the written examination for the Foreign Service with a grade of 74. I was glad to receive the news, as it restores a lot of confidence in my general knowledge since I did absolutely no studying for the test. The scores for the test were: General Ability (84), English Expression (64), and General background (74), with a weighted average grade of 74. (70 is passing) Since I was supposed to answer by September 20th I went to the Consul General to seek their advice and to obtain forms that Morton did not send. I used the typewriter at the Consulate and typed out a letter to the head of the Examination Board requesting further information on the Orals.

        Visited the Rijksmuseum in the morning and looked at the Rembrandt sketches and paintings that were on display. I must say that I wasn’t impressed with the exhibition, although some of the sketches were quite good. Viewed some of the other landmarks of the city, and toured the waterfront. Came upon one street with ugly, blonde, middle age whores practicing their profession in the middle of the day. Saw many bars, and decided to return in the evening to visit one or two. In the afternoon I met a New Zealand boy (Allan Notby) and we went around the city after supper. There wasn’t much to the bars, in fact, they seemed to cater mainly to the “rich” American serviceman. One obnoxious bar girl made me sick with her crude language which she thought to be very funny. I hope the majority of the people try to copy the better things from America instead of the filthy language (from servicemen) and the “Rock and Roll” records. Seems that is all I heard in these cheap bars.

​​OCT 04

        Al and I left Amsterdam early in the morning and rode to Harderwijk. We then proceed to walk on the earth dikes to one of the pumping stations located on Usel Lake. (formerly Zuydersea). The wind was extremely brisk and cold and I nearly froze during the 3-4 mile walk. The head of the station was extremely nice and he explained the process whereby 4 of such stations will empty the water out of this “Polder” and thus reclaim about 135,000 acres of land. The dike building period took 3 years on this section and it will take another 7 months to drain the water. This is the 3rd of 5 sections to be reclaimed from the Zuydersea, and when the total project is completed there will be an additional 550,000 acres of land. The water we were told is fresh water, since the sea has been shut out by a dike near the entrance of the Zuydersea. The man also said that it was not possible to reclaim all the land as they needed a lake to maintain a reservoir for the differences in level of the North Sea, and for the water from the rivers and canals which flow to the Zuydersea.

        It began to rain, so we asked a bus driver for a lift to a town on the dike – 25 Km. from Harderwijk and situated out in the water. As we talked a Dutch gentleman came up and introduced himself as Public Relations Director for the Dutch Gov’t for this area, and he said that we could ride in his car with his chauffeur (he would be with the bus & a group of people he was showing around) to the city (15-20 houses, restaurant, museum, workshops) and then to Urk. We thanked him and spent the next 3 hours riding along the dike (40-50 feet wide) and thence to Urk, a town located in the Northeast Polder, a section that was reclaimed about 10 years ago. The section consisted primarily of rich looking grazing land and I think I saw “millions” of dairy cows. Many new houses and prefabricated concrete barns were in the process of construction. At Urk we saw one of the locks and the difference in water level was about 20’ (a dramatic sight to behold. Took the bus to one of the brand new cities EMMELOORD and spent an hour walking around. From here we came back to Amsterdam.

​​OCT 05

        A little too much rain to suit me, as it drizzled all day long. It had hailed during the early morning and I debated about going to Alkmaar, but since I had nothing else to do until train time I decided to go. Really wasn’t much to the “fascinating & colorful” cheese market, but perhaps the rain spoiled the atmosphere. The market consisted of 5 or 6 trucks arriving between 8-9 AM and unloading 200-300 round (approx 8” dia) cheese balls on the ground in front of the weighing station. At 10 AM men in white dress with colored hats took the balls to the weighing house where they were weighed on huge scales. Then they carried (by means of a sled attached to straps on each of the 2 men) the cheese to a push cart where they were unloaded and taken to a large warehouse. From here I am not sure the next step.

        I took the 11 AM train back to Amsterdam and had another good, cheap (.35¢) meal at Ruteck’s Cafeteria. The meal consisted of soups, spaghetti, peas, cheese croquettes and dessert. The main reason why I had stayed in Amsterdam an extra day was so that I could visit a diamond-cutting factory. The factory that I visited had a small showroom and a well built Dutch girl pointed out the process. She showed me the small saw which they cut the diamond, the apparatus used in making the cut diamond round, and then I saw 2 men who were adding the 58 facets to the diamond. This latter work was done by hand, and magnifying glass and a diamond impregnated wheel turning at 3000 RPM. One of the workers performed at a high speed and it was interesting to see him work. There were also some interesting displays and glass replicas of the famous diamonds in the showroom.

        The train ride to Brussels was uninteresting and I arrived about 7 PM. There was no hotel information and so I had to find a cheap room for the night. Can’t say that I have a good opinion of Brussels after 1 night, but lets hope tomorrow changes my mind.

​​OCT 06

        One of the good features of having no set itinerary is that it is easy to alter ones plans and stay longer (Greece), go to another place (Sweden), or to leave a place earlier than planned (Belgium). After dodging the cold rain all day I decided to skip Ghent and Bruge and head south where I hope there is nicer weather. I spent the day in Brussels, trying to see as many of the outstanding sights as possible without getting too wet. I enjoyed the early Gothic church of St. Michel and Ste. Gudula, and was fortunate to overhear a guide explaining how they saved the beautiful stain glass windows during the war. It cost $200,000 to put the glass back. 

        The Grand Place is an interesting square composed of the Town Hall, and many old guild houses with gold leaf decorations and baroque figures splashed everywhere. A guide showed me thru the Town Hall, and perhaps the most interesting feature was a man who was repairing the gold leaf decorations on a door. He used 4” squares of gold leaf, which he placed in spots where the old gold had worn away. The guide said that a special varnish would then be applied to the leaf to make it wear better. Not too far from the square was the famous little statue of the Manneken-Pis, which is a little bronze statuette (1619) showing a small boy pissing. I understand that there are many different costumes for the boy to wear, however, he was in the nude today. In the afternoon I wandered up to the Palace of Justice, a huge building in Classical architecture, and supposedly the largest building of the 19th century.

        Met an Israeli boy at the Town Hall, and we walked and talked for about an hour. He was born in Rumania and emigrated to Israel in 1950. We discussed the Israel retaliation methods (which he feels is needed to let the Arabs know that the Israelis will not sit by and let their people be killed); the language problem (Hebrew being a dead language, more or less) and other problems. In the evening I went with him to see the Opera “Carmen.”

​​OCT 07 (SUNDAY - WEEK 94)

        I am glad that I decided to leave Brussels, as it was cold, wet and nasty I when I got up in the morning. The train to Paris was an express and we arrived in about 4 hours. While I was on the train I read 3 of Sophocles’ plays, “Electra,” “Ajax,” and “Women of Trachis.” At the beginning I wasn’t sure whether I would like them, but they proved to be quite interesting and easy to read.

        I checked my big bag (oh will I be glad to store it when I get home) and went to the hotel Al had suggested. The hotel, however, was full, and so were most of the others in the neighborhood. I inquired about the prices and when they quoted from 1000-1300 francs, I headed for the Latin Quarter on the left bank. Luckily I obtained a nice size room, (only freezing col water, no bath, dirty WC) for 500 francs, and I guess this will be home during my week in Paris. I think the 5 flights of stairs will be the end of me yet.

        The weather in Paris is cold and somewhat wet, however, there are many “inside” attractions that I can visit when it rains. It was 3 PM, and I had some time that could be put to good use, so I walked over to the Louvre Museum. Today being Sunday, there was no admission charge and I think all of Paris must have been there and later walking on the Champs Elysees. Thousands of people roamed the halls and crowded around the pictures, and it was difficult to move at times. Not being a great Art lover, I tried to see the main “public acclaimed” pieces and to notice others that I thought interesting. Thus I saw the “Mona Lisa,” “Venus de Milo” and “Winged Victory.” I enjoyed the Greek section most of all.

        In the evening I walked around the Champs Elysees (beautiful shops, merchandise and women), and then in the Latin Quarter (not much visible to the inexperienced eye). Later I went to Pigale and had a beer at a jazz bar and then walked along the streets admiring the nude pictures in front of the strip (and grip) joints.

OCT 08

        Slept very well and awakened around 8. Straightened out my things and then began a morning of getting some “little things” taken care of. At American Express I got my mail (and newspapers) and inquired of trains to the South. Checked at some tourist and travel agencies and bought a ticket for the opera this evening. Finally finished around 1 PM and went back to my room where I washed my hair in the frigid water. Must admit that the thought of having water and showers in the not too distant future is an appealing thought.

        The weather is cool, but nice, and consequently I set out to see some of the sights. First stop was Notre Dame Cathedral, and I must admit that it is one of the finest. I can’t figure out why the Catholics haven’t cluttered up the interior with their usual trash, but they haven’t; and it is much the finer for its simplicity. The interior is somewhat different than many early Gothic churches as it has a narrow nave with double aisles on each side, and its transepts are short and placed near the center of the E-W axis which makes for a long chancel. Some of the circular stain glass windows are very attractive.

        Leaving the Cathedral I walked to the 2nd of the Islands on the Seine River – Ile St. Louis – and observed the old buildings which once were occupied by the wealthy. Stopped for a few minutes at the Place de la Bastille (just a column) and then headed home, observing 2 churches and the city hall (Hotel de Ville) along the way.

        In the evening I went ot the opera (huge building – not filled not this evening) and thought the production – The Phantom Ship by Wagner – was so-so. On the way “home” I had a few glasses of wine at a student hangout on L’Abbaye street. The students are sure different from the Oxford crowd, and I enjoyed watching their actions and observing their sloppy dress. Both the boys & girls let their hair grow long, with girls allowing the hair to just hang over their shoulders. The girls also use a lot of eye make-up.

OCT 09

        Another busy day. In the morning I got tickets for the Opera (actually a ballet) and for the Folies Berger. At American Express I took the big plunge and paid the rest of my fare on the “Constitution.” So it appears that my travels will be about over once the 29th of October rolls around. I looked for a self service restaurant, but couldn’t find any, so I had to go into a local restaurant which seemed reasonably cheap. I ordered veal “something” and it turned out to be tongue (at least I think so). Tried my best to eat it but just couldn’t, so I had to order an omlet. The bill, including wine and 1 piece of bread was 460 francs, which sold me on self service restaurant. (cheaper and you can see what you are getting.) At this “cheap” restaurant I paid 80 for bread & cover and 50 for service. Ridiculous). Actually I think Paris is very expensive, and not only does the tourist pay for the name, but I can’t imagine how the Parisians manage to live.

        Spent the afternoon sightseeing. Walked up to the Montmartre District where I visited the Sacre Coeur Church and later the district around the church. Supposedly this is an artist hangout, and I did see 2 or 3 men on the street painting pictures. Took the subway (Metro) to Madeleine Church which is constructed in Greek Classical style – very similar to the Parthenon. (So-so). Meandered around Place de la Concorde (with its Obelisk) and the Jardin des Tuileries near the Louvre. Walked along the Champs Elysees and admired the shops and people. Passed through the Arc de Triumphe and head down Foch Avenue to Bois de Boulogne Park. The avenue is quite attractive with its many fine apartments lining its sides. Visited the Automobile Show at the Grand Palais and looked with envy at the many fine autos. The American cars sure dwarf the European models.

        In the evening I headed for Pigalle, and intended to visit one of the strip shows but the 400 cover and 1000 franc drink price sent me scurrying for the little bar that I found last night. Had 2 beers (50 francs each) and enjoyed the atmosphere.

OCT 10

        The weather has been great lately, cool, but sunny and with no rain. I took the early train to Versailles, and spent 2 hours walking through the immense gardens and on a tour of the apartments. I wasn’t as impressed as I thought that I would be, in fact, other than its huge proportions I was somewhat disappointed. One thing I did like was the manner in which the trees were laid out – so evenly spaced as such a vast forest.

        Arriving back in the city, I went to the Eiffel Tower, the famous iron landmark that watches over Paris. The Tower was taller than I thought and I was amazed at the mass of steel framework and millions of bolts. I climbed (can’t say that it was worth say saving the 100 francs) to the 2nd floor and spent some time viewing the city, which lay before my eyes. The day was clear and consequently I could see all the way across town to the Sacre Coeur Church. I took a picture of the tower from the Parc du Champs de Mars as the sun was out and everything stood out just right. Walked by the Military School (where Napoleon went) and thence to Hotel des Invalids where Napoleon is buried in fine grandeur. (Huge block of granite serving as his sarcophagus). Took the bus to the Luxembourg Park - where hundreds of mothers were watching their children play – and then walked to the Sorbonne University.

        The French student seems to have no inhibitions, and one sees dress of all kinds and generally ragged appearances. Many of the fellows grow beards and their hair is long. The girls use a lot of eye make-up and have all kinds of hair-do. One often sees a fellow kissing his girl on the street as if it were the thing to do. In a way I admire the attitude of the students, but sort of feel that they aren’t too practical. One thing I can’t figure out is how the Frenchman can afford the expensive food, for the place du jour is always around 385 francs and to order otherwise you are forced to pay a cover and other ridiculous prices. Went to the Opera in the evening and saw a very fine ballet – ”Romeo and Juliet.” (very good) and “Soir de Fete” (also quite good)

OCT 11

        There are some day when much is accomplished and there are others  – like today – when not many impressive things are seen or done. I attempted to phone Bill Shuber in the morning, and had no luck; however, I was able to talk to him later on in the day. After inquiring of his work and family, we made plans to meet Saturday afternoon at Chartres.

        Visited some museums today (all museums are free this week) among them being: National Museum of Modern Art (pretty good); Museum of Monumental Art (fair); Museum Guimet (Ascetic Art – fair) and once again the Louvre. The Louvre occupies a huge palace, – one of the largest and finest in the world. It has art objects of all sorts – sculpture, paintings, vases, etc – and the collection is said to total over 200,000 pieces. I had seen many of the paintings and statues on Sunday, so today I went back to see the famous pictures, and some antiquities that I had not seen before.

        One of the things that I did in the afternoon was to take a short, guided tour of the sewers. We went in boats and drifted about 500 yards downstream; and other than the fact that it was a swerve (huge concrete pipe with narrow walkways on each side) I did not get much from the trip and the guide who spoke in French. I think they ought to have one English speaking guides (didn’t have one at Versailles either) as there are over 60,000 English speaking people who come to Paris in the summer alone. Frankly, I think the French just don’t give a damn about tourists except for their money.  Incidentally I was approached by two men to exchange dollars for francs, but the difference now (390-$1, vs official 350-1 – I bought 410 - $1 in Switzerland) doesn’t justify the risk involved for me.

        In the evening I went to the famous Foiles Bergere. There were certain things that I liked – great scenery and costuming, good comedy – but on the whole I was disappointed. The dancing and singing was lousy, and not enough of the nudes!

OCT 12

        Glanced at the sub-title and realized that it is Carolyn’s birthday. Well, hope to be with her next year on her birthday. In the morning I spent some time making further plans for my trip; before heading to the Pantheon where many famous Frenchmen are buried; ie Voltaire, Rousseau, etc. The building is in classical style and quite pretentious on the interior, particularly the paintings on the walls. The crypts below are just the opposite and the drabness therein adds much to the atmosphere of the purpose of the building – tombs. Had another bad experience with a fixed price menu, and now will refrain – when possible – from entering such places until my French gets better. (Very unlikely)

        Walked about the city for a couple of hours, spending part of the time gazing in the windows. Fortunately I didn’t see anything I wanted to buy, for my money is getting mighty low. Spent 2 ½ hours at American Express in order to pick up my boat and bus tickets, and to say the least, I was most perturbed. I kick myself everytime I deal with these people. Also, spent an hour at the USO, drinking free coffee and catching up on the latest news.

        In the evening I went to a small little bar – L’Abbaye, where 2 ballad type singers entertained a packed house of French and American people. Al Doré had recommended the place to me, and I must say that he has good taste for the singers were good and the atmosphere “just right.” Talked with some American girls – some in their 3rd year of college (now at the Sorbonne for 1 year) and others just tourists. One of the girls knew and has dated Al Serinsky.

        As I prepare to leave Paris I have mixed reactions concerning the city. The bread and wine are tops; many of their public monuments are works of beauty; the city itself is quite pretty; – but prices are far too high for what you get. London – which I liked better – is ½ as expensive as Paris. Also, I don’t think the people are especially friendly. The women are quite good looking though, in spite of their coldness – to me.

OCT 13

        For the first time, I got on the wrong subway, but fortunately it did not prevent me from catching the train to Chartres. The day was extremely misty and during the train ride and for the greater portion of the morning, it was difficult to see more than 50 feet in any direction. The town of Chartres is a quaint old French village, with perhaps the most outstanding cathedral in France. The cathedral is constructed in early Gothic style and is very simply furnished and decorated on the inside. The blue and other stain glass windows are the most beautiful that I have seen during my travels. Since Bill and Horte were a little late in arriving, I had a good opportunity to study the exterior sculpturing, design and construction. I particularly liked the manner in which the flying buttresses are incorporated in the construction, – not obvious and decorated with small statues.

        Bill and Horte and little “Chipper” arrived about 2 PM and it was good to see them and to talk to them about their experiences in Europe and on their miscellaneous travels. Since I had thought that they were going to the Auto show in Paris, I had left my bags there, consequently we had to go back to Paris to pick up my luggage before going to Orleans. Bill had sold his Plymouth and had bought a French car which rode quite well although it is a little cramped in the bad seat.

        We did so much talking on the way to Orleans that I didn’t have much of a chance to observe the countryside. Did notice the old buildings in the towns that we drove through and the fact that the new buildings are constructed in the same style as the ones built hundreds of years ago. Bill’s house in Orleans is quite nice and they have some excellent records – which we listened to after supper. We talked of things in general and I enjoyed their company. They had a roll-away bed which I used for a bed for the night.

OCT 14 (SUNDAY - WEEK 95)

        We all slept late, and then it was awhile before Horte fixed breakfast. Some of their friends came in while we were eating and I got an opportunity to meet them and to talk to them about things in general. The weather was misty at first but it gradually cleared up and the sun came out. Around 2 PM we left the house and took a ride to the Loire River Valley to visit a couple of Chateaus.

        The first Chateau we stopped at was the one at Blois, a huge building overlooking the river. It was inside the town and had little ground around it, so it was not possible to capture the whole beauty of the building. The other Chateau we visited – at Chambord – is the largest of the Chateaus and is surrounded by acres and acres of grass lawns and uniform trees. The building was unique in 2 ways (at least to me); one, concerned the many unusual “chimney like” objects and spires that projected upward from the roof; and second, the double spiral staircase in the center of the building. A person going up or down the stairs can not see another person going up or down who is at the same level. The building is about 350 years old and is constructed on a solid basis, ie thick walls and brick floors.

        We then drove back to the house where we spent the evening talking about different subjects. Bill and Horte appear to be very happily married and they have a cute son called “Chipper.” The more I talk to him, the more that I am convinced that Bill will be a top notch surgeon one of these days. I believe I would have full confidence in letting him cut me up. I had decided to take the evening night train to Perigueux where there are located some of the famous prehistoric caves. The trains were crowded and I got little sleep, but I saved time by going at nighttime.

OCT 15

        It was a rough night last nite. I didn’t get much sleep on the train as the compartment was crowded the major portion of the journey. I arrived in Perigueux at 5 Am and went to the waiting room where I got about 2 ½ hours sleep. After checking my bags I began inquiring of passage to Les Eyzies and the other prehistoric caves. It developed that there were are no buses to the caves (grottos) and the first train wasn’t until noon. I thought that I would be able to hitch hike, but after a fruitless 1 ½ hours of waving my right thumb I decided to take the noon train.

The town of Perigueux is a medium size, old French village, most likely untouched during the last war. Its streets are narrow and dirty and there isn’t a lot of activity going on. One thing unusual were the cathedral and churches with their round roofs,  unlike any that I have seen in Europe thus far. In many ways the churches resembled mosques, as they had the circularly vaulted roof, thick walls, no nave or aisle, and didn’t appear to be in the shape of a cross.

        Arriving in Les Eyzies on the noon train, I set out for the 2 well known prehistoric grottos in the immediate locale. The first grotto – ”Combarelles” – consisted of a long, irregular cave with stalagmites and stalactites hanging from the ceiling. On the walls were scratches and crude designs of bison, fish and other objects, supposed to have been placed there by prehistoric man 15,000-30,000 years ago. The remarkable thing is that they found anything at all, and not the engraving, for this is quite a thing to have been done so long ago and to last until the present time. The second cave – “Font-de-Gaume” – had some paintings, and it was quite easy to recognize the outlines of the deer, and bison. Most of the colors are gone, the outline color being the only thing that remains.

I dallied and consequently missed a train, and thus spent an additional 4 hours in Les Eyzies. Must admit that the town is very peaceful and beautifully situated on the Vezere River and nestled among the limestone cliffs.

OCT 16

        Rough night again last nite. I arrived in Toulouse at midnight and had 5 hours to wait before the train left for Barcelona. I tried to sleep in the waiting room but had very little success. To top it off, I needed to cash in some dollars for francs and the exchange office was closed. Fortunately, there was one decent trainman who sold me a ticket anyway. The train ride to Barcelona, Spain was quite long – 10 hours – and at times it was crowded. I slept a little bit, but not very much. About the only thing I did with success was almost complete Homer’s “The Odyssey” which I had begun last night.

        Although fog was close in at the beginning of the trip, it soon cleared up later on and the sun came out in its full “Spanish” glory. I really hadn’t given the people and their environment much thought, so I guess what I saw didn’t phase me either one way or the other. The land was rocky in parts, and well-tilled in others. The houses were light colored, and both new and old. Barcelona is a bigger city than I had come to believe, and I was surprised at the many cars and modern shops. Room, board and transportation are very cheap in Spain, and I get a full pension for $1.70. I also decided to travel 3rd class, so I bought my ticket to Madrid, keeping my fingers crossed as I did. I traveled from the French border to Barcelona 3rd class, and other than the fact that it was crowded and noisy, I didn’t mind it too much. Sort of enjoyed watching the typical Spaniard as he went about his conversation and eating. The clothes of those in my compartment were quite shabby and torn and I guess the average Spaniard has a rough time of it. One sees the Spanish police everywhere.

        Spent the afternoon walking about Barcelona and sitting on a thoroughfare and watching the people go by. Visited the ultra modern Church of the Sagrada Family (not yet finished) with its huge spires which make a fine outline against the blue sky.

OCT 17

        Started off the day by visiting the Barrio Gotico or old section of Barcelona. The main attraction was the Cathedral which is of early Gothic style – with Spanish variations – dating from the 12th century. A service which going on while I entered the church, so I sat and waited until it was completed. The chanting, bowing, shaking a pot of incense, reciting and other religious tasks made me sick. The money, given by the poor Spaniards to build elaborate and costly churches, clothe the priests in nice ceremonial garb and to feed and house them. I chuckled to myself when 3 big, fat, well-fed priests passed the spot where I was sitting. If this was not worse enough, but let me continue.I walked around the interior of the church and noticed white objects made of wax, tied to the various gates in front of the numeral altars in the ambulatory. On taking a closer look, I found the objects to be in the shapes of arms, legs, hearts, brains and other parts of the body. While I didn’t see anybody do it, I imagine these inane objects are a mother’s tent to aubonction efforts to pray for her illness, or her child. 

        From here I visited Pueblo Español the remains of a World Wide Exposition built in 1929, and which contains authentic reproductions of Spanish houses. There were some tradesmen, but in many of the houses, working by hand as did their forefathers before them. Had two interesting conversations in the afternoon: one was with an intelligent, self educated museum guide. His English is good and thus should go for to substantiate his claim of having spent over 4 years to have a tabla another language at ones his command. The second discussion concerned the pensions where I stayed. I was under the impression that drinks were included in full board, but evidently not. Consequently I refused to pay the full cost of a bottle of wine from which I had ½ a glass. I think I was wrong, and most likely should have paid the full price and taken the wine with me. Got my things together and caught the night (3rd class) train to Madrid.

        

OCT 18

        Spent a terrible night on the train. The seats (in 3rd class) were hard and straight up and down, making for miserable traveling. The occupants in my compartment proceded to get high on wine, consequently they jabbered – with the light on – until after 1 AM. I dozed off for a couple hours of sleep, but counted the half hours and hours from 4 AM until we arrived in Madrid at 9 AM. I thought that I wouldn’t have much difficulty in obtaining lodging but after 2 hours of pounding the pavement and getting about 30 negative replies, I was almost ready to head for Portugal. Luckily I found a place, and fortunately I was able to get just a room and not the complete pension so common in Spain.

        After getting settled, I set out to see the sights and take in the Spanish atmosphere. The first place I visited was the Prado Museum, a world famous art museum housing many paintings of Velazquez, Goya, El Greco, etc. (Can’t say that I was impressed. The art appreciation “bug” hasn’t bitten me yet). Nearby was Retiro Park, a huge, green area with shady walks, bridle paths and ponds. It was a pleasure to amble down the walls and watch the Spaniards doing the same. Later in the afternoon I took a trip through the Royal Palace, erected by the Bourbons in the 18th century, and now used occasionally by Franco for State functions. Franco, himself, lives about 20 miles from Madrid.

        Madrid is quite a pretty city, and there are many modern buildings being constructed. The people appear happy, and in Madrid (and Barcelona) the people are well dressed. The Spanish girls are quite attractive and seem to be quite well built. Most of the people have black hair, common for South Europe. The streets are clean, and some of them are very broad. The traffic police control the pedestrians with strict authority and one has to walk where and when they say. The National Police are everywhere, doing little, and wearing crazy looking hats. The army is sloppy looking and not very impressive.

OCT 19

        Almost overslept, but I managed to get up and on my way to Toledo, one of the most famous Spanish towns. The train ride was lousy but we arrived around 11 AM, – much blacker than when I had left. The city is built on a hill, and is surrounded by the Tagus River which sort of serves as a moat. The streets are steep and winding and made to keep the sun away (by being narrow) and not for the modern automobiles that move about. The city, – rich in historical treasures – has been declared a national monument. One reason for this declaration is the fact that a Franco group of cadets held out in the Alcazar Citadel for a long period during the Civil War before succumbing to the Loyalist forces. History sure changes things; – I can remember when most people supported the Loyalist movement, but now we are “friends” with Franco and one must remember that the Russians were on the Loyalist side. Big joke.

        Toledo has some “listed” sights to see, but I was mainly impressed with the city itself and its ancient atmosphere and wonderful location on the hill. Still one has to visit the sights so I started first with the 13th Century Cathedral, a Spanish Gothic structure with much too much ornamentation on the interior. As in the Barcelona Cathedral, there was the unusual wall across the choir which allows only a limited amount of seating between the choir and the altar. This wall – highly decorated – also tends to prevent ones attention from always focusing on the altar. Other places that I saw were: an ancient Jewish Synagogue with Hebrew writing on the interior, the ruins of the Alcazar, another church and old town gate. I had time before the next train, so I began hitch-hiking and was lucky to get a ride with some G.I.’s who were headed for Madrid.

        After a late supper I walked about town looking for an interesting bar to visit, however, I didn’t find anything that had the type of entertainment that I was looking for. Consequently, I headed home and decided to catch up on some writing before hitting the sack.

OCT 20

        I was resolved to spend as much as the day as I needed in order to get Mom some kind of gift. Fortunately, I found a table cloth (linen) that I liked at my second stop, and decided to buy it and hope that she likes it. This purchase completes my gift problem, and I must say it relieves me of a big worry. Shortly before I went shopping, I bought a train ticket to Cordoba, and will head South tomorrow night and thus by-pass Portugal.
