After doing some checking, I found that it takes too long to get to Lisbon and from there to Seville. Consequently, I will head South and after visiting the Andalusian cities, I will probably spend a day or two in Gibraltar and Tangier, Spanish Morocco.

        In the afternoon I went by train to El Escorial, a monastery erected in a barren and severe setting, about 43 Km from Madrid. Philip II built this huge monastery (and palace) to in memory of his famous father, Charles V. The main sights are the church – in the shape of a Greek cross; the palace furnishings (only things I thought interesting were a huge painting of a battle, and some Spanish tapestries); and the Royal Pantheon where all the Spanish kings are buried with the exception of two. The building occupies a position on the side of the hill, and from the windows one can see for miles. There are a few buildings here and there – plus the small town of El Escorial – but mainly one sees only rock, sage brush and poor land. For a building that is acclaimed the 8th wonder of the world, I must say that I was a little disappointed.

        In the evening I went to a theater (at 11 PM) ostensibly to see Spanish dancing, but it turned out to be more of a vaudeville show. The house was packed and cheered a comedian and singer everytime they did some novel vocal expressions. Spain is an interesting country: people eat at 8-9, 2-3 and 9-10, and after 10 PM they go out. Consequently, the streets were crowded with people when I went back at 2 AM. It also seems that there are no front door keys, – one has to clap his hands for a night watchman who opens the doors for you. (Stupid).

OCT 21 (SUNDAY - WEEK 96)

        I slept late since I didn’t get home until after 2 AM last night. I had planned on visiting the University, but it got so late owing to my packing and ironing, that I decided to skip it. In regard to the ironing, I was fortunate to be able to borrow the iron at the pension, and thus press most of my shirts and pants.

        After lunch I started for the bull ring, the main reason for my staying an extra day in Madrid. I walked for almost an hour and one half along Alcala Street; but didn’t mind the exercise and besides I enjoyed the scenery. The sun was shining and many people were either out strolling or having a drink at one of the many sidewalk cafes, on the sidewalk. I find that most of the men wear coats (the museum guard in Barcelona said they have to) and the women are well dressed and groped. I think that outside of the Scandanavian women, I like the Spanish girls best of the remaining Europeans.

        The Bull Ring is quite modern (1929) and designed with a Spanish feeling. The Ring is circular, about 3 tiered and holds approximately 20,000 people. Today, I would say there were ½ that number – mostly men. In some respects I was disappointed, as I wanted to hear the exciting bull fight music (as in movies) but there were only 2 puny bands that afternoon. Also, none of the bull fighters were able to kill their bull on the first thrust and some of them took from 3-8 thrusts before killing the thin helpless bull. I enjoyed the men who stuck the little sticks in the bull’s back and some of the bull fighters were quite adept with the cape. I can see why some associations are trying to ban bull fighting, as it is a cruel, bloody sport. I am glad though that I waited to extra day to see this afternoon activity.

        Had some time to spend before my train was to leave, so I had a glass of wine at a sidewalk cafe, and watched “Madrid” stroll by. Spanish wine isn’t nearly as good as the French wine though.

OCT 22

        I went 2nd class last night and after seeing the 3rd class wooden benches in the other train to Cordoba, I was sure pleased with my decision. Second class is no picnic, though, and I only got a few hours of sleep. I hope that last night was my final night for sleeping on a European train – that is, I should have one more night of sitting up before I reach St. Louie. I arrived in Cordoba at 7 AM, and spent the morning in this quaint town in the Andalusian section of Spain. The main attraction is a wonderful Arab Mosque, built in 796 AD, converted into a christian church in the 13th century, and now is an odd mixture of Moorish, Gothic and Renaissance styles. I was fascinated by the Moorish architecture with its elegant use of archways. The Mosque or Cathedral has 19 aisles and is a huge panorama of double arches with alternating red and yellow stripes on the arches. The Moorish arch is a circle at the top and the doorway sides hit the circle at a chord that is smaller than the diameter. The Mosque is in good condition and I think it is the best thing that I have seen thus far in Spain.

        I enjoyed walking around the town, peering into the homes and admiring their patios with their plants and small trees. The streets are narrow, and appear to be quite clean. I noticed many women scrubbing the stones pavement leading to their house. The houses are painted either white or yellow, and seem to be repainted quite frequently. Many of the houses had plants and flowers in their windows which added to the charm. I must say that I was fascinated by my introduction to Southern Spain.

        I rode 3rd class to Seville in the afternoon and sat among among the others in the filth that has accumulated in the cars. Still this is the way the average Spaniard travels, and so I am willing to travel this way in order to learn from them and to save money. Generally, there is a song or two going for the first part of the journey, but later on everybody just stares out the window. In contrast to the well-dressed in Madrid, the people today had on old and well worn clothing. Southern Spanish countryside reminds me of the countryside of India. The fields are dry and very rocky in places. The villages are small, and many of the houses are made of mud. Occasionally one sees fine homes, and also, even the mud houses are white washed regularly. The main difference between Spain & India is that the former uses the donkey where the latter uses the oxen. Arrived in Seville and walked about town – again fascinated by the narrow streets and the large crowds of shoppers and people sitting at sidewalk cafes.

OCT 23

        The Cathedral in Seville is of Gothic architecture, and has some fine vaulted ceilings. The building is huge, and is supposed to be the 3rd largest Catholic building. Still don’t like the boxed in choir and altar style, nor the chapels on the aisles with their iron bar doors. The Cathedral, while immense and of great proportions, leaves something to be desired for a religious building as far as I am concerned. Many pamphlets mention the Santa Cruz district (former medieval Jewish ghetto) as being particularly interesting, but I though it was just a duplicate of the other fascinating, narrow street districts in Seville. Traffic is barely even one way and when a car passes you have to hug the building. The houses are similar to those in Cordoba, however, the shopping district is more extensive, and there are many streets for pedestrians only.

        I guess the main thing that happened today was that I almost didn’t get to Granada. There are only a certain number of places on Spanish trains and consequently when I went to get my reservation in the morning, the man said it was “complete.” From here I went to the station – “No, dice” and then did a lot of changing of plans. Fortunately one man said to go about an hour before train time as occasionally there are seats available that the officials don’t use. This I did and obtained a seat to the change point and luckily from there to Granada. During my morning running around I also visited the old Alcazar & its gardens. (fair)

OCT 24

        The light in my hotel room is exceedingly bad, but I guess I won’t go blind on just one page. Today differed from yesterday as it was full of interesting things. First thing that I saw that I must comment on, (and I saw it 3 times during the day) was a stage coach with 2 horses and 2 soldiers up front, with an Army officer in the back. After seeing the shabby Army in Spain – and it is pitiful – and observing horse drawn carts, I guess I should have expected the stage coach, but I didn't and it sure amused me. In contrast to the ordinary soldier, the officers, particularly the Air Force officers, look half way decent. Still there is far too many unnecessary police and soldiers in this country, particularly when the economy can’t stand the drain.

        I spent almost the whole day at the famous Alhambra, a true gem of a sight. The Alhambra was begun in 1248 and is of Moorish architecture and exists in a well preserved condition. The carving engraving and design of the sandstone walls, doorways and window frames are truly marvelous. The detail and extent of the engravings are unbelievable unless one views it in person. Intricate designs and Arabic letters are cover all the walls and the ceilings are either of inlaid wood or clusters of plaster in some sort of design. The buildings are of the light colors typical of Spain, and are spread among gardens and/or contain pools and fountains. The Alhambra and its related buildings are located on a hill overlooking Granada and the valley that extends to the Sierra Nevada Mountains. I also visited the matchless gardens of the “Generalife,” which use to be a summer place for one of the Moorish Kings. I wasn’t impressed with it as much as the Alhambra itself.

        In the evening I was fortunate (?) to see a religious parade and celebration. I think the more that I see of the Catholic religion the less I think of it. The parade was composed of hundreds of children and the older members of the particular church that sponsored the celebration, most of the people carrying candles. Many priests were in the procession and they carried crosses or other symbols, ie flags or banners. The main portion consisted of 3 floats, or platfords carried by people. On each were ridiculous figures, symbolizing an angel, Madonna and Saint (I guess). Also in the procession were some of the ubiquitous police, some of whom carried rifles. One of the main places of honor was given to an officer of the police. Later they had colored lights, a few fireworks and a blistering speech by one of the priests over the loud speaker set up in front of the church. I don’t know, I just can’t buy this crap – when I see rich churches and clerical clothes and poverty stricken people, and soldiers with rifles in a religious procession!

OCT 25

        I hope that the train ride from Granada to Algeciras (6 hours) was the last of the long train rides for a spell. I don’t know why the trains rock the way they do, but it makes reading a heavy strain on the eyes. Consequently, I spent the time looking out of the window and observing the landscape, houses and people. The land is strictly farm and/or grazing land, and some of it appears quite poor. There are a surprising number of rocky hills and plateaus in the Southern part of Spain. The houses are of mud and brick, but I liked the fact that they are whitewashed quite regularly.

        Arriving in Algeciras I checked on boat departures to Tangiers, and decided to go immediately when I found that the lost boat to Spain or Gibraltar came back Sat. afternoon. Finding no suitable storage room I lugged my bags on the boat with me. At first, I regretted my decision, but I lucked into a private home deal and I think I will have decent and cheap accommodations. My first impression concerned the Arab dress – which I haven’t seen for 3 ½ months – and the veiled women in particular.

​​OCT 26

        I met an American fellow at the place where I am staying (a fine Spanish couple who take in a few boarders as they have a huge, modern apartment) and helped him move to a nice place right after breakfast. Then we headed for the Arab section of town – Casbah – where we walked around for a few minutes. He then left and I spent the rest of the morning wandering through the narrow, dirty winding streets, stopping occasionally to take pictures. A couple of times people made threatening gestures at the camera as the Arabs don’t like to be photographed, particularly to have their women photographed.

        While much of what I saw today, I had seen previously in the Middle East, still I enjoyed the time spent in this section of Tangier. The men wore western clothes, night-shirts or the baggy pants variety. The women all wore the long gown, with the hood and a veil that covered the face except for the eyes. This was the first Arab country that I have seen this type of veil, as the Pakistanis cover the comp head completely, and the Egyptians and Turks don’t cover the face at all. Must admit that eyes can be quite enticing, especially when one can’t see the rest of the face.

        The Arabs are a poor and I think dirty people. They live in filth and don’t seem to have any pride in their health at all. It is no wonder that there is so much disease. Today beigh being the Moslem sabbath, the market wasn’t very crowded, however, many Berber people had come in from the country to sell their food. The market place is a huge open space and the people spread their goods on the ground or on crude carts. The Berber women are hardy looking souls, and are funny looking in their sombrella hats and occasionally leather legging.

        Since I was am planning to revisit the Casbah tomorrow, I sauntered down to the beach in the afternoon, observing the modern buildings that have sprung up in various sections of Tangier. The beach is of fine sand and one of the finest beaches that I have ever seen. It is also free.

​​OCT 27

        I shared a room with another border – a policeman of Tangier - at the place where I stayed. The fellow is quite friendly and somewhat interested in learning English, so I spent about 20 minutes with him reviewing words in his little book, ie hat, hand, head etc. After the school lesson, I departed once again for the Casbah, as I thought it would be a very busy day at the market. I was partially correct, as it was more crowded than yesterday, however, it wasn't jammed as I thought it would be. People were buying and selling food, policemen were attempting to keep a road open for automobiles and occasional tourists like myself strolled about, taking pictures and ignoring the souvenir beaches. After tiring somewhat of just standing, I once again walked through the winding streets, observing the shops and people. I noticed that there were quite a few Indian shops in the Casbah.

        Around noon, John – the American – helped me lug my bags to the boat which was to depart at 1 PM for Gibraltar. The ride across was uneventful, except that an American gentleman who overheard me say that I was going home on the Constitution, came up to me and spoke a few words about his recent trip on the boat. I presume he was quite wealthy as he planned to stay on the Riviera until next summer and I saw him with a “cool looking” thunderbird in Gibraltar. Some people amaze me with their friendliness.

        Gibraltar is a huge rock, stuck on the end of the Spanish mainland and consisting of one long main street. An American that I had met on the ship accompanied me as I strolled up the street, peering into the numerous souvenir shops, bars, and food stores. Really not much to see on the “Rock”, and I imagine it is a little boring for the British troops stationed there. I did see some of the famous Gibraltar monkeys climbing about the walls of a building. Later in the evening I took a ferry boat to Algeciras and checked in a cheap hotel.

OCT 28 (SUNDAY - WEEK 97)

        It seemed that most of the day I spent trying to convince myself that my travels were almost behind me. I went to the American Export Lines office in the morning and they informed me that I was to be ready around 9:30 tomorrow morning, and that the boat will sail around 1 PM. I must admit that I am looking forward to the trip home and the subsequent meeting with the family. The travels have been wonderful, – yet I have been on the go now for 5 solid months, and it will be nice not to worry about room and board, planning ahead; in other words, just to relax awhile. Also, I have noticed in Spain that my interest has somewhat waned for the small objects, only the big and exciting sights tend to move me to any enthusiasm.

        The experiences I have had, places I have been, and people that I have seen and spoken to are invaluable. The money spent is nothing compared to the broadening of my knowledge and appreciation of life on our planet. The trip has wetted my appetite for further travels, and I am sure it will influence me in future years, regarding jobs, vocations and life in general. My diary, slides and recollection of people whom I have met will provide a vicarious thrill in the future. Yes, – I can honestly say, “It has been a fine trip and experience!”

        I actually did little of anything today. In the morning I walked about Algeciras, and spent an interesting hour on the docks watching the fishermen prepare their catch for shipment. They cut the fish, weighed them, packed them in crates and added ice, salt and some kind of fern plant for a reason of which I did not find an answer. It did me good to see all the dead sharks on the flood with their bellies cut open. In the afternoon I returned to a cliff overlooking the bay and Gibraltar in the distance, and I sat, thought and read a while.

Route as of October 28th, 1956 – end of Chapter 17.

CHAPTER 18 - HOMEWARD BOUND

October 29th, 1956 - November 10th, 1956

​​OCT 29

        I slept pretty good – at least considering that I was soon to leave Europe. Around 9:15 I reported to the dock, and boarded the tender that was to take the passengers boarding at Algeciras to the SS Constitution which was anchored in the bay. We waited about an hour until all the luggage was loaded, and then steamed out ot the double stacked ship which was to take us to the USA. The ride out was a little rocky and I found myself constantly praying that the trip across will be smooth.

        The new passengers – about 80 – boarded the Constitution at about 11:30 and were assigned our cabins and dinner sittings. I have a 4 man cabin (with 3 Italians) and eat during the 2nd sitting. Around 1:30 AM we pulled up the anchor and about an hour later the ship passed Tangier, probably the last land we will see for 7 days. The weather is quite nice and the water smooth with only occasional white caps. The meals were very good, at least to one that hasn’t eaten very well for the past 5 months. I usually ordered most everything on the menu, and I am sure that I will gain back some of my lost weight if I keep on eating like a hog – a high one at that!

        Met 4 or 5 interesting people in tourist class, and I think they will be good companions during the voyage. One man is a social worker (been in Europe 7 months); one just graduated from college (5 months); a girl working in NY (2 months); an intelligent and amusing writer for the Saturday Review (3 months) and an older lady who has a fine personality and comes from a top-notch Bostonian family. Mrs. Edsel – the latter woman – told an interesting story about her brother-in-law who is a Communist (a brilliant, friendly fellow yet with these warped ideas on Communism) and who after the McCarthy hearings has gone to Canada to live and to take up with another woman.

​​OCT 30

        First full day at sea, and it was quite a pleasant day at that. The sun was shining and the cool breeze had died down and I spent most of the day outdoors on the sun deck. I didn’t know it when I booked passage but I have since found out that the ship is actually on a cruise and is consequently steaming further more South than usual. Today we steamed close to the Madeira Islands, and we were able to observe the cities, houses and general layout of these islands noted for their linen and wine. The landscape was quite rugged and mountain peaks shot up into the sky. From what I understand, we will now head almost due West and come up turn north near the Isle of Bermuda.

        I am attempting to read Marx’s “Capital” but don’t seem to get very far. Seems that every time I get started, I am interrupted and it then takes me awhile to get back into the thought of the book. The book is quite complicated, but since it is supposed to be one of the best criticisms of the capitalistic system, I thought I should make an effort to learn some of the basic concepts.

        In the evening Eric Rudd (the free lance writer – presently doing a story for Saturday Review) and I went to Cabin Class to see how the other half lived. He met some friends and so we joined them for a couple of hours. Actually I got bored of talking to the people, but he didn’t want to leave so we stuck it out. The singer wasn’t very good, however, the band was quite good and the evening passed very quickly.

​​OCT 31

        I awoke feeling pretty good, but after an hour or so, the rocking and rolling began to get to me. At No time did I actually throw up, but it was the most that I could do to keep what I had eaten down in my little old  belly. It rained in the morning and it wasn’t until the middle of the afternoon before the clouds drifted away and the sun dared to shine through the haze. In the afternoon I saw the fine movie, “Trial”, which concerns segregation and how communists use minority group to further their cause.

        Yesterday I received a phone call from a Mrs. Kohn in 1st class and I called her to see who she was and to find out what she wanted. It developed that she is a cousin of Gladys from Dallas, and Gladys had sent her a telegram saying that I was aboard the ship. She invited me for supper and afterwards to attend the halloween party. Everything was very nice and I enjoyed meeting her and her friends. While there was a little larger selection, plus thicker steaks, I can’t say that there isn’t too much difference in the food.

        The big news yesterday and especially today concerned the outbreak of hostilities in the Near East. Israel sent a armed force 100 miles into Egypt to wipe out some suicide bases, and England and France used (or provoked) the opportunity to send some troops and bombers to protect “their” interests in the Suez. It now appears that it is a small war between Israel, France and England against Egypt and I guess the other Arabs. The US and Russia have thus far stayed out and the US brought the matter to the UN only to have England and France veto the resolution. It is horrible to have such important news going on in the world – including the revolution in Hungary – and not be able to get the news. They have a small newspaper on board the ship but it doesn’t print much other than small news columns.

​​NOV 01

        Today was a much calmer day than yesterday, and most of the people on the ship were feeling a lot better. It is funny how the time flies, and also how little I get done regarding my book “Capital.” Seems as if there is always something coming up, ie movies or lectures (cabin class) or I talk to people and people interrupt my reading to gab with me. Thus, all the good intentions that I had for occupying my time on the ship are about out the “port hole.”

        Wasn’t nice enough to sit outside in the afternoon, so I saw a fair movie, “Julia.” In the evening I thought we were going to have a costume party, so I put on a cowboy hat and scarf so that I could be a part of the fun. It turned out to be only a costume contest, and I am afraid I looked pretty cheesy. After the contest I played bridge for a couple of hours before hitting the sack. We have some pleasant people in tourist class – along with the many Italian immigrants – and consequently there is always somebody to talk to or to discuss ones travels with. Won’t be long before we are in NY – today was half way I believe – and I am anxious to get ahold of some newspapers to find out what is happening in the Middle East and in Eastern Europe. (Also, interested in getting home!)

​​NOV 02

        Passed the half way mark last night and now we haven’t far or long to go before we reach the United States and New York in particular. This morning the sun came out in full force and I made the most of it by sitting out on the deck with my head facing the sun. Can’t say that I got a good tan, but I am pealing a little on and near my nose.

        In the afternoon I entered the chess and checkers tournament and managed to get “skunked” in chess, but saved face by eaking eking out a victory in checkers. Gee, but it has been a long time since I played either of these two pastimes. One of my new favorite games on this trip has been shuffleboard, which is located in the bar. Generally in the late afternoon and after dinner, there is always a hard fought game going on, and the outcome is usually uncertain owing to the pitching and rolling of the boat.

        Joined a group of the fellows and girls in the Cabin Class Bar where we danced awhile – if one can call it dancing on this “rock and rolling” boat – and listening to a fine entertainer who sings and plays the piano. The lack of a dance band in tourist class is one of my gripes on this ship, but it really doesn’t make too much difference as the crew doesn’t seem to care if we go up to Cabin and/or First Class. Will say, though, that the people that I have met in Tourist Class are far more enjoyable than those that I have talked to or seen in the other classes.

​​NOV 03

        The weather hasn’t been very nice since yesterday afternoon, and consequently the boat has changed its proposed course so as to bypass some rough water and heavy winds. Consequently, we are by-passing Bermuda, and are now heading for New York. Also, heard that a threatened dock strike has been postponed for 15 days, so we will be able to dock as planned this coming Monday morning.

        I stayed inside all day as it was too windy outside and there was always salt spray blowing across the deck. In the afternoon I entered a bridge tournament and didn’t fare too well. I always thought that I was as bad as they come in this game, but after this afternoon, I think I can name a couple others that or as bad and perhaps a little worse. I now can see why it is so painful for a good bridge player to play with poor players.

        Didn’t do much in the evening, – played a little bridge and again went up to Cabin Class. It is funny to ee how there are increasing number of tourist passengers in the Cabin Class bar, and I guess if the trip would be any longer, either tourist class would take over the bar or by be barred from it. Ever since I have been on the boat, we have been putting back our time pieces one hour each night, so that we will add the 6 hour difference between New York and Europe. I have now made up the day that I “lost” when I crossed the International Date Line back in February 1955.

​​NOV 04 (SUNDAY - WEEK 98)

        It was a little rocky last night, but I guess I was too sleepy to be bothered by the motion. Generally, I get to bed around 1 or 2 AM, wake up around 6 or 7 AM to go to the bathroom, am keep kept awake about ½ hour as the other 3 men in my room get up and dress, and then I fall back asleep until 8:30-9. Breakfast is at 9:15 and consists of almost everything imaginable that one would like. It is a real pleasure on my part to have good American breakfasts after the roll and coffee affairs in Europe.

        This morning I headed for the First Class lounge after washing my white shirt preparatory for the NY landing. Wrote in my diary for awhile and then read in my book – Capital. I sure didn’t do much reading or writing on this trip, but most of the time I didn’t feel like doing it, or someone was bothering me. While crossing the Atlantic by ship is somewhat relaxing, I am pretty well convinced that the Airplane is the way to travel if one has the money. I haven’t been sick during the trip, but I can admit that I have never felt tip-top or in No. 1 shape during the whole trip. Seems as if the rolling and vibrations of the ship combine to cause a little discomfort.

        Packed in the afternoon and got ready to leave in the morning. Hard to believe that I will soon be in the US., and subsequently in St. Louis. It will be good to see the family and my friends again and to stop moving about for awhile. I am sure, though, that I will never be satisfied to stay in one place, and will always be wanting, and I hope it will come about, to travel in the US and in other parts of the world.

​​NOV 05

        Todays the day – People in my cabin were up at 5:00 and even though I had gone to bed at 2 AM last nite, I found that I couldn’t sleep. Around 6:15 I got up, dressed and headed for the deck where I saw the outline of the buildings of New York City and Jersey. We were just passing the Statue of Liberty and it was a thrill and also a funny sensation to see her standing in the water with her torch blazing for all to see. We docked at 7 and then waited 2 hours while custom people and other officials came on board, or got ready on the dock. Meanwhile the passengers ate breakfast and had their passport stamped.

        I left the boat around 9:10 and by 9:30 I was finished with customs. Took the bus to the Sloane House YMCA and checked in for 2 days. I don’t really have much to do and see in New York, but I thought I would look around, see a play and perhaps see Chapman & Doré. At American Express I picked up my mail and received my absentee ballot. Voted right away – for Stephenson and Hennings –  and sent it air mail special delivery back to St. Louis. Met Allan Chapman for lunch and enjoyed seeing him and talking to him about the “Rock.” In the evening I had dinner at his house and met his wife and little daughter.

        Called home around 7:30 and spoke to Mom, Morton and Carolyn. It was good talking to them and finding out how things are. I told them that I would probably be home Saturday. Also, visited the district office of the NLRB where I talked to one of their attorneys about job prospects and the labor relations field in general. He suggested that I talk to the Washington main office which I plan to do this Thursday–

​​NOV 06

        I guess I was pretty tired out after the excitement and lack of sleep Sunday nite for I sleep 10 hours. I didn’t have my alarm – the girl on the boat who borrowed it left it on the boat – and so I dozed until 11 AM. After getting dressed, I went to the lobby where I phoned Al Doré and made plans to see him for lunch. Al is presently going to Columbia graduate school and plans to get a PHD in European history and cultural thought. We had lunch at his apartment, and then spent the next 4 hours discussing various topics, including a heated discussion on the Suez problem.

        Since he had a paper due for tomorrow, I thought it best to leave, and consequently caught the subway for Rockefeller Center. I spent some time walking around this area – quite impressive – and stopped in St. Patrick’s Cathedral. I think this Cathedral is one of the finest Catholic Cathedrals that I have seen on my trip. The structure is huge and its impressive size is not cancelled out by an excess of religious statues, paintings, crosses and other “works of art” common to churches in Europe. The altar is also quite simple and nice.

        Saw the musical “Damn Yankee” in the evening and thought it to be pretty good. The dancing was excellent and there were 4 or 5 good songs. (Didn’t like the $2.90 price though). After the show, I went to Times Square, where signs put up by the NY Times told of an Eisenhower landslide. I felt a little sorry for Stephenson AS he tried hard but IKE is just too popular plus the worsening of foreign events made Eisenhower’s victory almost certain. I stopped at the Roosevelt Hotel to see the Republicans in their victory hotel – not impressive – and then went back to the Y.

​​NOV 07

        Awoke earlier than I had planned, consequently I decided to get up and read the final results of the election. (Poor Adlai). Oh yes, I forgot to mention yesterday that I bumped into Bob Willis at the YMCA. He is the fellow I met in Cairo, and later bumped into in Athens and Tel Aviv. Also, I met a fellow whom he had just left in Greece and later he met Ray (whom I travelled with) in Venice. Small world —

        I I took the 8 AM bus to Washington and didn’t mind the 5 ½ hour ride. The Greyhound buses are sure different from the buses that I have riden in Europe and Asia. For part of the trip, a fog blocked our view but it faded as we went into Maryland. Nothing unusual to see, but the countryside was interesting in that I could compare it with other landscapes that I have seen. One thing I did like was were the 4 lane, divided highways we were on from NY to Washington. It sure made for smooth riding.

        In Washington I checked into the YMCA (expensive $3.19) and then set out for a few places that I intended to contact. First place on my list was the NLRB office, and I spoke to the personnel man concerning a field examiner’s position. (not too encouraging). Next I went to the Senate Office Bldg and stopped in to see – and congratulate – Senator Hennings, but he was still in St. Louis. I did talk with his staff and got a few ideas on what they do and the type of personnel they use. It got pretty late, so I headed for S & W cafeteria – good, reasonable food – and later went to see the movie “Giant.” The picture was about Texas and was one of the best I have seen this year. I must say that it isn’t too flattering for Texas.

​​NOV 08

        Today was spent in visiting – and talking to people in – – various firms and Government offices in which I had a little interest. At General Electric I obtained information of their program in which engineers work as patent research men during the day and go to law school in the evening. (Good for potent men). Talked with one of the executives of the International Trade Fair Organization. He told me about the organization and the type of positions I might fill, – ass’t fair mgr, and administrative assistant. There were no openings at present, but he said I should keep in contact.

        Stopped by the AFL CIO building, but learned that they do not have any national Industrial Engineering or Labor Relations departments and/or jobs. One man told me to go and see Dave Beck of the Teamsters, but I decided not to, for the Teamsters are not exactly the clean-cut type of outfit I would like to get become a part of. Talked to a man at International Cooperation Asse. (ICA) but they need older engineers who had specific experience in certain fields. Rounded out the afternoon by discussion admission with the personnel at the George Washington Law School. Most likely if I came to Washington, I would try to enter this particular law school.

        Didn’t do much in the evening. Attended a dinner-speaker meeting at the YMCA, and enjoyed – in a way – the “pray or be damned” speach of the minister who spoke. I don’t know, – I just can’t buy this type of religion, for I feel one does not need to make such out ward expressions of being good in order to be good. My theory is that actions speak louder than words. Went to another movie after the meeting and enjoyed seeing “The Solid Gold Cadillac.” Judy Holiday and Paul Douglas are a fine comedy team.

NOV 09                         CHARLES’ BIRTHDAY

        27 years old – hard to believe. This old man is aging mighty fast. Since there wasn’t much more to do in Washington, so I decided to take the afternoon bus to St. Louis. Consequently, I wrote a brief note to Mom explaining when I will arrive, and then I sent it air mail special delivery to 520 Kingsland.

        I had a few hours to kill before my bus was to leave, so I walked to the Mall and gazed in reverence at the Lincoln, Jefferson and Washington Memorials. Although I had seen these monuments about 3 years ago, I still got a thrill from seeing them again, and to read the speeches these men made, and which are inscribed on the walls of the buildings. The Gettysburg Address and some of Jefferson’s sayings are truly great, and it makes me proud to think of them as men from my country.

        I took the 1:30 bus, and tried to keep occupied during the insuing trip. However, the poorly regulated temperature – too hot – and the many turns in the West Virginia hills made it a pretty time-dragging trip. Some of the scenery was interesting, however, it became dark around 5 PM, and thus there wasn’t much doing from then until around 11 PM when I managed to get a little sleep. I really don’t regret taking the bus, but I must admit that it is pretty confining and boring.

NOV 10

        Todays the day. Not only will I be home for the first time in 22 months, but it will complete my writing in this book. This diary has been a weight which I have labored under ever since I left home, but I think it will be time well spent when I re-read it in later years.

        The trip from Washington continued until 4:30 PM when we finally rolled into St. Louis. It was a long, hot trip and I lived from rest stop to rest stop but the time finally managed to pass. In the afternoon I read the literature that I had picked up at Senator Hennings’ office (good man) plus a pocket book on American History.

        I got off the bus, got my other bag and walked inside the bus terminal. Since they didn’t announce the bus, the family didn’t know I had arrived and I walked up to Morton to say hello and inform him I was home. He then had me sit and got Mom and Carolyn to walk over my way, and they were quite surprised to see me sitting there. Mom was disappointed she didn’t see me get off the bus, so I went back to the entrance and walked in again.

        And so I am home. It was mighty good to see Mom, Morton and Carolyn – they all look well – and to hear their voices. Larry Richt was also at the station and it was good to see him.

        We drove to 520 Kingsland, and passed some of the housing developments on the way. St. Louis appears to have finally shaken their lethargic stupor and are is now a new and growing city. Saw the Chervitz family including Lyle and Carol Ann and Norty and his wife. Called the family, to say hello, and settled down to straightening out my affairs.

THE END.
